title: JDK, JVM and your first program
summary: A Java toolchain compiles source with javac and runs bytecode with a compatible Java runtime.
body:
A Java toolchain compiles source with javac and runs bytecode with a compatible Java runtime.

Working model

Use a supported JDK that matches your project. Check java -version and javac -version in the same terminal. Different versions usually mean PATH points at two installations. Keep the public class name and source filename identical.

Code

public class OrderReceipt {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Order received: ORD-1042");
    }
}

Save as OrderReceipt.java. Compile with javac OrderReceipt.java, then run java OrderReceipt. The output is Order received: ORD-1042. Run from the directory containing the compiled class, or supply a classpath.

Cost and design choices

Compilation checks names and types. Execution can still fail because a dependency is missing or an input violates an assumption. Start with this small program before adding an IDE or a build tool.

Separate three failure stages

A compiler error means no valid class file was produced for that compilation. A class-not-found error means the launcher could not locate the requested compiled entry point. A stack trace from main means execution started and the program failed later. Keep the command and working directory in the bug report.

The source filename must match a public top-level class name. Java class names are case-sensitive, so a filename accepted on one filesystem can still hide a portability problem. Run the compiled name without a .class suffix.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java variables and primitive types, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Running java OrderReceipt.class is incorrect: java expects a class name here. A newer compiler can emit bytecode that an older JVM cannot run; use --release when targeting an older supported runtime.

Separate toolchain failures from program failures

Check both java -version and javac -version before investigating a program. A machine can launch one installed runtime while its compiler comes from another installation. Keep the compiler release target separate from the compiler installation; javac --release 8 on a newer JDK checks the stated platform API and language boundary.

Compile into a dedicated output directory, then give that directory to the class path. Launch a packaged class by its full binary name, not by a source-file pathname. A missing class and an exception thrown from main occur at different stages; preserving the actual error makes that distinction visible.

The small program verifies compilation and launch. It does not validate an IDE’s test configuration, a dependency resolver or deployment packaging. Once the command-line build works, reproduce the same source roots, release target and runtime selection in the IDE.

title: Java variables and primitive types
summary: A Java variable has a declared type that determines its permitted values and operations.
body:
A Java variable has a declared type that determines its permitted values and operations.

Working model

Use integer types for counts. For this receipt, money is stored as an integer number of paise; the sample excludes currencies whose smallest unit differs. Floating-point values are unsuitable for exact decimal accounting.

Code

long unitPricePaise = 129900L;
int quantity = 3;
long invoiceTotalPaise = Math.multiplyExact(unitPricePaise, quantity);
boolean eligibleForDispatch = quantity > 0;
System.out.println(invoiceTotalPaise);
System.out.println(eligibleForDispatch);

The output is 389700, followed by true. Math.multiplyExact reports overflow rather than silently wrapping. A long has a wider range than an int, but neither grows without a limit.

Cost and design choices

Primitive assignment copies a value. Reference assignment copies a reference; two variables can then identify the same mutable object. That distinction matters when a method changes a list it receives.

Range and initialization boundaries

int arithmetic can wrap without throwing. Widening the destination variable after an overflowing int calculation does not recover the lost value. Convert an operand before the calculation or use checked arithmetic when overflow should reject the operation.

Fields and array elements receive default values; local variables need a definite assignment before use. A default zero may also be a valid business value, so explicitly track absence instead of assuming an unassigned field will be obvious.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java operators and numeric promotion, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Local variables require initialization before use. Integer overflow is not automatically an exception for ordinary arithmetic. For financial systems, validate units, currency, and rounding rules explicitly.

Choose the representation for the allowed values

A quantity that can never be fractional should not become double merely because a parser accepted a decimal token. Integral ranges, overflow behavior and nullability belong to the field contract. A primitive has no null sentinel; an Integer may be absent and can fail during unboxing.

Local variables need a definitely assigned value before reading. Fields have initialization defaults, but a default zero is not evidence that a business value was supplied. Model missing input explicitly at the parsing boundary rather than allowing field defaults to stand in for validation.

Assignments to reference variables copy references. They do not duplicate a list, an array or its nested members. Declare which component owns mutation and test changes through a second alias before describing a value as a snapshot. final prevents reassignment of that variable; it does not freeze a referenced array.

title: Java operators and numeric promotion
summary: Java operators compute values, compare operands, and combine boolean conditions.
body:
Java operators compute values, compare operands, and combine boolean conditions.

Working model

Integer division discards the fractional part. Cast an operand before division when the fraction matters; casting the result afterward cannot recover what was already discarded.

Code

int completedJobs = 7;
int submittedJobs = 10;
double completionRate = (double) completedJobs / submittedJobs;
boolean shouldRetry = submittedJobs > 0 && completionRate < 0.9;
System.out.println(completionRate);
System.out.println(shouldRetry);

The output is 0.7 and true. The cast changes the division to floating-point arithmetic. In a general method, check submittedJobs before computing the rate.

Cost and design choices

The && and || operators short-circuit. A guard on the left can prevent an unsafe expression on the right from executing. A single & on boolean operands evaluates both sides.

Promotion before assignment

For byte and short arithmetic, most ordinary numeric operations promote operands to int. A narrowing assignment needs an explicit conversion or a compound-assignment rule, and narrowing can lose information. The destination type does not select the intermediate expression type.

&& and || short-circuit: the right operand may not execute. Avoid hiding required side effects there. Integer division truncates toward zero; switching the final assigned variable to double does not undo division that already happened as int arithmetic.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java conditions and loops, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Guard against a zero denominator before division. Do not use == to compare string contents. Parentheses are cheap; use them when precedence would force a reader to pause.

Evaluate types before trusting the final value

Two int operands produce int arithmetic unless a conversion changes the operand types first. A long destination does not fix an overflow inside an earlier int addition. Use a widened operand or checked arithmetic when a rejected overflow is the business rule.

Integer division discards the fractional part toward zero. Floating-point division introduces its own rounding and special values; it is not an automatic substitute for decimal money. BigDecimal arithmetic still needs a declared scale and rounding policy at the operation boundary.

Short-circuit boolean operators can skip the right operand. That is useful for a null check followed by a dereference, but it also means a right-hand side effect might never happen. Keep required state changes out of boolean conditions, and parenthesize a compound business rule when precedence could hide its intent.

title: Java conditions and loops
summary: Conditions choose a branch; loops repeat work while a condition or iteration source permits it.
body:
Conditions choose a branch; loops repeat work while a condition or iteration source permits it.

Working model

Separate a skip condition from a stop condition. continue skips the remaining work for one iteration; break exits the loop. The difference can leave later records unprocessed.

Code

int[] retryCounts = {0, 1, 4, 2};
int acceptedJobs = 0;
for (int retries : retryCounts) {
    if (retries > 3) {
        continue;
    }
    acceptedJobs++;
}
System.out.println(acceptedJobs);

The output is 3. Each retry count is visited once, so the work is O(n) with O(1) extra space. The enhanced loop fits this case because the code does not need an index.

Cost and design choices

Use a while loop when the number of iterations depends on an external state, but make the state change visible. For bounded retries, a counted loop makes the limit harder to miss.

Loop invariants and exit policies

A loop should make progress toward a condition that can become false. Updating the wrong counter or comparing against an unchanging value can create an infinite loop even when the body appears small.

Use half-open index bounds for arrays: start at zero and stop before length. continue still permits a for loop’s update step, while return exits the method. Do not replace an error with break when the caller needs to know that processing stopped early.

Connected lessons

Continue with Values and control flow, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

A loop ending at index <= array.length accesses one element past the end. Replacing continue with break changes this example to stop at the first rejected record. Unbounded retries can consume resources indefinitely.

State the loop invariant and exit condition

A loop should keep a condition true after every completed iteration: a processed prefix is valid, a remaining counter is non-negative, or the current search interval contains every possible answer. Naming that condition gives the update and exit test something concrete to preserve.

A continue can skip an update when the update lives in the body. A rejected input can therefore repeat forever if the loop retries without consuming it. A break exits only its defined loop or switch scope, so nested search code needs an explicit result boundary rather than assuming every break leaves the method.

Test the zero-iteration case and the final legal iteration. For an array, the final valid position is length minus one. For a half-open search range, the upper boundary is excluded. Switching between these conventions halfway through a method is a common source of missed values or out-of-bounds access.

title: Java arrays and bounds
summary: An array is a fixed-length, indexed container whose elements share a component type.
body:
An array is a fixed-length, indexed container whose elements share a component type.

Working model

Allocate the array when its length is known. Indexing is O(1), but valid indices stop at length - 1. An array with length zero is valid and has no readable element.

Code

int[] dailyOrders = {12, 0, 8, 15};
int totalOrders = 0;
for (int orders : dailyOrders) {
    totalOrders += orders;
}
System.out.println(totalOrders);

The output is 35. Summation visits every element: O(n) time and O(1) extra space. A larger input may overflow an int total, so select the accumulator type from the expected range.

Cost and design choices

An array reference can be shared. Passing dailyOrders into a method does not create a separate array. Copy it when a caller must keep an unchanged snapshot.

Aliasing, covariance, and copying

Arrays.copyOf creates another array but only copies references for object elements. If an element is mutable, both arrays still reach that element. A two-dimensional Java array is an array of row references, so copying the outer array also shares the original rows.

A reference array can be assigned to a wider reference-array type. Its actual component type still controls writes, so storing an incompatible element throws ArrayStoreException. Generic lists use a different invariance rule that catches many such assignments at compilation.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java strings and content equality, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Do not assume every row of a two-dimensional array has the same length. Validate an index before accessing it. An array of object references initially contains null unless each element is assigned.

Distinguish membership copies from nested copies

An array has fixed membership length and mutable slots. Assigning it to another variable shares those slots. clone makes another outer array, but a nested array or mutable element can still be shared. Decide whether callers need independent rows or merely independent outer membership.

Java multidimensional arrays are arrays of arrays. Rows can have different lengths and can be null. A loop using the first row’s length for every row invents a rectangular-shape contract that the representation itself does not guarantee.

Bounds checks protect access at runtime but do not make an off-by-one algorithm correct. Test empty input, one element and the final position. A copied snapshot also adds allocation and O(n) element-reference work; it should appear in the method’s space cost rather than vanish behind the word copy.

title: Java strings and content equality
summary: String is an immutable sequence of characters; operations return a result rather than editing the existing object.
body:
String is an immutable sequence of characters; operations return a result rather than editing the existing object.

Working model

Use equals for content comparison. The == operator compares references. A constant on the left of equals handles a nullable candidate without dereferencing it.

Code

String paymentStatus = new String("PAID");
boolean dispatchAllowed = "PAID".equals(paymentStatus);
String receiptLabel = paymentStatus.toLowerCase(java.util.Locale.ROOT);
System.out.println(dispatchAllowed);
System.out.println(receiptLabel);

The output is true and paid. paymentStatus remains PAID. Locale.ROOT makes this machine-facing transformation independent of a user locale.

Cost and design choices

Repeated concatenation inside a large loop can create many intermediate strings. Use StringBuilder for incremental construction. A StringBuilder is mutable, so do not share one between threads without a coordination policy.

Text length is not always character count

String.length counts UTF-16 code units. Some Unicode characters occupy two code units, and a user-perceived character can combine several code points. Indexing and substring boundaries therefore need a defined text model when the input is not restricted to a simple identifier alphabet.

String is immutable, but repeated concatenation in a loop can create intermediate strings and repeated copying. Use a StringBuilder for a growing report, and limit total output size. A small one-off concatenation is a different workload.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java classes and objects, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Strings are not passwords vaults; an immutable string cannot be wiped in place. Unicode characters can span more than one char. Do not assume length counts user-visible characters.

Define equality, positions and encoding separately

String.equals compares the represented character sequence; == compares whether two references point to the same object. Interning can make some reference comparisons appear to work until input comes from a parser or another allocation. Use the value contract directly.

String positions are UTF-16 code-unit positions. A supplementary code point can occupy two units, and several code points can form one displayed unit. A UI character limit and a protocol byte limit therefore need different measurements. Use an explicit charset when moving text across a byte boundary.

The String object does not change when concatenation returns another String. Repeated accumulation in a loop can create substantial copying and temporary objects; a builder makes the intended mutable assembly phase explicit. That optimization does not decide whether the final value needs normalization or a language-specific comparison rule.

title: Java classes and objects
summary: A class defines state and behavior; an object is one instance of that definition.
body:
A class defines state and behavior; an object is one instance of that definition.

Working model

Keep state private when arbitrary writes would violate an invariant. The public operations below permit a task to change status without exposing the stored boolean as a writable field.

Code

public class DispatchTask {
    private boolean completed;

    public void complete() {
        completed = true;
    }

    public boolean isCompleted() {
        return completed;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DispatchTask task = new DispatchTask();
        task.complete();
        System.out.println(task.isCompleted());
    }
}

The output is true. Each task has its own completed field. A static field would instead belong to the class and would be shared by all instances.

Cost and design choices

Objects are accessed through references. Assigning task to another variable does not clone its state. Make copying explicit when a separate lifecycle is required.

Reachability and object ownership

A constructor does not automatically deep-copy the values passed into it. Storing a caller’s mutable collection keeps a shared reference. If the object promises a snapshot, copy the relevant structure and state how mutable elements are handled.

Garbage collection reclaims unreachable objects, not objects merely labelled temporary in a method name. Static fields, listeners, and captured callbacks can keep entire object graphs reachable. Releasing a reference also does not promptly close an external file or socket.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java constructors and validated state, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Do not expose mutable fields simply to reduce accessor code. A null reference does not identify an object. Calling an instance method through it fails before the method can inspect its arguments.

Make object state valid at publication

A constructor should establish the invariant that every permitted public operation can rely on. A stock object with a negative available count is already invalid before reserve is called. Reject that input rather than requiring every future operation to repair it.

An object can be referenced by several components. Returning its mutable internal list gives callers another mutation path around the class’s validation. Publish a copied or explicitly read-only view according to the required lifetime; a read-only live view still changes when the owner changes its backing state.

Instance fields belong to a particular object, while static fields belong to the loaded class. Moving state to static can accidentally merge independent accounts or requests. It also adds a shared lifetime and coordination requirement that did not exist when each request owned its own object.

Apply this contract in Spring

Spring ApplicationContext: construct and close an object graph, Spring bean scopes: singleton identity is not thread safety. These lessons keep framework assembly separate from the Java contract.

title: Java constructors and validated state
summary: A constructor initializes a new object and can reject inputs that would leave it unusable.
body:
A constructor initializes a new object and can reject inputs that would leave it unusable.

Working model

Require the identifier at creation. The constructor below validates the supplied value before storing it. This keeps every successfully created ticket usable without a later initialize call.

Code

public class SupportTicket {
    private final String ticketId;

    public SupportTicket(String ticketId) {
        if (ticketId == null || ticketId.trim().isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("ticketId is required");
        }
        this.ticketId = ticketId;
    }

    public String id() {
        return ticketId;
    }
}

A constructor has the class name and no return type. this.ticketId distinguishes the field from the parameter. final prevents reassignment of this field after construction; it does not make every object referenced by a final field immutable.

Cost and design choices

Validation adds work once per creation. That is often cheaper than requiring every operation to recover from missing state. Keep expensive I/O out of constructors when failures need a separate retry policy.

Keep partially built objects private

Do not publish this to another thread or callback before construction finishes. The observer can see an object whose invariants have not been established. Calling an overridable method from a constructor can also dispatch to subclass code before subclass initialization completes.

Validate related fields together. Two fields can each be individually valid while their combination is invalid, such as an end timestamp before a start timestamp. Constructor success should mean the complete object state is usable.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java encapsulation and object ownership, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Adding a return type turns the declaration into a method. Do not call overridable methods from constructors: subclass state may not yet be initialized. Avoid storing mutable input collections without deciding who owns later edits.

Validate before the object escapes

Constructor chaining should lead to one place that establishes the state contract. Duplicated validation in several overloads can drift until one constructor permits a state another rejects. A factory can name distinct creation policies without making callers guess which positional argument combination applies.

Avoid registering this with an external listener or starting a worker while construction is still in progress. Another component can then observe fields before the invariant is established. Finish creation, then let an explicit owner publish the object or start its resources.

Construction can allocate more than the outer object: copied collections, parsed metadata and acquired resources all contribute cost. If the constructor can fail after acquiring a resource, cleanup needs an explicit scope. A simple immutable value constructor should not quietly own a long-lived connection or executor.

title: Java encapsulation and object ownership
summary: Encapsulation keeps an object’s representation behind operations that preserve its rules.
body:
Encapsulation keeps an object’s representation behind operations that preserve its rules.

Working model

Private fields alone do not protect a mutable collection. If a getter returns the internal list, callers can alter it without using your methods. Return a snapshot when that behavior is unwanted.

Code

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Collections;
import java.util.List;

public class AuditBatch {
    private final List<String> eventIds = new ArrayList<>();

    public void record(String eventId) {
        if (eventId == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("eventId");
        eventIds.add(eventId);
    }

    public List<String> snapshot() {
        return Collections.unmodifiableList(new ArrayList<>(eventIds));
    }
}

Copying takes O(n) time and O(n) space. The returned list cannot be modified through its own methods, and later additions to eventIds do not appear in the copy.

Cost and design choices

This is a shallow copy. It is enough for immutable String values. If the list contains mutable records, their fields can still be shared and changed unless those values are copied too.

A getter can leak ownership

Returning the internal mutable list gives callers a route around the object’s validation methods. An unmodifiable wrapper blocks writes through that wrapper but still reflects changes made through another reference to the backing list.

Choose a snapshot, read-only live view, or explicitly shared collection according to the contract. The choice affects both memory and what a reader can observe over time. Hiding fields with private does not by itself establish that contract.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java inheritance and method overriding, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

An unmodifiable wrapper around the original list is a view, not a snapshot. This class is not thread-safe; copying while another thread writes requires coordination.

Protect every mutation route

Private fields are only one part of encapsulation. A public setter, returned array, live collection view or callback can still permit callers to bypass the intended invariant. Review the whole public surface and every alias it publishes.

Expose an operation such as reserve(quantity) when the rule spans available and reserved counts. Two unrelated setters make the caller responsible for preserving a relation it cannot update atomically. Validate before changing either field and specify the unchanged state on rejection.

An unmodifiable wrapper prevents updates through that wrapper but can still reflect owner updates and expose mutable elements. Independent snapshots need a copy at the correct layer. If multiple workers share the object, the class also needs one stated synchronization rule for reads and compound writes.

title: Java inheritance and method overriding
summary: Inheritance permits a subclass to extend a class; overriding supplies a different implementation of an inherited instance method.
body:
Inheritance permits a subclass to extend a class; overriding supplies a different implementation of an inherited instance method.

Working model

Use inheritance when the subtype must satisfy the same contract. Extending a class just to reuse a helper couples unrelated behavior and can expose operations the subtype should not support.

Code

public class DeliveryCharge {
    public int chargePaise() {
        return 5000;
    }

    static class PickupCharge extends DeliveryCharge {
        @Override
        public int chargePaise() {
            return 0;
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        DeliveryCharge charge = new PickupCharge();
        System.out.println(charge.chargePaise());
    }
}

The output is 0. The reference type permits the call; the object’s runtime class supplies the overridden implementation. The annotation catches a mismatched signature at compilation.

Cost and design choices

Prefer composition when pricing policies should be replaceable independently of the object hierarchy. A contained policy object makes that dependency explicit.

Substitution has behavioral limits

A subclass inherits more than names: callers already have assumptions about the parent’s accepted inputs, results, and state changes. A child that unexpectedly rejects valid parent inputs or changes units breaks those assumptions even if the code compiles.

Prefer composition when the new type needs to use another object without promising that it can replace that object. Inherited mutable protected fields can make invariants harder to control because several layers can alter them.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java interfaces and replaceable behavior, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

Overloading changes the parameter list and is a different operation from overriding. Static methods do not dispatch like overridden instance methods. A subclass must preserve expectations established by the parent contract.

Preserve the parent contract

An override must keep the behavior callers of the parent type are entitled to use. Narrowing an accepted input range or introducing an unrelated failure can break a caller that never names the subtype. Choose inheritance for substitutable behavior, not merely for reusing a few implementation lines.

Instance-method dispatch uses the actual object type after overload selection has chosen a method signature. Static methods and fields do not follow that same dispatch rule. Inspect the declared receiver and argument types before explaining an overloaded call trace.

A base constructor that invokes an overridable method can call subtype code before subtype initialization is complete. Keep construction-time invariant setup away from that virtual dispatch. Composition often makes resource ownership and independent policy changes easier to represent than a deep inheritance chain.

title: Java interfaces and replaceable behavior
summary: An interface defines a contract that an implementation agrees to provide.
body:
An interface defines a contract that an implementation agrees to provide.

Working model

Declare the capability a caller needs. A job service can depend on a notification contract without committing to email transport, vendor-specific APIs, or a console implementation.

Code

public class JobNotifier {
    interface NotificationChannel {
        void send(String message);
    }

    static class ConsoleChannel implements NotificationChannel {
        public void send(String message) {
            System.out.println(message);
        }
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NotificationChannel channel = new ConsoleChannel();
        channel.send("Job JOB-42 completed");
    }
}

The output is Job JOB-42 completed. A production transport would define failure handling, timeouts, and delivery semantics. The interface does not supply those guarantees by itself.

Cost and design choices

Keep contracts narrow. A method that needs only send should not require unrelated administration methods. Interfaces can reduce coupling, but an excessive number of tiny contracts can hide the actual flow of work.

Default methods still need conflict rules

An interface can provide a default instance method, but that does not give it per-instance field storage. If unrelated interfaces supply conflicting defaults, an implementing class may need to resolve the conflict explicitly.

A method signature is only part of a contract. Document null handling, ownership, side effects, and any required performance bound. Two implementations with the same signature can still behave incompatibly when those rules differ.

Connected lessons

Continue with Methods and objects, Java Tutorial.

Common Mistakes

An interface reference can still be null. Do not suppress transport failures and report success. Specify whether repeated calls can deliver duplicate notifications.

Describe behavior without promising an implementation

An interface names the operations and behavior a caller can require. List and Deque expose different permitted actions even when LinkedList implements both. Choose the narrower contract that actually represents the caller’s requirement rather than publishing every available method.

A default method can share behavior but does not automatically add object state or resolve every multiple-interface conflict. A class combining conflicting defaults must choose an implementation explicitly. Static interface methods also do not become ordinary virtual instance methods.

Thread safety, ownership and cost still depend on the chosen implementation and its documented contract. Accepting a List parameter does not imply constant-time indexing, immutable membership or safe concurrent traversal. If an algorithm needs one of those properties, state it or change the representation.

title: Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases
summary: LinkedList<E> is a doubly linked implementation of List and Deque that stores an element between references to its previous and next nodes.
body:
LinkedList<E> is a doubly linked implementation of List and Deque that stores an element between references to its previous and next nodes.

What the nodes buy you

There is no backing array to shift when an endpoint changes. The list keeps a head and a tail. Adding a node at either end changes a small set of references; reading an arbitrary position requires a walk from one of those ends.

Indexing costs time. The structure has no equivalent of an array address computed from an index. For a list with n elements, get(i) can traverse roughly half the list even though its return type looks identical to ArrayList.get(i).

Build a task queue

import java.util.LinkedList;

public class TaskQueueDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> pendingTasks = new LinkedList<>();
        pendingTasks.addLast("Validate invoice");
        pendingTasks.addLast("Send receipt");
        pendingTasks.addFirst("Check account");
        System.out.println(pendingTasks);
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.pollFirst());
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.peekFirst());
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.size());
    }
}

Save as TaskQueueDemo.java. Compile with javac TaskQueueDemo.java and run java TaskQueueDemo. The program prints the following values.

[Check account, Validate invoice, Send receipt]
Check account
Validate invoice
2

addFirst inserts urgent work before the existing head. pollFirst removes that head; peekFirst reads the replacement without removing it. The sample is single-threaded and in-memory. It does not guarantee job durability or exactly-once processing.

List, Queue, or Deque?

The reference type decides which methods the compiler exposes. A List<String> reference supports positional operations. Queue<String> exposes offer, poll, and peek. Deque<String> adds operations on both ends. Choose the contract the caller needs rather than exposing every method of the implementation.

Use Queue<String> pendingTasks = new LinkedList<>(); when the caller should treat the structure as FIFO. Use Deque when both ends matter. A List reference does not expose addFirst in Java 8; later Java releases added sequenced collection methods, so check the target release before relying on them.

Methods worth knowing

  • addFirst(value) / addLast(value): insert an element at the selected end.
  • offer(value): append an element using the Queue contract. LinkedList is not a capacity-bounded queue.
  • peekFirst() / peekLast(): read an endpoint, returning null for an empty list.
  • pollFirst() / pollLast(): remove an endpoint, returning null for an empty list.
  • getFirst() / getLast(): read an endpoint but throw NoSuchElementException when empty.
  • removeFirst() / removeLast(): remove an endpoint but throw when empty.
  • get(index) / set(index, value): walk to a valid position; set replaces its value.
  • add(index, value): insert at a position from zero through size(). Locating that position can dominate the operation.
  • remove(index): remove by position and return the removed element.
  • remove(Object): search for and remove the first equal value, returning a boolean.
  • contains(value): search by equality. It does not provide constant-time lookup.
  • listIterator(): obtain a cursor that can move in either direction and edit through its own methods.
  • size(): read the stored element count without traversing the nodes.

Performance is about locating the node

Endpoint insertion and removal perform O(1) link work. Searching by value and accessing an arbitrary index take O(n) in the worst case. Traversing every element once with an iterator takes O(n). The list uses O(n) storage, including one node object per element and its links; exact byte counts depend on JVM settings and object layout.

Insertion through a ListIterator already positioned at the target has O(1) link work. Getting that cursor to an arbitrary index can take O(n). These are separate costs. “LinkedList inserts in constant time” is incomplete when the caller first searches for a position.

Avoid a loop that calls get(index) for every index. It repeats traversal and can do O(n²) work. An enhanced for loop or iterator visits the chain once. Allocation and cache behavior still matter; Big O alone does not identify the faster collection for a real workload.

Insert with a positioned cursor

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.ListIterator;

public class ListEditDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> stages = new LinkedList<>(
            Arrays.asList("Received", "Packed", "Dispatched"));
        ListIterator<String> cursor = stages.listIterator();
        while (cursor.hasNext()) {
            if ("Packed".equals(cursor.next())) {
                cursor.add("Quality checked");
                break;
            }
        }
        System.out.println(stages);
    }
}
[Received, Packed, Quality checked, Dispatched]

The cursor is after Packed when add runs. It inserts at that cursor position and leaves Dispatched after the new element. Finding Packed takes O(n); adding after it takes O(1) link work. Iterator navigation remains valid because the edit goes through that iterator.

Removal overloads can surprise you

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedList;

public class RemovalTrapDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<Integer> retryCodes = new LinkedList<>(
            Arrays.asList(7, 11, 7));
        retryCodes.remove(1);
        System.out.println(retryCodes);
        retryCodes.remove(Integer.valueOf(7));
        System.out.println(retryCodes);
    }
}
[7, 7]
[7]

The literal 1 selects remove(int), which removes the value at index one: 11. Integer.valueOf(7) selects remove(Object), which removes the first matching 7. Autoboxing does not make those two calls mean the same thing.

Edit during iteration through the iterator

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.LinkedList;

public class IteratorCleanupDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> jobs = new LinkedList<>(
            Arrays.asList("done:1", "pending:2", "done:3"));
        Iterator<String> cursor = jobs.iterator();
        while (cursor.hasNext()) {
            if (cursor.next().startsWith("done:")) {
                cursor.remove();
            }
        }
        System.out.println(jobs);
    }
}
[pending:2]

Iterator.remove removes the element returned by the last next call. Calling it before next, or twice for the same element, is invalid. Calling jobs.remove from inside an enhanced for loop structurally edits the list outside its iterator and can trigger ConcurrentModificationException. Fail-fast behavior is a bug signal, not a concurrency guarantee.

Choose against ArrayList and ArrayDeque

Use ArrayList as a starting point for an ordered sequence that needs indexed reads. It uses a backing array of references and avoids allocating a linked node per element. Appending is amortized O(1), while inserting into the middle shifts later references.

For a queue or stack that does not need null values, evaluate ArrayDeque. It stores elements in a resizable array and typically avoids LinkedList’s node allocation costs. Its endpoint operations are generally amortized O(1). Do not choose LinkedList merely because the requirement says queue.

Choose LinkedList when its combined List/Deque behavior or cursor-based edits match a measured need. Benchmark realistic element counts, access patterns, allocation rates, and GC behavior. An isolated timing of one insertion does not represent a service workload.

Edge Cases

LinkedList permits null. That makes a null result from poll or peek ambiguous: it can mean an empty list or a stored null element. A queue of application jobs should usually reject null at its boundary.

Duplicates are permitted. remove(Object) removes only the first match. An empty list has no index zero, and get(size()) is out of bounds. add(size(), value) is valid because it inserts after the last current element.

The implementation is not synchronized. Protect an entire multi-step operation when several threads share it; individually coordinated calls do not automatically make check-then-remove atomic. A concurrent queue may fit the requirement better.

Common Mistakes

Do not combine “not empty” and removeFirst as separate unprotected actions across threads. Do not expect a shallow list copy to copy mutable task objects. Keep indexed loops out of long linked lists, and decide whether removal means a position or a value before choosing the overload.

title: Java ArrayList and indexed access
summary: ArrayList is a resizable-array implementation of List that supports constant-time indexed reads.
body:
ArrayList is a resizable-array implementation of List that supports constant-time indexed reads.

Start with the access pattern

If a UI needs the item at row 500 repeatedly, an indexed sequence fits. ArrayList reads that position directly. Inserting near the front shifts later references, so a workload with many such changes needs a separate analysis.

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ReceiptBatch {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> receiptIds = new ArrayList<>();
        receiptIds.add("R-104");
        receiptIds.add("R-105");
        receiptIds.set(0, "R-104-corrected");
        System.out.println(receiptIds.get(0));
    }
}

The output is R-104-corrected. Appending may resize the backing array; over many appends the cost is amortized O(1). A resize copies references and can produce a latency spike. The stored objects themselves are not duplicated.

Capacity and public views

Capacity is backing storage; size is the number of accessible elements. ensureCapacity does not add readable elements. get(size) is still invalid even when extra capacity has already been reserved.

subList is a view, not a detached ArrayList. Structural edits to the parent outside the view can invalidate assumptions made by the view. Copy the sublist when a reader needs independent structure, and include that O(k) copying cost.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases, Java LinkedList quiz.

Capacity and ownership are separate decisions

Capacity is storage reserved for references; size is the number of elements currently in the list. new ArrayList(100) does not create one hundred usable indexed elements. Calling get(0) before adding anything still fails. Use a measured capacity hint when a batch size is known, but do not reserve enormous buffers for every small request.

Growing the backing storage can copy existing references. Adding at the end is amortized constant work under ordinary growth, but one individual addition may perform a resize. Inserting or removing near the start shifts later references, so repeated front edits can produce quadratic work.

An ArrayList copy retains the same element references. If Receipt objects are mutable, a caller changing one receipt can affect both lists. The view and snapshot lesson distinguishes membership copies from independent object state.

Choose a mutation and traversal policy

Removing by index from a List of integers is not the same overload as removing an Integer value. Make the value type explicit when the business operation asks to remove a particular numeric ID.

Editing the list structurally during an ordinary enhanced-for traversal can invalidate its iterator. Use the iterator’s supported removal path, removeIf for a predicate, or a separate transformed result. Fail-fast behaviour detects mistakes on a best-effort basis; it is not a thread-safety guarantee.

Use ArrayDeque for a single-owner endpoint queue and a bounded blocking queue for producer/consumer admission. A collection choice should follow access patterns rather than its name.

Common Mistakes

Do not assume an unmodifiable List is an ArrayList. Removing while iterating needs an iterator or a deliberately chosen filter operation. A capacity setting is not an element count.

Compare the Python boundary

Python lists: slicing copies the outer sequence, not nested objects.

title: Java ArrayDeque for queues and stacks
summary: ArrayDeque is a resizable-array deque for inserting and removing elements at either end.
body:
ArrayDeque is a resizable-array deque for inserting and removing elements at either end.

FIFO work order

import java.util.ArrayDeque;
import java.util.Deque;

public class TaskDequeDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Deque<String> pendingTasks = new ArrayDeque<>();
        pendingTasks.addLast("Validate invoice");
        pendingTasks.addLast("Send receipt");
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.pollFirst());
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.pollFirst());
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.pollFirst());
    }
}

The output is Validate invoice, Send receipt, and null. A stack instead pairs push with pop at the same end. Do not mix that convention with addLast and assume the result is FIFO.

Most endpoint operations are amortized O(1). The deque has no List-style get(index) operation. It rejects null elements, which leaves null available as an empty result for poll and peek.

Endpoint absence and memory retention

ArrayDeque rejects null elements, so poll returning null can clearly mean no element was available. It is not a blocking queue and does not wait for a producer to add another element.

A deque can grow to absorb a burst and may retain backing-array capacity after removals. Empty size is not proof that all storage returned to the runtime. Bound queued work according to the application’s memory budget.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases, Java LinkedList quiz.

An empty queue needs an explicit policy

pollFirst returns null when no element exists, while removeFirst throws. Use poll when empty is an expected state and the caller can choose another task; use a throwing operation when emptiness violates a proven application precondition.

ArrayDeque does not permit null elements, which keeps the null result from poll unambiguous. A LinkedList can contain null, so copying the same interpretation to a LinkedList-backed queue without controlling elements changes the meaning of an empty-looking result.

A stack uses push/pop or consistent first-end operations. A FIFO queue adds at the back and removes from the front. Mixing ends unintentionally changes processing order while every call remains individually valid.

Endpoint speed does not solve shared ownership

Endpoint insertions and removals have amortized constant work; resizing can copy stored references. Searching by value or removing an occurrence can require a full scan. The deque stores O(n) references and implementation capacity, rather than one separately allocated link node for every element.

ArrayDeque is not a concurrent queue. Giving it to two workers without coordination can corrupt the assumptions behind a compound empty-check and remove. A synchronized access policy must cover all participating operations, or use a concurrent collection designed for the required producer/consumer contract.

Clearing pending membership does not cancel a task another worker already removed. Completion, cancellation and queue size are separate facts. See bounded queues for admission and shutdown boundaries.

Common Mistakes

ArrayDeque is not thread-safe and has no fixed capacity limit. Use a bounded or concurrent queue when producers, backpressure, or multiple consumers require those properties.

title: Java LinkedList exercises with checked solutions
summary: LinkedList exercises should distinguish value removal, endpoint behavior, and iterator-safe edits.
body:
LinkedList exercises should distinguish value removal, endpoint behavior, and iterator-safe edits.

Requirements

  • Remove only the first matching retry code, without treating it as an index.
  • Remove completed jobs during a traversal.
  • Verify that polling an empty queue returns null.

Reference solution

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.LinkedList;

public class LinkedListChecks {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<Integer> retries = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList(2, 5, 2));
        boolean removed = retries.remove(Integer.valueOf(2));
        if (!removed || !retries.equals(Arrays.asList(5, 2))) {
            throw new AssertionError("Remove first matching value");
        }
        LinkedList<String> jobs = new LinkedList<>(Arrays.asList("done:1", "pending:2"));
        Iterator<String> cursor = jobs.iterator();
        while (cursor.hasNext()) {
            if (cursor.next().startsWith("done:")) cursor.remove();
        }
        if (!jobs.equals(Arrays.asList("pending:2"))) {
            throw new AssertionError("Remove completed jobs");
        }
        LinkedList<String> emptyQueue = new LinkedList<>();
        if (emptyQueue.pollFirst() != null) throw new AssertionError("Empty queue");
        System.out.println("3 checks passed");
    }
}

The checks throw directly, so they run without an assertions flag. Value removal and filtering each require a traversal in the worst case. Polling the empty queue is O(1). This is a local verification program, not a server-side code judge.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases, Java LinkedList quiz.

Common Mistakes

Calling remove(2) removes at index two. A second Iterator.remove without another next is invalid. Test duplicates and an empty list before using the same code for application data.

Add boundary cases that distinguish the overloads

Repeat value removal with a target that is absent and require false without changing membership. Test equal duplicates so the answer proves that only the first matching value is removed. For position removal, test zero, the last valid index and an index equal to size; these cases use a different contract.

For iterator cleanup, put completed jobs at the first and last positions as well as next to each other. A loop that advances twice after removal can skip adjacent matches. Keep the removal on the same iterator that supplied the current element.

A null member can make a polling result ambiguous with an empty queue. Use a non-null element policy for a task queue, and test the policy before insertion. These checks run as a local Java program; they do not describe an online judge or synchronized queue.

title: Java LinkedList interview questions
summary: LinkedList interview questions test whether you can separate API behavior from the cost of finding a node.
body:
LinkedList interview questions test whether you can separate API behavior from the cost of finding a node.

Is insertion always O(1)?

No. Endpoint insertion has constant link work. Adding at an arbitrary index can spend O(n) finding that position. Inserting through an already-positioned ListIterator changes links in O(1). State which operation you mean.

Why can indexed traversal become quadratic?

Each get(index) starts another traversal. A loop over all indices sums those walks. Use an iterator to follow each link once instead.

What does remove(1) mean for LinkedList<Integer>?

It removes the element at index one. To remove the first integer value one, call remove(Integer.valueOf(1)). The two overloads also have different return types.

Does ConcurrentModificationException make it safe to share?

No. Fail-fast detection is best-effort. It cannot replace coordination across reads and structural edits. Choose an explicit locking policy or a collection designed for the required concurrent behavior.

Would you use it for a service queue?

Not without checking the requirements. ArrayDeque may fit single-threaded endpoint work with fewer allocations. A service queue may also require capacity limits, concurrent access, persistence, ordering guarantees, and retry policy.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases, Java LinkedList quiz.

Common Mistakes

Do not invent fixed node sizes without naming a JVM layout. Do not claim LinkedList avoids all copying: copying a list still visits its elements and allocates storage.

Follow up on the representation choice

Ask what the caller already knows at insertion time. An already-positioned iterator avoids a fresh position search, but a caller holding only a numeric index may need to traverse. A claim about link-editing cost should identify that precondition rather than call every insertion constant time.

Ask whether a shallow copy isolates a mutable element. It does not. The copied node sequence holds the same referenced elements, so a field change on one shared element can be seen through both lists. Snapshot membership and element ownership are separate answers.

Ask how to stop a worker waiting for task admission and what survives restart. Neither LinkedList nor ArrayDeque supplies a blocking wait or durable retry record. Changing an implementation without adding those contracts does not create a production service queue.

import java.util.LinkedList;

public class TaskQueueDemo {

        LinkedList<String> pendingTasks = new LinkedList<>();
        pendingTasks.addLast("Validate invoice");
        pendingTasks.addLast("Send receipt");
        pendingTasks.addFirst("Check account");
        System.out.println(pendingTasks);
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.pollFirst());
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.peekFirst());
        System.out.println(pendingTasks.size());
    }
}
[Check account, Validate invoice, Send receipt]
Check account
Validate invoice
2

Insertion after a matching stage

import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.LinkedList;
import java.util.ListIterator;

public class ListEditDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        LinkedList<String> stages = new LinkedList<>(
            Arrays.asList("Received", "Packed", "Dispatched"));
        ListIterator<String> cursor = stages.listIterator();
        while (cursor.hasNext()) {
            if ("Packed".equals(cursor.next())) {
                cursor.add("Quality checked");
                break;
            }
        }
        System.out.println(stages);
    }
}
[Received, Packed, Quality checked, Dispatched]

The queue uses endpoints. The stage editor locates a matching value before it inserts. Both return an ordered sequence, but their costs differ because the second program searches.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases, Java LinkedList quiz.

Common Mistakes

Compile each public class in a file of the same name. These examples are single-threaded. Do not mistake printed output for a persistence or delivery guarantee.

Read the operation order as a state trace

Write the list after each mutation before checking the final print. addFirst and addLast place values at different ends, and pollFirst removes the value that currently occupies the head. Duplicate descriptions remain separate elements because this example has no identity or deduplication rule.

The ListIterator editor first searches for a matching stage. Once positioned, add inserts relative to that cursor. Locating the stage can visit the whole list, so the program’s total cost includes search even though changing the nearby links requires constant work.

Compare a missing stage and an empty list with the printed success case. Neither should create a quality-check stage at a guessed position unless that fallback is part of the contract. A null stage also needs a stated input policy; invoking a method on a null member will not be repaired by using a linked representation.

title: Java task-deque project: command parsing, endpoint order and rejected work
summary: A task deque accepts normal work at the tail and urgent work at the head, then removes the next pending item from the head.
body:
A task deque accepts normal work at the tail and urgent work at the head, then removes the next pending item from the head.

Java 8+. This is a complete program using JDK classes.

Make each command a small boundary

The command grammar supports add, urgent, next and list. add and urgent require a nonempty task description; next and list take no argument. An unknown command or extra argument is rejected rather than silently interpreted as a task.

Two equal descriptions remain distinct items. This contract has no task identifiers or deduplication. Urgent work can delay earlier normal work indefinitely, so it is an ordering rule rather than a fairness guarantee.

The implementation depends on Deque<String> but stores a LinkedList. Swapping the implementation to ArrayDeque preserves these operations for the validated non-null input. A concurrent or durable queue needs different coordination and storage decisions.

Keep input ownership outside the queue

The demonstration executes a fixed sequence so it can be compiled and checked without waiting for stdin. A CLI loop can pass each complete line to execute and decide how to display rejected inputs. It should not close a shared System.in reader merely because one command completed.

Working program

import java.util.Deque;
import java.util.LinkedList;
public class TaskDequeCommands {
    final Deque<String> pending=new LinkedList<>();
    String execute(String line){
        if(line==null||line.trim().isEmpty())throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing command");
        String[] parts=line.trim().split("\\s+",2);String command=parts[0];String argument=parts.length==2?parts[1].trim():"";
        if(command.equals("add")||command.equals("urgent")){
            if(argument.isEmpty())throw new IllegalArgumentException("Missing task");
            if(command.equals("add"))pending.addLast(argument);else pending.addFirst(argument);
            return "accepted";
        }
        if(!argument.isEmpty())throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unexpected argument");
        if(command.equals("next")){String task=pending.pollFirst();return task==null?"empty":task;}
        if(command.equals("list"))return pending.toString();
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown command");
    }
    public static void main(String[] args){
        TaskDequeCommands queue=new TaskDequeCommands();
        queue.execute("add Audit stock");queue.execute("add Print label");queue.execute("urgent Verify address");
        System.out.println(queue.execute("list"));System.out.println(queue.execute("next"));
        System.out.println(queue.execute("list"));
        try{queue.execute("add");}catch(IllegalArgumentException rejected){System.out.println("Empty task rejected");}
    }
}

Output

[Verify address, Audit stock, Print label]
Verify address
[Audit stock, Print label]
Empty task rejected

Costs and boundaries

Endpoint insertion and removal use O(1) linked-node work; parsing visits the command characters and list rendering visits O(n) tasks. The queue retains descriptions until removed. It is in memory only and has no bounded admission policy; the calling CLI must limit admitted work if input is not trusted to stay small.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not promise persistence across restart.
  • Urgent-at-head ordering can starve normal work.
  • A Deque interface does not make a LinkedList thread-safe.

title: Java LinkedList method notes
summary: LinkedList method choice depends on the endpoint, the empty-case contract, and whether removal targets a value or an index.
body:
LinkedList method choice depends on the endpoint, the empty-case contract, and whether removal targets a value or an index.

Endpoint pairs

  • FIFO: offer or addLast, then poll or pollFirst.
  • LIFO: push, then pop; pop throws when empty.
  • Read without removing: peekFirst or peekLast returns null when empty.
  • Strict endpoint read: getFirst or getLast throws when empty.
  • Position: remove(int) returns an element.
  • First equal value: remove(Object) returns a boolean.

Costs

Endpoints use O(1) link work. Searching and arbitrary indexing are O(n) in the worst case. A full iterator traversal is O(n). A get(index) loop over the entire list can be O(n²). Each element requires linked-node storage.

Connected lessons

Continue with Java LinkedList: operations, internals and failure cases, Java LinkedList quiz.

Common Mistakes

Null elements make poll and peek results ambiguous. The class does not coordinate access between threads. A shallow copy preserves references to mutable elements.

Remember which result means absence

pollFirst and peekFirst return null for an empty list, while removeFirst and getFirst reject that empty state with an exception. An actual null element makes a null result ambiguous, so an application queue can choose to reject null elements even though LinkedList permits them.

remove(int) returns the removed element at that position. remove(Object) returns whether a first equal value was found and removed. An Integer argument can select different behavior depending on whether the call supplies a primitive int or an explicitly boxed value; read the argument type before explaining the result.

Iterator traversal follows links once. Repeated get(i) asks for a new location search on each call. A shallow copy also traverses values to build another membership structure without cloning arbitrary elements. Do not treat fail-fast exceptions as an access-coordination mechanism.

Choose and explain an answer

subject: java-quizzes

questions.prompt: What does remove(1) do on LinkedList<Integer>?
options: Removes the first value equal to 1
questions.explanation: The int argument selects positional removal. Use Integer.valueOf(1) to select value removal.

questions.prompt: What does pollFirst return on an empty LinkedList?
questions.explanation: pollFirst returns null. removeFirst throws NoSuchElementException when empty.

questions.prompt: What is the worst-case cost of get(index)?
questions.explanation: The list walks from an endpoint to find the indexed node.

questions.prompt: How should a traversal remove its current element?
options: Call list.remove inside an enhanced for loop
Use the iterator remove method after next
questions.explanation: An iterator supports removal of its last returned element. Its state must be respected.

questions.prompt: Does a LinkedList copy clone its mutable element objects?
questions.explanation: A shallow list copy has separate nodes but still shares element references.

questions.prompt: Which claim about insertion is complete?
options: An endpoint insert has constant link work; finding an arbitrary index can take O(n)
An indexed insert always costs O(log n)
questions.explanation: Location and link edits are different parts of the operation.

questions.prompt: What does LinkedList.descendingIterator start with on a nonempty list?
questions.explanation: The descending iterator traverses the list from the tail toward the head; it does not sort the values.

questions.prompt: Which call reads the last element without removing it and returns null when empty?
questions.explanation: peekLast uses the nullable empty-result contract and leaves membership unchanged.

questions.prompt: Does replacing an element with set(index,value) ordinarily add a node?
questions.explanation: It replaces a stored value at the located position rather than adding membership.

questions.prompt: Can a ListIterator add after reaching a chosen position without a fresh index search?
options: Only when the list is empty
questions.explanation: The positioned cursor identifies the local link location, though reaching that cursor position still had a cost.

questions.prompt: Does fail-fast behavior guarantee detection of every unsynchronized race?
questions.explanation: Detection is best-effort and cannot be the program’s coordination policy.

questions.prompt: Why can a null poll result be ambiguous in a LinkedList allowing null?
options: It can represent an empty result or a removed null value
questions.explanation: The class permits null elements, so applications often choose a stricter queue element policy.

title: Java HashMap: keys, collisions, and update operations
summary: HashMap associates keys with values through hash buckets; key equality decides whether an insertion creates a mapping or replaces an existing one.
body:
HashMap associates keys with values through hash buckets; key equality decides whether an insertion creates a mapping or replaces an existing one.

Lookup is a two-part contract

Hashing narrows the search. Equality finishes it. Two keys can share a hash without being equal, so a collision does not mean one entry overwrites the other. Read equals and hashCode before introducing an application object as a key.

A receipt counter needs one entry per payment status. Updating an existing status should change its count, not append another row. A map expresses that requirement directly; a list would require a search before each update.

HashMap does not promise iteration order. An observed order in a small test is not an API contract. Use LinkedHashMap for encounter order or TreeMap for key ordering. Sorting the display and choosing the storage structure are separate decisions.

Update without an unnecessary second lookup

merge supplies the first value when a key is absent and combines it with the existing non-null value otherwise. The counter uses Integer::sum. The merge operation on a plain HashMap is not an atomic update shared safely among threads.

Null needs care. get returns null for both a missing mapping and an entry explicitly mapped to null; containsKey distinguishes those states. This counter never stores null, which removes that ambiguity from its caller contract.

The counters describe an in-memory batch. They are not an audit ledger: process exit loses them, repeated delivery increments them again, and concurrent updates need a different ownership model.

Internal working: a Java 8 implementation view

The Java 8 implementation stores entries in a bucket array. It spreads a key hash with a shifted portion of the hash and selects a bucket using a mask against the current power-of-two capacity. Equality is still checked inside that bucket. These are implementation details of the inspected Java 8 source, not extra promises made by the Map interface.

The default load factor is 0.75. Capacity and load factor determine when growth is needed, but an initial capacity is not a fixed maximum number of mappings. During a resize, stored hash bits decide whether an entry remains at its old index or moves by the old capacity. Keys still need stable equality and hash behavior; growth cannot repair a mutated key.

The inspected Java 8 source declares a treeification threshold of eight and a minimum treeification capacity of sixty-four. A collision-heavy bucket can trigger growth rather than tree conversion when the array is smaller. Treating eight colliding insertions as a portable guarantee of a tree is therefore wrong. The insertion path, current capacity and release matter.

Tree bins limit many collision cases, but a blanket claim that every hostile key set gives logarithmic lookup is too broad. Equal-hash keys and their comparability affect how the implementation searches. Iteration also visits capacity and stored mappings, so allocating a huge sparse map can make scanning expensive even when lookups are usually quick. Validate adversarial keys and measure the application distribution before choosing a capacity.

Working program

import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class ReceiptCounter {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, Integer> counts = new HashMap<>();
        String[] statuses = {"paid", "declined", "paid", "pending", "paid"};
        for (String status : statuses) {
            counts.merge(status, 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        System.out.println("paid=" + counts.getOrDefault("paid", 0));
        System.out.println("refunded=" + counts.getOrDefault("refunded", 0));
        System.out.println("statuses=" + counts.size());
    }
}

Output

paid=3
refunded=0
statuses=3

Cost and design choices

For well-distributed hashes, each map update has expected constant lookup cost. With n input statuses and k distinct statuses, the batch requires expected O(n) time and O(k) stored entries. String hashing and equality themselves depend on key length, so treating arbitrarily long keys as free work would be misleading.

Capacity is the bucket budget, not the number of mappings already present. Growth allocates storage and moves entries. Excessive preallocation also costs memory and can make iteration expensive. Measure the actual batch size before selecting a capacity.

A key whose equality-relevant fields change after insertion may no longer be found by a later lookup. Store stable identifiers or immutable key objects. Resizing a map does not repair a broken key contract.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not depend on HashMap iteration order in tests or API responses.
  • Do not mutate keys after inserting them.
  • Do not assume merge on HashMap is safe for simultaneous writers.
  • Do not let Integer counters wrap silently when batch totals can exceed their range.

title: Java HashSet: deduplication and equality
summary: HashSet stores distinct elements using hashing and equality, with no promised iteration order.
body:
HashSet stores distinct elements using hashing and equality, with no promised iteration order.

Choose what counts as the same value

Deduplication is a policy. Are two receipt IDs equal when their letter case differs? Are leading spaces meaningful? Decide before inserting values. A set can enforce your chosen equality rule; it cannot infer the business meaning of an identifier.

This import treats trimmed receipt strings as case-sensitive identifiers. It rejects an empty identifier and counts duplicates. It does not normalise letter case, because changing a case-sensitive provider ID could incorrectly merge two receipts.

A HashSet permits a null element, but this pipeline does not. Restricting inputs makes downstream work easier: a reader knows every stored value is a usable identifier. For original encounter order, choose LinkedHashSet instead of sorting after each insertion.

Use the result of add

add returns false when an equal element already exists. Checking contains and then calling add repeats the search and creates a wider race window if the code is later shared incorrectly between threads.

If the imported record is a custom type, its equality and hash contract determine deduplication. Object identity is often the wrong rule for a record reconstructed from a file.

A process-local set is not a permanent idempotency store. Separate service instances have separate sets, and restarting a process clears its history. Use a durable uniqueness constraint when accepting an ID twice would create an external side effect.

Working program

import java.util.HashSet;
import java.util.Set;

public class ReceiptDeduplicator {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        String[] importedIds = {" rcpt-41 ", "rcpt-82", "rcpt-41", ""};
        Set<String> acceptedIds = new HashSet<>();
        int duplicates = 0;
        int rejected = 0;
        for (String rawId : importedIds) {
            String receiptId = rawId.trim();
            if (receiptId.isEmpty()) {
                rejected++;
            } else if (!acceptedIds.add(receiptId)) {
                duplicates++;
            }
        }
        System.out.println("accepted=" + acceptedIds.size());
        System.out.println("duplicates=" + duplicates);
        System.out.println("rejected=" + rejected);
    }
}

Output

accepted=2
duplicates=1
rejected=1

Cost and design choices

Processing n bounded-length IDs takes expected O(n) time with well-distributed hashes and O(k) entry storage for k distinct IDs. Trimming can allocate new strings; account for input text length when estimating a large import.

HashSet uses hashing storage rather than a sorted index. If the main operation is checking membership, that is a sensible fit. If the application needs nearest values, ordered ranges, or a floor entry, study ordered maps instead.

An unbounded stream of distinct IDs creates an unbounded memory requirement. A maximum batch size, retention window, or external store is a design decision the collection will not make for you.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assert the order of HashSet.toString().
  • Do not use mutable fields in an element’s hash while it is stored.
  • Do not claim process-local deduplication guarantees exactly-once delivery.

title: Java TreeMap: ordered keys and range views
summary: TreeMap stores mappings in key order and exposes range and nearest-key operations through the NavigableMap contract.
body:
TreeMap stores mappings in key order and exposes range and nearest-key operations through the NavigableMap contract.

Search an ordered domain

Hashing answers exact lookup. A pricing schedule has a different question: which threshold is the greatest one not above this order quantity? floorEntry answers it directly. The keys are thresholds, not individual purchases.

Natural ordering works for integer thresholds. A custom comparator changes the definition of key uniqueness: keys that compare as zero occupy the same mapping even if equals says otherwise. Keep those contracts consistent unless the disagreement is intentional and documented.

For a case-insensitive string comparator, two differently capitalised strings can address the same mapping. This can be useful for a lookup, but it is unsuitable when the original identifiers must remain distinct. Compare the contract with HashMap before replacing a storage type.

Range views share storage

subMap produces a view of the parent map, not an independent snapshot. Changes through either side can be visible through the other. Copy into a new map when a reader needs a stable snapshot owned by that reader.

The four-argument overload makes inclusive and exclusive endpoints explicit. A threshold exactly equal to the lower bound belongs in an inclusive range; one equal to an exclusive upper bound does not.

floorEntry can return null. An order below the smallest configured threshold has no matching rule. The program checks that case rather than converting absence into a zero price.

Working program

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.NavigableMap;
import java.util.TreeMap;

public class QuantityPricing {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        NavigableMap<Integer, Integer> centsPerUnit = new TreeMap<>();
        centsPerUnit.put(1, 240);
        centsPerUnit.put(10, 220);
        centsPerUnit.put(50, 195);
        int quantity = 24;
        Map.Entry<Integer, Integer> price = centsPerUnit.floorEntry(quantity);
        if (price == null) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Quantity must meet a threshold");
        }
        System.out.println("unitCents=" + price.getValue());
        System.out.println("thresholds=" + centsPerUnit.subMap(10, true, 50, false).keySet());
    }
}

Output

unitCents=220
thresholds=[10]

Cost and design choices

Key lookup, insertion, and removal require O(log n) tree work for n entries, assuming key comparisons have bounded cost. Returning a range view does not copy every mapping. Traversing k selected mappings still costs work proportional to those visited entries.

Tree nodes allocate references and metadata per entry. A sorted array can use less memory for an immutable small schedule, but insertion into that representation requires moving elements. Match the representation to the update rate.

Prices use integer cents here so the example isolates threshold selection. A real multi-currency pricing engine must define currency, rounding, tax, and bounds; BigDecimal addresses decimal arithmetic, not those policy choices.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not dereference a missing floorEntry.
  • Do not assume a subMap is a detached copy.
  • Do not insert keys that your comparator cannot compare, including null when unsupported.

title: Java LinkedHashMap: encounter order and a bounded cache model
summary: LinkedHashMap combines hash-based key lookup with a linked encounter order that can follow insertion or access.
body:
LinkedHashMap combines hash-based key lookup with a linked encounter order that can follow insertion or access.

Order is part of the contract

A plain HashMap deliberately leaves ordering unspecified. LinkedHashMap maintains an order so an application can produce repeatable output or identify the least recently accessed entry.

Insertion order is the default. Access order requires the constructor’s third argument to be true. Reading an existing entry then moves it to the most recently accessed end. That read can change structural iteration state; it is not a harmless shared read for concurrent code.

The program models a two-entry cache. It overrides removeEldestEntry to remove an old entry after a new mapping exceeds the capacity. Reading account-a before inserting account-c means account-b becomes the eviction candidate.

Bounded entries are not bounded bytes

A maximum entry count only bounds the number of mappings. One value might contain a large payload. Production caches need a memory budget or weighted sizing when payload sizes vary.

An eviction policy does not supply expiration, load coalescing, failure caching, or thread safety. This small model is useful for understanding access order. It is not a replacement for a tested cache library when a service has those requirements.

Cache values also need an ownership rule. A cached mutable object can be changed by any caller holding its reference. If the cached value is a configuration snapshot, prefer immutable content or return a defensive copy.

Working program

import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;

public class AccessOrderedCache {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Map<String, String> cache = new LinkedHashMap<String, String>(4, 0.75f, true) {
            @Override
            protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<String, String> eldest) {
                return size() > 2;
            }
        };
        cache.put("account-a", "active");
        cache.put("account-b", "paused");
        cache.get("account-a");
        cache.put("account-c", "active");
        System.out.println(cache.keySet());
        System.out.println("account-b=" + cache.containsKey("account-b"));
    }
}

Output

[account-a, account-c]
account-b=false

Cost and design choices

Expected hash lookup cost remains constant with good key distribution. Maintaining encounter links adds per-entry references and constant bookkeeping for an access-order move. Iterating n entries follows encounter links in O(n) time.

The demonstration stores two entries, giving O(1) entry-count space under this fixed limit. For a configured maximum k, storage is O(k) entries plus the memory owned by their keys and values.

Do not hold an iterator while repeatedly calling get on the same access-ordered map. A design that needs both traversal and updates should define a snapshot or lock strategy explicitly.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call this cache thread-safe.
  • Do not confuse containsKey with an access-order get operation.
  • Do not interpret an entry-count limit as a guaranteed byte limit.
