title: Java dynamic proxies: define Object-method behavior explicitly
summary: A java.lang.reflect.Proxy routes interface calls through an InvocationHandler, including equals, hashCode, and toString declared by Object.
body:
A java.lang.reflect.Proxy routes interface calls through an InvocationHandler, including equals, hashCode, and toString declared by Object.

Operational contract

The adapter counts receipt reads and delegates the business call. It implements identity-based equals and hashCode for the proxy itself, and a fixed diagnostic toString. That avoids accidentally forwarding Object calls to an unrelated delegate, recursing through the proxy, or returning a value with the wrong type. A dynamic proxy only implements interfaces; a concrete class cannot be proxied this way. The method handler runs on the caller's thread, so a blocking delegate still blocks that caller.

Failure case

A metrics registry inserts a receipt-reader proxy into a hash map. If hashCode returns null or changes with a read count, lookup breaks even though the read method works. This adapter preserves stable identity semantics.

Java code

import java.lang.reflect.Proxy;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

public class ReceiptReaderProxy {
    public interface Reader { String read(long receiptId); }

    public static Reader counting(Reader delegate, AtomicLong reads) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(delegate);
        Objects.requireNonNull(reads);
        return (Reader) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
                Reader.class.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[] { Reader.class },
                (proxy, method, arguments) -> {
                    if (method.getDeclaringClass() == Object.class) {
                        return switch (method.getName()) {
                            case "equals" -> proxy == arguments[0];
                            case "hashCode" -> System.identityHashCode(proxy);
                            case "toString" -> "ReceiptReaderProxy";
                            default -> throw new UnsupportedOperationException(method.getName());
                        };
                    }
                    if (!method.getName().equals("read"))
                        throw new UnsupportedOperationException(method.getName());
                    reads.incrementAndGet();
                    return delegate.read((long) arguments[0]);
                });
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Each call adds proxy dispatch and an atomic increment before the delegate's work. Storage is O(1) per proxy. A hot call path can make the shared counter contended, so measure it before placing a single counter on every high-volume invocation.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not forget equals, hashCode, and toString can reach the handler.
  • Do not return null for primitive-returning methods such as hashCode.
  • Do not expect Proxy to subclass a concrete class or make a blocking delegate asynchronous.

title: Java ServiceLoader: treat provider discovery as fallible startup work
summary: ServiceLoader locates implementations registered for a service interface. Iteration can fail when provider metadata, construction, or linkage is broken.
body:
ServiceLoader locates implementations registered for a service interface. Iteration can fail when provider metadata, construction, or linkage is broken.

Operational contract

The loader selects one provider during startup and converts ServiceConfigurationError into a clear configuration failure. It does not silently skip a broken provider, because doing so could change the selected receipt codec. The classpath registration file or named-module provides directive belongs in the deployment artifact; a service interface alone does not register implementations. ServiceLoader lazily discovers and instantiates providers, so moving iteration into a request path can turn a packaging problem into a customer-visible failure. If multiple providers are legal, selection needs an explicit stable policy.

Failure case

A deployment lists a provider whose constructor throws. The service fails initialization instead of pretending no codec exists and processing receipts with an unintended fallback.

Java code

import java.util.Iterator;
import java.util.ServiceConfigurationError;
import java.util.ServiceLoader;

public class ReceiptCodecDiscovery {
    public interface ReceiptCodec { byte[] encode(String receipt); }

    public static ReceiptCodec requiredProvider() {
        try {
            Iterator<ReceiptCodec> providers = ServiceLoader.load(ReceiptCodec.class).iterator();
            if (!providers.hasNext())
                throw new IllegalStateException("No receipt codec registered");
            ReceiptCodec selected = providers.next();
            if (providers.hasNext())
                throw new IllegalStateException("Multiple receipt codecs registered");
            return selected;
        } catch (ServiceConfigurationError broken) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Receipt codec registration is invalid", broken);
        }
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Discovery scans P registered providers and instantiates at least those visited, costing O(P) startup time and provider-dependent memory; this sample visits enough to reject a second provider. Holding the selected provider afterward makes per-request discovery cost O(0).

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect an interface declaration to register a provider.
  • Do not swallow ServiceConfigurationError and select a different provider without policy.
  • Do not repeat lazy discovery on every request when providers are deployment configuration.

title: Java Class.forName: inspect an allowlisted class without initializing it
summary: Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links a class without requesting its initialization. The three-argument form makes loader and initialization policy explicit.
body:
Class.forName(name, false, loader) loads and links a class without requesting its initialization. The three-argument form makes loader and initialization policy explicit.

Operational contract

The method maps a short trusted key to a fixed receipt implementation name, then verifies that the loaded type implements the expected interface. Using arbitrary user text as a class name could load unrelated types or increase attack surface. The false flag avoids initialization during discovery; constructing an instance or using a static member later can still initialize the class. Linkage errors can occur while loading, and loader identity determines whether a class is assignable to this service interface.

Failure case

A configuration key names the built-in warehouse codec. The service checks its type at startup without constructing it. A key that is not on the allowlist fails before any class lookup.

Java code

import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptCodecTypeGate {
    public interface ReceiptCodec { byte[] encode(String receipt); }
    public static class WarehouseCodec implements ReceiptCodec {
        public byte[] encode(String receipt) {
            return receipt.getBytes(java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        }
    }

    private static final Map<String, String> ALLOWED = Map.of(
            "warehouse", WarehouseCodec.class.getName());

    public static Class<? extends ReceiptCodec> resolve(String configurationKey)
            throws ClassNotFoundException {
        String className = ALLOWED.get(Objects.requireNonNull(configurationKey));
        if (className == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown receipt codec key");
        ClassLoader loader = ReceiptCodecTypeGate.class.getClassLoader();
        return Class.forName(className, false, loader).asSubclass(ReceiptCodec.class);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The allowlist lookup is O(1) average for a fixed small map. Class loading and linking may perform I/O and verification once per loader; class initialization is deferred, not removed. Retaining references to classes can retain their defining loader.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not pass an untrusted class name directly to Class.forName.
  • Do not claim false prevents later static initialization.
  • Do not assume two classes with the same name but different defining loaders are interchangeable.

title: Java modules: distinguish exported APIs from open packages
summary: A named module's exported package supports access to public API types; an open package permits deeper reflection to another module. Module inspection exposes these separate conditions.
body:
A named module's exported package supports access to public API types; an open package permits deeper reflection to another module. Module inspection exposes these separate conditions.

Operational contract

The helper reports whether the provider module exports or opens its class package to a consumer module, and whether the consumer reads the provider. These checks describe module relationships, not whether a particular private member may be invoked; member accessibility, caller context, and lookup mode still matter. Unnamed modules report broad export/open behavior. For a named plugin, declaring exports is not a substitute for opens when a framework needs deep reflection. Code should prefer a public interface if possible and validate module setup at startup.

Failure case

A public receipt interface remains callable after a plugin removes opens. A serializer that reads private fields can fail. The report shows that exported and opened are separate deployment decisions.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;

public class PluginModuleVisibility {
    public record Access(boolean consumerReadsProvider,
                         boolean packageExported, boolean packageOpen) { }

    public static Access inspect(Class<?> providerType, Module consumer) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(providerType);
        Objects.requireNonNull(consumer);
        Module provider = providerType.getModule();
        String packageName = providerType.getPackageName();
        return new Access(consumer.canRead(provider),
                provider.isExported(packageName, consumer),
                provider.isOpen(packageName, consumer));
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The inspection uses O(1) application data and small module-graph lookups. It is a configuration check, not a performance path; run it when a plugin is registered rather than for each receipt.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat exports as permission for private-member reflection.
  • Do not ignore the consumer's readability relationship.
  • Do not interpret a package-level report as proof a particular Method or Field is accessible.

title: Java MethodHandle.invokeExact: make the call-site type part of the contract
summary: MethodHandle.invokeExact requires the call site's argument and return types to match the handle's MethodType exactly; a mismatch raises WrongMethodTypeException.
body:
MethodHandle.invokeExact requires the call site's argument and return types to match the handle's MethodType exactly; a mismatch raises WrongMethodTypeException.

Operational contract

The sample caches a public String.substring handle with receiver String and two int arguments. Its cast to String establishes the return type of the invokeExact call site. A Long argument in place of int, or discarding the return value, changes the call-site type and fails; invoke is the adapting form when conversions are deliberate. The handle is resolved once and its lookup obeys access rules. Index validation belongs to the business boundary, not to MethodHandle, so this method checks the requested slice first.

Failure case

A receipt code is sliced from index 8 to 10. The result is 47. A refactor that changes one index to long without changing the handle type fails at the exact invocation boundary rather than silently choosing a different overload.

Java code

import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandle;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles;
import java.lang.invoke.MethodType;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptCodeSlice {
    private static final MethodHandle SLICE = findSlice();

    private static MethodHandle findSlice() {
        try {
            return MethodHandles.publicLookup().findVirtual(String.class,
                    "substring", MethodType.methodType(String.class, int.class, int.class));
        } catch (ReflectiveOperationException failure) {
            throw new ExceptionInInitializerError(failure);
        }
    }

    public static String read(String receiptCode, int start, int end) throws Throwable {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receiptCode);
        if (start < 0 || end < start || end > receiptCode.length())
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid receipt-code slice");
        return (String) SLICE.invokeExact(receiptCode, start, end);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The cached lookup is paid once per class initialization. Each invocation adds method-handle dispatch and substring's O(L) copy for L selected characters, with O(L) new string storage. Wrong call-site types are contract failures, not a fallback lookup mechanism.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not confuse invokeExact with the adapting invoke call.
  • Do not omit the return cast when it defines the expected call-site type.
  • Do not assume a handle bypasses public-lookup access rules or input range validation.

title: Java BitSet: distinguish logical length, capacity, and set-bit count
summary: BitSet.length returns one beyond the highest set index, cardinality counts true bits, and size reports implementation storage capacity. These values answer different questions.
body:
BitSet.length returns one beyond the highest set index, cardinality counts true bits, and size reports implementation storage capacity. These values answer different questions.

Operational contract

The method reports the highest active receipt slot and total active slots without mistaking allocated capacity for a business identifier. An empty BitSet has length zero, so the highest index is represented as -1. A sparse set with only slot 82 active has cardinality one and length 83. BitSet grows to hold high indexes, which can make a single erroneous ID expensive. Validate identifiers before calling set; BitSet is not synchronized for concurrent mutation.

Failure case

The importer marks slot 82 and then clears it. Its logical length returns to zero even though its backing storage may remain allocated. Using size as the number of processed receipts would report capacity instead of work done.

Java code

import java.util.BitSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ActiveReceiptSlots {
    public record Summary(int highestSlot, int activeCount) { }

    public static Summary summarize(BitSet activeSlots) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(activeSlots);
        int logicalLength = activeSlots.length();
        return new Summary(logicalLength == 0 ? -1 : logicalLength - 1,
                activeSlots.cardinality());
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Computing cardinality scans the words used by the bit set, taking O(W) time for W stored machine words; highest-set-bit lookup is tied to that representation. The method adds O(1) result storage. A very high index can enlarge the underlying bit vector far beyond the number of true bits.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use size as the count of true bits.
  • Do not return length as the highest index without subtracting one for a nonempty set.
  • Do not set unvalidated huge indexes in a sparse business ID space.

title: Java BitSet nextSetBit: scan a bounded index range without walking gaps
summary: BitSet.nextSetBit finds the next true bit at or after a starting index, returning -1 when none exists. A bounded scan must still enforce its end index and result cap.
body:
BitSet.nextSetBit finds the next true bit at or after a starting index, returning -1 when none exists. A bounded scan must still enforce its end index and result cap.

Operational contract

The method returns at most 47 receipt slots in a half-open interval. It validates nonnegative ordered bounds, then jumps between set bits rather than testing every possible index. The loop stops before the exclusive upper bound. Because every visited bit is strictly less than an int upper bound, incrementing that bit cannot overflow here. A cap protects output memory and prevents one request from enumerating an enormous set. The input is caller-owned and must not be mutated concurrently without synchronization.

Failure case

Active slots are 3, 47, and 82. A scan of [40, 82) returns only 47. Slot 82 is outside the half-open range even though its bit is set.

Java code

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.BitSet;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptSlotWindow {
    public static List<Integer> active(BitSet slots, int fromInclusive, int toExclusive) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(slots);
        if (fromInclusive < 0 || toExclusive < fromInclusive)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid slot range");
        List<Integer> found = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int slot = slots.nextSetBit(fromInclusive);
                slot >= 0 && slot < toExclusive;
                slot = slots.nextSetBit(slot + 1)) {
            if (found.size() == 47) throw new IllegalStateException("Too many active slots");
            found.add(slot);
        }
        return List.copyOf(found);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

The scan visits K set bits and searches the underlying words across the requested span, rather than performing one test per missing index. Result memory is O(K) with K capped at 47. The returned immutable list copies its elements once.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not include the exclusive end slot.
  • Do not forget that nextSetBit returns -1 when no later bit exists.
  • Do not scan an unbounded range into an unbounded output list.

title: Java EnumSet complementOf: derive a default-deny capability set
summary: EnumSet.complementOf returns a new set containing enum constants absent from the supplied EnumSet. Its universe is the entire enum type, not just constants known to one caller.
body:
EnumSet.complementOf returns a new set containing enum constants absent from the supplied EnumSet. Its universe is the entire enum type, not just constants known to one caller.

Operational contract

The helper constructs a fresh denied set from an allowed capability set. Adding a new enum constant automatically puts it in denied until the policy explicitly allows it, which is appropriate for this default-deny design. The result is a separate mutable EnumSet; changing allowed later does not update the previous result. If a product instead interprets the complement as granted permissions, a newly introduced constant could become granted accidentally. The allowed set itself still requires an authorization source and review.

Failure case

A release adds ARCHIVE. Existing callers allow only READ and EXPORT. The computed denied set includes ARCHIVE without changing the callers' allowlists.

Java code

import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptCapabilityPolicy {
    public enum Capability { READ, EXPORT, DELETE, ARCHIVE }

    public static EnumSet<Capability> denied(EnumSet<Capability> allowed) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(allowed);
        return EnumSet.complementOf(allowed);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Complement construction visits the enum universe and copies a compact bit representation, taking O(E) work in the number of enum constants under a portable cost model and O(E) result bits. The policy computation is small but should not replace explicit authorization checks at the action boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a complement as granted permissions without reviewing new enum constants.
  • Do not assume the returned set is a live view of allowed.
  • Do not treat enum membership alone as proof that a caller is authorized.

summary: EnumSet.copyOf a non-EnumSet collection needs at least one element to infer its enum type; noneOf states the element class explicitly and works for an empty source.
body:
EnumSet.copyOf a non-EnumSet collection needs at least one element to infer its enum type; noneOf states the element class explicitly and works for an empty source.

Operational contract

The helper starts with a typed empty EnumSet, then adds supplied review states. It returns an independent mutable set even when the source is empty. Duplicate states collapse by set semantics, and null elements are rejected. If the API promises an immutable result, wrap or copy it separately; returning EnumSet transfers mutation ownership to the caller. This lesson concerns type inference and collection ownership, not permission policy.

Failure case

An intake has no review flags. Building EnumSet.copyOf from an ordinary empty List throws because the enum type cannot be inferred. The typed empty set returns normally.

Java code

import java.util.Collection;
import java.util.EnumSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptReviewStates {
    public enum State { NEW, CHECKED, HELD, RELEASED }

    public static EnumSet<State> copy(Collection<State> states) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(states);
        EnumSet<State> result = EnumSet.noneOf(State.class);
        result.addAll(states);
        return result;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Copying N source elements costs O(N) time and compact O(E) bit storage for E enum constants. It is a new set, so later mutation of the source does not change the result.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call EnumSet.copyOf on an ordinary empty collection and expect type inference.
  • Do not assume the returned EnumSet is immutable.
  • Do not silently accept null states; EnumSet rejects them.

title: Java NavigableSet subSet: account for a live backed range
summary: NavigableSet.subSet returns a backed view of keys in a specified range. Mutations through either view or source are visible through the other.
body:
NavigableSet.subSet returns a backed view of keys in a specified range. Mutations through either view or source are visible through the other.

Operational contract

The method returns a half-open receipt-ID range. Its caller owns the underlying set and must keep it alive and coordinate any concurrent access; TreeSet itself is not thread-safe. Inserting an out-of-range value through the view throws IllegalArgumentException. If a stable snapshot is needed, copy the view into a new TreeSet under appropriate synchronization. Comparator order defines the meaning of from and to; this sample assumes natural long ordering. The range validates reversed endpoints before construction.

Failure case

A report asks for IDs [40, 80). After the view is created, the owner adds ID 47 to the source set. The view now contains 47. Attempting to add 82 through the view fails as out of range.

Java code

import java.util.NavigableSet;
import java.util.Objects;

public class ReceiptIdRangeView {
    public static NavigableSet<Long> between(NavigableSet<Long> receiptIds,
            long fromInclusive, long toExclusive) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(receiptIds);
        if (toExclusive < fromInclusive)
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Reversed receipt range");
        return receiptIds.subSet(fromInclusive, true, toExclusive, false);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Creating the view uses O(1) wrapper state. Tree-based lookup or insertion through it is O(log N) for N stored IDs; iterating K matching IDs is O(K) after locating the start. A stable copy costs O(K) storage and additional insertion work.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat the returned range as a snapshot.
  • Do not insert outside its bounds.
  • Do not mutate an unsynchronized TreeSet concurrently through source and view.

title: Java PriorityBlockingQueue: add an admission limit to an unbounded priority queue
summary: PriorityBlockingQueue orders retrieval by priority but is logically unbounded; its constructor argument is an initial capacity, not a maximum backlog.
body:
PriorityBlockingQueue orders retrieval by priority but is logically unbounded; its constructor argument is an initial capacity, not a maximum backlog.

Operational contract

The wrapper acquires one of 47 permits before offering a job and releases it when a worker takes that job. This bounds jobs waiting in the queue, not jobs already being processed by workers. The queue comparator orders priority descending and receipt ID ascending for a defined tie break. A failed offer releases the permit. The queue remains private so callers cannot bypass the gate with direct insertion or removal. A production service must also cap producer concurrency and define shutdown and task-failure handling.

Failure case

All 47 waiting slots are filled. A new receipt job is rejected immediately even though PriorityBlockingQueue itself would otherwise accept it and grow. A worker take releases one waiting slot.

Java code

import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.PriorityBlockingQueue;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;

public class BoundedPriorityReceiptInbox {
    public record Job(int priority, long receiptId) { }
    private final Semaphore waitingSlots = new Semaphore(47);
    private final PriorityBlockingQueue<Job> jobs = new PriorityBlockingQueue<>(47,
            Comparator.comparingInt(Job::priority).reversed()
                    .thenComparingLong(Job::receiptId));

    public boolean submit(Job job) {
        Objects.requireNonNull(job);
        if (!waitingSlots.tryAcquire()) return false;
        boolean added = false;
        try {
            added = jobs.offer(job);
            return added;
        } finally {
            if (!added) waitingSlots.release();
        }
    }

    public Job take() throws InterruptedException {
        Job job = jobs.take();
        waitingSlots.release();
        return job;
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Insertion and removal are O(log N) heap operations for N queued jobs, capped here at 47 by the permit gate. The gate uses O(1) extra state. Worker execution and producer tasks are outside this queue bound.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat initial capacity or remainingCapacity as a backlog cap.
  • Do not expose the underlying queue for bypass insertion or removal.
  • Do not forget that priority service can starve low-priority jobs even with bounded storage.

title: Java CopyOnWriteArraySet: publish against a stable listener snapshot
summary: CopyOnWriteArraySet provides snapshot iterators and copies its backing array on writes. It fits small listener registries with frequent reads and infrequent changes.
body:
CopyOnWriteArraySet provides snapshot iterators and copies its backing array on writes. It fits small listener registries with frequent reads and infrequent changes.

Operational contract

A receipt listener added during one publication is absent from that publication's iterator and can participate in the next one. Removing a listener likewise does not retroactively remove it from an iterator already obtained. Duplicate listeners are judged by equals, not object identity. Callbacks run on the publisher's thread; one slow or failing listener can delay or abort later callbacks. The sample leaves callback failure visible so the service can set an explicit isolation policy.

Failure case

A listener registers an audit listener while handling receipt 47. The audit listener does not receive 47 from that in-progress publication, but it can receive receipt 82 afterward.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArraySet;

public class ReceiptListenerRegistry {
    public interface Listener { void received(long receiptId); }
    private final CopyOnWriteArraySet<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArraySet<>();

    public boolean add(Listener listener) {
        return listeners.add(Objects.requireNonNull(listener));
    }

    public boolean remove(Listener listener) {
        return listeners.remove(listener);
    }

    public void publish(long receiptId) {
        for (Listener listener : listeners) listener.received(receiptId);
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

Publishing to L listeners is O(L) callback dispatch without copying for each read. Adding or removing is O(L) search plus an O(L) array copy on change, with a temporary second array. This is expensive for high-churn large sets.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect a newly added listener to join an iteration already in progress.
  • Do not treat callbacks as asynchronous or isolated from each other's failures.
  • Do not choose copy-on-write for frequent writes and large registries without measuring allocation.

title: Java LinkedBlockingDeque: bound urgent and normal work in one queue
summary: LinkedBlockingDeque can enforce a fixed capacity while admitting work at either end. offerFirst and offerLast report a full queue without blocking.
body:
LinkedBlockingDeque can enforce a fixed capacity while admitting work at either end. offerFirst and offerLast report a full queue without blocking.

Operational contract

The inbox uses 47 slots. Urgent receipts enter at the front, normal receipts at the back, and workers take from the front. Both admission paths share the same capacity. Repeated urgent arrivals can starve older normal items, so a production scheduler may need fairness or separate reserved capacity. The dequeue operation is interruptible. The wrapper owns the queue and does not expose mutating methods that could circumvent admission policy.

Failure case

There are 47 waiting receipts. Both urgent and normal submission return false rather than growing memory. When a worker takes one, exactly one slot opens for either class.

Java code

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingDeque;

public class ReceiptWorkDeque {
    private final LinkedBlockingDeque<String> waiting = new LinkedBlockingDeque<>(47);

    public boolean submitUrgent(String receiptId) {
        return waiting.offerFirst(Objects.requireNonNull(receiptId));
    }

    public boolean submitNormal(String receiptId) {
        return waiting.offerLast(Objects.requireNonNull(receiptId));
    }

    public String take() throws InterruptedException {
        return waiting.takeFirst();
    }
}

Performance and ownership cost

End insertion and removal are O(1) queue work aside from lock contention or blocking, with O(N) node storage capped at 47. The cap covers waiting items; worker execution and upstream request retention need separate limits.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use the no-argument constructor when a real queue cap is required.
  • Do not ignore false from offerFirst or offerLast.
  • Do not assume urgent-first ordering guarantees fair service for normal work.

title: Spring Data JPA entity graph for a bounded to-one read
summary: Load a required to-one association with the receipt query instead of discovering an N+1 after mapping begins.
body:
Load a required to-one association with the receipt query instead of discovering an N+1 after mapping begins.

Make the read shape explicit

A receipt detail endpoint returns 47 rows and shows each account name. If mapping touches receipt.account and the association was left lazy, the ORM can issue one root query plus a separate account query for each uncached association. A repository method with an entity graph requests the account in the same read plan. The method remains tenant-scoped. This is a narrow application of fetch-plan design, not a reason to mark every association eager.

Keep pagination away from collection fetches

A to-one graph has at most one account per receipt, so it does not multiply receipt rows. A collection graph is different: joining receipt lines can multiply rows, interfere with page boundaries, or force expensive deduplication. For a list endpoint that needs a collection, page receipt IDs first and fetch details for those bounded IDs in a second query. Page and Slice still need a stable order.

Verify the actual SQL

Run the endpoint against 47 receipts that reference different accounts. Capture statement count and compare it with the query without a graph. Assert the response still contains only the authenticated tenant's receipts. An entity graph chooses fetch shape; it does not add an authorization predicate or guarantee one SQL statement under every provider and mapping.

Implementation contract

interface ReceiptReadRepository extends JpaRepository<ReceiptEntity, UUID> {
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "account")
    List<ReceiptEntity> findTop47ByTenantIdOrderByCreatedAtDescIdDesc(
        UUID tenantId);
}

Cost and verification

A to-one join transfers account columns with each receipt row. That is often cheaper than dozens of round trips, but wider rows can be wasteful when the response does not need account data. Compare SQL and payload size on a representative read.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not use a collection entity graph on a paged query without checking row multiplication and page correctness.
  • Do not assume a graph filters another tenant's rows; keep the tenant predicate.
  • Do not replace SQL inspection with a repository mock.

title: Spring Data JPA Specifications with a mandatory tenant predicate
summary: Compose optional search filters around a tenant condition that callers cannot remove.
body:
Compose optional search filters around a tenant condition that callers cannot remove.

Separate optional filters from mandatory scope

A back-office receipt search accepts an optional status and a date range. The tenant condition is not optional. Build it inside the service from the authenticated identity, then combine user-selected filters with it. A Specification describes a predicate; it does not decide whether a principal may read the tenant. Resolve that decision first through tenant identity checks.

Make the query bounded

Passing an unbounded Pageable does not protect the database. Cap the requested page size, sort by createdAt and id, and decide whether the UI needs a total count. A Slice can omit the count when the UI only needs a next-page flag. An index beginning with tenantId and supporting the chosen filter and order can matter more than the Java predicate syntax.

Test composition, not just each piece

Seed receipts for two tenants with the same status and timestamp. Search with status supplied and absent; both results must stay inside the authenticated tenant. Then test an empty date interval and a malicious tenant ID supplied in request data. The service must ignore that caller-supplied scope. Inspect the generated SQL for repeated joins before adding more Specifications.

Implementation contract

static Specification<ReceiptEntity> visibleReceipts(
        UUID authenticatedTenantId, ReceiptStatus requestedStatus) {
    Specification<ReceiptEntity> tenant = (root, query, builder) ->
        builder.equal(root.get("tenantId"), authenticatedTenantId);
    if (requestedStatus == null) return tenant;
    return tenant.and((root, query, builder) ->
        builder.equal(root.get("status"), requestedStatus));
}

Cost and verification

Predicate composition itself is small. Database work depends on selectivity, indexes, joins, and whether a count query is requested. An optional filter that prevents an index range scan can dominate the endpoint's cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not accept the tenant ID from a request field as an authorization decision.
  • Do not return an unbounded search because the Specification reads cleanly.
  • Do not assume individually tested predicates prove the combined query is tenant-safe.

title: Spring Data JPA Page versus Slice: pay for totals only when needed
summary: A Slice reports whether another window exists without the total-count work a Page may require.
body:
A Slice reports whether another window exists without the total-count work a Page may require.

Match the return type to the screen

An activity feed needs 47 receipts and a next button. It does not display an exact page count. Returning Page asks the repository infrastructure for total metadata and can issue a count query; returning Slice fetches enough rows to determine whether another slice exists. That saves count work, but it does not make the data query free. Use a deliberate count query when an admin report truly needs an exact total.

Use a deterministic order

Ordering only by createdAt is unstable when two receipts share a timestamp. Add id as a tie-breaker, and keep both columns in the query's order. With offset pagination, a new row inserted between requests can still shift later results. For deep scrolling or strong continuation semantics, use a keyset cursor with an index matching the filter and order.

Prove the query budget

Request the first and second slices from a dataset larger than one page; assert hasNext is accurate and IDs do not repeat in the unchanged dataset. Record the SQL. Then request a large offset to observe the database work, and cap page size with input bounds. A Slice is a count-cost choice, not a cure for deep offset scans.

Implementation contract

interface ReceiptFeedRepository extends JpaRepository<ReceiptEntity, UUID> {
    Slice<ReceiptEntity> findByTenantId(
        UUID tenantId, Pageable page);
}

Pageable firstWindow = PageRequest.of(0, 47,
    Sort.by(Sort.Order.desc("createdAt"),
            Sort.Order.desc("id")));

Cost and verification

A Slice typically reads one extra row to determine hasNext. A Page can require a separate count query, especially expensive with joins. Both offset forms may scan or skip increasing work as the requested page number grows.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not request Page totals for a screen that never displays them.
  • Do not sort on a non-unique timestamp alone.
  • Do not describe Slice as keyset pagination; it still uses an offset with Pageable.

title: Spring Data JPA count query for a joined Page
summary: Count distinct parent rows when a filter joins a to-many relationship, and verify the page metadata against real SQL.
body:
Count distinct parent rows when a filter joins a to-many relationship, and verify the page metadata against real SQL.

A joined row is not always one receipt

A receipt with three matching lines can appear three times in a SQL join. If the content query selects distinct receipts but the count query counts joined rows, the UI may claim more receipts than exist. Define the count expression explicitly for a Page query that filters on receipt lines. The example counts distinct receipt IDs and keeps the tenant predicate in both queries.

Know when the count is worth it

Count distinct may require extra sorting or hashing in the database, depending on the plan and index. If the screen only needs a next button, a Slice may avoid the total count; still test the joined content query for duplicates and stable boundaries. For a large report where exact totals matter, benchmark the count separately and consider a dedicated read model rather than hiding the expense in a repository method.

Compare content and total

Seed one receipt with multiple matching lines, one with a single matching line, and a matching receipt in another tenant. The first page must contain two distinct local receipts and report totalElements as two. Run the test against the actual database dialect used in deployment. A unit mock cannot expose a wrong JPQL count or provider-specific pagination behavior.

Implementation contract

@Query(
    value = "select distinct receipt from ReceiptEntity receipt " +
        "join receipt.lines line where receipt.tenantId = :tenantId " +
        "and line.sku = :sku",
    countQuery = "select count(distinct receipt.id) from ReceiptEntity receipt " +
        "join receipt.lines line where receipt.tenantId = :tenantId " +
        "and line.sku = :sku")
Page<ReceiptEntity> findByTenantAndLineSku(
    UUID tenantId, String sku, Pageable page);

Cost and verification

The content query and count query are separate database work. DISTINCT can add memory and sort/hash work; an index on line sku and join keys plus a tenant-selective access path may help, but inspect the actual execution plan.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not count joined rows when the page displays distinct parent entities.
  • Do not forget the tenant predicate in the count query.
  • Do not trust in-memory repository doubles to validate JPQL, SQL plans, or page totals.

title: Spring Data JPA saveAndFlush is a SQL boundary, not a commit
summary: Flush can surface a database constraint error before method return while the surrounding transaction may still roll back.
body:
Flush can surface a database constraint error before method return while the surrounding transaction may still roll back.

Distinguish three events

save places or merges entity state in the persistence context. Flush synchronizes pending changes with the database inside the current transaction. Commit makes the transaction durable and visible according to database isolation. Calling saveAndFlush can force a unique-key rejection earlier, but a later failure still rolls back the flushed row. Transaction ownership remains at the service boundary, not the repository call.

Do not publish on flush

An order acceptance service writes a receipt and an outbox row in one transaction. If it sends a broker message immediately after saveAndFlush, a later rollback can leave a message announcing a receipt that never committed. Persist an outbox obligation in the same database transaction and deliver it later through the relay boundary. A flush also does not make a concurrent transaction see an uncommitted row.

Exercise the rollback path

Save a receipt with a unique tenant and external key, flush it, then throw a test exception before method exit. Assert the row is absent in a new transaction. Repeat with a duplicate key to check when the exception appears for the chosen database and constraint mode. Some constraints are deferred until commit, so do not promise that every violation is caught by flush.

Implementation contract

@Transactional
public UUID accept(ReceiptCommand command) {
    ReceiptEntity receipt = receipts.saveAndFlush(
        ReceiptEntity.from(command));
    outbox.save(OutboxEvent.receiptAccepted(receipt.getId()));
    return receipt.getId();
}

Cost and verification

An explicit flush adds a synchronization point and can reduce batching opportunities. Use it when an earlier database check or generated value is required, not after every save. The transaction still holds resources until commit or rollback.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat saveAndFlush as a durable commit.
  • Do not send an external message after flush and before commit.
  • Do not assume every database constraint is checked before commit.

title: Spring read-only transaction: performance hint, not a write guard
summary: Use readOnly for a read unit of work, but enforce write permissions and invariants elsewhere.
body:
Use readOnly for a read unit of work, but enforce write permissions and invariants elsewhere.

Name the promise accurately

A receipt view service loads a tenant-scoped row and maps it to an immutable response within a read-only transaction. Spring passes the read-only flag to transaction infrastructure; with Hibernate, the chosen flush behavior can skip dirty-check work for a large loaded graph. The flag is not an authorization rule and should not be used as the only defense against a mutation. Proxy invocation still controls whether the annotation is applied.

Keep reads bounded and contained

Return a DTO while the transaction is active rather than exposing a lazy entity to the controller. Pair the read with disabled Open EntityManager in View so a later response serializer cannot silently query the database. A projection may avoid loading an entire entity graph. Inherited Spring Data CRUD reads are commonly configured read-only, while declared query methods and outer service transactions deserve explicit review.

Test what matters

Assert that a denied principal cannot call the write path; do not use a readOnly test as proof of denial. Measure statement count and allocation for a representative read, then inspect the transaction attributes at the service proxy. A database driver or provider may treat read-only differently, so benchmark instead of promising a fixed speedup.

Implementation contract

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public ReceiptView readReceipt(UUID tenantId, UUID receiptId) {
    ReceiptEntity receipt = receipts.findByTenantIdAndId(
        tenantId, receiptId).orElseThrow(ReceiptNotFound::new);
    return new ReceiptView(receipt.getId(), receipt.getTotalMinor());
}

Cost and verification

A read-only hint can reduce flush and dirty-check overhead with some providers. The dominant cost may still be SQL, hydrated columns, and N+1 reads. A read transaction holds a connection until it exits.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not interpret readOnly as a security boundary or universal database write prohibition.
  • Do not return a lazy entity to be serialized after the transaction closes.
  • Do not assume a self-invoked annotated method entered a transaction proxy.

title: Spring Data JPA auditing: record the actor at the write boundary
summary: Populate created-by and modified-by fields from authenticated context without treating audit metadata as access control.
body:
Populate created-by and modified-by fields from authenticated context without treating audit metadata as access control.

Capture actor identity deliberately

A receipt write records who created or last changed it. Enable JPA auditing, attach the auditing listener to the entity, and provide AuditorAware from the current authentication. Store a stable subject identifier, not a display name that changes next month. The audit field answers who the application recorded; it does not prove a caller was authorized. Method security and tenant predicates remain separate.

Define non-request writers

Scheduled jobs, queue consumers and migration programs may have no HTTP security context. Choose an explicit service actor for each path or reject the write; do not silently invent a human identity. An imperative SecurityContextHolder is thread-local, so worker threads need their own authenticated execution context and transaction. Keep the actor in the same transaction as the row so a rollback removes both changes.

Verify the lifecycle

Create and update a receipt through Spring-managed repository methods and assert the two actor fields in a fresh persistence context. Test an unauthenticated write path and a worker job. Bulk JPQL updates bypass ordinary entity listeners, so use a separate audit design for those operations; bulk-update behavior is its own contract.

Implementation contract

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing
class ReceiptAuditConfiguration {
    @Bean AuditorAware<String> currentActor() {
        return () -> Optional.ofNullable(
            SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication())
            .filter(actor -> actor.isAuthenticated()
                && !(actor instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken))
            .map(Authentication::getName);
    }
}

@Entity
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
class ReceiptEntity {
    @Id UUID id;
    @CreatedBy @Column(nullable = false) String createdBy;
    @LastModifiedBy String modifiedBy;
}

Cost and verification

Auditing callbacks write extra columns and inspect caller context on entity changes. The overhead is usually small beside SQL, but bulk imports and high-volume updates need a measured design because entity callbacks may not run.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not treat an audit field as proof of authorization.
  • Do not let a background writer silently record an absent or misleading human actor.
  • Do not expect JPQL bulk updates to invoke entity auditing callbacks.

title: Spring Boot Open EntityManager in View: close the response-time query gap
summary: Disable request-wide persistence access and fetch or project the data needed before the service returns.
body:
Disable request-wide persistence access and fetch or project the data needed before the service returns.

A serializer can become a query caller

A controller returns a JPA entity. After the service transaction ends, JSON serialization touches a lazy association. With Open EntityManager in View enabled, that traversal can issue SQL during response rendering, outside the deliberate service read plan. With it disabled, the missing fetch becomes visible as a lazy-loading failure. Prefer a DTO whose fields were assembled inside a bounded service transaction. A to-one graph or a projection can supply the required fields.

Choose one read boundary

Set spring.jpa.open-in-view=false in application configuration, then identify endpoints that returned entities. Move mapping into the service and make the required associations explicit. Do not respond by turning every relationship eager; that expands unrelated queries and can multiply rows on collections. A read-only service method states intent, while the hint alone does not pick the correct fetch plan.

Test serialization end to end

Run a real HTTP test with SQL statement counting. Assert that serialization performs no unexpected database queries and that the response stays correct after the service transaction closes. An endpoint that needs 47 records should not accidentally make 47 association round trips. Watch connection hold time and response latency before and after the change; disabling Open EntityManager in View exposes assumptions that must be repaired endpoint by endpoint.

Implementation contract

spring.jpa.open-in-view=false

Cost and verification

Closing the request-wide persistence context avoids late SQL and may shorten connection use. Deliberate DTO mapping can add code and additional targeted queries; count those queries instead of assuming the configuration alone improves latency.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not return a JPA entity as an HTTP response and rely on serialization to choose its fetch plan.
  • Do not fix a lazy-loading failure by making every association eager.
  • Do not assume switching the property repairs existing endpoints without response-level tests.

title: Spring Data JPA test: flush and clear before trusting a read
summary: A persistence-context cache can make a repository test pass without proving that the database contains the expected row.
body:
A persistence-context cache can make a repository test pass without proving that the database contains the expected row.

Test the stored state

A repository test saves a receipt, then calls findById in the same persistence context. JPA may hand back the already managed object. That proves little about column mapping, database defaults, or a query predicate. Flush pending SQL, clear the persistence context, then read again. A flush can expose a constraint failure, while the clear forces a later lookup to materialize data from the database. Flush remains different from commit].

Choose the assertion boundary

For a derived tenant query, persist one local receipt and one foreign-tenant receipt, flush and clear, then assert only the local row appears. A unit mock cannot validate JPQL or the actual tenant predicate. For a test of joined page totals], seed multiple matching child rows and assert both content and totalElements after clearing. Keep the dataset small enough to diagnose a failure, but varied enough to expose row multiplication.

Account for rollback

@DataJpaTest normally wraps each test in a transaction and rolls it back. That isolates many repository tests, but it does not prove a commit-time constraint, an after-commit listener, or what another transaction sees. Use a separate committed-boundary test for those contracts. If you inspect SQL counts, reset the counter after setup; fixture inserts otherwise contaminate the measurement.

Implementation contract

@DataJpaTest
class ReceiptTenantQueryTest {
    @Autowired ReceiptRepository receipts;
    @Autowired EntityManager entityManager;

    @Test void excludesOtherTenantAfterDatabaseRoundTrip() {
        receipts.save(ReceiptEntity.forTenant(NORTH_TENANT, "R-47"));
        receipts.save(ReceiptEntity.forTenant(SOUTH_TENANT, "R-47"));
        entityManager.flush();
        entityManager.clear();

        assertThat(receipts.findByTenantId(NORTH_TENANT))
            .extracting(ReceiptEntity::getTenantId)
            .containsExactly(NORTH_TENANT);
    }
}

Cost and verification

Flush adds a database synchronization point; clear discards managed objects and requires another read. That extra work is useful in persistence tests but would be needless ceremony in a plain unit test with no JPA context.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not assert against the same managed entity and call it a database round trip.
  • Do not treat a rolled-back slice test as proof of commit-time behavior.
  • Do not include setup statements in the query budget being measured.

title: Spring Data JPA test against the deployment database dialect
summary: Keep fast repository tests, then run dialect-sensitive SQL and migration cases against the actual database engine.
body:
Keep fast repository tests, then run dialect-sensitive SQL and migration cases against the actual database engine.

An in-memory substitute changes the contract

A query that passes against an embedded database can fail against the deployment engine because of SQL functions, locking, collation, JSON operators, generated columns, or index behavior. @DataJpaTest keeps the persistence slice small, while a database container gives the slice a realistic engine. Disable embedded-database replacement for that test. Container lifecycle] and migration ownership] still need explicit setup.

Select tests by risk

Run ordinary mapping and simple query tests quickly. Put a smaller set of dialect-sensitive cases against the deployment engine: unique constraints, pessimistic locks, case-sensitive comparisons, pagination under joins, and migration compatibility. Compare the engine major version with production. A container image is not proof that production extensions, collation or configuration match; record those differences as test assumptions.

Force a database-specific failure

Insert duplicate tenant and external-reference pairs, assert the database rejects the second write, then verify the transaction outcome. For a locking test, use two independent transactions and bounded timeouts, not two reads inside one test transaction. Inspect the SQL emitted by the fetch plan] and the plan for a bounded page].

Implementation contract

@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class ReceiptRepositoryDialectTest {
    @Container
    @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> database =
        new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17");

    @Autowired ReceiptRepository receipts;
}

Cost and verification

A container adds startup time and memory use. Share an appropriate lifecycle across tests and reserve this path for behavior that depends on the real engine; do not trade away isolation by reusing dirty database state without cleanup.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not infer deployment SQL behavior from an embedded database alone.
  • Do not run two lock participants in the same test transaction.
  • Do not assume an engine version match also matches collation, extensions or schema migrations.

title: Spring Boot HTTP test: client rollback does not own server writes
summary: A real HTTP server handles requests on another thread, so a test-managed transaction cannot be assumed to roll back those writes.
body:
A real HTTP server handles requests on another thread, so a test-managed transaction cannot be assumed to roll back those writes.

Track the thread boundary

A test starts a random-port Spring Boot server and calls POST /receipts. The test method may be annotated @Transactional, but the server processes the request on its own thread and transaction. Rolling back the test thread does not rewind the server's committed receipt. This differs from a repository slice where test and repository usually share the test-managed transaction. Transaction context] is bound to its execution thread.

Own cleanup explicitly

Give each test a unique tenant or receipt key and remove its rows through a controlled cleanup path, or reset an isolated database between tests. Query the database in a fresh transaction after the HTTP response so the assertion sees committed state. A MockMvc test can share more of the test thread, but it does not exercise the network stack; choose it for MVC behavior], not a real port contract.

Test both success and failure

For a command that writes a receipt and outbox event, assert both exist after a successful HTTP response. Then cause a database rejection and assert neither durable row remains. This proves the rollback invariant] through the actual request path. Never rely on a cleanup rollback that runs only in the test thread.

Implementation contract

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureTestRestTemplate
class ReceiptHttpCommitTest {
    @Autowired TestRestTemplate client;
    @Autowired ReceiptRepository receipts;
    String externalKey;

    @Test void acceptedReceiptIsCommitted() {
        externalKey = "receipt-http-" + UUID.randomUUID();
        ResponseEntity<Void> response = client.postForEntity(
            "/receipts", new ReceiptRequest(externalKey, 4700), Void.class);
        assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
        assertThat(receipts.existsByExternalKey(externalKey)).isTrue();
    }

    @AfterEach void removeCommittedFixture() {
        if (externalKey != null)
            receipts.findByExternalKey(externalKey).ifPresent(receipts::delete);
    }
}

Cost and verification

A real server test loads the full context and opens a port. It is slower than a repository or MVC slice, so use it for behavior that crosses HTTP, transaction and persistence boundaries; isolate its committed data deliberately.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect a test-method rollback to undo a server-thread commit.
  • Do not leave committed test rows for later tests to discover.
  • Do not claim a MockMvc-only test proved real HTTP listener behavior.

title: Spring MockMvc security test: run the application filter chain
summary: A controller assertion is not an authorization test unless the request passes through the configured security chain.
body:
A controller assertion is not an authorization test unless the request passes through the configured security chain.

Keep the filter path real

A controller test calls a handler with a mocked principal and gets the expected JSON. That does not show whether the deployed SecurityFilterChain permits the route, checks a bearer token, or rejects a missing tenant claim. Build MockMvc from the application context with security filters active, or use a full-context auto-configured MockMvc. Standalone setup] is useful for mapping logic but needs explicit filter wiring.

Assert a denial matrix

Send an anonymous request, a caller with a valid identity but missing authority, and a caller with authority for the wrong tenant. Assert status and absence of writes for each. A helper that injects a mock JWT can exercise authorization rules, but it skips cryptographic token decoding; use a separate test for the decoder configuration. JWT web-context tests] and filter-chain rules] divide those responsibilities.

Watch the service boundary

A passing HTTP 403 does not prove a scheduled job or message listener is protected. Test method authorization] through a Spring-injected bean as well. For the web test, verify that a rejected request does not call the write service. Avoid mocking the SecurityFilterChain itself; doing so removes the behavior under examination.

Implementation contract

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class ReceiptAuthorizationHttpTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

    @Test void rejectsMissingWriteAuthority() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/receipts")
                .with(jwt().authorities(
                    new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_receipt.read")))
                .with(csrf())
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"externalKey\":\"R-47\",\"minorUnits\":4700}"))
            .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
    }
}

Cost and verification

A full-context MockMvc test starts more beans than a web slice and still avoids a real network port. Keep a small denial matrix here; use focused service tests for detailed tenant and policy permutations.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not bypass the filter chain and call the result an HTTP authorization test.
  • Do not treat a mock JWT as proof of signature or issuer validation.
  • Do not rely only on controller security when non-web callers reach the same service.

title: Spring TestContext cache: keep equivalent tests on one context shape
summary: Profiles, property overrides, bean overrides and test configuration affect whether Spring can reuse an application context.
body:
Profiles, property overrides, bean overrides and test configuration affect whether Spring can reuse an application context.

A cached context has a key

Two integration tests that request equivalent configuration can share one cached ApplicationContext inside a test process. Add a different active profile, a per-class property, or a distinct @MockitoBean override and the cache key may differ; startup work repeats. The cache is process-local, so separate build forks do not share it. Context tests] should prove wiring, not create a fresh application for every assertion.

Consolidate by contract

Group tests that need the same profile, database connection and bean graph. Use explicit fixtures and reset test data between methods instead of changing properties merely to alter a row value. Avoid @DirtiesContext as routine cleanup: it evicts the context and makes later tests pay startup cost again. Never share mutable singleton test state across classes without reset; a fast reused context must still be isolated at the data and mock level.

Measure before restructuring

Enable test-context cache statistics while running the suite and inspect hit, miss and eviction counts. Change one configuration dimension at a time, then rerun the same set. A context cache hit is useful only if the test still covers production-relevant wiring. Container ownership] can add its own lifecycle and property differences.

Implementation contract

@SpringBootTest
@ActiveProfiles("integration")
@Transactional
abstract class ReceiptIntegrationContext {
    @Autowired protected ReceiptRepository receipts;
}

class ReceiptLookupIT extends ReceiptIntegrationContext {
    @Test void tenantQueryDoesNotLeakRows() {
        UUID north = UUID.randomUUID();
        UUID south = UUID.randomUUID();
        receipts.save(ReceiptEntity.forTenant(north, "R-47"));
        receipts.save(ReceiptEntity.forTenant(south, "R-48"));
        assertThat(receipts.findByTenantId(north))
            .extracting(ReceiptEntity::getTenantId)
            .containsExactly(north);
    }
}

Cost and verification

Context startup can dominate a small test suite. Reuse saves startup time and memory, while overly broad contexts increase the cost of each miss. Cache size and build forking limit the benefit; measure suite wall time, not annotation count.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not add per-class profile or property overrides without recognizing the cache-key cost.
  • Do not use @DirtiesContext as a substitute for fixture cleanup.
  • Do not share unreset mutable state just to gain a cache hit.

title: Spring @MockitoBean override: a mock can remove advice from the tested bean
summary: Replace a collaborator for a boundary test, but keep the advised service real when verifying transactions, caching or method security.
body:
Replace a collaborator for a boundary test, but keep the advised service real when verifying transactions, caching or method security.

Choose which bean is under test

@MockitoBean replaces a bean in the Spring test context. The replacement is a Mockito object, not the original advised service. A controller test may safely mock a receipt service while checking request validation and response mapping. A test that claims to verify @Transactional, @Cacheable or @PreAuthorize on that same mocked service is empty: the method body and its advice have been removed. Proxy mechanics] still matter in the real service.

Keep the seam narrow

Mock an external gateway or a downstream collaborator, then invoke the real Spring-managed service when testing service advice. Use a spy only with care: a spy can retain an advised proxy shape, but stubbing and verification around proxies are easy to misunderstand. An integration test with a real repository is stronger evidence for rollback] than verification that a mock repository method was called.

Check the override itself

If several beans share a type, qualify the intended replacement explicitly; a test can fail at context startup or replace an unintended bean. Count distinct override combinations across classes because each can alter context caching]. State in the test name what remains real and what has been substituted.

Implementation contract

@SpringBootTest
class ReceiptServiceAdviceTest {
    @Autowired ReceiptWriteService realService;
    @Autowired ReceiptRepository receipts;
    @MockitoBean PaymentGateway paymentGateway;

    @Test void failedChargeLeavesNoReceipt() {
        String externalKey = "rejected-" + UUID.randomUUID();
        when(paymentGateway.charge(any())).thenThrow(
            new PaymentDeclinedException("declined"));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> realService.accept(
            new ReceiptCommand(externalKey, 4700)))
            .isInstanceOf(PaymentDeclinedException.class);
        assertThat(receipts.existsByExternalKey(externalKey)).isFalse();
    }
}

Cost and verification

A mock keeps the test local and fast, but replacing a bean changes the graph and may create another cached context. A database assertion costs more than mock verification and is warranted when the claim is about committed or rolled-back state.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not mock the service whose transaction or authorization advice you claim to test.
  • Do not assume a Mockito interaction proves durable database state.
  • Do not leave bean selection ambiguous when several candidates share a type.

title: Spring transactional event test: cross an actual commit boundary
summary: An AFTER_COMMIT listener cannot be proved by a test transaction that always rolls back.
body:
An AFTER_COMMIT listener cannot be proved by a test transaction that always rolls back.

The phase is the behavior

A service publishes ReceiptAccepted inside a transaction and an @TransactionalEventListener with AFTER_COMMIT starts follow-up work. A test method annotated @Transactional rolls back by default, so the listener should not run in that test. Verifying only that publishEvent was called does not prove after-commit delivery. Transaction events] separate event publication from phase execution.

Commit in a controlled test

Use TestTransaction to mark the active test transaction for commit and end it, then assert a synchronous listener's observable result. Or run the service without a test-managed transaction and verify committed state in a fresh transaction. Do not send irreversible external traffic from a unit test; substitute the final gateway while keeping the service, transaction manager and listener real. For durable cross-process delivery, an outbox] remains the stronger contract.

Cover rollback too

Invoke the service on a path that throws after publication, and assert the AFTER_COMMIT listener did not perform its action. If the listener is asynchronous, wait on a bounded observable completion signal rather than sleeping a guessed duration. Test both commit and rollback with the same event type so a misplaced plain @EventListener cannot quietly pass.

Implementation contract

@SpringBootTest
@Transactional
class ReceiptCommittedEventTest {
    @Autowired ReceiptWriteService receipts;
    @Autowired ReceiptNotificationProbe probe;

    @Test void notifiesOnlyAfterCommit() {
        receipts.accept(new ReceiptCommand("R-47", 4700));
        assertThat(probe.count()).isZero();
        TestTransaction.flagForCommit();
        TestTransaction.end();
        assertThat(probe.count()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

Cost and verification

A commit test writes durable rows and needs cleanup or isolated data. It is slower than a publisher mock but exercises the phase that matters. An asynchronous listener adds a scheduling boundary and needs bounded synchronization.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not expect AFTER_COMMIT to fire after a test transaction rolls back.
  • Do not equate publishEvent invocation with listener completion.
  • Do not use an unbounded sleep to wait for asynchronous delivery.

title: Spring scheduled worker test: inject a clock and call the work once
summary: Test a due-time rule without waiting for a real scheduler tick or relying on wall-clock races.
body:
Test a due-time rule without waiting for a real scheduler tick or relying on wall-clock races.

Separate trigger from work

@Scheduled decides when to call a method. A reminder worker decides which due rows to claim and how many to process. Put that decision in a callable service with an injected Clock; keep the scheduled adapter small. A test can advance a fixed clock and call one work cycle directly. The scheduled outbox pattern] still needs database ownership rules across replicas.

Make time a precise input

At 09:47 UTC, a reminder due exactly at 09:47 should be included if the contract says dueAt less than or equal to now. Seed one row just before, one equal, and one after the boundary. Assert a bounded batch of 47 and the resulting state. Do not use Thread.sleep or depend on the CI machine timezone. Test shutdown and draining] separately because a fixed clock does not exercise scheduler lifecycle.

Keep concurrency in another test

A direct call proves selection logic, not that two application replicas cannot claim the same row. Use an integration test with two independent workers and a real database lock or claim update for that invariant; poller integration tests] cover it. Capture failures as retryable state rather than letting a scheduled method's exception lose a work item.

Implementation contract

final class ReminderWorker {
    private final Clock clock;
    private final ReminderStore reminders;

    ReminderWorker(Clock clock, ReminderStore reminders) {
        this.clock = clock;
        this.reminders = reminders;
    }

    int runOneCycle() {
        return reminders.claimDueBeforeOrAt(clock.instant(), 47).size();
    }
}

class ReminderWorkerClockTest {
    @Test void usesFixedCutoff() {
        Instant cutoff = Instant.parse("2026-10-05T09:47:00Z");
        ReminderStore store = mock(ReminderStore.class);
        when(store.claimDueBeforeOrAt(cutoff, 47)).thenReturn(List.of());
        Clock fixed = Clock.fixed(cutoff, ZoneOffset.UTC);
        assertThat(new ReminderWorker(fixed, store).runOneCycle()).isZero();
        verify(store).claimDueBeforeOrAt(cutoff, 47);
    }
}

Cost and verification

A fixed clock removes waiting and makes boundary tests fast. It does not replace a database concurrency test or a scheduler lifecycle test; those cost more because they exercise real threads and storage ownership.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not sleep until a scheduled tick in a unit test.
  • Do not let system timezone decide a UTC due-time assertion.
  • Do not mistake a single-worker fixed-clock test for multi-replica claim safety.

title: Spring BeanFactoryPostProcessor: inspect definitions before instances exist
summary: A bean-factory post-processor works on registration metadata before ordinary application beans are created.
body:
A bean-factory post-processor works on registration metadata before ordinary application beans are created.

The definition is the input

A receipt signer must be one shared instance because it owns a limited key handle. At container startup, a BeanFactoryPostProcessor can inspect the signer definition and reject a non-singleton scope before the application serves traffic. It operates on bean definitions, not the signer object. Scope choice] and constructor wiring] remain the ordinary first options; use a post-processor when one policy spans registrations you do not own.

Do not instantiate during definition work

Calling getBean inside the post-processor constructs an object before normal post-processing has finished. That object may miss proxy advice, property injection, or another extension step. The static @Bean method in the example lets the container register the post-processor without first creating its configuration object. BeanPostProcessor] works later on instances and has a different lifecycle risk.

Test failure at refresh

Register a prototype receiptSigner in a small application context and require refresh to fail with the scope message. Repeat with the singleton definition and assert one constructed signer. A unit call to the post-processor function can test the predicate, but only a context refresh proves Spring discovered it at the intended phase. Avoid using this hook for ordinary request validation or database access.

Implementation contract

@Configuration
class ReceiptDefinitionPolicy {
    @Bean
    static BeanFactoryPostProcessor signerScopeGuard() {
        return factory -> {
            BeanDefinition signer =
                factory.getBeanDefinition("receiptSigner");
            if (!signer.isSingleton()) {
                throw new IllegalStateException(
                    "receiptSigner must use singleton scope");
            }
        };
    }
}

Cost and verification

The policy runs during context creation, so a failure blocks startup rather than a later request. A metadata scan is cheap; calling getBean here can trigger broad, premature initialization and make startup ordering hard to reason about.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not call getBean from definition processing to inspect an application object.
  • Do not declare a stateful non-static factory method for an early post-processor without understanding initialization order.
  • Do not use container metadata hooks when a direct bean definition or constructor check expresses the rule.

title: Spring BeanPostProcessor: instance callbacks and the early-bean trap
summary: A bean post-processor sees created instances, but it and its direct dependencies are initialized before ordinary proxy processing is complete.
body:
A bean post-processor sees created instances, but it and its direct dependencies are initialized before ordinary proxy processing is complete.

Operate on instances

A BeanPostProcessor can inspect or replace a freshly initialized connector. The receipt connector policy below runs after initialization and leaves the same object in the container. Unlike definition processing], this callback has an instance to inspect. Use it sparingly: ordinary validation belongs in a constructor or initialization method when only one class is affected.

Keep the processor's dependency graph small

The container creates post-processors early so they can advise later beans. If a processor injects an application service, that service can also be instantiated early and miss transaction, cache or method-security proxying. Register the processor with a static @Bean method and avoid pulling runtime services into its constructor. Proxy boundaries] already require care; early initialization can remove the proxy entirely.

Check both identity and advice

Start a context with the connector and an advised service. Verify the processor saw the connector, then call the advised service through the injected bean and assert its transaction or authorization advice still runs. A log line that says a bean was processed is not proof the rest of the application kept its proxies. If the callback wraps a bean, preserve its exposed interface and inspect identity-sensitive consumers.

Implementation contract

@Configuration
class ReceiptConnectorPolicy {
    @Bean
    static BeanPostProcessor connectorGuard() {
        return new BeanPostProcessor() {
            @Override
            public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(
                    Object candidate, String registeredName) {
                if (candidate instanceof ReceiptConnector connector) {
                    connector.verifyStartupPolicy();
                }
                return candidate;
            }
        };
    }
}

Cost and verification

A processor callback can run for many bean instances, so keep its type check and validation bounded. The larger risk is startup side effects and early dependencies that lose advice, not the nanoseconds of the instanceof test.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not inject a broad service graph into an early BeanPostProcessor.
  • Do not assume a post-processed bean kept every expected AOP proxy without a context test.
  • Do not replace an object with a wrapper that drops its interface or lifecycle contract.
