title: Embedding migrations: keep query and document vectors in one space
summary: Version embedding models, dimensions and normalization rules as one index contract, then cut over only after query parity checks.
body:
Version embedding models, dimensions and normalization rules as one index contract, then cut over only after query parity checks.

Record the vector contract

An embedding is meaningful only relative to the model and preprocessing that produced it. Store model ID, revision, vector dimension, distance metric, text normalization and any title-prefix policy beside each index generation. A query vector from model B must not be compared to document vectors from model A merely because both have 768 coordinates. Even identical dimensions do not imply shared geometry. Embedding diagnostics belong before promotion.

Build a separate generation

Create a new index rather than overwriting old vectors in place. Re-embed every active, permitted document revision; index tombstones and access metadata at the same time. Reject vectors with non-finite values, wrong dimensions or an empty source span. Keep the old index available while the new one is validated. If the model changes its tokenizer or input prefix, capture that too; a silent query-side change can look like an index outage.

Compare on the same judgments

Run a frozen query set against old and candidate indexes with the same permission snapshot. Report recall at the candidate cutoff, first relevant rank, exact-ID failures and latency by query family. A higher average similarity is not evidence of better retrieval because score scales move with models. Inspect newly missed answer-bearing passages, especially minority languages and long documents. Release gates turn this comparison into a decision.

Switch and recover

Point readers to one versioned alias only after the candidate is complete and validated. Include the generation ID in result metadata and cache keys. Keep the previous alias target for a rollback window, then retire it under the corpus deletion policy. A rollback must restore matching query encoder and document index together. A mixed pair can return plausible neighbors while quietly losing relevant evidence.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import isfinite

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class VectorContract:
    model_revision: str
    dimensions: int
    metric: str

def accept_vector(values: list[float], query_contract: VectorContract,
                  index_contract: VectorContract) -> tuple[float, ...]:
    if query_contract != index_contract:
        raise ValueError("query and index vector contracts differ")
    if len(values) != index_contract.dimensions or not all(map(isfinite, values)):
        raise ValueError("invalid vector")
    return tuple(values)

active = VectorContract("receipt-embed-r8", 3, "cosine")
assert accept_vector([0.2, 0.4, 0.8], active, active) == (0.2, 0.4, 0.8)
try:
    accept_vector([0.2, 0.4, 0.8], VectorContract("receipt-embed-r9", 3, "cosine"), active)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("mixed embedding generations were accepted")

Performance and operating cost

Validating one d-dimensional vector takes O(d) time and O(d) output space here. Re-embedding N passages costs N model calls plus index construction and temporarily doubles vector storage during overlap. Migration planning should include that peak, query encoder rollout, cache invalidation and a measured rollback window.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming equal vector dimensions imply compatible embedding spaces.
  • Replacing document vectors before deploying the matching query encoder.
  • Comparing raw similarity scores across model versions as if they shared a scale.
  • Deleting the previous generation before rollback and permission tests pass.

Validation drill

Take 83 judged queries with identifier, paraphrase and multilingual slices. Build a candidate index under a new model revision, verify dimension and access metadata, then record recall and latency deltas before moving the alias.

title: Filtered vector search: measure ANN recall inside the permitted set
summary: Approximate nearest-neighbor speed is useful only if access filters and candidate limits still surface relevant permitted passages.
body:
Approximate nearest-neighbor speed is useful only if access filters and candidate limits still surface relevant permitted passages.

Name the reference set

Approximate nearest-neighbor search trades some exact-neighbor recall for latency and memory behavior. Evaluate it against an exact search over the same eligible documents, query embedding and distance metric. If the exact baseline includes another tenant's records, its recall number is meaningless for a permission-filtered product. Apply tenant, revision and document-state filters before ranking, or use an index layout whose filtering semantics are proven. Access policy is a hard eligibility rule.

Test selective filters

A broad tenant with millions of passages and a small tenant with 47 passages may exercise different search paths. Some engines prefilter the graph; others use postfiltering or adaptive methods. Postfiltering the global top K can return zero permitted results even when a perfect permitted answer exists just outside K. Ask the engine what it actually does, then test the behavior. A filter that removes forbidden hits after they have already entered prompt assembly is too late.

Separate relevance from system recall

Measure exact top-K overlap to quantify approximation loss, then judge whether answer-bearing passages remain in the candidate pool. A candidate can differ from the exact top K yet still answer the question; conversely, excellent vector overlap can miss a literal error code. Compare by tenant size, filter selectivity, language and document length. Hybrid retrieval can recover some exact-token cases but is not a repair for access leakage.

Set a latency budget with an exit

Tune search breadth and K on a fixed judged set while measuring p50 and p95 latency. Keep a limit on vector comparisons, rerank candidates and total response time. When filtered ANN returns too few candidates, a bounded exact fallback may be reasonable for a small eligible set. Do not retry forever with a larger global K: that raises cost and can still miss the allowed island. Record when fallback runs, so an index regression is not hidden by the safety net.

Worked contract

def recall_at_k(returned_ids: list[str], exact_ids: list[str], k: int) -> float:
    if k < 1 or len(exact_ids) < k:
        raise ValueError("invalid recall cutoff")
    permitted_reference = set(exact_ids[:k])
    return len(set(returned_ids[:k]) & permitted_reference) / k

exact_permitted = ["west-r8-p4", "west-r8-p9", "west-r8-p2"]
ann_permitted = ["west-r8-p4", "west-r8-p2", "west-r8-p11"]
assert recall_at_k(ann_permitted, exact_permitted, 3) == 2 / 3

def allowed_candidates(candidates: list[dict], tenant_id: str) -> list[dict]:
    return [passage for passage in candidates if passage["tenant_id"] == tenant_id
            and passage["state"] == "active"]

assert allowed_candidates([{"tenant_id": "west", "state": "active"},
                           {"tenant_id": "east", "state": "active"}], "west") == [
                               {"tenant_id": "west", "state": "active"}]

Performance and operating cost

An exact scan costs O(Nd) distance work for N eligible d-dimensional vectors; an ANN index aims to reduce query work but adds build time, memory and tuning. The filter check shown costs O(K) over returned candidates and does not replace index-side authorization. Report recall and latency together at the production filter distribution.

Common Mistakes

  • Computing ANN recall against a reference set that includes forbidden documents.
  • Postfiltering only the global top K and calling an empty result a true no-answer.
  • Treating vector-neighbor overlap as answer-bearing passage recall.
  • Using an unbounded retry or exact fallback on a large tenant.

Validation drill

Create a large and a small tenant with overlapping language. Compare exact and ANN top-8 within each tenant, then revoke one document and prove it cannot appear in candidates, reranker inputs or citations.

title: Hybrid retrieval: fuse exact terms and semantic candidates by rank
summary: Run lexical and vector retrieval over the same permitted revision set, then fuse ranks without pretending their raw scores are comparable.
body:
Run lexical and vector retrieval over the same permitted revision set, then fuse ranks without pretending their raw scores are comparable.

Keep both candidate paths honest

A user may ask for a named status code and its meaning in different words. Keyword search protects exact strings, version tags and identifiers; dense retrieval helps with paraphrases. Each leg must apply the same tenant, document-state and revision constraints before its results reach fusion. If one leg indexes stale policy or ignores a revocation, its high rank cannot be made safe by later scoring. Filtered ANN tests the semantic leg independently.

Fuse ranks, then inspect the result

Reciprocal rank fusion awards a candidate one divided by a rank constant plus its position in each list. A passage appearing in both lists receives contributions from both. This avoids adding an unbounded keyword score to a cosine similarity on a different scale. It discards score margins, so a clear lexical winner and a weak lexical hit can be treated as neighboring ranks. Compare fusion against each leg on judged questions, particularly exact-ID queries.

Preserve identity while deduplicating

The key is a stable passage identity tied to document revision, not only display text. Two copied sections from different policies may have identical wording but different owners or effective dates. Deduplicate the same passage returned by both legs, then group near-duplicates for context selection rather than erasing provenance. Evidence packing decides how many passages from one document belong in the prompt.

Tune the window, not the formula alone

Each leg contributes only the candidates it retrieved. A fusion constant cannot recover a passage absent from both top-K lists. Measure candidate recall while changing lexical depth, vector depth and fusion constant; track p95 latency and reranker input size. If exact identifiers are mandatory, apply a hard exact-match gate before or after fusion according to the query contract, not an arbitrary score threshold on the fused rank.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def reciprocal_rank_fusion(lexical: list[str], semantic: list[str],
                           rank_constant: int = 37) -> list[str]:
    if rank_constant < 1:
        raise ValueError("rank constant must be positive")
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for ranking in (lexical, semantic):
        for position, passage_id in enumerate(dict.fromkeys(ranking), start=1):
            scores[passage_id] += 1 / (rank_constant + position)
    return sorted(scores, key=lambda passage_id: (-scores[passage_id], passage_id))

keyword_hits = ["policy-r8-ax47", "policy-r8-refunds", "guide-r3"]
vector_hits = ["policy-r8-refunds", "policy-r8-ax47", "manual-r6"]
ranking = reciprocal_rank_fusion(keyword_hits, vector_hits)
assert ranking[:2] == ["policy-r8-ax47", "policy-r8-refunds"]
assert len(ranking) == 4

Performance and operating cost

Fusion scans L + V ranked candidates and stores at most their union, so expected O(L + V) score work and O(U) memory, followed by O(U log U) sorting. It adds almost no model cost, while running two retrieval legs may double search traffic. Bound both depths and measure whether extra recall justifies their latency.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding raw keyword and vector scores without a tested normalization rule.
  • Fusing candidates from different permission or index generations.
  • Deduplicating by text and losing document ownership or revision.
  • Tuning the fusion constant while the needed passage never enters either list.

Validation drill

Judge 63 queries split across exact identifiers, paraphrases and mixed language. Compare keyword-only, vector-only and fused recall at 12; record the extra latency and every newly missed exact-token query.

title: Reranking: spend model budget on a bounded candidate window
summary: Rerank a diverse, permitted candidate set and measure whether the added cost moves answer-bearing passages into view.
body:
Rerank a diverse, permitted candidate set and measure whether the added cost moves answer-bearing passages into view.

Find before sorting

A reranker can reorder candidates; it cannot recover an answer omitted by first-stage search. Freeze a judged set and measure candidate recall at the exact window passed to the reranker. Include identifiers, paraphrases, negative questions and long documents. If recall is weak, repair routing before paying for a bigger ranker. Hybrid retrieval can supply a stronger starting window.

Budget the input

Set a maximum candidate count, passage length and total scoring budget. A 47-passage window at 1,400 tokens each can cost more than the final answer. Truncate at sentence or section boundaries while retaining title and source identity. Test long queries and the largest eligible tenant. On timeout, fall back to first-stage order with a degraded-mode signal; do not disguise a timeout as no evidence.

Keep eligibility outside the model

Filter access, active revision and deletion state before scoring. A reranker should never see forbidden material, even if final selection would discard it. A high relevance score says nothing about truth, freshness or permission. Winning passages still need claim support checks.

Measure rank movement

Track first relevant rank, context-cutoff recall and answer support with and without reranking. Report by query family; a ranker may improve paraphrases while pushing exact IDs down. Retain candidate IDs, truncation details and model revision so regressions can be reproduced.

Worked contract

def bounded_rerank_window(candidates: list[dict], tenant_id: str,
                          limit: int = 12) -> list[dict]:
    if limit < 1:
        raise ValueError("candidate limit must be positive")
    selected, seen = [], set()
    for passage in candidates:
        if passage["tenant_id"] != tenant_id or passage["state"] != "active":
            continue
        identity = (passage["document_id"], passage["revision_id"], passage["span_id"])
        if identity not in seen:
            selected.append(passage)
            seen.add(identity)
        if len(selected) == limit:
            break
    return selected

candidate = {"tenant_id": "west", "state": "active", "document_id": "policy",
             "revision_id": "r8", "span_id": "p4"}
assert bounded_rerank_window([candidate, candidate, {**candidate, "tenant_id": "east"}],
                             "west", 2) == [candidate]

Performance and operating cost

Selecting K eligible passages from N candidates takes O(N) time and O(K) space. Pairwise reranking costs roughly one model evaluation per candidate, so compute grows with K and passage length. Cap both, measure p95, and separate first-stage recall from reranker gain.

Common Mistakes

  • Increasing the reranker window when the answer is absent from all first-stage hits.
  • Scoring a forbidden passage before access filtering.
  • Truncating away the sentence that carries the answer.
  • Calling a timeout fallback a successful rerank.

Validation drill

Use 91 judged questions. Compare first-stage and reranked first relevant rank at windows of 8, 16 and 32; record p95 latency and exact-ID regressions before choosing a window.

title: Context packing: retain independent evidence under a token cap
summary: Select passages by answer coverage, document diversity and provenance instead of filling the prompt with near-duplicates.
body:
Select passages by answer coverage, document diversity and provenance instead of filling the prompt with near-duplicates.

Reserve the evidence budget

Allocate tokens for instructions, question, response and citations before retrieved text. Each passage needs title, revision, section and citation identity. A long high-ranked section can crowd out a short exception that changes the answer. Pack by paragraphs or table rows, not a cut through a condition. Chunk boundaries determine what can be selected intact.

Prevent one revision from monopolizing context

Near-duplicate chunks often rank together. Limit repeated passages from one revision unless the question needs several clauses. Prefer a second independent source when it adds a missing fact, but do not force diversity at the cost of the sole answer-bearing span. Deduplicate the same passage identity across lexical and vector legs; copied text in separate revisions retains separate provenance.

Preserve contradictions

When permitted sources disagree, packing must not hide the newer statement just because it ranked lower. Include effective dates and revision labels so the answer can explain the conflict or abstain. Test exceptions, date boundaries and footnotes. Packet quality is whether it contains every fact needed, not its average similarity score.

Inspect the packet actually sent

Store candidate IDs, included IDs, exclusions and token counts. Compare generated claims with this exact packet, not the entire index. If support is absent, a fluent answer still fails. Claim checks decide whether to cite, revise or abstain.

Worked contract

def pack_passages(candidates: list[dict], token_budget: int,
                  per_revision_limit: int = 2) -> list[dict]:
    if token_budget < 1 or per_revision_limit < 1:
        raise ValueError("positive limits required")
    selected, spent, per_revision = [], 0, {}
    for passage in candidates:
        revision = (passage["document_id"], passage["revision_id"])
        if per_revision.get(revision, 0) >= per_revision_limit:
            continue
        if spent + passage["tokens"] > token_budget:
            continue
        selected.append(passage)
        spent += passage["tokens"]
        per_revision[revision] = per_revision.get(revision, 0) + 1
    return selected

ranked = [{"document_id": "policy", "revision_id": "r8", "tokens": 33},
          {"document_id": "policy", "revision_id": "r8", "tokens": 41},
          {"document_id": "faq", "revision_id": "r3", "tokens": 29}]
packet = pack_passages(ranked, 67, 1)
assert len(packet) == 2 and sum(p["tokens"] for p in packet) == 62

Performance and operating cost

This bounded pass costs O(K) time and O(D) counters for K candidates and D revisions. Tokenization and model context cost dominate. Greedy packing can miss a better combination; add measured coverage-aware selection only if judged queries expose that ceiling.

Common Mistakes

  • Spending the whole context window on passages and leaving no response budget.
  • Suppressing a newer contradiction because its score is lower.
  • Confusing duplicate text with duplicate source identity.
  • Citing a passage that was retrieved but not included in the final packet.

Validation drill

For 37 questions, label required facts and revisions. Pack under a 540-token evidence budget and measure how often all facts survive, especially exceptions and conflicts.

title: Claim-level citations: verify each answer against its passage
summary: Bind each factual claim to a permitted, current passage and reject citations that are merely related to the topic.
body:
Bind each factual claim to a permitted, current passage and reject citations that are merely related to the topic.

Split answers into testable claims

‘Refunds arrive in 47 hours and managers can extend the window’ contains two claims. Each needs support from the selected evidence packet. A policy-title citation is too broad when its quoted span states only the first clause. Keep claim and passage IDs together. Distinguish direct support, contradiction, insufficient evidence and facts supplied by the user. Abstention is correct when a required claim lacks support.

Check passage identity

The cited span must belong to an active permitted revision and have been included in the generator context. Resolve it to a readable page or section. A valid-looking ID for a retired revision is insufficient. Extraction provenance supplies the source location.

Test support rather than overlap

A passage about refund windows may omit the 47-hour value. ‘Up to 47 hours’ does not justify ‘always within 47 hours.’ Numbers, negation, dates and exceptions deserve explicit checks. An entailment model can triage cases, but its confidence alone does not prove support; keep a human-judged sample.

Fail clearly

Remove or qualify unsupported claims and regenerate from the same permitted packet. If the core question remains unanswered, state which part cannot be verified. Log the unsupported claim and citation ID without putting private source text in public telemetry. Count unsupported-claim rate separately from retrieval misses.

Worked contract

def validate_claim_citations(claims: list[dict], packet_ids: set[str],
                             active_ids: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    failures = []
    for claim in claims:
        cited = set(claim["citations"])
        if not cited or not cited <= packet_ids or not cited <= active_ids:
            failures.append(claim["claim_id"])
        elif claim["support"] != "supported":
            failures.append(claim["claim_id"])
    return failures

claims = [{"claim_id": "hours", "citations": ["policy-r8-p4"], "support": "supported"},
          {"claim_id": "extension", "citations": ["policy-r8-p4"], "support": "insufficient"}]
assert validate_claim_citations(claims, {"policy-r8-p4"}, {"policy-r8-p4"}) == ["extension"]

Performance and operating cost

Identity checking takes O(C + E) expected time for C claims and E citation edges, with O(C) failure output. Semantic support review is costlier and may need model calls or human adjudication. Sample high-impact claims first; do not hide unsupported claims in an average answer score.

Common Mistakes

  • Accepting a citation because its document title matches the topic.
  • Using a retired passage or one absent from the final context packet.
  • Treating ‘up to’ and ‘always’ as equivalent.
  • Reporting retrieval recall as proof of answer support.

Validation drill

Write 29 answers with a numeric claim, an exception and a distractor citation each. Mark support from the exact packet and count unsupported claims that survive automation.

title: Retrieval caches and conversation turns: recheck access every time
summary: Prevent cached evidence and follow-up questions from crossing tenant, principal or document-revision boundaries.
body:
Prevent cached evidence and follow-up questions from crossing tenant, principal or document-revision boundaries.

Key on authorization context

A cache entry keyed by query text alone is unsafe. Include tenant, principal or authorization scope, policy version, corpus generation, query normalization and retrieval configuration. Even then, a revoked document can invalidate an old answer before TTL expires. Revalidate cached passage IDs against current access and deletion state, or invalidate them on revocation. Document lifecycle defines the invalidation event.

Carry resolved conversation state

A follow-up like ‘What about the other case?’ needs a specific, permitted antecedent. Store document and revision IDs, not an indiscriminate replay of previous passages. Recheck access before reuse. If two antecedents fit, ask for clarification. A conversation ID is not an authorization token; shared browser sessions and role changes expose that mistake.

Separate candidate and answer caches

Cached candidates depend on index generation, access scope and search configuration. A cached final answer also depends on the prompt, model, evidence packet and answer policy. Give these caches separate lifetimes. Never serve a final answer whose citations no longer resolve, and avoid storing user secrets in a shared cache.

Prove revocation works

Test identical query text from two tenants, role change mid-session, document deletion and index swap. Each must produce only a newly permitted answer or an explicit no-answer. Log cache hit, authorization recheck and corpus generation without private text in metric labels. Index swaps need matching invalidation.

Worked contract

from hashlib import sha256

def retrieval_cache_key(tenant_id: str, principal_id: str, policy_revision: str,
                        corpus_generation: str, query: str) -> str:
    fields = (tenant_id, principal_id, policy_revision, corpus_generation,
              " ".join(query.casefold().split()))
    if any(not field for field in fields):
        raise ValueError("incomplete cache scope")
    return sha256("\x1f".join(fields).encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()

base = retrieval_cache_key("west", "analyst-47", "acl-r8", "index-r8", " AX-47 status ")
assert base != retrieval_cache_key("east", "analyst-47", "acl-r8", "index-r8", "AX-47 status")
assert base != retrieval_cache_key("west", "analyst-47", "acl-r9", "index-r8", "AX-47 status")

Performance and operating cost

Key construction is O(q) for query length q. Rechecking K cached passage IDs is O(K) plus authorization lookup cost. That recheck adds latency but prevents stale permissions from leaking. If it becomes expensive, use a policy-version or revocation index with a measured freshness bound.

Common Mistakes

  • Caching by query text without tenant or principal scope.
  • Assuming TTL handles emergency revocation.
  • Using previous-turn passages after the user's role changes.
  • Serving a cached answer after its citations disappear.

Validation drill

Run the same 19 questions as two principals with different access. Revoke a document after a warm cache and prove no old passage, claim or citation appears next.

title: Retrieval release gates: evaluate slices before changing an index
summary: Promote a retriever only after judged recall, support, access and latency checks pass for distinct query families.
body:
Promote a retriever only after judged recall, support, access and latency checks pass for distinct query families.

Freeze the comparison

Store query, permitted corpus snapshot, expected answer-bearing passage IDs, acceptable abstention and query family. Run current and candidate versions against the same access snapshot. Keep exact IDs, paraphrases, multilingual queries, long documents, stale revisions and no-answer cases separate. A global average can rise while one small tenant loses its only correct passage. Retrieval and answer quality remain separate measurements.

Measure decisions

For each query, measure answer-bearing candidate recall, required-fact survival in the final packet, first relevant rank and unsupported answer claims. Record p95 latency and forbidden-passage exposure; the latter must stay at zero. Some questions have no answer, so abstention matters. Compare equal cutoffs and token budgets across versions.

Set slice floors before testing

Write thresholds before seeing candidate results. A release may require no access violations, no decline in exact-ID recall and a bounded p95 increase while accepting a defined paraphrase improvement. Such thresholds are product policies, not universal constants. Inspect every newly failed query and retain it for regression work.

Canary and recover

After offline gates pass, send a small permitted traffic slice to the candidate alias and watch latency, empty-result rate and citation resolution before widening. Record encoder, extraction, corpus, filter and ranker revisions. Rollback query encoder and index alias together. Embedding migrations fail quietly when only one half is reverted.

Worked contract

def release_decision(current: dict, candidate: dict) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    failures = []
    if candidate["access_violations"] != 0:
        failures.append("access violation")
    if candidate["exact_id_recall"] < current["exact_id_recall"]:
        failures.append("exact-ID recall regression")
    if candidate["answer_support"] < current["answer_support"]:
        failures.append("answer support regression")
    if candidate["p95_ms"] > current["p95_ms"] + 47:
        failures.append("latency budget exceeded")
    return not failures, failures

baseline = {"access_violations": 0, "exact_id_recall": .94,
            "answer_support": .91, "p95_ms": 168}
candidate = {"access_violations": 0, "exact_id_recall": .95,
             "answer_support": .92, "p95_ms": 199}
assert release_decision(baseline, candidate) == (True, [])
assert release_decision(baseline, {**candidate, "access_violations": 1})[0] is False

Performance and operating cost

Evaluation of Q queries and K candidates costs at least O(QK) identity work, plus search, rerank and answer calls. Keep a small smoke set for each change and a broader judged set before promotion. The 47 ms allowance in this example is product-specific; choose a measured budget for the actual service.

Common Mistakes

  • Promoting on one average while an important tenant slice regresses.
  • Changing the judged corpus between baseline and candidate runs.
  • Reporting answer quality without candidate recall or access exposure.
  • Rolling back the index while leaving the new query encoder active.

Validation drill

Build 120 judged questions across six slices. Compare two generations at identical top-12 and 600-token packet limits, list newly failed queries and record the rollback target.

title: Project: ship a permission-aware hybrid retrieval release gate
summary: Build a small corpus, two search legs, rank fusion, evidence packing and a failing release gate with reproducible checks.
body:
Build a small corpus, two search legs, rank fusion, evidence packing and a failing release gate with reproducible checks.

Define the corpus and questions

Create 83 passages from policy revisions, case notes and help articles. Give every passage an immutable ID, tenant, document revision, state and source location. Add two tenants, one revoked passage, duplicated wording in two revisions and one table-like exception. Write 47 judged questions across exact IDs, paraphrases, mixed intent, no-answer and conflicting-revision cases. Keep judgments outside the search implementation.

Implement a transparent baseline

Start with a simple token-based lexical ranker and a precomputed semantic ranking supplied as data. Both legs must filter tenant and active state before fusion. Use rank fusion with stable passage identity; show each leg's rank and the final order for a query. Add a bounded context packet and store included IDs. This project tests retrieval logic without requiring paid model calls.

Break it deliberately

Remove an access filter from one leg and demonstrate that the test fails before a private passage reaches fusion. Swap in a stale revision and verify rejection. Make a candidate absent from both lists and show that reranking cannot recover it. Generate one unsupported numeric claim and prove citation validation catches it. Each failure should name its query and passage IDs.

Gate the release

Compare baseline and candidate on answer-bearing recall at 12, first relevant rank, forbidden exposures, packet fact coverage and p95 local query latency. Write a release decision that refuses any exposure or exact-ID regression. Package corpus manifest, judgment set, executable checks, measured output and rollback target. A screenshot of a plausible answer is not completion evidence.

Worked contract

def release_gate(rows: list[dict]) -> dict[str, object]:
    if not rows:
        raise ValueError("judged queries required")
    exposed = [row["query_id"] for row in rows if row["forbidden_seen"]]
    missed = [row["query_id"] for row in rows
              if row["exact_id_query"] and not row["answer_passage_found"]]
    return {"promote": not (exposed or missed), "exposed": exposed,
            "missed_exact_ids": missed}

checks = [{"query_id": "q-47", "forbidden_seen": False,
           "exact_id_query": True, "answer_passage_found": True},
          {"query_id": "q-63", "forbidden_seen": True,
           "exact_id_query": False, "answer_passage_found": True}]
assert release_gate(checks) == {"promote": False, "exposed": ["q-63"],
                                "missed_exact_ids": []}

Performance and operating cost

For Q judged rows the gate scans O(Q) time and uses O(Q) failure space. Building lexical rankings naively across N passages costs O(QN) token comparisons; production indexes avoid that scan. Keep this project small enough to inspect each failure, then scale only after the contracts are proved.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a high fused rank as permission to show a passage.
  • Judging only answers and omitting candidate recall.
  • Testing the same queries used to hand-tune every threshold without a held-out slice.
  • Calling the project complete before deletion and rollback checks pass.

Validation drill

Deliver a repository folder with the 83-passage manifest, 47 questions, runnable gate, failure log and a one-page promotion decision. Revoke one passage after building the index and rerun all checks.

title: Multi-hop retrieval: build evidence chains with bounded searches
summary: Answer questions whose facts sit in separate documents without letting a plausible first hit become an unsupported final answer.
body:
Answer questions whose facts sit in separate documents without letting a plausible first hit become an unsupported final answer.

Represent the missing link

A multi-hop question needs two or more supported joins. A support ticket may name shipment SH-47, while the carrier notice names only its dispatch batch. First retrieve the ticket and extract its batch ID. Then search that exact ID in the permitted carrier corpus. Keep each edge as a tuple of source passage, extracted entity, target passage and match rule. The final answer must cite both ends of the join. Claim support should reject a chain whose second edge is only a semantic resemblance.

Search in a fixed budget

Give each hop its own candidate limit, time limit and permission filter. The planner can propose the next lookup, but application code should validate the proposed identifier against the preceding passage before executing it. Stop after a bounded number of hops; a loop between two documents is a failed search, not deeper reasoning. If the first document names two batches, branch into two explicit chains and keep their evidence separate until a source disambiguates them.

Preserve uncertainty

The chain may support that SH-47 belongs to batch BX-83 and that BX-83 was delayed. It does not prove the customer's delivery date changed unless a permitted source states that consequence. Distinguish a missing edge from a contradictory edge. Missing means the lookup exhausted its budget; contradictory means two eligible sources disagree and require revision or time resolution. Abstention is the correct output when a required edge has no evidence.

Evaluate the joins

Judgments should name the expected intermediate entity and answer-bearing passages, not only the answer text. Record success at hop one, success at hop two, chain precision and final claim support independently. A fluent answer can hide a bad join. Include decoy IDs with similar spelling, revoked passages, duplicate entity names across tenants and an answer that requires three documents. A single overall accuracy score will obscure which hop fails.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Evidence:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    entity_id: str
    linked_id: str

def trace_shipment(shipment_id: str, tenant: str,
                   tickets: list[Evidence], notices: list[Evidence]) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    chains = []
    for ticket in tickets:
        if ticket.tenant != tenant or ticket.entity_id != shipment_id:
            continue
        for notice in notices:
            if notice.tenant == tenant and notice.entity_id == ticket.linked_id:
                chains.append((ticket.passage_id, notice.passage_id))
    return chains

tickets = [Evidence("ticket-47-r2", "north", "SH-47", "BX-83")]
notices = [Evidence("notice-83-r4", "north", "BX-83", "late"),
           Evidence("notice-83-private", "south", "BX-83", "cancelled")]
assert trace_shipment("SH-47", "north", tickets, notices) == [
    ("ticket-47-r2", "notice-83-r4")]
assert trace_shipment("SH-47", "south", tickets, notices) == []

Performance and operating cost

The transparent nested-loop baseline costs O(TN) time for T tickets and N notices and O(C) space for C chains. Index notices by tenant and entity to reduce the join to O(T + N + C) build-and-probe time. Each extra retrieval hop adds latency and new failure opportunities, so cap depth and branch count before generation.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a model-generated intermediate ID that is absent from the cited passage.
  • Combining passages from different tenants because the entity text matches.
  • Claiming a downstream consequence that neither source states.
  • Allowing repeated hops to search indefinitely.

Validation drill

Create 37 questions: 19 valid two-hop chains, six ambiguous branches, five missing second edges, four decoy IDs and three revoked intermediates. Report first-hop and full-chain recall separately.

title: Table retrieval: keep numeric cells attached to their labels
summary: Retrieve tabular evidence without losing row keys, column units, revision dates or the calculation needed for an answer.
body:
Retrieve tabular evidence without losing row keys, column units, revision dates or the calculation needed for an answer.

Treat a cell as a qualified fact

The value 47 has no useful meaning alone. A searchable fact needs table ID, revision, row key, column name, unit, effective period and access label. Store a compact row rendering for discovery, but preserve typed cells for comparison and arithmetic. A question about the West queue's 47-hour target must not match a North queue row or a 47-day retention policy. Extraction provenance should point back to the original table location.

Separate discovery from computation

Use lexical or semantic search to locate a candidate table, then execute an approved operation over its typed rows. Do not derive a total by reading the top few text snippets; omitted rows silently bias the result. Exact row and column filters should run before aggregation. If the requested metric is not defined, ask for the metric rather than inventing a sum. Record the row IDs used so the answer can be audited after a table revision.

Handle headers and units

Merged headings, repeated page headers and blank cells need explicit parsing rules. A blank value can mean unknown, not zero. A percentage column cannot be summed like a count, and a currency column cannot be combined across currencies without a declared conversion rule. If a table changes from hours to minutes in a new revision, the retrieval layer must not silently mix both. Index swaps should move the searchable row text and typed table together.

Test answer coverage

Judged queries should include an exact cell lookup, a filter plus sum, a percentage with denominator, a missing cell and a superseded revision. Evaluate table discovery separately from calculation correctness. A system that retrieves the right table but adds the wrong rows still fails. For each calculated answer, retain the operation, selected row keys, table revision and resulting value.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class QueueRow:
    region: str
    week: int
    resolved: int | None
    revision: str

def resolved_total(rows: list[QueueRow], region: str, weeks: set[int],
                   revision: str) -> int:
    selected = [row for row in rows if row.region == region
                and row.week in weeks and row.revision == revision]
    if len(selected) != len(weeks) or any(row.resolved is None for row in selected):
        raise ValueError("incomplete table coverage")
    if len({row.week for row in selected}) != len(selected):
        raise ValueError("duplicate row key")
    return sum(row.resolved for row in selected if row.resolved is not None)

queue_rows = [QueueRow("West", 31, 47, "r8"),
              QueueRow("West", 32, 29, "r8"),
              QueueRow("North", 31, 81, "r8")]
assert resolved_total(queue_rows, "West", {31, 32}, "r8") == 76
try:
    resolved_total(queue_rows, "West", {31, 33}, "r8")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("missing week was accepted")

Performance and operating cost

The baseline scans N rows in O(N) time and stores O(K) selected rows. A typed index on revision, region and week avoids a full scan in a large warehouse; query cost then depends on matching rows and index lookup. Preserve row lineage even if it adds metadata, because a wrong numeric answer is harder to diagnose than a slow lookup.

Common Mistakes

  • Embedding isolated numeric cells without their row and column labels.
  • Treating blank cells as zero during aggregation.
  • Summing a top-k snippet sample instead of the full filtered table.
  • Combining rows from different revisions or units.

Validation drill

Build a 29-row queue table with two revisions and three regions. Answer 12 cell questions and eight aggregate questions. Make two cells blank and one row duplicated; require explicit errors for both cases.

title: Multimodal retrieval: connect images, OCR and text to one asset identity
summary: Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.
body:
Search image-bearing documents while keeping captions, OCR text, crop coordinates and permissions tied to the exact source revision.

Define the asset graph

A diagram may have a text caption, OCR labels, a surrounding paragraph and a visual embedding. Give all views one immutable asset revision, then store their own modality and location. A match in OCR is evidence for visible words, not for a visual relation that OCR cannot read. A visual similarity match locates candidate images; it does not prove that two valves have the same operating limit. Source provenance must survive the modality change.

Retrieve and fuse carefully

Text queries can search captions and OCR; image queries can use visual embeddings. Fuse candidate asset IDs only after permission and revision checks. Preserve the match route in the result: caption, OCR, surrounding text or image similarity. This matters when a reviewer asks why a drawing ranked first. Rerank with the full question and a bounded set of candidate assets, not a collection of detached crop embeddings.

Resolve the cited region

An answer about a label in the upper-left crop should cite that region and its parent page. Store normalized crop coordinates and the original image dimensions so a viewer can highlight the right area. If preprocessing rotates or resizes the image, transform coordinates back before presenting them. A citation to an entire manual page may be too broad when the claim depends on a tiny annotation. Support checks should confirm the cited modality can prove the claim.

Measure modality-specific misses

Maintain query slices for exact OCR strings, paraphrased captions, visual resemblance and questions requiring both text and image. Evaluate candidate recall by modality and asset revision. A high combined score can conceal that OCR systematically misses rotated labels. Keep a no-answer slice where a visually similar image lacks the requested label, and require the system to say so.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AssetView:
    asset_id: str
    revision: str
    tenant: str
    modality: str
    content: str

def find_label(views: list[AssetView], label: str, tenant: str,
               active_revisions: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted({view.asset_id for view in views
                   if view.tenant == tenant and view.modality == "ocr"
                   and active_revisions.get(view.asset_id) == view.revision
                   and label.casefold() in view.content.casefold()})

views = [AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r2", "plant-a", "ocr", "Outlet 73 kPa"),
         AssetView("pump-47", "r3", "plant-b", "ocr", "Outlet 47 kPa")]
assert find_label(views, "47 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == ["pump-47"]
assert find_label(views, "73 kPa", "plant-a", {"pump-47": "r3"}) == []

Performance and operating cost

The sample scans V views in O(V) time and uses O(A) result space for A matching assets. Production retrieval can index each modality, but storage and embedding work grow with the number of views and crops. Set crop limits and deduplicate near-identical renders; otherwise one document can flood the candidate window.

Common Mistakes

  • Using visual similarity as proof of a printed numeric label.
  • Returning a crop without its parent asset and revision.
  • Mixing a fresh caption with OCR from an old image revision.
  • Showing a broad page citation when only one crop supports the answer.

Validation drill

Index 17 diagrams with captions and OCR, including three rotated scans and two superseded revisions. Judge exact-label, visual and mixed queries separately; verify every cited crop opens at the correct page and coordinates.

title: Incremental retrieval ingestion: replay events without reviving deleted passages
summary: Apply document revisions, permission changes and deletions safely when source events arrive late, twice or out of order.
body:
Apply document revisions, permission changes and deletions safely when source events arrive late, twice or out of order.

Make the event contract explicit

Each source event needs tenant, document ID, monotonic source version, action and a stable event ID. The index writer should compare versions before replacing passages. At-least-once delivery means duplicate events are normal; processing the same revision twice must yield the same searchable state. A late upsert for version 6 cannot restore a document deleted at version 8. Index freshness depends on this ordering rule.

Separate removal from embedding work

Delete and permission-revocation events should invalidate answer caches and remove eligible passages promptly. A new revision may take longer because extraction and embeddings run asynchronously. During that interval, either keep an explicitly permitted old revision under a defined policy or mark the document unavailable. Do not show a half-written revision whose metadata and vectors disagree. Publish the new generation only after all required passages and filters are ready.

Retain a tombstone

A tombstone records the latest delete version even after the vector rows are removed. Without it, a replayed old upsert can recreate a deleted passage. Keep the tombstone until upstream retention guarantees make older events impossible, and test that guarantee rather than guessing. A permission change also needs a versioned marker; it may be independent of content revision and should not wait for re-embedding.

Observe lag and recovery

Measure event age at application, pending extraction count, index generation and deletion-to-unavailability delay. Replay a durable event log into a staging index, compare eligible document sets, then atomically switch the alias. Encoder migrations need the same generation boundary. A process restart should resume from a checkpoint without losing the version guard.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DocumentEvent:
    document_id: str
    version: int
    action: str
    text: str = ""

def apply_event(state: dict[str, tuple[int, str | None]],
                event: DocumentEvent) -> None:
    current_version = state.get(event.document_id, (-1, None))[0]
    if event.version <= current_version:
        return
    if event.action == "delete":
        state[event.document_id] = (event.version, None)
    elif event.action == "upsert" and event.text.strip():
        state[event.document_id] = (event.version, event.text)
    else:
        raise ValueError("invalid document event")

index_state: dict[str, tuple[int, str | None]] = {}
apply_event(index_state, DocumentEvent("policy-47", 8, "delete"))
apply_event(index_state, DocumentEvent("policy-47", 6, "upsert", "old policy"))
apply_event(index_state, DocumentEvent("policy-47", 8, "delete"))
assert index_state["policy-47"] == (8, None)

Performance and operating cost

The version guard is O(1) expected time per event with a hash map and O(D) state for D documents. Extraction and embedding dominate CPU and queue time. Tombstones consume storage, but deleting them too early risks data resurrection. Report end-to-end publication lag and revocation lag separately.

Common Mistakes

  • Deleting vector rows without retaining the latest source version.
  • Assuming queue delivery is exactly once or ordered across partitions.
  • Waiting for slow re-embedding before enforcing a permission revocation.
  • Publishing metadata for a new revision before its passage set is complete.

Validation drill

Replay 53 events with duplicates, delayed upserts, revisions and deletes into an empty index. Shuffle events while preserving per-document source versions; assert that eligible final documents and tombstones match the source of truth.

title: Retrieval traces: locate the stage that lost the answer
summary: Trace routing, filtering, candidate generation, reranking and context packing so a failed answer can be explained and repaired.
body:
Trace routing, filtering, candidate generation, reranking and context packing so a failed answer can be explained and repaired.

Record stage boundaries

A single total latency and final answer are not enough. Give each query a trace ID and record route, index generation, encoder revision, allowed corpus scope, candidate counts, reranker cutoff, context IDs and answer citations. Keep the original query in a protected audit store when policy permits; avoid putting private text, user IDs or document contents into metric labels. Routing and packing need separate spans.

Name the first failing stage

If the answer-bearing passage is absent from candidate retrieval, changing the prompt will not fix it. If it appears at rank 12 but the reranker receives only eight, the candidate window is the failure. If it reaches the context packet but the model cites another passage, investigate answer synthesis and support checking. Diagnose against a judged passage ID, not a vague statement that search felt poor.

Keep traces safe and bounded

Trace metadata can itself expose sensitive document names or tenant relationships. Hash or redact identifiers in broad telemetry, reserve full IDs for access-controlled debugging, and apply retention limits. Sample routine traffic, but retain all permission denials, deletion races and release-gate failures under an approved policy. A trace with every passage text can cost more to store than the retrieved context and may violate the source's access boundary.

Use paired comparisons

Replay a fixed query against current and candidate releases with the same corpus snapshot and permission scope. Diff each stage: route, top-k identities, filters, rerank order, context selection and citations. This isolates a changed encoder from a changed index or prompt. Release gates should attach these traces to failures so a rollback decision has evidence.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetrievalTrace:
    expected_passage: str
    candidates: tuple[str, ...]
    reranked: tuple[str, ...]
    context: tuple[str, ...]
    cited: tuple[str, ...]

def first_loss(trace: RetrievalTrace) -> str:
    stages = (("candidate retrieval", trace.candidates),
              ("reranking", trace.reranked),
              ("context packing", trace.context),
              ("answer citation", trace.cited))
    for stage_name, passage_ids in stages:
        if trace.expected_passage not in passage_ids:
            return stage_name
    return "supported path"

incident = RetrievalTrace("policy-47-r3", ("policy-47-r3", "memo-29"),
                          ("memo-29",), ("memo-29",), ("memo-29",))
assert first_loss(incident) == "reranking"
assert first_loss(RetrievalTrace("missing", (), (), (), ())) == "candidate retrieval"

Performance and operating cost

Finding the first loss scans at most the four recorded stage lists, O(K) time for K total IDs and O(1) extra space. A full trace pipeline adds serialization, storage and review cost proportional to captured candidates. Sample successful queries and store compact IDs; preserve richer traces for judged failures under access control.

Common Mistakes

  • Blaming generation when the answer passage never entered candidate retrieval.
  • Logging private passage text or principal IDs in broad metric labels.
  • Comparing releases against different corpus snapshots.
  • Recording only final scores and losing stage identities.

Validation drill

Create 41 judged traces with deliberate failures at each stage. Produce a count by first-loss stage and inspect one trace from each category before changing any retrieval parameter.

title: Query expansion: add recall terms without changing the user's question
summary: Use controlled synonyms and subqueries while retaining exact IDs, exclusions, dates and authorization scope.
body:
Use controlled synonyms and subqueries while retaining exact IDs, exclusions, dates and authorization scope.

Split immutable constraints from optional terms

Parse exact identifiers, quoted phrases, exclusions, tenant scope and time bounds before expansion. Keep those constraints attached to every generated subquery. A query for case AX-47 after September must not turn into a general query about delayed cases. Expansion is useful for vocabulary mismatch: ‘chargeback’ may appear as ‘payment dispute’ in a permitted document. It is not permission to relax an exact case ID. Routing should decide whether expansion is needed at all.

Bound candidates and weights

Start with a small, reviewed synonym list or a validated reformulator. Search the original query as one leg and each expansion as a separate leg, then merge by passage ID. Preserve which leg found each candidate. Weight the original query and exact-match leg so a broad synonym cannot bury the literal target. Rank fusion is a useful merge baseline because score scales from different legs are not directly comparable.

Reject drift

A proposed rewrite fails when it drops an identifier, changes a number, reverses a negation, broadens a tenant, or shifts a date interval. Compare parsed constraints before executing the rewrite. Some vocabulary changes are context dependent: ‘hold’ can mean a payment hold or warehouse hold. For ambiguous terms, retrieve with both senses only inside the authorized corpus and let evidence disambiguate; otherwise ask the user.

Measure value by query family

Expansion should improve recall for jargon and paraphrase queries without harming exact-ID precision or latency. Build paired judgments with original-only and expanded runs. Report newly found answer passages, false positives, average additional calls and p95 latency. Retain a no-answer set; a system that answers more questions by matching unrelated synonyms has not improved. Traces should expose which expansion introduced each candidate.

Worked contract

import re

def safe_expansions(question: str, synonyms: dict[str, tuple[str, ...]]) -> list[str]:
    required_ids = set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", question.upper()))
    variants = [question]
    for term, replacements in synonyms.items():
        if not re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(term)}\b", question, re.IGNORECASE):
            continue
        for replacement in replacements[:2]:
            candidate = re.sub(rf"\b{re.escape(term)}\b", replacement,
                               question, count=1, flags=re.IGNORECASE)
            if required_ids <= set(re.findall(r"\bAX-\d+\b", candidate.upper())):
                variants.append(candidate)
    return variants[:4]

variants = safe_expansions("AX-47 chargeback status",
                           {"chargeback": ("payment dispute", "card dispute")})
assert variants == ["AX-47 chargeback status",
                    "AX-47 payment dispute status", "AX-47 card dispute status"]
assert all("AX-47" in variant for variant in variants)

Performance and operating cost

For Q query characters and at most S reviewed replacements, this small implementation scans O(SQ) time and stores at most four variants. Search cost can grow roughly with the number of variants, so cap expansion count and parallel calls. This demonstration protects exact IDs only; production validation must also compare negations, dates, tenant scope and other parsed constraints before dispatch.

Common Mistakes

  • Replacing an exact identifier with a likely-looking related identifier.
  • Dropping ‘not’ or a date bound while rewriting.
  • Merging scores from different search legs as if their scales were equal.
  • Celebrating recall gains without measuring no-answer false positives.

Validation drill

Judge 61 requests across exact IDs, jargon synonyms, negations, date bounds and no-answer cases. Compare original-only search with a maximum of three expanded variants; reject any rewrite that changes parsed constraints.

title: Knowledge graph retrieval: prove every edge in the path
summary: Use entity links to find candidate evidence while retaining the passage, relation type, revision and access rule that made each edge valid.
body:
Use entity links to find candidate evidence while retaining the passage, relation type, revision and access rule that made each edge valid.

Define the graph's evidence contract

Graph retrieval stores entities and typed relations so a question can follow connections that text similarity misses. Consider a service case linked to a replacement part, which is linked to a supplier bulletin. A bare edge saying that a case uses a part is insufficient: the edge also needs the source passage, relation type, effective time, extraction method and tenant. The graph is a navigation index, not an authority separate from its documents. Passage provenance lets a reviewer inspect the statement behind each edge.

Resolve entities before traversal

An identifier can be reused across tenants, and two supplier names can refer to one organization. Resolve an entity only within its namespace and permitted source set. Keep aliases as attributed claims rather than overwriting the canonical node. For an ambiguous name, return candidate entities with their disambiguating attributes; do not silently merge them. A false merge makes every later traversal look plausible. Exact identifiers should remain exact even when a semantic retriever proposes a near match.

Bound traversal and evidence assembly

Start from an authorized seed, expand only allowed relation types, cap hop count and degree, and reject a route if any edge lacks an active supporting passage. A popular supplier node may have thousands of neighbors; unrestricted breadth-first traversal can dominate latency and swamp the answer with irrelevant paths. Score the path by the weakest required edge and the question's relation sequence. Multi-hop stop rules should halt when the requested join is proven or the search budget expires.

Treat updates as graph operations

A document deletion must remove or invalidate all edges supported solely by that revision. If another active passage also supports an edge, the edge may survive with that other provenance. Keep an edge-to-passage reverse map to make revocation prompt. During a rebuild, compare node and edge counts by tenant, then test a set of known paths and forbidden paths before swapping the graph generation. Versioned ingestion prevents an old event from reviving a revoked relation.

Judge paths, not fluent answers

Create questions with known seed nodes, expected relation sequences and expected supporting passages. Report seed resolution, edge recall, valid-path recall and final claim support separately. Include a shared-name trap, a stale edge, a missing middle relation, a high-degree hub and a cross-tenant decoy. If the result uses a correct answer reached through unsupported edges, mark the path wrong: the route will fail on the next corpus revision.

Worked contract

from collections import deque
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SupportedEdge:
    source: str
    target: str
    relation: str
    tenant: str
    passage_id: str

def evidence_paths(edges: list[SupportedEdge], start: str, goal: str,
                   tenant: str, allowed: tuple[str, ...], degree_cap: int = 24):
    adjacency: dict[str, list[SupportedEdge]] = {}
    for edge in edges:
        if edge.tenant == tenant and edge.passage_id:
            adjacency.setdefault(edge.source, []).append(edge)
    frontier = deque([(start, ())])
    while frontier:
        node, path = frontier.popleft()
        if len(path) == len(allowed):
            if node == goal:
                return path
            continue
        candidates = [edge for edge in adjacency.get(node, ())
                      if edge.relation == allowed[len(path)]]
        for edge in candidates[:degree_cap]:
            if edge.target not in {start, *(part.target for part in path)}:
                frontier.append((edge.target, path + (edge,)))
    return ()

links = [SupportedEdge("case-47", "part-83", "uses", "north", "case-r2"),
         SupportedEdge("part-83", "bulletin-29", "covered-by", "north", "notice-r4"),
         SupportedEdge("part-83", "bulletin-91", "covered-by", "south", "private-r3")]
path = evidence_paths(links, "case-47", "bulletin-29", "north",
                      ("uses", "covered-by"))
assert [edge.passage_id for edge in path] == ["case-r2", "notice-r4"]
assert evidence_paths(links, "case-47", "bulletin-91", "north",
                      ("uses", "covered-by")) == ()

Performance and operating cost

Building the in-memory adjacency map costs O(E) time and space for E eligible edges. A bounded traversal can still examine up to the degree cap raised to the hop count; keep both limits small and index relation plus tenant in persistent storage. The example returns the first valid path, not the globally best path, and production ranking needs judged evidence quality.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating an extracted relation as fact after its supporting passage was deleted.
  • Merging two tenants' same-named entities into one node.
  • Allowing a high-degree node to expand without a cap.
  • Citing only the final bulletin when the answer depends on two edges.

Validation drill

Construct 43 questions against a small case-part-bulletin graph. Remove six supporting passages and verify that the affected paths disappear, while paths with independent support remain.

title: Corrective retrieval: retry only when evidence is insufficient
summary: Diagnose a weak retrieval result, choose a specific repair, and stop before retries turn into unsupported answer fishing.
body:
Diagnose a weak retrieval result, choose a specific repair, and stop before retries turn into unsupported answer fishing.

Separate absence from weak ranking

Corrective retrieval is a controlled second search after a first result fails an evidence check. It is not a request to regenerate an answer until one sounds convincing. A missing exact case ID suggests indexing or filter trouble; a correct passage outside the reranker window suggests candidate-window trouble; a passage in context that does not support the claim suggests answer validation trouble. Stage traces reveal which repair has a chance to work.

Define a sufficiency test

For a question asking whether order OR-47 qualified for a refund on a stated date, require evidence for the order state, applicable policy revision and date condition. A high similarity score alone does not satisfy those slots. Use deterministic checks for exact IDs, active revisions and permission scope; use a judged support check where meaning cannot be reduced to a field match. Record the missing slot and the retrieved passage IDs before another search begins.

Pick one bounded repair

If vocabulary differs, run a constrained query expansion. If the required passage was cut before reranking, enlarge that stage's candidate window within its latency budget. If the corpus lacks the source, ask for clarification or abstain; searching unrelated collections is not a repair. Keep the original constraints on every attempt, including tenant, negation, identifier and date. Maximum attempts should be part of the application contract, not left to a model's willingness to continue.

Compare attempts against the same target

Log route, corpus generation, repair reason, new candidate IDs and sufficiency outcome per attempt. A retry counts as useful only if it introduces eligible support that the first attempt lacked. Repeated retrieval of the same passages is an exhaustion signal. If two eligible sources contradict one another, stop and present the conflict with dates; another paraphrase may merely hide it. Abstention remains an acceptable final result.

Evaluate repair yield

Build a set with first-pass successes, fixable vocabulary misses, candidate-window misses, truly missing evidence and contradictions. Measure recovered supported answers, extra retrieval calls, p95 latency and false-answer rate. A policy that retries every request can raise latency with no quality gain. The target is recovery on the fixable slice while keeping no-answer cases unanswered.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Attempt:
    passage_ids: frozenset[str]
    covered_slots: frozenset[str]
    route: str

def decide_repair(attempts: list[Attempt], required_slots: frozenset[str],
                  max_attempts: int = 2) -> str:
    latest = attempts[-1]
    if required_slots <= latest.covered_slots:
        return "answer with evidence"
    if len(attempts) >= max_attempts:
        return "abstain: budget exhausted"
    if any(latest.passage_ids == prior.passage_ids for prior in attempts[:-1]):
        return "abstain: repeated candidates"
    if latest.route == "literal":
        return "retry with constrained synonyms"
    return "abstain: no justified repair"

needed = frozenset({"order", "policy", "date"})
first = Attempt(frozenset({"order-47-r2"}), frozenset({"order"}), "literal")
second = Attempt(frozenset({"order-47-r2", "policy-83-r4"}), needed, "synonym")
assert decide_repair([first], needed) == "retry with constrained synonyms"
assert decide_repair([first, second], needed) == "answer with evidence"
assert decide_repair([first, first], needed) == "abstain: budget exhausted"

Performance and operating cost

The decision function scans prior attempts in O(AK) time in the worst case for A attempts and K passage IDs per attempt; the deliberately small attempt cap keeps that bounded. The real cost is another retrieval and possible rerank call, so track added p95 latency and recovered answers together. Slot coverage must be derived from verified evidence rather than a model's untested self-rating.

Common Mistakes

  • Retrying because the answer sounded uncertain, without identifying a missing evidence slot.
  • Dropping an exact identifier or authorization filter in a rewrite.
  • Calling a second search successful when it returns the same unsupported passages.
  • Continuing after two eligible sources contradict each other.

Validation drill

Label 55 requests by first-loss stage and whether a repair exists. Allow one corrective attempt; count supported recoveries, unchanged candidates and false answers separately.

title: Retrieval evaluation labels: build a trustworthy judged set
summary: Create passage-level judgments with time, permission and disagreement rules so release scores mean the same thing across runs.
body:
Create passage-level judgments with time, permission and disagreement rules so release scores mean the same thing across runs.

Define the unit of judgment

A retrieval test needs a question, corpus snapshot, principal scope, answerable state and one or more supporting passage IDs. Labeling only a final answer string loses the evidence path: two passages may express the same value, but only one may be active for the query date or visible to the principal. Include the exact fact or relation each passage supports. Claim-level support can then be checked without treating a merely related document as a positive hit.

Collect questions from distinct failures

Sample real query shapes only where consent and access rules allow it. Add exact-ID requests, paraphrases, two-hop joins, table calculations, time-bounded questions, revoked documents, ambiguous names and no-answer cases. Synthetic queries are useful for rare traps, but they should be reviewed against an actual corpus snapshot. Keep a held-out set that prompt and ranker tuning cannot see. Otherwise the next release may memorize the test's wording instead of improving retrieval.

Make disagreement visible

Two reviewers should independently judge a difficult slice. If one marks a passage relevant because it mentions the same topic while the other requires the answer-bearing sentence, the rubric is incomplete. Record both labels and a resolution reason; do not silently average them. A third reviewer can adjudicate disputed examples. Store the rubric version with each label, because changing 'relevant' from topical to supporting changes every reported metric.

Lock the evaluation context

A query that was answerable on Monday may be unanswerable after a Tuesday deletion. Freeze or identify the corpus generation, permission policy and query-as-of time for each run. When the source changes, create a new judgment revision instead of overwriting the old one. Generation swaps and access rules are part of the test context, not incidental metadata.

Report slices with uncertainty

Measure recall at the candidate window, recall after reranking, citation support and abstention accuracy by question family. A single mean hides a catastrophic permission regression in a small slice. For a tiny slice, show counts along with percentages rather than implying precision the data cannot support. Attach first-loss traces for every regression; that makes adjudication and repair practical instead of a debate over one aggregate score.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Judgment:
    question_id: str
    corpus_generation: str
    visible_passages: frozenset[str]
    supporting_passages: frozenset[str]
    candidate_passages: tuple[str, ...]

def recall_at_window(judgments: list[Judgment]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    found = eligible = 0
    for judgment in judgments:
        gold = judgment.supporting_passages & judgment.visible_passages
        if not gold:
            continue
        eligible += 1
        found += bool(gold & set(judgment.candidate_passages))
    return found, eligible

cases = [Judgment("q-47", "g-8", frozenset({"policy-r3"}),
                  frozenset({"policy-r3"}), ("policy-r3", "memo-r2")),
         Judgment("q-48", "g-8", frozenset({"memo-r2"}),
                  frozenset({"private-r7"}), ("private-r7",)),
         Judgment("q-49", "g-8", frozenset({"manual-r4"}),
                  frozenset({"manual-r4"}), ("notice-r1",))]
assert recall_at_window(cases) == (1, 2)

Performance and operating cost

This simple metric scans each candidate list once, O(C) time for C total candidates, and builds temporary sets up to the window size. Human labeling and adjudication dominate cost. The example excludes questions with no eligible supporting passage; report those separately as no-answer and permission slices rather than burying them in recall.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a topical passage as if it supported the requested fact.
  • Changing the corpus or permission scope while comparing two releases.
  • Discarding reviewer disagreement instead of fixing the rubric.
  • Reporting only a pooled metric that conceals no-answer or restricted-document failures.

Validation drill

Label 72 questions in six families, including 12 no-answer cases. Double-label 18 difficult examples and adjudicate disagreements before comparing two retrieval releases on the same corpus generation.

title: Federated retrieval: search multiple stores without losing policy or time budgets
summary: Coordinate independent search sources, preserve each source's access checks, and merge evidence without pretending their scores share a scale.
body:
Coordinate independent search sources, preserve each source's access checks, and merge evidence without pretending their scores share a scale.

Keep source ownership explicit

Federated retrieval sends a query to more than one store: perhaps a policy index, a ticket database and a table catalog. Each adapter must enforce the caller's authorization under that store's rules, and the coordinator must not infer that permission in one store grants access in another. Return source ID, passage ID, revision, eligibility and match route with every hit. Corpus access belongs at the source boundary as well as the final response boundary.

Budget each leg

Give the whole request a deadline and each source a smaller timeout. A slow table catalog should not stall a simple policy answer until the client disconnects. Cancel or ignore work after the deadline, and mark the result as partial. Partial results can support an answer only if all required evidence slots are covered; a missing source may require a clear abstention. The timeout policy should be visible in retrieval traces so a missing document is not mistaken for a ranking failure.

Merge identities, not raw scores

A cosine score of 0.79 and a lexical score of 11.4 are not comparable magnitudes. Deduplicate by stable source-and-passage identity, then use per-source rank, calibrated relevance or a judged fusion rule. Record which source returned each duplicate and why a candidate survived. Rank fusion offers a baseline when adapters expose rankings but not aligned probabilities. Keep source diversity when the answer needs both a ticket and a policy.

Handle source-specific freshness

One source may have a fresh transaction row while another holds yesterday's indexed document. Store source revision and observed-at time on every hit; do not present their join as a single current snapshot unless the application defines consistency semantics. For a question about historical eligibility, apply the requested as-of time to each adapter. If one store cannot answer as-of queries, say which part is unavailable rather than silently reading its current state.

Test partial and contradictory outcomes

Run evaluations where every source succeeds, one times out, a source returns forbidden hits, two stores disagree on a revision, and one store returns an exact ID absent elsewhere. Measure required-evidence coverage, p95 latency and per-source failure rates. A high overall recall score does not excuse a coordinator that leaks a restricted hit or hides a missing source behind a confident answer.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchHit:
    source: str
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    rank: int
    text: str

def merge_hits(source_hits: dict[str, list[SearchHit]], tenant: str,
               per_source_cap: int = 3) -> list[SearchHit]:
    eligible = []
    for source, hits in source_hits.items():
        ranked = sorted((hit for hit in hits if hit.source == source
                         and hit.tenant == tenant), key=lambda hit: hit.rank)
        eligible.extend(ranked[:per_source_cap])
    seen: set[tuple[str, str]] = set()
    merged = []
    for hit in sorted(eligible, key=lambda item: (item.rank, item.source)):
        identity = (hit.source, hit.passage_id)
        if identity not in seen:
            seen.add(identity)
            merged.append(hit)
    return merged

results = {"policy": [SearchHit("policy", "refund-r4", "north", 1, "47 days"),
                      SearchHit("policy", "refund-r4", "north", 2, "duplicate")],
           "tickets": [SearchHit("tickets", "case-83", "south", 1, "private"),
                       SearchHit("tickets", "case-47", "north", 2, "eligible")]}
assert [(hit.source, hit.passage_id) for hit in merge_hits(results, "north")] == [
    ("policy", "refund-r4"), ("tickets", "case-47")]
assert all(hit.tenant == "north" for hit in merge_hits(results, "north"))

Performance and operating cost

For N returned hits, filtering and sorting costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space. Concurrent source calls can lower wall time toward the slowest successful leg, but only with explicit deadlines and a shared request budget. This example does not execute network calls or enforce source authorization; production adapters must perform their own checks before returning candidates.

Common Mistakes

  • Sorting raw scores from unrelated retrieval engines as if they were calibrated.
  • Letting a single slow adapter consume the entire request deadline.
  • Assuming an aggregator-side filter replaces authorization in each source.
  • Answering as though all stores were current when their revisions differ.

Validation drill

Federate three mocked stores over 38 judged questions. Inject timeouts, duplicate hits, stale revisions and cross-tenant decoys; count partial results and unsupported final answers independently.
