title: Hierarchical retrieval: find a section before selecting its evidence
summary: Route through document structure while keeping answer citations on the smallest passage that actually proves the claim.
body:
Route through document structure while keeping answer citations on the smallest passage that actually proves the claim.

Index two useful levels

Hierarchical retrieval searches a document tree before choosing answer-bearing passages. A maintenance manual's chapter heading may say 'hydraulic pressure', while the relevant sentence appears in a child paragraph about pump P-47. Store a parent summary and child passages with stable IDs, revision and access label. The parent helps locate the right region; the child proves the claim. A heading alone is not evidence for a numeric limit. Chunk identity should preserve the original section path rather than replacing it with a generated synopsis.

Route with reversible decisions

A top-level search can choose candidate manuals, then section headings, then paragraphs. Keep more than one plausible branch when the query is ambiguous, and record each routing decision in the trace. If the first branch fails an evidence test, a bounded sibling search can recover a missed section. Do not let a model invent a chapter name or crawl indefinitely. Corrective retrieval needs a named failure and a fixed search budget, not an open-ended promise to look harder.

Apply permissions at both levels

A parent section might be visible while a child appendix is restricted. Filtering only the parent can expose child text; filtering only the child can reveal restricted section names through the navigation path. Bind tenant, role and revision to every node. If a parent is revoked, descendant eligibility must be recomputed or removed. An index generation should publish its tree and its passage store together, so a parent does not point to a child from an older revision. Document lifecycle rules still govern tree traversal.

Avoid parent dominance

Long section summaries can match many queries and crowd out precise passages. Allocate a small number of candidate parents, then a separate child window per parent; finally merge child passages with diversity controls. The result should carry its route and its actual supporting span. If the answer requires two sections, preserve both branches instead of concatenating one chapter's unrelated paragraphs. Context packing should count evidence coverage, not just total tokens.

Judge routing and support separately

Evaluation should report whether the right document was found, whether the right section survived routing, whether the supporting child reached the candidate window, and whether the answer cited it. Include misleading headings, appendices, renamed chapters, cross-section questions and restricted child nodes. A router may have high document recall but poor child recall. Preserve first-loss traces to locate that gap before changing the model or the prompt.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PassageNode:
    passage_id: str
    parent_id: str
    tenant: str
    revision: str
    text: str

def children_for_section(nodes: list[PassageNode], section_id: str,
                         tenant: str, revision: str, term: str) -> list[str]:
    return [node.passage_id for node in nodes
            if node.parent_id == section_id and node.tenant == tenant
            and node.revision == revision and term.casefold() in node.text.casefold()]

manual = [PassageNode("pump-47-limit", "hydraulics-r3", "plant-a", "r3",
                      "Pump P-47 relief limit is 83 kPa."),
          PassageNode("pump-47-old", "hydraulics-r2", "plant-a", "r2",
                      "Pump P-47 relief limit is 71 kPa."),
          PassageNode("private-limit", "hydraulics-r3", "plant-b", "r3",
                      "Pump P-47 relief limit is 99 kPa.")]
assert children_for_section(manual, "hydraulics-r3", "plant-a", "r3", "83 kPa") == [
    "pump-47-limit"]
assert children_for_section(manual, "hydraulics-r3", "plant-a", "r3", "99 kPa") == []

Performance and operating cost

This transparent child scan is O(N) time for N nodes and O(K) space for K matches. A production index keyed by parent, tenant and revision reduces the eligible scan, but tree traversal adds parent-search and child-search latency. Keep branch count and depth bounded; broad hierarchies can cost more than one flat retrieval call without improving support.

Common Mistakes

  • Citing a section summary that does not contain the claimed number.
  • Pruning every branch except the first plausible heading.
  • Applying access control to a parent but not its children.
  • Publishing a parent tree and child passages from different document revisions.

title: Late-interaction retrieval: score token matches without one-vector blur
summary: Compare multi-vector passage ranking with single-vector search while accounting for storage, candidate pruning and token-level false matches.
body:
Compare multi-vector passage ranking with single-vector search while accounting for storage, candidate pruning and token-level false matches.

Keep token evidence visible

A single vector compresses a whole passage into one representation. Late-interaction ranking keeps multiple token vectors for the query and passage, then combines their best token-level matches. This can preserve a rare part number alongside broad topic words. It is a ranking signal, not a proof that a passage answers the question: matching 'P-47', 'pressure' and 'limit' in separate sentences could still miss the requested limit. Claim support must inspect the actual text after ranking.

Separate candidate generation from scoring

Scoring every passage token against every query token is expensive. First build a candidate set with lexical or approximate vector search, apply tenant and revision filters, then run token-level scoring on a bounded window. If the correct passage never enters that window, late interaction cannot rescue it. Filtered candidate recall and reranker window size should be measured before debating score formulas.

Explain the aggregation

One simple late-interaction score takes each query token's best similarity to any passage token and sums those maxima. It rewards coverage of query terms while allowing different passage tokens to satisfy them. Normalize or calibrate for query length when comparing across questions; within one query, ranking scores can be compared directly. Stop words, duplicated tokens and template boilerplate can distort results. A document containing twenty copies of a part label should not gain twenty independent votes from one query term.

Budget memory and CPU

Multi-vector passages consume more index space than a single vector per passage. Token pruning, low-precision storage and candidate caps reduce cost, but each can reduce recall. Measure bytes per passage, index build time, p95 query latency and judged passage recall together. Keep encoder version and tokenization version on the index; a query encoded with a different vocabulary or model revision can change rankings without any corpus update. Embedding migrations need paired tests.

Test the hard queries

Include near-identical part numbers, terms scattered across unrelated sections, long passages, short passages and one genuinely absent answer. Report candidate recall, rank after late interaction, and final support separately. A high ranking score for a passage with all query words but no answer is an expected failure mode to catch, not a reason to weaken the citation check.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def cosine(left: tuple[float, ...], right: tuple[float, ...]) -> float:
    numerator = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(left, right, strict=True))
    left_norm = sqrt(sum(value * value for value in left))
    right_norm = sqrt(sum(value * value for value in right))
    if not left_norm or not right_norm:
        raise ValueError("zero-length token vector")
    return numerator / (left_norm * right_norm)

def token_coverage(query_tokens: list[tuple[float, ...]],
                   passage_tokens: list[tuple[float, ...]]) -> float:
    if not query_tokens or not passage_tokens:
        raise ValueError("empty token sequence")
    return sum(max(cosine(query, passage) for passage in passage_tokens)
               for query in query_tokens)

pressure_query = [(1.0, 0.0), (0.0, 1.0)]
complete_passage = [(1.0, 0.0), (0.0, 1.0)]
partial_passage = [(1.0, 0.0), (1.0, 0.0)]
assert token_coverage(pressure_query, complete_passage) == 2.0
assert token_coverage(pressure_query, partial_passage) == 1.0

Performance and operating cost

For Q query tokens, P passage tokens and D vector dimensions, direct scoring costs O(QPD) time and O(1) extra space beyond the vectors. For C candidates, multiply that work by C. Index storage grows with passage token count rather than passage count alone, so use a candidate stage and measure the cost of any compression or token pruning.

Common Mistakes

  • Running token-level scoring over the entire corpus without a candidate bound.
  • Treating token coverage as proof that the passage states the requested fact.
  • Mixing encoder or tokenizer revisions between query and index.
  • Ignoring storage growth when comparing against a single-vector baseline.

Validation drill

Judge 49 part-number questions with close distractors. Compare a single-vector baseline and a bounded token-level reranker on candidate recall, supported top-one answers, index bytes and p95 latency.

title: Temporal retrieval: answer as-of questions from valid evidence
summary: Distinguish when a fact was true from when it was indexed, and resolve overlapping revisions before producing a dated answer.
body:
Distinguish when a fact was true from when it was indexed, and resolve overlapping revisions before producing a dated answer.

Store two clocks

Temporal retrieval answers questions about a specified point in time. A policy may be valid from 1 March to 30 June yet ingested on 4 March. Valid time describes when the policy applies; system time describes when the search system learned or changed it. Conflating the two makes historical answers wrong after a late upload or backdated correction. Record both intervals and the source revision. Index freshness explains availability, while valid time determines which fact belongs in the answer.

Parse the user's time boundary

An as-of question needs a date, time zone and boundary convention. 'On 30 June' may mean any instant that day; an interval ending at midnight on 30 June may already be invalid then. Choose half-open intervals consistently: start inclusive, end exclusive. If the user gives only a month, do not quietly pick its last day for a rule that changed mid-month. Ask for a date or return the change range. Query routing should preserve the time constraint across every retrieval leg.

Filter before ranking

Restrict candidates to the requested valid-time interval and authorized corpus before semantic ranking. A newer policy is often lexically similar and may rank above the old one even when the user asks about last year. An answer must cite the applicable revision and the effective interval. For a comparison across dates, retrieve each date separately and keep the two evidence sets distinct. A revision's publication timestamp is not a substitute for its effective timestamp.

Resolve overlap explicitly

Two active records may cover the same instant because of a correction, overlapping jurisdiction or bad source data. Prefer a documented supersession rule only if the source provides one. Otherwise report the conflict with both citations and abstain from a single definitive value. A deletion may remove public availability without erasing the historical audit record; retrieval policy decides whether that archived evidence remains eligible. Access control applies even to historical answers.

Judge temporal slices

Build cases just before and after effective boundaries, retroactive corrections, delayed ingestion, unknown end dates, conflicting overlaps and no eligible history. Measure valid-revision recall and answer support separately from plain passage recall. A search that finds the right policy family but the wrong revision should fail the dated slice. Keep the corpus generation in the judgment so a changing source does not invalidate the comparison.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PolicyRevision:
    revision: str
    tenant: str
    valid_from: date
    valid_until: date | None
    refund_days: int

def applicable_policy(revisions: list[PolicyRevision], tenant: str,
                      as_of: date) -> PolicyRevision | None:
    matches = [policy for policy in revisions if policy.tenant == tenant
               and policy.valid_from <= as_of
               and (policy.valid_until is None or as_of < policy.valid_until)]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError("overlapping eligible policy revisions")
    return matches[0] if matches else None

policies = [PolicyRevision("r3", "north", date(2026, 3, 1), date(2026, 7, 1), 47),
            PolicyRevision("r4", "north", date(2026, 7, 1), None, 29),
            PolicyRevision("private", "south", date(2026, 3, 1), None, 83)]
assert applicable_policy(policies, "north", date(2026, 6, 30)).refund_days == 47
assert applicable_policy(policies, "north", date(2026, 7, 1)).refund_days == 29
assert applicable_policy(policies, "north", date(2026, 2, 28)) is None

Performance and operating cost

The example scans R revisions in O(R) time and stores O(M) matches, where M is the number valid at the requested instant. A database interval index and tenant key can reduce candidate reads. Store valid-time and ingestion-time metadata separately; two extra timestamps are cheap compared with an unsupported historical answer.

Common Mistakes

  • Using ingestion time as the policy's effective date.
  • Treating an interval end as inclusive in one service and exclusive in another.
  • Returning the newest revision for every historical question.
  • Silently choosing one of two overlapping eligible revisions.

Validation drill

Create 61 dated questions around four policy transitions, including six backdated corrections and five overlaps. Require explicit ambiguity when the source cannot determine the applicable revision.

title: Near-duplicate retrieval: collapse copies without hiding independent evidence
summary: Deduplicate copied passages by lineage and revision while preserving genuinely independent sources for corroboration.
body:
Deduplicate copied passages by lineage and revision while preserving genuinely independent sources for corroboration.

Separate copies from corroboration

A retrieval result can contain a policy paragraph copied into twelve team notes. Twelve hits are not twelve independent confirmations. Store document lineage, source owner, passage hash and revision so the system can group copies. Exact hashes catch byte-identical text; normalized hashes catch whitespace and formatting changes; semantic similarity can suggest near duplicates for review. A separate independent bulletin stating the same limit may be valuable corroboration and should not disappear merely because its wording is similar. Provenance decides which case applies.

Collapse at the right boundary

Group near duplicates after access filtering. A user who can see the public manual but not a private support note must not see the private note's title or existence in the collapsed result. Within an eligible group, choose an authoritative active revision and retain a list of permitted copies for audit. Do not pick a superseded revision only because it has a higher lexical score. Revision rules take precedence over ranking.

Protect the candidate window

Repeated template text can consume most of top-k, leaving no room for another document needed to answer the question. Collapse copies before context selection and reserve slots for distinct source lineages. Track both raw hit count and independent-lineage count in traces; a result of 20 hits from one copied memo is effectively one source. Evidence diversity should be measured at lineage level rather than URL count.

Choose a conservative similarity rule

A shared heading and two similar sentences do not prove two passages are duplicates. Numeric values, negations, dates and identifiers can differ while the rest of the text matches. Treat changes in those fields as blockers to automatic collapse. For uncertain pairs, keep both or flag them for review. False merging removes possible contradictions; false separation mostly wastes context. This asymmetry argues for conservative thresholds and explicit field checks.

Test both errors

Create copied passages, lightly reformatted copies, stale revisions and independently authored confirmations. Measure duplicate-group purity and answer-bearing passage recall after collapse. Include two near-identical policies whose refund windows differ and a copied note with a missing negation. The system should retain both contradictory policies for resolution, not merge them into a false consensus. Judged sets need lineage labels to make this visible.

Worked contract

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceCopy:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    lineage: str
    revision: int
    text: str

def normalize_copy(text: str) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text.casefold()).strip()

def collapse_copies(passages: list[EvidenceCopy], tenant: str) -> list[EvidenceCopy]:
    chosen: dict[tuple[str, str], EvidenceCopy] = {}
    for passage in passages:
        if passage.tenant != tenant:
            continue
        key = (passage.lineage, normalize_copy(passage.text))
        if key not in chosen or passage.revision > chosen[key].revision:
            chosen[key] = passage
    return list(chosen.values())

copies = [EvidenceCopy("manual-r2", "north", "manual-47", 2, "Limit: 47 days"),
          EvidenceCopy("manual-r3", "north", "manual-47", 3, "Limit:  47 days"),
          EvidenceCopy("notice-r1", "north", "notice-83", 1, "Limit: 47 days"),
          EvidenceCopy("private-r4", "south", "manual-47", 4, "Limit: 47 days")]
assert {hit.passage_id for hit in collapse_copies(copies, "north")} == {
    "manual-r3", "notice-r1"}

Performance and operating cost

The hash-based baseline scans N passages in O(NL) time for average passage length L and stores O(U) groups for U unique lineage-text pairs. Semantic near-duplicate detection adds candidate-pair and review cost; avoid an O(N squared) all-pairs scan on a large corpus by blocking on lineage, source type or approximate fingerprints first.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting copied team notes as independent evidence.
  • Grouping before access checks and exposing restricted source metadata.
  • Merging passages that differ in a number, negation or effective date.
  • Keeping the highest-ranked stale copy instead of the active revision.

Validation drill

Make 79 passages across 12 lineages with exact copies, formatting changes, copied notes and three contradictory revisions. Verify that collapse preserves all independent answer-bearing sources and no restricted metadata leaks.

title: Multilingual retrieval without losing names, units or permissions
summary: Search across languages while preserving exact entities and measuring answer support in the language of the source.
body:
Search across languages while preserving exact entities and measuring answer support in the language of the source.

Treat language as a retrieval constraint

Multilingual retrieval finds evidence when the question and the answer-bearing document use different languages or scripts. A Hindi request for a pump's pressure limit might need an English maintenance sheet. Translate or encode the request for candidate generation, but retain the original request and its entity spans. A translated product name can become a common noun; a model number or unit can be silently changed. Keep the original tokens beside any expansion so the exact identifier remains searchable. Expansion tests should fail when an alias changes the requested entity.

Use two candidate paths

A multilingual vector index can find semantically related passages across languages; an exact or transliterated term index can recover names and part numbers that an embedding misses. Merge bounded candidate lists, then rank the original passages. Transliteration is a controlled alias for a named entity, not a general translation engine. Store aliases with locale, entity ID and review status. If two entities share the same Roman spelling, an alias must not erase that ambiguity. Hybrid merging gives a practical way to combine the two paths without pretending their raw scores are comparable.

Preserve the source's meaning

Retrieve source text, revision, locale and passage ID together. A translated display excerpt may help the reader, but the citation must still point to the original passage. Numbers, negation, effective dates and units require explicit checks across the translation boundary. Do not answer a question in the user's language from a passage whose translation has inverted 'must not' or converted 47 psi into 47 kPa. Claim-level support is judged against the source, not against a fluent paraphrase.

Filter before mixing languages

Tenant permissions, document status and jurisdiction apply to every language variant. A public English summary is not evidence that a private Spanish appendix can be searched or surfaced. Deduplicate translations by source lineage only after access filtering; separate independently authored statements even if they are translated similarly. Track source revision across language copies because a translated page may lag behind the original. Corpus lifecycle determines which variant is eligible.

Evaluate language pairs, not one average

Build judged queries for each query-language and document-language pair, including mixed-script queries, transliterated names, similar identifiers and documents with no valid answer. Report candidate recall, supported answer rate and entity preservation per pair. A strong English-English score can hide total failure on Hindi-English or Arabic-English searches. Review wrong answers with both original and translated passages. If no reviewer can establish the meaning of the source, mark support unknown rather than accepting the answer by fluency.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
import unicodedata

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ServicePassage:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    locale: str
    text: str
    entity_id: str

def normalized(text: str) -> str:
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).casefold()

def exact_entity_candidates(passages: list[ServicePassage], tenant: str,
                            requested_entity: str, aliases: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    entity_id = aliases.get(normalized(requested_entity))
    if entity_id is None:
        return []
    return [passage.passage_id for passage in passages
            if passage.tenant == tenant and passage.entity_id == entity_id]

service_notes = [ServicePassage("sheet-en-r4", "north", "en",
                                "Pump P-47 relief limit is 83 kPa.", "pump-p47"),
                 ServicePassage("sheet-hi-r2", "south", "hi",
                                "P-47 limit is 99 kPa.", "pump-p47")]
reviewed_aliases = {normalized("पी-47"): "pump-p47", normalized("P-47"): "pump-p47"}
assert exact_entity_candidates(service_notes, "north", "पी-47", reviewed_aliases) == ["sheet-en-r4"]
assert exact_entity_candidates(service_notes, "north", "P-48", reviewed_aliases) == []

Performance and operating cost

The transparent candidate scan costs O(N) time over N passages and O(K) output space for K eligible matches. A production entity index keyed by tenant and entity ID reduces lookup work but requires reviewed aliases and refreshes when documents change. A second multilingual vector path adds index storage and query latency; measure its incremental supported recall by language pair before accepting the cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating transliteration as an unambiguous entity identifier.
  • Dropping the original query after translation and losing exact numbers or negation.
  • Citing only a generated translation rather than the source passage.
  • Reporting one aggregate recall score across uneven language pairs.

Validation drill

Build 53 questions across three query languages and two document languages. Include twelve mixed-script identifiers and eight restricted passages. Record entity preservation, authorized candidate recall and supported answers for every language pair.

title: Code repository retrieval by symbol, call site and commit
summary: Find implementation evidence in a changing repository without confusing symbol matches, generated files and stale revisions.
body:
Find implementation evidence in a changing repository without confusing symbol matches, generated files and stale revisions.

Index code as code

Code repository retrieval searches declarations, call sites, configuration and tests as related but distinct evidence. A question about how InvoiceLedger.post records a refund needs the method body and perhaps its caller; a README mentioning the same method is insufficient. Parse source into language-aware symbols with file path, line span and commit ID. Preserve surrounding imports and enclosing class for interpretation. Stable chunk identity helps trace a symbol across index rebuilds, but a changed body must receive a new revision identity.

Use the repository graph carefully

Exact symbol search should usually run before semantic search for named functions, exception types or environment keys. Then collect bounded callers, callees and tests to explain behavior. A call graph is only an approximation in languages with reflection, runtime dispatch, generated code or dependency injection. Do not claim a path is unreachable because a static extractor missed it. Edge provenance should identify whether an edge came from parsing, a build artifact or a test trace.

Bind every result to a revision

Branch names move. A result retrieved from main yesterday may contradict today's implementation. Store commit, file hash and language in the index; include the commit in the answer trace. For a question about a deployment, use the deployed commit rather than the latest default branch. For a historical bug, retrieve the failing revision and a candidate fix separately. Temporal evidence is particularly important when a config flag changed between releases.

Respect boundaries and noise

Filter repositories and paths by permission before presenting symbol names or snippets. Skip vendored libraries, generated files and copied lockfile text unless the question specifically concerns them. Merge duplicate definitions only when lineage and revision match. Keep tests accessible as evidence of intended behavior, but do not treat a passing test as proof that every production call follows the same path. Duplicate handling should not collapse a test and implementation into one source.

Judge answer-bearing spans

Create questions about exact symbols, renamed methods, inherited calls, generated bindings, stale commits and behavior described only by a caller. Measure whether the correct file and line span entered the candidate set, whether the required call path was retrieved, and whether the final explanation cited the right revision. A high lexical hit on a symbol name is not a supported answer if its body never entered context. Keep line links pinned to commit hashes so they remain valid after later edits.

Worked contract

import ast
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CodeSymbol:
    name: str
    path: str
    commit: str
    first_line: int
    last_line: int

def python_symbols(source: str, path: str, commit: str) -> list[CodeSymbol]:
    tree = ast.parse(source, filename=path)
    symbols: list[CodeSymbol] = []
    for node in tree.body:
        if isinstance(node, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
            symbols.append(CodeSymbol(node.name, path, commit, node.lineno, node.end_lineno))
        elif isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef):
            for method in node.body:
                if isinstance(method, (ast.FunctionDef, ast.AsyncFunctionDef)):
                    symbols.append(CodeSymbol(f"{node.name}.{method.name}", path,
                                              commit, method.lineno, method.end_lineno))
    return symbols

ledger_source = "class InvoiceLedger:\n    def post_refund(self, amount):\n        return -amount\n"
found = python_symbols(ledger_source, "billing/ledger.py", "c47e2a")
assert found == [CodeSymbol("InvoiceLedger.post_refund", "billing/ledger.py", "c47e2a", 2, 3)]

Performance and operating cost

AST extraction visits O(S) syntax nodes and stores O(M) symbols for M declarations. An exact symbol index is cheap to query but misses indirect behavior; graph expansion can grow rapidly with call depth, so cap neighbors and inspect the highest-value paths first. Parsing each changed file once per commit is cheaper than rescanning the full repository on every question.

Common Mistakes

  • Answering from a README when the question asks what code actually executes.
  • Mixing snippets from different commits in one behavior claim.
  • Assuming a static call graph captures reflective or injected calls.
  • Indexing vendored and generated code as if it were the repository's own implementation.

Validation drill

Index 47 source files at two commits. Judge 41 questions about named methods, indirect callers and renamed symbols; report correct commit, symbol span and supported call-path coverage separately.

title: Audio and video retrieval with timecoded evidence
summary: Retrieve a precise spoken or visual moment while retaining timestamps, speakers and media-version identity.
body:
Retrieve a precise spoken or visual moment while retaining timestamps, speakers and media-version identity.

Make time part of the passage ID

Audio and video retrieval uses timed segments, transcript words and sometimes frame descriptions as searchable evidence. A transcript paragraph without a start and end time cannot support a jump to the original recording. Store media asset ID, version, track, speaker label, start and end milliseconds on every segment. Re-captioning or editing the recording changes the time map; keep the old version rather than silently reusing stale links. Asset identity must survive storage moves but change when the underlying cut changes.

Separate modalities in candidate generation

Transcript search works for spoken terms; frame descriptions or image embeddings may find a visual action with no spoken mention. Run each path within a budget, then combine candidates using calibrated ranks and overlap rules. A camera view of a valve does not prove that the narrator's pressure number belongs to that valve. Preserve which modality supplied each clue. Federated budgets prevent one long transcript from consuming every result slot.

Account for timing errors

Automatic speech recognition can mishear part numbers, names and negation. Speaker diarization can swap labels after cross-talk. Store word-level confidence or review status where available, and include a small playback margin around candidate spans. Avoid letting margins turn a thirty-second citation into an unrelated ten-minute clip. When the spoken answer is uncertain, retrieve nearby segments or abstain rather than silently repairing the transcript. Abstention should remain available after a high ranking score.

Check the answer at playback time

A timestamp is a pointer, not proof. The final claim should be checked against the media span and any displayed text within it. For a question about who approved a release, both speaker attribution and the words of approval matter. If the text says 'not approved', a frame showing a green button cannot reverse it. Keep transcript and frame citations separate when both are needed. Support checks must inspect the exact moment behind each claim.

Evaluate with time tolerance

Judge answer-bearing intervals, not just media IDs. Measure whether the right asset entered the candidate set, whether an overlapping interval appeared in the top window, and whether the final answer cited a span narrow enough to inspect. Include edits, repeated phrases, noisy speech, overlapping speakers and purely visual evidence. Report timing error and missing-evidence abstention separately. A result that finds the correct meeting but points nine minutes late should fail the timestamp test.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MediaSegment:
    asset_id: str
    version: str
    start_ms: int
    end_ms: int
    speaker: str
    transcript: str

def timed_matches(segments: list[MediaSegment], asset_id: str,
                  version: str, phrase: str) -> list[tuple[int, int, str]]:
    matches = []
    for segment in segments:
        if segment.start_ms < 0 or segment.end_ms <= segment.start_ms:
            raise ValueError("invalid media interval")
        if segment.asset_id == asset_id and segment.version == version \
                and phrase.casefold() in segment.transcript.casefold():
            matches.append((segment.start_ms, segment.end_ms, segment.speaker))
    return matches

meeting = [MediaSegment("release-briefing", "cut-3", 83000, 97000,
                        "release-lead", "The patch remains blocked."),
           MediaSegment("release-briefing", "cut-2", 79000, 93000,
                        "release-lead", "The patch is approved.")]
assert timed_matches(meeting, "release-briefing", "cut-3", "blocked") == [
    (83000, 97000, "release-lead")]
assert timed_matches(meeting, "release-briefing", "cut-3", "approved") == []

Performance and operating cost

The baseline scans S segments in O(S) time and stores O(K) matches. A transcript term index narrows spoken candidates; visual embeddings add frame-sampling, index storage and ranking costs. Higher sampling density improves access to brief events but increases storage and search work. Evaluate timestamp recall against that cost, rather than indexing every frame by default.

Common Mistakes

  • Returning a meeting title without a timecoded supporting span.
  • Mixing transcript timestamps from one cut with video from another.
  • Treating noisy automatic captions as verified words.
  • Using a visual match to assert a speaker's words without checking the audio.

Validation drill

Judge 39 questions over six edited recordings. Include repeated phrases, overlapping speakers and silent visual events; measure asset recall, interval overlap, speaker accuracy and cited-span width.

title: Hard-negative mining without training against true answers
summary: Choose informative retrieval distractors while auditing labels, lineage and split leakage before model training.
body:
Choose informative retrieval distractors while auditing labels, lineage and split leakage before model training.

Define the negative precisely

A hard negative is a passage that resembles a relevant answer but does not satisfy the query. For a request for pump P-47's current relief limit, an old revision or P-48's limit may be informative distractors. A second valid P-47 passage is a false negative even if the judgment file omitted it. Before mining, specify query intent, time boundary, tenant and what counts as support. Judgment labels should allow multiple positives and an uncertain state; a missing label is not proof of irrelevance.

Mine from several candidate pools

Lexical search yields near-word matches; dense retrieval yields semantic neighbors; a reranker can find subtle confusions. Sample within authorized, training-eligible corpora and record which model and index version produced each candidate. Balance easy and hard distractors so training does not only distinguish almost-identical policies. A candidate that is too hard may actually be another answer, especially when multiple documents repeat the same fact. Lineage checks help distinguish a copied positive from a real contradiction.

Audit false negatives before training

Compare each mined candidate with all known positives by document lineage, answer entity, valid interval and evidence span. Flag near-identical answers and ambiguous cases for human review. Do not automatically turn every high-scoring unlabeled passage into a negative. If the corpus has a corrected revision, the old passage may be a legitimate negative for a current-policy query but a positive for an as-of query. Temporal eligibility belongs in the label, not only the search filter.

Prevent split leakage

A test question and a training question can differ in wording while pointing to the same source paragraph. Split by source lineage or entity family when the evaluation asks for transfer to unseen material. Keep mined examples from a fixed training snapshot; a later corpus refresh must not add evaluation positives to the training pool. Log query ID, passage ID, source revision, mine score, decision and reviewer. Release gates should compare held-out supported recall, not training loss alone.

Measure the cost of hardness

Run an ablation with the same query set and candidate budget: baseline negatives, reviewed hard negatives, and mixed difficulty. Track false-negative audit rate, candidate recall, top-k judged relevance and answer support on held-out slices. If mining improves ranking for common queries but harms a rare language or recent-policy slice, do not ship the aggregate gain as universal. Keep a small manual audit of top-ranked new negatives after each mining cycle; retriever changes alter which mistakes are selected next.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class MinedPassage:
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    lineage: str
    entity_id: str
    label: str
    score: float

def reviewed_negatives(candidates: list[MinedPassage], tenant: str,
                       positive_lineages: set[str], entity_id: str) -> list[str]:
    selected = [candidate for candidate in candidates
                if candidate.tenant == tenant and candidate.label == "negative"
                and candidate.lineage not in positive_lineages
                and candidate.entity_id != entity_id]
    return [candidate.passage_id for candidate in
            sorted(selected, key=lambda item: item.score, reverse=True)]

pool = [MinedPassage("pump-48", "plant-a", "manual-48", "pump-p48", "negative", .94),
        MinedPassage("copied-p47", "plant-a", "manual-47", "pump-p47", "negative", .99),
        MinedPassage("unreviewed", "plant-a", "manual-52", "pump-p52", "unknown", .96),
        MinedPassage("private", "plant-b", "manual-49", "pump-p49", "negative", .98)]
assert reviewed_negatives(pool, "plant-a", {"manual-47"}, "pump-p47") == ["pump-48"]

Performance and operating cost

Filtering N mined candidates costs O(N log N) time because the sample sorts by score, with O(N) extra space; a bounded top-k heap can reduce sorting work when N is large. The expensive part is creating and auditing labels: retrieval calls, cross-source comparisons and human adjudication. Spend that budget on candidates likely to change a decision, not on repeated copies of the same mistake.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating every unlabeled retrieved passage as a negative.
  • Mining a copied positive into the negative pool because it has a new URL.
  • Letting test-source lineages enter the training candidate pool.
  • Judging the mining run only by training loss or one aggregate retrieval score.

Validation drill

Mine 79 candidates for 23 queries from lexical and dense pools. Review ambiguous matches, split by document lineage, and compare held-out top-five relevance and supported-answer rate before accepting the new negatives.

title: OCR retrieval: preserve reading order, page regions and uncertainty
summary: Index scanned documents as positioned evidence rather than flattening columns, captions and doubtful characters into one text stream.
body:
Index scanned documents as positioned evidence rather than flattening columns, captions and doubtful characters into one text stream.

Keep the page geometry

OCR retrieval searches text extracted from scans while preserving where each token appeared. The page image is the source; recognized text is a fallible interpretation. Store document revision, page number, bounding box, block type, reading-order position and extraction confidence with each passage. A two-column safety sheet can interleave warnings with unrelated specifications if its text is flattened by coordinate order alone. Extraction provenance should let a reviewer reopen the precise image region behind a candidate.

Reconstruct blocks before chunks

Detect headings, paragraphs, footnotes, tables and captions as separate blocks, then connect them in a plausible reading order. A caption can belong to a diagram beside it rather than the paragraph directly above it. Chunk within a block or a justified parent section; crossing column boundaries can invent a sentence that was never printed. Keep alternative reading-order hypotheses when a page is ambiguous. Hierarchical retrieval can route by section while leaving the cited evidence on the original page region.

Handle uncertain characters

A scan may confuse P-47 with P-41 or 83 kPa with 88 kPa. Record character- or token-level confidence when the OCR engine provides it. Exact-match retrieval of identifiers should search the recognized string and, within a bounded error budget, reviewed alternatives. Do not silently replace low-confidence digits with a fluent guess. For a numeric answer, require the number and unit to be legible in the image or verified by an independent source. Numeric cell context matters even when the table was recognized correctly.

Separate search from support

OCR text is useful for candidate generation, but an answer citing a scan needs a page and a region. A high ranking score cannot validate an illegible number. If a candidate's decisive token is below the review threshold, send the region to a human or abstain. Preserve redaction masks in both OCR text and image crops; otherwise a search result might expose text that the displayed image hides. Permission rules apply to page metadata and crops as well as text.

Judge image-grounded retrieval

Build queries for split columns, rotated labels, handwriting, captions, tables, near-identical part numbers and pages with no answer. Score page recall, region overlap, reading-order integrity and final claim support separately. A system that finds the correct PDF but cites the wrong column should fail. Record OCR engine and layout model versions so a model upgrade can be compared on exactly the same scanned pages. Review regressions on low-resolution and multilingual slices rather than accepting one aggregate score.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PageBlock:
    document_id: str
    page: int
    column: int
    order: int
    confidence: float
    text: str

def ordered_evidence(blocks: list[PageBlock], document_id: str,
                     minimum_confidence: float) -> list[PageBlock]:
    if not 0 <= minimum_confidence <= 1:
        raise ValueError("confidence threshold outside [0, 1]")
    eligible = [block for block in blocks if block.document_id == document_id
                and block.confidence >= minimum_confidence]
    return sorted(eligible, key=lambda block: (block.page, block.column, block.order))

scan = [PageBlock("manual-r4", 3, 2, 1, .97, "Pump P-47 limit: 83 kPa"),
        PageBlock("manual-r4", 3, 1, 1, .99, "Hydraulic system"),
        PageBlock("manual-r4", 3, 2, 2, .44, "Unclear value: 88?"),
        PageBlock("manual-r3", 3, 2, 1, .99, "Pump P-47 limit: 71 kPa")]
assert [block.text for block in ordered_evidence(scan, "manual-r4", .85)] == [
    "Hydraulic system", "Pump P-47 limit: 83 kPa"]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting B blocks costs O(B log B) time and O(B) output space. OCR and layout inference cost far more than the ordering operation, so cache extraction by document hash and model version. Crops, coordinates and alternate transcripts add storage. Higher-resolution rescans can improve evidence quality but increase processing and review cost; target them at low-confidence answer-bearing regions.

Common Mistakes

  • Concatenating two columns into a fabricated sentence.
  • Treating an OCR guess for a digit as verified evidence.
  • Citing only a PDF title when the answer lives in one page region.
  • Redacting the image but leaving its recognized text searchable.

Validation drill

Scan 47 pages with columns, tables and captions. Judge 37 questions and require page-region overlap, correct number and unit, and an abstention when the decisive characters remain uncertain.

title: Geospatial retrieval: combine meaning, distance and jurisdiction
summary: Find nearby eligible evidence with explicit coordinate systems, radius limits and geographic provenance.
body:
Find nearby eligible evidence with explicit coordinate systems, radius limits and geographic provenance.

Define what the location means

Geospatial retrieval finds records whose physical coverage matters to the query. 'Show repair notices near station P-47' could mean notices located at a point, assets within a radius, or policies applying to a jurisdiction polygon. Those are different predicates. Store geometry type, coordinate reference system, accuracy, valid interval and source identity with the record. A document mentioning a city name is not necessarily located there. Query routing should distinguish place intent from a text-only mention before choosing a spatial operation.

Filter space before semantic rank

Apply tenant permission, active revision and geographic eligibility before semantic ranking. A nearby restricted maintenance ticket should not appear in a result count, map marker or generated answer. Use an indexed radius predicate for point proximity, then compute exact distance for candidates; use containment or intersection for coverage areas. Do not compare raw latitude-longitude degree differences with a radius in meters. Corpus permissions remain part of the spatial query, not a presentation-layer patch.

Keep uncertainty visible

A geocoded address may identify a street rather than a building. A device location can drift; a service district boundary can change. Store location accuracy and boundary version, and avoid a definitive inside/outside claim when an uncertainty circle crosses the edge. For a 'within 2 km' question, state whether distance is straight-line, walking route or drive time. The retrieval result should include the location source and the calculated distance, so the claim can be checked. Temporal retrieval governs historical boundaries.

Combine place and text without score confusion

A spatial index can return a bounded set of eligible records, after which lexical or vector ranking identifies the relevant notice. For broad areas, text search may produce candidates first, followed by exact geometry checks. Choose order from selectivity and cost, but keep both filters mandatory. Ranking a notice highly cannot make an out-of-area record eligible. Do not merge kilometers and semantic similarity into one unexplained scalar. Source budgets can reserve results across nearby notices and region-wide rules.

Test boundaries, not just centers

Judge cases on both sides of a district border, exactly at the radius, with missing coordinates, stale geocodes, overlapping regions and different tenant scopes. Report eligible-record recall separately from relevance and answer support. Include a named location that appears in a document body but lies outside its service area. A system that finds the right topic and wrong jurisdiction must fail even if its prose sounds plausible. Capture geometry version and distance method in the evaluation trace.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from math import asin, cos, radians, sin, sqrt

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ServiceNotice:
    notice_id: str
    tenant: str
    latitude: float
    longitude: float
    text: str

def distance_km(lat_a: float, lon_a: float, lat_b: float, lon_b: float) -> float:
    if any(not -90 <= lat <= 90 for lat in (lat_a, lat_b)):
        raise ValueError("invalid latitude")
    if any(not -180 <= lon <= 180 for lon in (lon_a, lon_b)):
        raise ValueError("invalid longitude")
    north = radians(lat_b - lat_a)
    east = radians(lon_b - lon_a)
    arc = sin(north / 2) ** 2 + cos(radians(lat_a)) * cos(radians(lat_b)) * sin(east / 2) ** 2
    return 2 * 6371.0088 * asin(min(1.0, sqrt(arc)))

def nearby(notices: list[ServiceNotice], tenant: str,
           latitude: float, longitude: float, radius_km: float) -> list[str]:
    if radius_km < 0:
        raise ValueError("negative radius")
    return [notice.notice_id for notice in notices if notice.tenant == tenant
            and distance_km(latitude, longitude, notice.latitude, notice.longitude) <= radius_km]

notices = [ServiceNotice("pump-47", "north", 28.6139, 77.2090, "Valve inspection"),
           ServiceNotice("pump-83", "north", 28.7041, 77.1025, "Valve inspection"),
           ServiceNotice("private", "south", 28.6139, 77.2090, "Valve inspection")]
assert nearby(notices, "north", 28.6139, 77.2090, 2) == ["pump-47"]

Performance and operating cost

The transparent scan costs O(N) distance calculations and O(K) output space for K matches. A spatial index narrows large corpora before exact distance checks; maintaining it adds storage and write work. Haversine computes a spherical straight-line approximation, not route distance or polygon coverage. Use a geography-aware database predicate for production radius searches and measure boundary errors where accuracy matters.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing coordinate degrees directly with kilometers.
  • Treating a place name in text as a verified record location.
  • Filtering geography after showing restricted candidate metadata.
  • Ignoring location uncertainty near a boundary.

Validation drill

Prepare 61 notices across two districts with five missing geocodes and seven boundary cases. Compare point-radius and jurisdiction queries, reporting eligible recall, false inclusions and supported location claims.

title: Database retrieval: link a question to schema and trace the rows
summary: Retrieve structured answers with approved query plans, row-level permissions and verifiable source identifiers.
body:
Retrieve structured answers with approved query plans, row-level permissions and verifiable source identifiers.

Retrieve a schema contract first

Database retrieval maps a question to tables, columns, joins and filters before reading rows. A request for unpaid invoices from branch 47 should identify invoice status, branch ID and billing date; an embedding over column descriptions may help discover candidates but cannot define the final join. Store approved schema descriptions, key relationships and field meanings. A column named amount may be gross, net or settled. Intent routing should distinguish a row lookup from a policy explanation or a calculation.

Keep query generation bounded

Treat a proposed SQL query as untrusted input. Constrain it to an allowlisted read-only view or a small set of approved query templates. Bind values as parameters, cap rows and time, and reject mutations or cross-tenant joins. Parsing a generated string for the word SELECT alone is not a security boundary; database permissions and row-level security must enforce scope. Access control belongs at the data source as well as in the retrieval layer.

Carry row provenance into the answer

Return primary keys, source table or view, query template version, data snapshot and effective filters with each result. An aggregate such as '47 unpaid invoices' needs a traceable query and the population definition, not merely a plausible sentence. If a join multiplies rows, count distinct invoice IDs or fix the join before answering. For a cell-level claim, identify both the row and column. Table evidence requires the unit and row context that make a number meaningful.

Separate retrieval from computation

A row set may require arithmetic after retrieval, but that computation should be deterministic and reviewable. Currency conversion needs an explicit rate and as-of date; a missing rate should cause a partial answer or abstention. A result that combines transactional rows with a document policy needs separate citations to each source. Evidence chains should show which source supplies the rule and which supplies the transaction facts.

Evaluate query and result failures

Judge schema linking, authorized row recall, predicate accuracy, join cardinality and final answer support separately. Include duplicate line items, soft-deleted records, null status, renamed columns and time-zone boundaries. A syntactically valid query can be semantically wrong: selecting posted_at instead of due_at may produce credible but incorrect overdue counts. Compare the executed query and returned row IDs against a reviewed reference set; do not grade only the final prose.

Worked contract

import sqlite3

connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
connection.execute("CREATE TABLE invoices (invoice_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, tenant TEXT, branch INTEGER, status TEXT, amount_cents INTEGER)")
connection.executemany("INSERT INTO invoices VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    ("INV-47", "north", 47, "unpaid", 8300),
    ("INV-48", "north", 47, "paid", 4700),
    ("INV-49", "south", 47, "unpaid", 9900),
])

def unpaid_invoices(tenant: str, branch: int) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    return connection.execute(
        "SELECT invoice_id, amount_cents FROM invoices "
        "WHERE tenant = ? AND branch = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY invoice_id LIMIT 83",
        (tenant, branch, "unpaid"),
    ).fetchall()

assert unpaid_invoices("north", 47) == [("INV-47", 8300)]
connection.close()

Performance and operating cost

With an index on tenant, branch and status, a selective lookup can avoid scanning every invoice; the exact cost depends on the planner and row count. The in-memory example is tiny, but a production read needs a row cap, execution timeout and query plan check. Materializing R result rows costs O(R) memory; stream large exports rather than placing them in an answer context.

Common Mistakes

  • Executing free-form generated SQL with broad database privileges.
  • Using a similarly named amount column without checking its business definition.
  • Counting joined line items as distinct invoices.
  • Omitting row IDs and filter values from an aggregate's audit trace.

Validation drill

Create 43 questions against invoices, payments and branch tables. Include duplicate line items, nulls and two tenants. Require matching row IDs, approved schema paths, correct aggregate populations and no cross-tenant disclosure.

title: Conversational retrieval: rewrite the follow-up without changing its scope
summary: Resolve references in a dialogue while carrying only the constraints that still apply to the current search turn.
body:
Resolve references in a dialogue while carrying only the constraints that still apply to the current search turn.

Make the current turn searchable

Conversational retrieval turns a context-dependent follow-up into a standalone search request. After 'What is the P-47 limit in revision r4?', 'What about the old one?' may refer to the same pump and a prior revision. A rewrite should capture that relation without inventing a date or unit. Keep the raw user text, the selected antecedent and the resolved query in the trace. Query routing should use the resolved intent only after checking that the reference is unambiguous.

Carry constraints with expiration

Tenant identity and authorization come from the active session, never from an earlier answer string. Topic, entity and date constraints may carry forward for one turn, but they can also be overridden. 'Now compare P-48' replaces P-47; 'in the south plant' changes place but must not grant access to south-plant records. Track each constraint's origin, confidence and scope, then apply explicit user changes before searching. Conversation caches need the resulting permission and constraint identity in their keys.

Ask when reference resolution is unsafe

'What about that one?' may point to two passages from the previous answer. Picking one silently can produce a well-cited answer to the wrong question. Clarify when multiple antecedents remain plausible, or search both only if a comparison was requested and permissions allow both. Do not use the last retrieved passage as the default referent merely because it was ranked first. A bounded clarification step is cheaper than a confident but irrelevant retrieval. Abstention also applies to unresolved dialogue state.

Prevent answer contamination

The previous assistant answer may be wrong, incomplete or injected. Rewrites should rely on authenticated conversation metadata and user turns, then retrieve fresh source evidence. Do not copy a previous answer's unsupported number into the next query as though it were a fact. When the user asks 'why did that change?', retrieve both applicable revisions and compare their cited text. Temporal retrieval preserves the two evidence sets rather than blending old and new values.

Judge turn-by-turn retrieval

Evaluate follow-ups with pronouns, topic switches, corrections, permission changes, long gaps and contradictory prior answers. Score resolved entity and constraints before measuring passage recall and final support. A system can retrieve the correct passage for a wrong rewrite by luck; that should not hide the rewrite defect. Store the conversation turn ID and corpus generation in the trace. When a user revokes or changes scope, previously cached passages must not reappear in later turns.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchTurn:
    entity: str | None
    revision: str | None
    tenant: str

def resolve_follow_up(previous: SearchTurn, current_text: str,
                      active_tenant: str) -> SearchTurn:
    text = current_text.casefold()
    if "p-48" in text:
        entity = "P-48"
    elif "p-47" in text:
        entity = "P-47"
    elif "old one" in text and previous.entity:
        entity = previous.entity
    else:
        raise ValueError("ambiguous entity; ask for clarification")
    revision = "previous" if "old one" in text else None
    return SearchTurn(entity, revision, active_tenant)

last_turn = SearchTurn("P-47", "r4", "north")
assert resolve_follow_up(last_turn, "What about the old one?", "north") == SearchTurn(
    "P-47", "previous", "north")
assert resolve_follow_up(last_turn, "Now compare P-48", "north") == SearchTurn(
    "P-48", None, "north")

Performance and operating cost

The example resolves one turn in O(L) time for text length L and O(1) additional state. A production resolver may inspect a bounded window of T turns, increasing work with that window and with each retrieval retry. Avoid feeding the entire dialogue into every search when only an explicit entity and recent correction are needed. Record and evaluate clarification frequency as part of latency and success.

Common Mistakes

  • Carrying an old entity after the user explicitly switched topics.
  • Treating a prior assistant answer as a verified source for the next query.
  • Taking tenant access from dialogue text instead of the active session.
  • Resolving an ambiguous pronoun to the first-ranked passage without asking.

Validation drill

Write 59 multi-turn queries with corrections, topic changes and ambiguous references. Record rewrite accuracy, authorized passage recall and final support, and require clarification for turns with no unique antecedent.

title: Image-region retrieval: cite the object, not merely the image
summary: Retrieve a bounded visual region and preserve its asset version, crop coordinates and supporting labels.
body:
Retrieve a bounded visual region and preserve its asset version, crop coordinates and supporting labels.

Index regions with their parent asset

Image-region retrieval searches a part of an image that can support a specific claim. A maintenance photo may show several pumps, warning tags and gauges; an image-level match for 'P-47 gauge' says little about which gauge carries the reading. Store asset ID, version, image dimensions, region coordinates and any reviewed label. A crop is not an independent source: it inherits access rules and revision from the parent image. Asset identity prevents a crop coordinate from silently pointing at a replacement photograph.

Generate and score candidates

Regions can come from reviewed annotations, object proposals or a grid of crops. Search their labels and visual representations, then cap the candidate window before expensive inspection. Overlapping proposals for one object should not consume every slot. Group them by parent asset and approximate overlap, retaining a precise box when evidence supports it. A predicted label is a search hint, not proof that the pictured valve is P-47. Duplicate control helps keep copied crops from masquerading as independent sightings.

Ground the claim spatially

The answer should point to a region whose visible pixels support it. A caption outside the crop may identify the object, but the caption and image need separate provenance. If the query asks whether a red lockout tag is attached, a close crop of the tag alone might hide whether it is attached to the requested pump. Keep enough surrounding context to verify the relationship without turning the citation into the whole image. Claim support must inspect the crop and its parent context.

Account for transformations

Resizing, rotation and cropping change coordinates. Store boxes in a stable source coordinate system and record any display transform; never reuse pixel positions on a newly cropped image without mapping them. Check privacy masks at the source and crop levels. A face blurred in the full image can reappear if an unredacted original is cropped and served separately. Reject regions whose bounds fall outside the asset or whose version mismatches the current display. Lifecycle rules include withdrawing all derived crops after an asset is removed.

Evaluate region-level evidence

Judge both parent-image recall and region overlap with the answer-bearing object. Include small objects, similar gauges, partially occluded labels, repeated components and misleading captions. A system that finds the correct photo but draws a box around the wrong gauge should fail. Track unsupported confident labels and missing-evidence abstentions separately. Measure the cost of finer crops against their improvement in supported claims, rather than indexing thousands of near-identical patches without a clear gain.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ImageRegion:
    asset_id: str
    version: str
    width: int
    height: int
    box: tuple[int, int, int, int]
    label: str

def checked_region(region: ImageRegion, expected_version: str) -> tuple[float, float, float, float]:
    if region.version != expected_version:
        raise ValueError("asset version mismatch")
    left, top, right, bottom = region.box
    if region.width <= 0 or region.height <= 0 or not (0 <= left < right <= region.width):
        raise ValueError("invalid horizontal bounds")
    if not 0 <= top < bottom <= region.height:
        raise ValueError("invalid vertical bounds")
    return (left / region.width, top / region.height,
            right / region.width, bottom / region.height)

gauge = ImageRegion("plant-photo-47", "v3", 1200, 800,
                    (240, 160, 600, 560), "P-47 pressure gauge")
assert checked_region(gauge, "v3") == (.2, .2, .5, .7)
try:
    checked_region(gauge, "v2")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("stale crop accepted")

Performance and operating cost

Validating one region is O(1) time and space. A full image with R proposed regions needs storage and embedding work proportional to R, plus overlap grouping if many proposals duplicate the same object. Candidate generation can be bounded by asset and region counts; visual inspection is the costly stage. Keep source-resolution crops only for regions that survive retrieval and access checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Citing an image when the requested object is not identifiable within it.
  • Using crop coordinates from a different image version.
  • Treating a detector's label as verified identity.
  • Serving an unredacted crop of a redacted parent asset.

title: Event-window retrieval: answer from complete time slices
summary: Retrieve logs and measurements with explicit event time, observation time, window bounds and missing-data behavior.
body:
Retrieve logs and measurements with explicit event time, observation time, window bounds and missing-data behavior.

Define the clock and window

Event-window retrieval finds records that occurred in a requested interval, not merely records indexed recently. A query about pump P-47 alarms between 09:00 and 09:30 must use event time; observation time describes when the collector received a record. Late arrivals and device clock drift can make those differ. Store both clocks, source ID, event ID and a normalized time zone. Use half-open windows so adjacent intervals do not count the same event twice. Temporal retrieval supplies the same boundary discipline for document validity, but event streams have additional lateness and completeness issues.

Join events by stable identity

A trace ID, asset ID or incident ID can join logs from several services. Free-text similarity between two error messages is not sufficient to claim they describe the same incident. Apply tenant and asset filters before joining, then retain each event's source and original timestamp. A repeated warning may be a retry of one operation or many separate failures; deduplicate only with a stable event or request identity. Duplicate evidence rules keep retries from inflating a count.

Treat gaps as unknown

No retrieved alarm is not proof that no alarm occurred. The collector may have been offline, the index may lag, or the query may cover a shard not searched. Record source watermarks and missing intervals. When a window is incomplete, report the covered interval and abstain from a global zero count. A late event can change a previously computed result; either revise the answer or pin it to a snapshot and explain the cutoff. Freshness controls should expose that cutoff in the trace.

Separate retrieval from aggregation

Retrieve the eligible events first, then compute counts, maxima or sequences deterministically. A p95 latency claim requires enough samples and an explicit percentile method; a single high value is not the percentile. For a sequence question, preserve ordering by event time and break ties with stable IDs. Apply units and sampling rates before combining sensor readings. Numeric context is as important for telemetry as it is for a table cell.

Evaluate late and partial data

Build cases with out-of-order arrivals, clock skew, duplicate retries, collector outages, overlapping windows and no matching events. Judge event recall, window-boundary correctness, join identity, completeness detection and final answer support separately. A high recall score on available records can still mask an incorrect 'nothing happened' answer when a source is missing. Keep both query time and data snapshot in the evaluation record so later backfills do not silently change the expected result.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timezone

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class AlarmEvent:
    event_id: str
    tenant: str
    asset_id: str
    occurred_at: datetime
    observed_at: datetime

def window_events(events: list[AlarmEvent], tenant: str, asset_id: str,
                  start: datetime, end: datetime) -> list[str]:
    if start.tzinfo is None or end.tzinfo is None or end <= start:
        raise ValueError("window needs ordered aware datetimes")
    seen: set[str] = set()
    selected: list[str] = []
    for event in sorted(events, key=lambda item: (item.occurred_at, item.event_id)):
        if event.tenant == tenant and event.asset_id == asset_id \
                and start <= event.occurred_at < end and event.event_id not in seen:
            seen.add(event.event_id)
            selected.append(event.event_id)
    return selected

utc = timezone.utc
event_time = datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 17, tzinfo=utc)
alarms = [AlarmEvent("alarm-47", "north", "P-47", event_time,
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 39, tzinfo=utc)),
          AlarmEvent("alarm-47", "north", "P-47", event_time,
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 40, tzinfo=utc))]
assert window_events(alarms, "north", "P-47",
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 0, tzinfo=utc),
                     datetime(2026, 10, 7, 9, 30, tzinfo=utc)) == ["alarm-47"]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N events costs O(N log N) time and O(N) space in the example; an index ordered by tenant, asset and event time narrows production windows. Watermarks and coverage records add modest metadata but are necessary for trustworthy zero-result answers. Wider windows increase scanned events and aggregation cost, so apply a query limit and stream large results.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering by collector arrival time when the question asks when an event occurred.
  • Calling an incomplete window empty.
  • Counting duplicate retries as independent alarms.
  • Using naive local timestamps across a daylight-saving boundary.

Validation drill

Build 67 events over three assets with delayed arrivals and two collector gaps. Judge 31 window questions, requiring correct half-open boundaries and an explicit incomplete-data result where coverage is missing.

title: Entity linking for retrieval: resolve aliases before searching facts
summary: Map mentions to stable entity IDs while retaining ambiguity, alias provenance and out-of-catalog behavior.
body:
Map mentions to stable entity IDs while retaining ambiguity, alias provenance and out-of-catalog behavior.

Separate mention from identity

Entity linking maps a surface mention in a query to a canonical entity ID. 'P-47' might identify a pump in one plant and a permit in another; spelling alone is not identity. Store type, tenant, site, active interval and reviewed aliases with each entity. Preserve the original mention in the search trace, and do not replace it with a canonical ID until context establishes the match. Multilingual retrieval may supply transliterated aliases, but an alias can still be shared by distinct entities.

Generate candidates then decide

Exact alias search produces candidates. Type constraints, nearby words, site and time narrow them; semantic similarity can rank the remainder. Keep a no-match outcome for an unknown entity instead of forcing every mention onto the closest catalog entry. If two candidates remain plausible, ask for a clarifier or search both as explicitly separate interpretations. Conversation state can supply an antecedent, but an old assistant answer is not authoritative identity evidence.

Carry identity through evidence

After linking, retrieve passages tagged with the stable entity ID and current authorization scope. A document can mention several entities, so a page-level tag may be too coarse: the cited span must actually refer to the selected entity. If an entity is renamed, maintain alias history and effective dates rather than rewriting old documents. If IDs are merged or split, preserve the mapping event; otherwise historical citations can point to a different object. Chunk identity and entity identity solve different problems and both belong in the trace.

Guard against alias poisoning

User-submitted content may claim that an unrelated part number is an alias for a restricted asset. Accept aliases only from reviewed catalog changes, not from retrieved passages or prompt text. Apply access checks to candidate IDs and to their associated documents; even an ambiguous candidate list can leak a private device name. Normalize Unicode carefully, but do not erase distinctions that matter in identifiers. Tool boundaries keep source text from changing the resolver's catalog.

Evaluate more than top-one accuracy

Judge exact aliases, spelling changes, transliterations, shared names, unknown entities and historical renames. Measure candidate recall, correct-ID selection, abstention for unknown mentions, and downstream supported answers. A top-one metric alone rewards a resolver that confidently guesses on every unknown name. Track entity type and language slices separately. Review cases where linking is correct but the retrieved passage refers to a different entity in the same document; that is an evidence-span error, not a linking success.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
import unicodedata

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CatalogEntity:
    entity_id: str
    tenant: str
    kind: str
    site: str
    aliases: tuple[str, ...]

def alias_key(value: str) -> str:
    return unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", value).casefold().strip()

def resolve_entity(catalog: list[CatalogEntity], tenant: str, kind: str,
                   site: str, mention: str) -> str | None:
    matches = [entry.entity_id for entry in catalog
               if entry.tenant == tenant and entry.kind == kind and entry.site == site
               and alias_key(mention) in {alias_key(alias) for alias in entry.aliases}]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError("ambiguous alias; request clarification")
    return matches[0] if matches else None

catalog = [CatalogEntity("pump-47-north", "north", "pump", "plant-a", ("P-47", "Pump 47")),
           CatalogEntity("permit-47-north", "north", "permit", "plant-a", ("P-47",)),
           CatalogEntity("pump-47-south", "south", "pump", "plant-b", ("P-47",))]
assert resolve_entity(catalog, "north", "pump", "plant-a", "P-47") == "pump-47-north"
assert resolve_entity(catalog, "north", "pump", "plant-a", "P-48") is None

Performance and operating cost

The transparent scan checks N catalog entries and up to A aliases per entry, costing O(NA) time with temporary alias sets. An alias index keyed by normalized mention, tenant and type reduces candidate lookup, but it must update atomically with catalog changes. Preserve multiple candidates until context resolves them; forcing one ID can be cheaper per query but costlier in downstream incorrect answers.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a shared alias as a globally unique entity ID.
  • Forcing unknown mentions onto the nearest catalog item.
  • Letting retrieved text edit the trusted alias catalog.
  • Tagging a whole document as support when its cited span refers to another entity.

Validation drill

Create 83 mentions across two tenants and three entity types, including 17 ambiguous aliases and nine unknowns. Score correct IDs, ambiguity handling, unknown abstention and supported downstream passages.
