title: Counterfactual retrieval tests: change one fact and trace the failure
summary: Probe retrieval and answer support with controlled evidence edits, plausible distractors and first-loss diagnosis.
body:
Probe retrieval and answer support with controlled evidence edits, plausible distractors and first-loss diagnosis.

Change one controlled variable

A counterfactual retrieval test alters an evidence fact while keeping the rest of the query and corpus stable. Replace a pump limit of 83 kPa with 67 kPa in a synthetic revision, or swap the relevant entity ID, then check whether retrieval and the answer respond to that change. The point is to expose reliance on memorized or distracting text. Use synthetic, clearly isolated fixtures; never mutate a production source or present a test revision as a real policy. Release evaluation can run these cases as a separate judged slice.

Keep labels and access coherent

When a fact changes, update the gold passage, expected answer, revision metadata and all copied evidence that derives from it. Leave unrelated passages unchanged. A distractor can be highly similar yet invalid because its entity, date, tenant or negation differs. If the counterfactual version conflicts with a legitimate original left in the same eligible corpus, the expected behavior may be conflict reporting, not a forced new number. Lineage controls help distinguish an accidental duplicate from independent contradictory evidence.

Locate the first loss

Trace whether the edited passage enters the lexical or vector candidate pool, survives filters and reranking, reaches the context window, and supports the final claim. A wrong answer with the correct passage in context is an answer-use failure; a correct answer after the passage was excluded may indicate memorization or leakage. Do not call both failures 'retrieval quality'. Retrieval traces should carry candidate IDs and score stages so the first bad decision is visible.

Probe distractors without gaming them

Vary one failure mode at a time: wrong part number, old revision, copied note, negated sentence, unit mismatch or unauthorized source. Include a genuinely unanswerable case. A model might pass a simple value swap but fail when the old value appears in a top-ranked stale document. Keep distractor language natural and the target question unchanged. Avoid test cases whose answer is visible in the file name or test label. Hard-negative audits keep distractors from accidentally becoming valid answers.

Report stability and sensitivity

The system should remain stable when irrelevant text changes and change when the supporting fact changes. Measure candidate recall, supported top-one answer, contradiction detection and abstention for each perturbation type. Compare against the same corpus snapshot and model versions. A pass rate that averages easy no-op edits with hard entity swaps obscures the actual weakness; keep per-perturbation slices. Review a sample of failures manually to confirm that the synthetic edit did not create an unintended second answer.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceRecord:
    passage_id: str
    entity_id: str
    revision: str
    value_kpa: int

def answer_limit(records: list[EvidenceRecord], entity_id: str,
                 revision: str) -> int | None:
    matches = [record.value_kpa for record in records
               if record.entity_id == entity_id and record.revision == revision]
    if len(matches) > 1:
        raise ValueError("conflicting eligible evidence")
    return matches[0] if matches else None

original = EvidenceRecord("manual-p47-r4", "pump-p47", "r4", 83)
distractor = EvidenceRecord("manual-p48-r4", "pump-p48", "r4", 83)
edited = replace(original, value_kpa=67)
assert answer_limit([original, distractor], "pump-p47", "r4") == 83
assert answer_limit([edited, distractor], "pump-p47", "r4") == 67
assert answer_limit([distractor], "pump-p47", "r4") is None

Performance and operating cost

Creating a synthetic variant costs O(C) for C copied records and running the baseline scan costs O(C) time with O(K) match space. The real expense is repeated retrieval and answer generation across perturbation suites. Keep fixtures small and deterministic for every commit, then run a wider judged sample before a release. Store only synthetic values in test logs so a reviewer cannot confuse them with production facts.

Common Mistakes

  • Changing a value without changing its expected answer and revision label.
  • Leaving an eligible original passage that makes the edited answer ambiguous.
  • Calling a memorized correct answer a retrieval success when evidence never entered context.
  • Averaging all perturbation types into one score that hides a severe slice failure.

Validation drill

Construct 47 synthetic question variants across value, entity, negation, date and permission edits. Record the first pipeline stage that loses the required evidence and whether the final answer changes only when it should.

title: Lexical retrieval: analyzers, fields and exact identifiers
summary: Keep text analysis and exact identifiers separate so keyword retrieval finds the right record without changing its identity.
body:
Keep text analysis and exact identifiers separate so keyword retrieval finds the right record without changing its identity.

Define an analyzer contract

A lexical analyzer converts source text and query text into comparable terms. Character cleanup, tokenization, case handling, stop words and synonym expansion all affect which documents can enter the candidate set. Record the analyzer version alongside the index; otherwise a query may be analyzed differently from the stored text after a configuration change. A simple token list is useful for an experiment, but a production inverted index also stores postings, field identity and often positions for phrase matching. Hybrid retrieval only benefits from its lexical arm when that arm can actually find the required term.

Do not normalize away identifiers

A part number such as P-47 is an identity constraint, not a bag of words. If punctuation splitting turns it into P and 47, a document about pump P-48 and drawing 47 can appear relevant. Store the canonical part ID in a keyword field with a deliberately narrow normalizer, and filter on it before ranking free text. Preserve the original display form for citations. Likewise, tenant, revision and document status belong in typed fields rather than prose. Entity linking may resolve aliases, but it must not silently replace a verified identifier with a nearby one.

Score fields for their job

A match in a reviewed title can deserve more weight than the same term buried in an attachment, but a title boost is not a permission or authority signal. Production BM25-style scoring accounts for term frequency, rarity and field length; field boosts then express how the application values each field. Apply hard eligibility filters first. Evaluate title-only, body-only and identifier-only queries separately so one tuned score does not hide a severe miss. Reranking cannot recover a document that lexical candidate generation excluded.

Treat synonyms as a release change

Search-time synonyms may improve recall for a controlled vocabulary, yet broad expansion can replace a specific engineering term with a general word and flood the candidate window. Test both index and search analysis with golden token streams, especially multiword synonyms, units and abbreviations. Version the rule set and record which rule produced an expanded term in the trace. Keep exact identity filters outside synonym expansion. Expansion drift tests should catch queries that begin retrieving a different asset family after a new synonym is deployed.

Measure candidate failure before answer failure

Build judged queries with misspellings, plural forms, hyphenated identifiers, long titles and repeated boilerplate. Measure eligible recall at the lexical candidate boundary and compare it with downstream supported answers. Inspect misses by analyzer version and field. A correct answer that came from a vector candidate does not prove the lexical index is healthy. During a migration, run old and new analyzers on the same snapshot and retain the old path until the new one passes the required slices.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass
import re

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ManualRecord:
    document_id: str
    part_id: str
    title: str
    body: str

def terms(text: str) -> Counter[str]:
    return Counter(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.casefold()))

def rank_manuals(records: list[ManualRecord], query: str,
                 required_part_id: str) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    query_terms = terms(query)
    scores = []
    for record in records:
        if record.part_id.casefold() != required_part_id.casefold():
            continue
        title_terms, body_terms = terms(record.title), terms(record.body)
        score = sum(min(count, title_terms[term]) * 4
                    + min(count, body_terms[term])
                    for term, count in query_terms.items())
        if score:
            scores.append((record.document_id, score))
    return sorted(scores, key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))

manuals = [
    ManualRecord("pump-p47-r4", "P-47", "P-47 seal pressure", "inspect the seal"),
    ManualRecord("pump-p48-r4", "P-48", "P-48 seal pressure", "drawing 47"),
]
assert rank_manuals(manuals, "seal pressure", "P-47") == [("pump-p47-r4", 9)]
assert rank_manuals(manuals, "seal pressure", "P-49") == []

Performance and operating cost

Building an inverted index is proportional to the indexed term count and stores postings in addition to source text. The standard-library demonstration scans N records with L terms each, costing O(NL) time and O(N) result space; it is intentionally a contract check, not a replacement for an inverted index or BM25. A keyword filter narrows the eligible set before ranking, while broader synonym rules increase postings visited and candidate pressure.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a text analyzer for an exact part ID or tenant key.
  • Changing query tokenization without testing compatibility with indexed terms.
  • Treating a title boost as proof that a document is authoritative.
  • Measuring only final answer quality while the lexical candidate pool loses required evidence.

Validation drill

Create 53 queries covering hyphens, aliases, plurals, units and title/body conflicts. Compare old and new analyzer token streams, exact-ID recall and eligible recall at the candidate boundary.

title: Vector compression: spend memory without losing the answer
summary: Measure how compressed vectors change candidate recall, then recover ordering with exact reranking where the budget permits.
body:
Measure how compressed vectors change candidate recall, then recover ordering with exact reranking where the budget permits.

Separate storage from ranking quality

A dense index can store full precision vectors or compressed codes. Product quantization and related codecs reduce per-vector storage by representing a vector with learned codebook entries, but the distance computed from a code is approximate. A smaller index does not automatically mean a better service: a support document that falls out of the candidate set cannot be rescued by the language model. Keep the original vector ID, embedding-model version and source revision alongside each compressed code. Embedding migration must rebuild or isolate incompatible spaces.

Budget the entire resident index

A 768-dimensional float32 vector uses 3,072 raw bytes before IDs, graph edges, partition metadata or replicas. A 48-byte code plus an eight-byte ID looks much smaller, but codebooks, coarse centroids, filtering structures and a raw-vector store for reranking still consume memory. Estimate each component against the actual number of vectors and replicas. If exact reranking reads remote raw vectors, account for that I/O in tail latency. Filtered ANN can lose still more candidates after permission or category constraints narrow the search space.

Use two stages deliberately

Retrieve a larger candidate set using compressed distances, apply eligibility filters, then compute exact similarity on the surviving vectors before final ranking. The second stage corrects ordering errors only when the correct item survived stage one. Increasing the approximate candidate count raises memory reads and exact-score work; it is not a free recall fix. Keep the rerank window tied to latency and access budgets. Candidate-window design makes this trade measurable rather than setting one global top-K by habit.

Train codes on representative data

A codebook trained on general prose may compress rare part numbers, source code or other specialized content poorly. Sample from the production distribution without including restricted documents in an unsafe shared training artifact. Evaluate queries by domain, language, document length and freshly added content. Rebuild when the embedding distribution changes enough to shift recall, and compare the new index with a full-precision baseline over the same corpus snapshot. A score difference across codec versions is not directly interpretable as a relevance change.

Gate on supported evidence

Measure exact-neighbor recall, answer-bearing passage recall, supported-answer rate, p95 latency and resident bytes together. A codec that preserves average neighbor recall but drops the only passage for safety-critical questions should fail its release slice. Record whether a miss arose in coarse partition selection, code distance, filter application or reranking. Keep a rollback index or a staged rollout until those failures are understood. Release gates should include both quality and resource limits.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class VectorCandidate:
    passage_id: str
    approximate_distance: float
    exact_distance: float

def exact_rerank(candidates: list[VectorCandidate], width: int) -> list[str]:
    if width < 1:
        raise ValueError("candidate width must be positive")
    shortlist = sorted(candidates, key=lambda item: item.approximate_distance)[:width]
    return [item.passage_id for item in sorted(
        shortlist, key=lambda item: (item.exact_distance, item.passage_id))]

def storage_bytes(vectors: int, dimension: int, code_bytes: int) -> tuple[int, int]:
    return vectors * dimension * 4, vectors * (code_bytes + 8)

candidates = [
    VectorCandidate("seal-procedure-r4", .18, .08),
    VectorCandidate("seal-catalog-r2", .09, .13),
]
assert exact_rerank(candidates, 2)[0] == "seal-procedure-r4"
assert exact_rerank(candidates, 1)[0] == "seal-catalog-r2"
assert storage_bytes(2_700_000, 768, 48) == (8_294_400_000, 151_200_000)

Performance and operating cost

For C retrieved candidates, sorting the approximate stage costs O(C log C), then sorting W shortlisted candidates costs O(W log W), with O(C) working space in this demonstration. Real ANN engines avoid a full corpus sort and add codec decoding and coarse-search costs. The byte calculation excludes codebooks, centroids, graph links, filtering metadata, replicas and any full-precision rerank store; measure those separately before committing to an index size.

Common Mistakes

  • Reporting code bytes as total index memory.
  • Assuming exact reranking can restore a relevant item absent from the shortlist.
  • Training compression on a corpus unlike the one served.
  • Comparing approximate distances from different codecs as if they shared a calibrated scale.

Validation drill

For 61 judged queries, compare full precision, compressed top-1 and compressed top-12 followed by exact reranking. Record the first lost answer-bearing passage, resident memory and p95 latency per domain.

title: Snapshot-consistent retrieval across changing indexes
summary: Pin lexical, vector and permission views to a compatible generation before merging evidence or paginating results.
body:
Pin lexical, vector and permission views to a compatible generation before merging evidence or paginating results.

Choose an answer-time snapshot

A retrieval request can span lexical postings, a vector index, metadata storage and a permission service. Each may refresh at a different time. If a document revision enters vector search before its permission update reaches the filter, combining the newest result from every component can create an answer that no coherent system state ever contained. Select a generation or snapshot token that all required components can serve. If one is behind, wait within a bounded budget, fall back to an older common generation, or abstain. Temporal validity answers which revision was true at a requested time; snapshot consistency answers which revision the search system actually observed.

Carry generation through each stage

Attach generation, document revision, tenant and source ID to candidates, reranker inputs and final citations. A merged list with two revisions of one document is not merely a ranking issue; the reader may be shown mutually incompatible facts. Keep tombstones and permission revocations in the same generation discipline. A cached result must include its snapshot and authorization scope, or it may outlive the state it claims to represent. Permission-aware caching handles the authorization half of this contract.

Paginate a frozen view

Offset pagination over a changing index can duplicate or skip documents when new records arrive between page requests. A point-in-time search view and a stable sort key let later pages continue the same result set. Expire the view deliberately and return a restart signal rather than silently switching generations halfway through. A user-facing search may tolerate a short-lived snapshot, while an audit export may need a longer frozen manifest and repeatable IDs. Retrieval traces should record snapshot token and page cursor for reconstruction.

Handle mixed-generation failures

During a blue-green index swap, query both old and new read paths against the same judged questions before activating the new generation. If vector generation 48 is ready but lexical generation 47 is still serving, a generation-48 hybrid answer is premature. A retry is useful only when the lag is expected to clear within the request budget. Never downgrade permission revocation to an old snapshot just to keep an answer available. Security-critical revocations require current authorization even if content indexes remain pinned. Index swap controls govern when a new generation becomes safe to serve.

Test observable consistency

Inject updates between candidate fetch, reranking and pagination. Include a deleted document, a permission withdrawal, a content revision and a vector rebuild that completes later than the lexical refresh. Check that every returned citation resolves to the claimed revision and that all pages share one snapshot. Measure waiting time and abstention separately; an apparently fast system that silently mixes generations has traded correctness for latency without declaring it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class IndexView:
    name: str
    ready_generation: int

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchHit:
    document_id: str
    revision: str
    generation: int
    source_index: str

def merge_snapshot(views: list[IndexView], hits: list[SearchHit],
                   generation: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    if not views or any(view.ready_generation < generation for view in views):
        raise ValueError("requested generation is not ready everywhere")
    allowed_sources = {view.name for view in views}
    revisions: dict[str, str] = {}
    for hit in hits:
        if hit.source_index not in allowed_sources or hit.generation > generation:
            continue
        previous = revisions.setdefault(hit.document_id, hit.revision)
        if previous != hit.revision:
            raise ValueError("conflicting document revisions in one snapshot")
    return revisions

views = [IndexView("lexical", 48), IndexView("vector", 47)]
hits = [SearchHit("pump-p47", "r4", 47, "lexical"),
        SearchHit("pump-p47", "r4", 47, "vector"),
        SearchHit("pump-p47", "r5", 48, "lexical")]
assert merge_snapshot(views, hits, 47) == {"pump-p47": "r4"}
try:
    merge_snapshot(views, hits, 48)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("mixed-generation read was accepted")

Performance and operating cost

The demonstration scans V component views and H hits in O(V + H) time with O(H) revision space. A real point-in-time view can retain old index segments and add storage pressure for its lifetime; waiting for the slowest component adds tail latency. Limit snapshot duration, expose timeouts and monitor generation lag. A permission revocation must still be checked against current policy even when content retrieval uses an older coherent generation.

Common Mistakes

  • Merging the latest response from each index without a shared generation.
  • Using an old permission snapshot after access was revoked.
  • Changing generation between search result pages without telling the client.
  • Dropping revision IDs before citations are assembled.

Validation drill

Replay 43 synthetic updates across two indexes and a permission view. Verify citation revisions, page continuity, revocation handling and bounded fallback when one index lags.

title: Corpus poisoning: admit evidence before ranking it
summary: Keep adversarial or unreviewed corpus additions from becoming authoritative evidence merely because they rank well.
body:
Keep adversarial or unreviewed corpus additions from becoming authoritative evidence merely because they rank well.

Separate relevance from authority

Corpus poisoning changes what the retriever can find. An attacker may add a plausible document that repeats the query terms, cites a fake update or embeds a misleading number, without writing an explicit instruction to the assistant. A high similarity score says the passage resembles the question; it says nothing about who published it or whether its claim is approved. Admit evidence through trusted ingestion metadata before ranking it for a consequential answer. Prompt-injection controls handle instructions inside retrieved text, but a false factual claim can be dangerous even when it contains no command.

Assign trust at ingestion

Capture source owner, collection, reviewer state, document signature or checksum, import channel and revision lineage outside the document body. A sentence inside the document claiming to be 'official' is not proof of authority. Give user uploads and external feeds a lower trust tier until their content is reviewed or corroborated under policy. Apply tenant and lifecycle rules before any trust comparison. Passage provenance should let an investigator trace an answer back to the exact admitted source and revision.

Guard candidate admission

A poisoned page can still consume the top candidate slots even if a downstream generator refuses its claims. Filter or partition sources by trust tier, then set candidate budgets so lower-trust material cannot crowd out the approved corpus. For exploratory search, show unreviewed material with a clear status; for a policy or safety answer, require an approved evidence tier. If a trusted source and an unreviewed source disagree, do not average their text or choose the one with the more fluent explanation. Context packing should preserve source diversity without confusing diversity with authority.

Detect suspicious change patterns

Watch for a burst of new documents that all answer the same rare question, unusual repetition of identifiers, copied authority language, and content whose owner cannot be verified. These signals are review triggers, not automatic proof of attack. Compare new-corpus and previous-corpus answers on stable judged queries, and record which admitted document changed each answer. Quarantine a source by source ID or ingest batch, then rebuild affected candidate stores and caches. Ingestion controls should make quarantine and deletion repeatable.

Evaluate the admission boundary

Test harmless user uploads, misleading but relevant documents, forged update notices and contradictions between two approved sources. Judge whether the system finds authorized evidence, labels uncertainty and abstains when approved evidence conflicts. A detector that blocks every new document may reduce attack success while destroying useful recall. Review false positives by source tier and query slice. Counterfactual tests can reveal when an answer changes only because a low-trust passage was introduced.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceCandidate:
    source_id: str
    policy_key: str
    value: str
    similarity: float
    verified_origin: bool
    approved_for_answers: bool

def admitted_value(candidates: list[EvidenceCandidate], policy_key: str) -> str | None:
    eligible = [candidate for candidate in candidates
                if candidate.policy_key == policy_key
                and candidate.verified_origin
                and candidate.approved_for_answers]
    values = {candidate.value for candidate in eligible}
    if len(values) > 1:
        raise ValueError("approved sources conflict; require review")
    return next(iter(values)) if values else None

records = [
    EvidenceCandidate("signed-manual-r4", "pump-p47-limit", "83 kPa", .71, True, True),
    EvidenceCandidate("unreviewed-upload-9", "pump-p47-limit", "67 kPa", .99, False, False),
]
assert admitted_value(records, "pump-p47-limit") == "83 kPa"
assert admitted_value(records, "unknown-policy") is None

Performance and operating cost

Admission scans C candidates in O(C) time and stores at most O(C) distinct admitted values. In production, source status should usually be indexed so unapproved material is excluded before expensive retrieval and reranking. Provenance verification, review queues and quarantine rebuilds add operational cost, but accepting a high-scoring forged source can corrupt every downstream answer that cites it. Keep metadata server-controlled and audit changes to approval state.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading an 'official' label from document text as if it were verified metadata.
  • Letting low-trust candidates fill the entire top-K window before filtering.
  • Assuming a prompt-injection detector also catches false factual claims.
  • Picking one of two conflicting approved claims solely by similarity score.

Validation drill

Add 37 synthetic unreviewed documents to a judged corpus. Record which enter the candidate pool, which are admitted for answers, how many legitimate passages are displaced and whether conflicts trigger review.

title: Score normalization: combine retrievers without inventing certainty
summary: Normalize lexical and vector rankings for fusion, then validate separately whether fused scores predict useful evidence.
body:
Normalize lexical and vector rankings for fusion, then validate separately whether fused scores predict useful evidence.

Keep score meanings separate

A lexical score, a vector similarity and a cross-encoder score are produced by different computations. Their raw values do not share a common unit, and even one retriever's range can shift with query length, corpus size or model version. Adding them directly lets the largest numeric scale dominate the merged ranking. Reciprocal-rank fusion avoids raw score arithmetic, while a weighted linear blend requires a stated normalization rule. Neither result is automatically a probability that the passage supports the answer. Hybrid fusion explains the candidate merge; this lesson covers the meaning and limits of its numeric scores.

Normalize inside the candidate window

For a given query, min-max scaling maps the observed lowest and highest candidate scores to zero and one. It is easy to inspect, but it depends on the candidate window: adding a single outlier changes every scaled value. A constant-score list needs a defined fallback rather than division by zero. L2 normalization and rank-based methods have different behavior. Select one with judged queries, keep its configuration version, and never compare a min-max value from one query to another as if both were calibrated relevance probabilities.

Apply eligibility before blending

Permission, tenant, revision and source-status filters are hard constraints. If an unauthorized record gets a high fused score and is removed only after top-K truncation, it can displace the answer-bearing record. Build separate eligible lexical and vector candidate lists, normalize within the eligible window, then fuse. Missing candidates need an explicit default contribution; they should not be assigned a fabricated high score merely to keep each branch represented. Corpus permissions must remain independent of ranking math.

Calibrate support on labeled evidence

A fused score can order passages well yet be a poor threshold for abstention. To decide whether to answer, collect judged query-passage pairs and measure supported-answer precision at candidate thresholds by domain, language and source. Calibrate a decision rule against that labeled set, then test it on held-out queries. Recalibrate after changing an encoder, lexical analyzer, candidate window or normalization method. Evidence-bound answers should use support checks, not a raw similarity cutoff that happened to work on a few examples.

Monitor score drift with release slices

Record the per-query lexical and vector score distributions, overlap between branches, fused top-K stability and the number of abstentions. A new corpus of short titles can raise lexical scores without improving evidence. An embedding update can narrow cosine-score spread while retrieval recall falls. Compare judged slices and score histograms against one fixed corpus snapshot before release. If the fusion change improves average ranking but loses exact-ID questions, keep a hard exact-ID path. Release gates should expose that regression.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BranchScore:
    passage_id: str
    lexical: float | None
    vector: float | None

def scale(values: list[float]) -> dict[float, float]:
    if not values:
        return {}
    low, high = min(values), max(values)
    return {value: (value - low) / (high - low) if high > low else 1.0
            for value in values}

def fused_rank(candidates: list[BranchScore]) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    lexical = scale([item.lexical for item in candidates if item.lexical is not None])
    vector = scale([item.vector for item in candidates if item.vector is not None])
    ranked = [(item.passage_id,
               .6 * lexical.get(item.lexical, 0.0)
               + .4 * vector.get(item.vector, 0.0))
              for item in candidates]
    return sorted(ranked, key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0]))

passages = [BranchScore("pump-p47-manual", 13.0, .82),
            BranchScore("pump-p47-note", 4.0, .78),
            BranchScore("pump-p48-manual", 2.0, .54)]
assert fused_rank(passages)[0][0] == "pump-p47-manual"
assert scale([.47, .47]) == {.47: 1.0}

Performance and operating cost

For C eligible candidates, finding per-branch extrema and scoring each item costs O(C) time; sorting the merged result costs O(C log C) time and O(C) working space. Min-max values are defined only relative to the observed window. Training a support threshold costs additional judged labels and must be repeated when branch distributions change. Filter eligibility before this work so a high-scoring forbidden candidate cannot consume the window.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding raw lexical and vector scores as if they had a shared scale.
  • Treating a fused score of 0.8 as an 80 percent chance of answer support.
  • Normalizing before removing ineligible documents that can distort the range.
  • Using a constant-score branch without defining how it contributes.

Validation drill

Run 47 labeled questions through rank fusion and two score normalizers. For each, record recall at 12, supported top-one precision, outlier sensitivity and exact-identifier misses.

title: Click feedback: correct exposure bias before tuning retrieval
summary: Use logged exposure probabilities and judged evidence to keep clicks from reinforcing the ranking that produced them.
body:
Use logged exposure probabilities and judged evidence to keep clicks from reinforcing the ranking that produced them.

A click is an observation, not a label

Search logs record what users were shown and what they clicked. A top-ranked result is usually examined more often than a lower-ranked result, so more clicks do not prove greater relevance. Snippet wording, device layout, query ambiguity and a satisfied user who never clicks can alter behavior as well. Keep impressions, rank positions, query class and click outcomes together. Do not label every unclicked result irrelevant, because it may never have been seen. Judged relevance labels remain the anchor for measuring whether retrieved evidence truly answers a question.

Log the policy that chose the result

Offline comparison of two rankings needs to know how likely the logging policy was to show each observed result in that position. Randomized or carefully designed interleaving traffic can provide such propensities, but changing the order of high-stakes evidence merely to collect data can be unacceptable. Record policy version and selection probability at impression time; reconstructing it later from final rankings is fragile. A target policy must have support wherever it assigns probability, otherwise logged data cannot estimate its behavior there. Retrieval traces give each exposure its candidate and policy identity.

Estimate with bounded weights

Inverse-propensity weighting gives greater weight to observations that were unlikely under the logging policy but likely under the target policy. Very small logging probabilities produce high-variance estimates, so define a floor or clip and report the resulting bias-variance tradeoff. Keep query-level confidence intervals and do not call an offline score a guaranteed online gain. A tiny code sample can demonstrate the arithmetic; real deployment evaluation needs a randomized logging design and careful outcome definition. Release evaluation should compare offline evidence with judged slices before any traffic change.

Avoid feedback loops

If a retriever promotes what was clicked yesterday, those results get more exposure today and may collect still more clicks. New or niche documents receive little data and can be unfairly buried. Keep some exploration within safe, eligible candidate sets, cap how quickly behavior changes ranking weights and audit exposure by source and topic. Never use clicks to bypass permission or source-trust filters. Evidence admission must happen before any learned click signal is applied.

Evaluate the outcome that matters

A click on a plausible but stale snippet can be worse than no click. Combine behavioral signals with supported-answer judgments, abandonment, reformulation and task-completion measures. Segment by mobile versus desktop, head versus rare queries and new versus established documents. Check for a ranking that improves click-through while reducing answer-bearing passage recall or increasing unsupported claims. Preserve a fixed holdout set and an escape path to the previous ranking policy if a monitored slice degrades.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class LoggedExposure:
    query_id: str
    clicked: bool
    logged_probability: float
    target_probability: float

def propensity_weighted_clicks(events: list[LoggedExposure]) -> float:
    if not events:
        raise ValueError("evaluation needs impressions")
    total = 0.0
    for event in events:
        if not 0 < event.logged_probability <= 1:
            raise ValueError("invalid logging probability")
        if not 0 <= event.target_probability <= 1:
            raise ValueError("invalid target probability")
        total += float(event.clicked) * event.target_probability / event.logged_probability
    return total / len(events)

impressions = [LoggedExposure("seal-pressure-1", True, .5, .25),
               LoggedExposure("seal-pressure-2", False, .5, .75)]
assert propensity_weighted_clicks(impressions) == .25

Performance and operating cost

Computing this illustrative inverse-propensity estimate costs O(E) time for E logged impressions and O(1) extra space. Collection and storage costs grow with impressions, policy metadata and retention period. Low logging probabilities increase estimator variance; clipping reduces that variance but changes the estimate. Use the code as an arithmetic contract, not as a complete causal evaluation design or a substitute for judged relevance and online safety checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating an unclicked low-ranked result as a negative relevance label.
  • Estimating a target policy where the logging policy never exposed its candidates.
  • Ignoring very large inverse-propensity weights and their variance.
  • Optimizing click-through while answer support and source trust get worse.

Validation drill

Design 31 judged queries with two safe ranking policies. Log impressions, positions, policy probabilities and support labels; compare raw clicks with weighted estimates and report uncertainty by query slice.

title: Personalized retrieval: preferences never grant access
summary: Apply explicit user preferences only after access checks, with clear consent, cache isolation and deletion behavior.
body:
Apply explicit user preferences only after access checks, with clear consent, cache isolation and deletion behavior.

Separate preference from permission

Personalized retrieval can rank eligible material using a reader's chosen topics, reading level or current project. That preference cannot make an unauthorized document eligible. First apply tenant, group and document lifecycle filters from the active authenticated session; only then adjust the rank of remaining candidates. A model's guess about a user's role is not an access token. Corpus permissions define the hard boundary; personalization operates inside it.

Collect only useful state

Store explicit preference fields with their purpose, consent state and expiration. A recent query may be useful for one follow-up without becoming permanent memory. Do not silently turn private questions or retrieved passages into a lasting user profile. Let the user inspect, correct or clear preference state, and make the default search path useful with no personalization at all. Conversation rewriting may carry a short-lived entity or constraint, but it should not import unrelated history into a new search.

Isolate caches and embeddings

A result cache keyed only by query text can leak personalized ranks or even snippets across accounts. Include identity scope, authorization version, preference version and corpus generation where those affect output, or decline to cache the result. User-specific embeddings create another derived-data copy that must be covered by retention and deletion rules. If consent is withdrawn, stop using the feature immediately and invalidate cached outputs. Permission-aware caches provide the same discipline for nonpersonalized conversation turns.

Keep explanations specific

When personalization changes order, show a concise reason such as 'your selected Java topic' rather than implying the top document is more authoritative. User preferences can help choose among equally eligible tutorials, but they should not override exact identifiers, current policy revision or evidence support. A strong preference for one source can create a narrow view that misses contradictory material, so diversify when the task calls for comparison. Evidence diversity helps prevent a preference filter from hiding necessary counterevidence.

Test consent transitions

Build cases for opt-in, opt-out, changed group membership, preference deletion, shared devices and two users with the same query. Verify that unauthorized documents never enter candidates, personalized ranks disappear after opt-out and no cached response crosses an identity boundary. Measure whether personalization improves task completion or merely raises clicks on familiar material. Review long-tail users separately; sparse history can make the model's inferred interests unstable.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReaderContext:
    tenant: str
    groups: frozenset[str]
    consent: bool
    preferred_topic: str | None

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchDocument:
    document_id: str
    tenant: str
    required_group: str
    topic: str
    relevance: float

def ranked_for_reader(reader: ReaderContext,
                      documents: list[SearchDocument]) -> list[str]:
    allowed = [document for document in documents
               if document.tenant == reader.tenant
               and document.required_group in reader.groups]
    return [document.document_id for document in sorted(
        allowed,
        key=lambda document: (-(document.relevance + (
            .1 if reader.consent and document.topic == reader.preferred_topic else 0)),
            document.document_id))]

reader = ReaderContext("north", frozenset({"engineers"}), True, "maintenance")
documents = [SearchDocument("pump-p47", "north", "engineers", "maintenance", .72),
             SearchDocument("salary-plan", "north", "finance", "maintenance", .99),
             SearchDocument("pump-p48", "south", "engineers", "maintenance", .97)]
assert ranked_for_reader(reader, documents) == ["pump-p47"]
assert ranked_for_reader(ReaderContext("north", reader.groups, False, None), documents) == ["pump-p47"]

Performance and operating cost

Filtering and sorting N candidates costs O(N log N) time and O(N) working space in this small implementation. An index should apply tenant and group constraints before ranking to avoid scanning ineligible documents. Per-user state and cache keys increase storage cardinality, so set retention limits and avoid caching low-reuse private results. Preference boosts should be evaluated separately from authorization and evidence support.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a predicted role or preferred topic as an access grant.
  • Caching personalized snippets under only the query text.
  • Keeping query history after a user withdraws personalization consent.
  • Letting a preference boost hide a newer or contradictory source.

Validation drill

Create 29 two-user scenarios with shared queries, group changes and opt-out events. Verify no cross-user snippet appears, then measure whether explicit preferences improve supported task completion.

title: Index watermarks: measure what the retriever has actually seen
summary: Use per-source progress markers to distinguish a fresh source document from an index that has not applied its latest update.
body:
Use per-source progress markers to distinguish a fresh source document from an index that has not applied its latest update.

Define freshness at the serving boundary

A document's edited-at timestamp says when its source changed, not when lexical, vector and metadata indexes became ready to serve that change. Track source event offsets and the highest contiguous offset applied to each serving component. A gap matters: processing event 94 while event 93 failed does not make 94 a safe watermark. Expose the minimum ready offset across components required for the query. Incremental ingestion supplies the event ordering and retry contract behind that marker.

Give queries a required freshness

A historical how-to question may tolerate a short index delay; an access-revocation or active incident question may not. Express the requirement as a source offset, snapshot token or bounded age tied to a documented source clock. If the serving watermark is behind, wait only within the request budget, then use an explicit stale-answer policy: return a labeled older snapshot, query an authoritative live source, or abstain. Do not quietly answer from stale evidence while presenting it as current. Abstention is the correct result when freshness is required and cannot be established.

Keep deletes in the same progress model

Deletion and permission revocation are not ordinary updates. A vector may linger after the document disappears from the source; a cache can still hold its snippet. Track a revocation watermark for every serving path that could expose the material and require it to reach the requested offset. Quarantine or deny a known revoked document immediately, even if rebuilding the full index takes longer. Deletion controls must cover the source, index and caches, not just a database flag.

Measure lag by source and slice

An average ingestion delay hides one stuck partition. Report p95 and maximum lag, oldest unapplied event age, contiguous watermark and count of failed events by source. The query trace should show the freshness requirement and the watermarks actually used. Alert on lag that threatens the service target, not merely on high queue depth. A queue can be empty while a poison event is parked in a dead-letter path and the watermark is frozen. Traces connect stale answers to the precise lagging component.

Test races with a fixed answer contract

Replay an update, a delete and a permission withdrawal while lexical and vector ingestion advance at different rates. Ask the same question before and after each watermark crosses the required offset. The answer may change only when a coherent serving view is ready; it must never reveal a revoked passage. Include event retries and out-of-order delivery. Snapshot consistency chooses a coherent generation once each component advertises progress.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class IndexProgress:
    component: str
    source_offset: int
    visible_offset: int
    revocation_offset: int

def ready_for_answer(progress: list[IndexProgress], required_offset: int,
                     must_cover_revocations: bool = True) -> bool:
    if not progress or required_offset < 0:
        return False
    return all(state.visible_offset >= required_offset
               and (not must_cover_revocations
                    or state.revocation_offset >= required_offset)
               for state in progress)

components = [IndexProgress("lexical", 93, 93, 93),
              IndexProgress("vector", 93, 92, 93)]
assert not ready_for_answer(components, 93)
assert ready_for_answer(components, 92)
components[1] = IndexProgress("vector", 93, 93, 93)
assert ready_for_answer(components, 93)

Performance and operating cost

A readiness check scans S serving components in O(S) time and O(1) extra space. Maintaining contiguous watermarks takes durable offset tracking and retry state per partition. A strict freshness target can increase latency or abstention when one component lags; measure those effects against the value of a current answer. Never trade away revocation checks to improve an apparent freshness score.

Common Mistakes

  • Using source edited-at time as proof that the vector index has applied an update.
  • Advancing a watermark past an unprocessed event gap.
  • Treating a delete as complete when a cached passage can still be served.
  • Reporting only average lag while one partition is stuck.

Validation drill

Simulate 37 ordered source events with two dropped updates and one revocation. Record each component watermark and verify exactly when a current answer becomes eligible.

title: Learned sparse retrieval: weighted terms without dense-vector search
summary: Understand weighted token expansion, inverted-list execution, exact-term safeguards and the real storage cost of sparse semantic search.
body:
Understand weighted token expansion, inverted-list execution, exact-term safeguards and the real storage cost of sparse semantic search.

Represent meaning as weighted terms

Learned sparse retrieval maps a query and a passage to small sets of vocabulary terms with nonzero weights. A model may assign weight to a related term that never appeared literally in the passage. That expansion can bridge wording differences while retaining an inverted-index execution path. It is not ordinary keyword search: the weights and extra terms come from a model, so their meaning depends on its training data and version. It is also not a dense embedding, where nearly every vector coordinate is populated. Lexical analysis remains valuable for exact strings that a model might split or suppress.

Build postings for nonzero coordinates

At index time, write each nonzero passage coordinate to a posting list keyed by vocabulary term, with passage ID and weight. At query time, visit only lists for nonzero query coordinates and accumulate the products of query and passage weights. A term absent from either side contributes zero. Pruning tiny weights can reduce disk and query work, but aggressive pruning can remove the only bridge for a rare question. Measure posting-list length, index bytes and recall at a fixed latency target before choosing a pruning threshold.

Keep identifiers on a literal path

A model-generated term for an equipment family must not replace an exact serial number, ticket ID or regulatory clause. Preserve raw identifiers in a separately analyzed field, route identifier-heavy queries through a literal match, and fuse its candidates with the learned sparse list. Keep authorization and document-status filters before final ranking. Hybrid fusion can combine branches without pretending that BM25 and sparse-model scores share one scale. A model expansion is a recall aid; it is never permission to rewrite a user's stated identifier.

Version both sides of the match

Query and passage term weights must come from compatible model and vocabulary versions. If the query encoder changes while old passage postings remain, the same term ID may have a different role or weight distribution. Store model and tokenizer IDs with the index generation, and switch serving traffic only after a complete compatible build. A dual-index migration allows comparison of labeled query slices before cutover. Embedding migrations follow the same generation discipline even though the storage format differs.

Evaluate where expansion helps and hurts

Build judged slices for paraphrases, abbreviations, rare identifiers, multilingual text and adversarial keyword stuffing. Compare learned sparse retrieval against a lexical baseline and a dense branch at the same candidate budget, measuring recall, latency, index size and unsupported-answer rate. Inspect which expansion coordinates caused a false positive; human-readable terms make diagnosis possible, but a readable term does not prove semantic correctness. An answer still needs source evidence and a claim-level support check.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def sparse_candidates(query_weights: dict[str, float],
                      passage_weights: dict[str, dict[str, float]],
                      allowed_ids: set[str]) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    postings = defaultdict(list)
    for passage_id, weights in passage_weights.items():
        if passage_id not in allowed_ids:
            continue
        for term, weight in weights.items():
            if weight > 0:
                postings[term].append((passage_id, weight))
    scores = defaultdict(float)
    for term, query_weight in query_weights.items():
        if query_weight <= 0:
            continue
        for passage_id, passage_weight in postings.get(term, ()):
            scores[passage_id] += query_weight * passage_weight
    return sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))

passages = {"pump-p47": {"seal": .8, "leak": .4},
            "pump-p48": {"seal": .2, "motor": .9},
            "private-plan": {"seal": 1.0}}
ranked = sparse_candidates({"seal": .6, "leak": .3}, passages,
                           {"pump-p47", "pump-p48"})
assert ranked == [("pump-p47", .6), ("pump-p48", .12)]

Performance and operating cost

For an already built index, query work is proportional to the total posting entries visited for nonzero query terms, plus sorting or top-K selection over scored candidates. The demonstration rebuilds postings in O(W) time and O(W) space for W nonzero passage weights; a production index stores them once and pays that cost during ingestion. Model inference, larger expanded vocabularies and long posting lists can dominate latency. Compare end-to-end cost, not just the dot product.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling model expansion a verified synonym dictionary.
  • Pruning weights solely for index size without a rare-query recall test.
  • Mixing query and passage encoders from incompatible generations.
  • Letting an expanded term outrank a required exact identifier or bypass access filters.

Validation drill

On 43 judged maintenance questions, compare lexical, learned sparse and fused top-12 recall. Keep separate slices for serial IDs, paraphrases and terms seen in only one manual revision; report p95 latency and index bytes alongside recall.

title: Retrieval shards: fanout, replica lag and incomplete top-K results
summary: Route queries across shards, merge local candidates and make partial failure visible instead of presenting an incomplete answer as complete.
body:
Route queries across shards, merge local candidates and make partial failure visible instead of presenting an incomplete answer as complete.

Split a corpus without splitting the answer contract

A sharded index places different documents on different serving units. A coordinator asks each relevant shard for local top-K candidates and merges them into a global top-K. This distributes storage and search work, but a query that fans out to every shard can become slower as the shard count rises. Tenant-aware or time-aware routing may reduce fanout when its key is a real query constraint. Routing by guessed topic is dangerous: one mistaken guess can make the answer-bearing shard invisible. Federated retrieval handles unlike sources; shard fanout concerns partitions of one logical index.

Merge with stable identity

Each shard returns a score, a stable passage ID, its index generation and the applied authorization scope. The coordinator must compare scores only when every shard uses the same model, scoring rules and compatible index generation. It then sorts by score and a deterministic tie key, deduplicates repeated passages, and clips to the requested count. One shard returning K candidates is sufficient for a global top-K when scores are comparable and each shard has the same eligibility filter; returning fewer can discard a candidate that belongs in the global result.

Replicas improve availability, not automatic freshness

A replica can answer a read while a primary is unavailable, but it may lag behind an update or permission withdrawal. Query routing should select only a replica that has applied the required source offset and revocation watermark; otherwise wait within budget, use an eligible replica, or fail closed. A generic 'healthy' check does not establish the freshness needed by this query. Index watermarks state what each serving copy has actually applied.

Treat a missing shard as missing evidence

If one of four required shards times out, the coordinator cannot claim that its top result is the best document in the corpus. For low-stakes exploratory search it may return explicitly labeled partial results; for an answer requiring complete policy coverage, abstention or retry is safer. Log shard IDs, generations, missing partitions, timeout budgets and candidate counts. Never hide a partial result behind a normal 200 response without a machine-readable completeness field. Evidence-bound answers should refuse to synthesize a confident claim from a known incomplete search.

Size and test the fanout budget

More small shards increase coordinator work, per-shard overhead and the chance that at least one request misses its deadline. Fewer large shards can create memory pressure and longer recovery. Benchmark representative query slices as shard count, replica count and local candidate window change. Inject a slow shard, one stale replica and a node loss; verify that global ranking is stable when complete and that the incomplete path reports precisely what was missed. Retrieval traces should make this diagnosis possible without replaying private query text.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ShardReply:
    shard_id: str
    generation: int
    candidates: tuple[tuple[str, float], ...]

def merge_complete(replies: list[ShardReply], required_shards: set[str],
                   generation: int, limit: int) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    if limit < 1 or {reply.shard_id for reply in replies} != required_shards:
        raise ValueError("incomplete shard set")
    if any(reply.generation != generation for reply in replies):
        raise ValueError("mixed index generations")
    best: dict[str, float] = {}
    for reply in replies:
        for passage_id, score in reply.candidates:
            best[passage_id] = max(best.get(passage_id, float("-inf")), score)
    return sorted(best.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))[:limit]

responses = [ShardReply("north", 47, (("pump-p47", .82),)),
             ShardReply("south", 47, (("pump-p48", .71),))]
assert merge_complete(responses, {"north", "south"}, 47, 1) == [("pump-p47", .82)]
try:
    merge_complete(responses[:1], {"north", "south"}, 47, 1)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("missing shard was accepted")

Performance and operating cost

With S shards each returning at most K candidates, this simple merge reads O(SK) entries, stores O(SK) unique IDs and sorts them in O(SK log(SK)) time. A bounded heap can reduce ranking work when SK is large. Network latency is controlled by the slowest required shard, not the average shard; replicas consume extra storage and indexing capacity. Reducing fanout is useful only if routing cannot exclude eligible evidence.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a missing shard as an empty shard.
  • Merging scores from different model or index generations as if comparable.
  • Reading from a stale replica after a permission withdrawal.
  • Increasing shard count without measuring coordinator and tail-latency costs.

Validation drill

Partition 59 documents across three shards. Remove one reply and delay another, then verify complete top-K ordering, generation checks and explicit partial-result behavior under a fixed latency budget.

title: Stable search pagination: point-in-time views and safe cursors
summary: Page through ranked results without duplicates or omissions while the corpus changes, and bind a cursor to the query and permission scope.
body:
Page through ranked results without duplicates or omissions while the corpus changes, and bind a cursor to the query and permission scope.

Why offsets drift

An offset asks for positions in the current ranking. If a document is inserted, deleted or reranked between page one and page two, those positions move: one hit may repeat and another may never be shown. Deep offsets also force an engine to inspect or hold many skipped hits. A cursor instead records the final sort key seen on the prior page, and a point-in-time view pins the index snapshot for the series. Snapshot consistency covers the same idea across multiple indexes; pagination applies it across successive requests.

Choose a total order

Sort by relevance plus a stable unique ID, or by timestamp plus ID for chronological browsing. Score alone is insufficient because many documents can tie. The next page requests records after the last full sort tuple, using the same query, filters, model and index view. If score computation changes midstream, the cursor cannot preserve a stable order. Keep the requested page size bounded and use a deterministic direction for every field.

Bind the cursor to authorization

A cursor is user-supplied input, even if the server created it earlier. Include a query fingerprint, tenant or principal scope, permission version, index snapshot ID, last sort tuple and expiry; sign it to detect alteration. On resume, recheck current permissions as well as the pinned snapshot, because a point-in-time view must not preserve access to a document after revocation. Do not place private query text or secrets in a merely encoded cursor. Permission-aware caches face the same identity and revision problem.

Budget snapshot lifetime

Holding a point-in-time view retains old index state while users page. Set a short keep-alive, close it when finished where supported, and return an explicit restart response after expiry. A refreshed snapshot can change the result order; silently replacing one mid-cursor defeats the contract. For exports, use a separate bounded job with checkpointing rather than leaving an interactive cursor open for hours. Document whether counts and facets correspond to the pinned view or a new live query.

Test writes and revocations between pages

Create tied scores, fetch one page, insert a high-ranked hit, delete a middle hit and revoke access to another. The next page should neither duplicate a previously returned ID nor reveal the revoked one; an expired cursor should fail clearly. Run the same test across replicas if the backend can route successive pages differently. Document lifecycle takes priority over pagination convenience.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchHit:
    passage_id: str
    score: float
    tenant: str

def page_after(hits: list[SearchHit], tenant: str, page_size: int,
               last_key: tuple[float, str] | None = None
               ) -> tuple[list[SearchHit], tuple[float, str] | None]:
    if not 1 <= page_size <= 47:
        raise ValueError("invalid page size")
    ordered = sorted((hit for hit in hits if hit.tenant == tenant),
                     key=lambda hit: (-hit.score, hit.passage_id))
    if last_key is not None:
        ordered = [hit for hit in ordered
                   if (-hit.score, hit.passage_id) > last_key]
    selected = ordered[:page_size]
    next_key = (-selected[-1].score, selected[-1].passage_id) if selected else None
    return selected, next_key

snapshot = [SearchHit("pump-p47", .91, "north"),
            SearchHit("pump-p48", .91, "north"),
            SearchHit("pump-p49", .76, "north"),
            SearchHit("private-plan", .99, "south")]
first, cursor = page_after(snapshot, "north", 2)
second, _ = page_after(snapshot, "north", 2, cursor)
assert [hit.passage_id for hit in first + second] == ["pump-p47", "pump-p48", "pump-p49"]

Performance and operating cost

This in-memory demonstration filters and sorts N hits on every page in O(N log N) time and O(N) space. A search engine can seek after the indexed sort tuple without rescanning all prior results, but maintaining a point-in-time view retains segment state and has a lifetime cost. The tuple shown is only the inner seek key; a public API must sign and scope its serialized cursor and enforce expiration plus fresh authorization before serving it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using offset pagination on a frequently updated ranking and assuming positions stay fixed.
  • Sorting by score alone when tied scores can reorder.
  • Treating base64 encoding as cursor integrity or confidentiality.
  • Allowing an old snapshot to bypass a new access revocation.

Validation drill

Fetch 11 pages from a fixed judged snapshot while inserting, deleting and revoking documents in the live corpus. Verify exact-once IDs for still-authorized results and a clear failure when the snapshot expires.

title: Chunk boundaries: test whether the answer survives the split
summary: Tune passage size and overlap against answer-span recall, citation precision, duplicate context and indexing cost.
body:
Tune passage size and overlap against answer-span recall, citation precision, duplicate context and indexing cost.

Chunking is a retrieval decision

A chunk is the smallest passage the index can return, so its boundaries determine what a retriever can prove. Splitting a procedure between a warning and the step it qualifies may produce a passage that looks relevant but is unsafe alone. Keeping an entire handbook as one chunk dilutes a precise answer and consumes context. Start with source structure: headings, paragraphs, table rows and transcript time ranges. Preserve parent document and revision identity so the original location remains auditable. Chunk identity defines stable IDs and citation boundaries after a split.

Treat overlap as a measured tradeoff

Overlap repeats material across adjacent chunks and can rescue an answer span crossing a fixed window. It also increases token storage, embedding work, candidate duplication and the chance that the same source is mistaken for independent support. A fixed percentage is not a guarantee: a table header, a negation or a section title may fall outside both useful windows. Prefer structure-aware boundaries; use overlap only where judged cases show a gain. Duplicate evidence must be collapsed before citing corroboration.

Record exact answer spans

For each judged query, annotate the source document, revision and minimal answer-bearing span, including qualifiers that change the claim. After chunking, ask whether at least one eligible returned chunk contains that full span. Measure answer-span recall at K, citation precision and the fraction of retrieved tokens that are duplicate overlap. This is more informative than measuring whether any chunk from the right document was returned. An answer can mention the right manual while omitting the limit value or exception that makes the result useful.

Use parent context without losing provenance

A small child chunk can retrieve accurately; a larger parent section can supply the surrounding condition. Keep the child's offset and the parent's revision, then expand context within a strict token budget. Never merge text across documents or policy revisions just because their headings match. For tables, keep header labels and units with each row. Parent-child retrieval describes the serving pattern, while table retrieval covers row-level evidence.

Run controlled chunking experiments

Hold corpus, queries, embedding model, retriever settings and K constant while changing only the splitting rule. Compare section-aware windows, fixed token windows and minimal overlap on the same answer-span labels. Inspect misses by document type: code blocks, tables, scanned PDFs and incident timelines behave differently. Count extra index entries and ingest time, not just recall. A higher recall score that doubles repeated context and citation confusion can worsen the final answer. Release gates should require both evidence quality and acceptable cost.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PassageWindow:
    document_id: str
    start: int
    end: int

def windows(document_id: str, token_count: int, size: int,
            overlap: int) -> list[PassageWindow]:
    if token_count < 0 or size < 1 or not 0 <= overlap < size:
        raise ValueError("invalid chunk settings")
    result = []
    step = size - overlap
    for start in range(0, token_count, step):
        end = min(start + size, token_count)
        result.append(PassageWindow(document_id, start, end))
        if end == token_count:
            break
    return result

def span_is_complete(chunks: list[PassageWindow], document_id: str,
                     answer_start: int, answer_end: int) -> bool:
    return any(chunk.document_id == document_id
               and chunk.start <= answer_start
               and answer_end <= chunk.end for chunk in chunks)

plain = windows("pump-p47-v3", 83, 30, 0)
with_overlap = windows("pump-p47-v3", 83, 30, 12)
assert not span_is_complete(plain, "pump-p47-v3", 24, 35)
assert span_is_complete(with_overlap, "pump-p47-v3", 24, 35)
assert with_overlap[-1].end == 83

Performance and operating cost

For T tokens, window size C and overlap O, the number of windows is roughly T divided by C minus O, so index entries and embedding work rise as overlap approaches C. The example emits windows in O(W) time and O(W) space for W windows; checking one answer span costs O(W) time. Actual tokenizer counts, structural parsing, retrieval and reranking add further cost. Keep offsets in the tokenization version used to build the index, or citations will drift after reprocessing.

Common Mistakes

  • Selecting chunk size from model limits alone without measuring complete answer spans.
  • Counting overlapping copies of one passage as independent evidence.
  • Splitting a table value away from its unit or header.
  • Changing tokenizer or parser without rebuilding offsets and citation IDs.

Validation drill

Annotate 53 answer spans across prose, tables and procedures. Compare three splitting policies at the same top-12 budget; report complete-span recall, duplicated retrieved tokens, index size and citation errors.

title: Safe search query parsing: operators, filters and literal identifiers
summary: Parse a small search grammar without allowing user text to become backend query syntax or corrupting exact identifiers.
body:
Parse a small search grammar without allowing user text to become backend query syntax or corrupting exact identifiers.

Separate user text from query instructions

A search box receives untrusted text. Some users want literal terms; others want a quoted phrase or a field filter. Treating every colon, quote or minus sign as an operator makes part numbers and copied error messages disappear. Sending the entire string to an engine's strict query-language parser also exposes backend syntax and brittle error behavior. Define a small public grammar and compile it to typed backend clauses. Keep literal identifier matching available even when the ordinary text analyzer stems or splits words.

Write down the grammar before the parser

For a maintenance archive, allow plain words, double-quoted phrases and one filter of the form site:plant-a. Make the allowed filter names explicit. Put bounds on query bytes, phrase length and operator count before parsing; a syntactically valid query can still consume excessive work. Reject unknown filters rather than silently treating them as authorization. A site filter narrows a search; it cannot grant access to a plant the user is forbidden to see. Corpus permissions must be applied by the server independently of the query.

Compile to data, never to a concatenated query string

The backend should receive structured term, phrase and filter values. It should escape or parameterize them using its own API, not string interpolation into a query-language expression. If an external search service accepts only a query string, encode literal tokens with that service's documented escaping rules and test metacharacters end to end. Do not reuse SQL quoting rules for search-engine syntax. Parse errors should be explicit and safe: show the offending span without echoing private backend diagnostics. Query expansion is a separate, measured step after the literal request is preserved.

Preserve exact tokens and interpretation

Store the raw query, parsed clauses, parser version and final backend request in a protected trace. A serial such as P-47/AC may need both a raw keyword field and a normalized text field; the slash and hyphen should not accidentally become operators. Search analytics can group equivalent grammar versions, but never rewrite a user's identifier into a guessed synonym without retaining an exact branch. When a result seems wrong, retrieval traces reveal whether the parser, analyzer, filter or ranker changed the request.

Test the contract at its boundaries

Build a table of valid and invalid requests: empty input, unmatched quotes, doubled filters, Unicode letters, copied stack traces, 47-word inputs and punctuation-heavy IDs. Check that forbidden sites stay excluded even when the user asks for them. Compare parsed intent with human judgments on realistic query logs after redacting personal data. A permissive fallback that sends a malformed query directly to the engine defeats the parser; return a clear error or treat the whole input as literal text according to one documented rule.

Worked contract

import re
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SearchRequest:
    terms: tuple[str, ...]
    phrases: tuple[str, ...]
    site: str | None

TOKEN = re.compile(r'"[^"\n]{1,80}"|[^\s"]+')
SITE = re.compile(r"site:([a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,31})$", re.I)

def parse_search(raw_query: str, allowed_sites: set[str]) -> SearchRequest:
    if len(raw_query.encode("utf-8")) > 384:
        raise ValueError("query too long")
    terms, phrases, site = [], [], None
    remaining = TOKEN.sub("", raw_query).strip()
    if remaining:
        raise ValueError("unmatched quote or unsupported syntax")
    for token in TOKEN.findall(raw_query):
        if token.startswith('"'):
            phrases.append(token[1:-1])
        elif token.startswith("site:"):
            match = SITE.fullmatch(token)
            if match is None or site is not None:
                raise ValueError("invalid site filter")
            site = match.group(1).lower()
            if site not in allowed_sites:
                raise ValueError("site not available")
        else:
            terms.append(token)
    if not terms and not phrases:
        raise ValueError("query needs search text")
    if len(terms) + len(phrases) > 47:
        raise ValueError("too many clauses")
    return SearchRequest(tuple(terms), tuple(phrases), site)

request = parse_search('P-47/AC "seal pressure" site:plant-a', {"plant-a"})
assert request.terms == ("P-47/AC",)
assert request.phrases == ("seal pressure",)
assert request.site == "plant-a"

Performance and operating cost

For N query characters, tokenization and parsing take O(N) time and O(N) space. The backend's cost depends on posting-list size, phrase positions, filters and top-K ranking; parsing is rarely the expensive part. The demonstration describes a deliberately narrow grammar, not a full search-language parser. Its caller must still enforce tenant authorization and compile the typed values through the backend's safe query API.

Common Mistakes

  • Passing raw user text to a strict backend query-language parser.
  • Using a user-supplied site filter as an access-control decision.
  • Dropping punctuation from an exact serial number before literal matching.
  • Silently falling back to unrestricted search after a syntax error.

Validation drill

Collect 63 redacted archive queries containing IDs, quotes and filters. Label each intended interpretation, then test parser acceptance, exact-token retention and permission enforcement before comparing top-12 recall.
