title: Search snippets: highlighting, offsets and safe evidence previews
summary: Build snippets from the correct source revision, escape text safely and keep private spans out of previews.
body:
Build snippets from the correct source revision, escape text safely and keep private spans out of previews.

A snippet is a provenance claim

A search result preview tells a reader why a passage matched. Its words must come from the same authorized source revision as the link and citation. Reconstructing a snippet from a model summary can make the result appear to contain text it never held. Preserve source offsets during source extraction, together with document ID, revision and field name. Render the original passage around a matched span; label transformed text when OCR or normalization means the display differs from the source.

Choose a window that retains the qualifier

A 30-character window around a matched number may omit its unit, negation or date. Expand to a sentence, table row or bounded section when structure is available. Limit output length, then mark truncation. For a query about a pressure limit, showing only the number is misleading if the next sentence says it applies only during startup. The claim support check should inspect the full evidence, not a clipped snippet. A preview is navigation help, not proof by itself.

Escape before adding markup

Source documents may contain HTML, scripts or text that looks like tags. Escape source text first, then insert only controlled highlighting markup around measured spans. Offset units matter: byte offsets, Unicode code-point indices and UTF-16 units are different. If the highlighter measures one representation and the renderer slices another, a match can move into the wrong word or break an encoded character. A safe renderer either uses offsets in its own string representation or converts them explicitly.

Redact under the current permission scope

A result can be searchable without every field being previewable. Mask personal data, secrets and restricted spans before selecting or rendering windows; highlight offsets then need recalculation against the redacted text. Cache previews only with a permission scope and source revision, and invalidate them when a document is deleted or access changes. Redaction is not achieved by hiding markup with CSS: the private text must never be sent to the browser. Permission-aware caching covers the same revocation boundary.

Evaluate both safety and usefulness

Judge whether a preview contains the answer-bearing phrase, relevant unit and limiting condition; also test whether it contains any restricted span. Include OCR artifacts, right-to-left text, emoji and strings such as angle brackets in the corpus. Compare snippet usefulness and render latency at a fixed window budget. Generating broad previews for every candidate before top-K selection can waste work; fetch and render only results that survive ranking. OCR layout changes what a nearby text window actually means.

Worked contract

from html import escape

def highlighted_preview(source_text: str, match_start: int,
                        match_end: int, radius: int = 47) -> str:
    if not 0 <= match_start < match_end <= len(source_text):
        raise ValueError("invalid match span")
    if not 0 <= radius <= 160:
        raise ValueError("invalid radius")
    start = max(0, match_start - radius)
    end = min(len(source_text), match_end + radius)
    before = escape(source_text[start:match_start])
    matched = escape(source_text[match_start:match_end])
    after = escape(source_text[match_end:end])
    return ("…" if start else "") + before + "<strong>" + matched + "</strong>" + after + ("…" if end < len(source_text) else "")

passage = "Pump P-47: <script> is literal text. Seal limit is 28 kPa."
start = passage.index("28 kPa")
preview = highlighted_preview(passage, start, start + len("28 kPa"))
assert "<script>" not in preview
assert "<script>" in preview
assert "<strong>28 kPa</strong>" in preview

Performance and operating cost

For a selected preview window of W characters, escaping and concatenation take O(W) time and O(W) space. Locating a match can be O(N) in an N-character passage without stored offsets; the example's index call has that cost. Index-time term vectors or stored offsets trade storage and ingest work for faster highlighting. Apply redaction before this function; escaped private text is still private text. The example emits controlled strong tags only after escaping source characters.

Common Mistakes

  • Inserting raw source text into HTML and highlighting it afterward.
  • Using offsets from a normalized or redacted string against the original source.
  • Showing a numeric hit without its unit or limiting condition.
  • Caching a preview beyond a permission change or document revision.

Validation drill

Annotate 37 result previews across HTML-like text, OCR and restricted fields. Require the answer span plus qualifier in allowed previews, zero leaked restricted spans and correct source revision after an update.

title: Index alias cutovers: switch retrieval generations without mixed results
summary: Build and verify a new index before switching readers, retain rollback and check cross-index compatibility.
body:
Build and verify a new index before switching readers, retain rollback and check cross-index compatibility.

Treat each index build as a generation

An index generation is an immutable serving candidate with a corpus snapshot, parser settings, analyzer configuration and model version. Updating a live index in place can mix old and new representations. Instead, build generation B while readers use A, replay changes until B reaches an acceptable ingestion watermark, and verify it before cutover. An alias or routing pointer lets the application switch the serving generation as one operation. The pointer is small; rebuilding the index is the costly work.

Check compatibility across every retrieval branch

A retrieval service may read a lexical index, vector index, metadata store and citation store for one answer. Changing only one alias can produce a passage ID that the other stores cannot resolve, or a query vector encoded with the wrong model. Record a manifest of compatible generations and switch that manifest atomically at the application boundary. Multi-index snapshots explain why a single consistent view matters; embedding migration covers vector-specific compatibility.

Gate the switch on observed evidence

Compare the candidate generation on labeled slices for exact identifiers, paraphrases, deleted documents, access restrictions and fresh updates. Inspect top-K recall, unsupported claims, p95 latency and index size. A green aggregate can hide a severe loss for rare serial-number queries. Run shadow traffic with identical authorization filters and no user-visible answers, then compare traces under a fixed sample budget. Keep a minimum freshness condition so the new index does not silently omit the last ingestion window.

Switch once and keep rollback bounded

Before cutover, pin in-flight requests to one generation. Change the alias or manifest pointer atomically, then start new requests on B. Retain A until rollback tests, cache invalidation and a short monitoring period complete. Reversing the pointer is a rollback only if A can still serve current permissions and deletion rules. A deleted document must not reappear after a rollback; apply tombstones to both generations or use a central authoritative filter. Delete races become more important during dual writes.

Audit the generation used by each answer

Log the serving manifest ID, corpus watermark and relevant model versions with each retrieval trace and citation. If an incident spans a cutover, those fields distinguish an index defect from a changed query distribution. Test partial failures: a stale replica, failed alias update and cache entry from A should never make one answer combine A and B without an explicit compatibility rule. An index alias is a routing device, not evidence that data or permissions are correct.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class IndexGeneration:
    name: str
    corpus_revision: int
    model_revision: str
    checked: bool

def choose_generation(current: IndexGeneration,
                      candidate: IndexGeneration,
                      required_corpus_revision: int,
                      query_model_revision: str) -> IndexGeneration:
    if not candidate.checked:
        raise ValueError("candidate has not passed release checks")
    if candidate.corpus_revision < required_corpus_revision:
        raise ValueError("candidate is behind the freshness gate")
    if candidate.model_revision != query_model_revision:
        raise ValueError("query and passage models differ")
    return candidate

active = IndexGeneration("lexical-a", 81, "encoder-r4", True)
next_index = IndexGeneration("lexical-b", 87, "encoder-r4", True)
selected = choose_generation(active, next_index, 85, "encoder-r4")
assert selected.name == "lexical-b"
assert active.name == "lexical-a"

Performance and operating cost

The gate shown uses O(1) time and space; index construction remains proportional to corpus size and token or vector count. Dual generations temporarily raise storage, ingestion and validation cost. Actual pointer updates need a backend operation that is atomic for readers, plus a consistent application manifest when several indexes are involved. The code models a gate, not a distributed alias update or a substitute for live permission checks.

Common Mistakes

  • Switching a lexical index and vector index independently without a compatibility manifest.
  • Treating a successful alias update as proof the candidate contains recent deletions.
  • Deleting the prior generation before rollback and in-flight requests are finished.
  • Using a rollback that restores documents whose access has since been revoked.

Validation drill

Build two generations from 113 documents and replay three changes, including a deletion. Verify a freshness gate, a failed candidate, an atomic pointer switch, in-flight request pinning and a rollback that does not reveal the deleted record.

title: Retrieval drift: monitor query slices and shadow a candidate safely
summary: Detect changes in retrieval quality without confusing clicks with labels or exposing shadow results to users.
body:
Detect changes in retrieval quality without confusing clicks with labels or exposing shadow results to users.

Drift is a change in the contract, not one number

Retrieval drift appears when query wording, corpus coverage, permissions, parser behavior or model representations change enough that relevant evidence is no longer found. A stable aggregate click rate can hide a severe miss for a low-volume query class. Define slices such as serial identifiers, recent procedures, multilingual requests and no-answer questions. Track corpus and index freshness alongside result behavior so a stale source is not mistaken for ranking drift. Release gates set initial quality thresholds; monitoring tests whether those assumptions still hold.

Use signals with different levels of trust

Labeled answer-bearing passages give direct recall measurements but are expensive and slow to update. Unlabeled operational signals include zero-result rate, filter rejection, latency, candidate overlap and sudden changes in query length. These indicate where to investigate; they do not prove relevance. Clicks are shaped by result position and interface design, so they cannot be treated as ground-truth judgments. Click bias needs explicit correction or a separate human review path.

Shadow candidates within the same security boundary

A shadow run sends a sampled query to the current and candidate retrievers, then shows only the current result to the user. Both branches must apply the same current permission filters and secret-handling rules. Log bounded, redacted comparisons rather than raw private queries. Record index, model and parser versions; otherwise a changed score distribution cannot be attributed. Compare result IDs, answer-bearing span recall on labeled traffic and latency at the same candidate budget. Do not call a shadow winner from score magnitude alone when scoring scales differ.

Set alert thresholds by slice and baseline

Use a fixed evaluation set for regression checks and a rolling operational baseline for distribution changes. A threshold should include minimum traffic, a window and an action: inspect, pause rollout or roll back. For rare slices, low sample count can make a weekly rate noisy; report numerator and denominator, not only a percentage. A sudden zero-result increase may be caused by a permission policy change, an ingestion delay or new user vocabulary. Traces help separate these causes.

Close the loop with adjudicated cases

When an alert fires, sample misses, attach source revision and permission context, and have reviewers identify the expected evidence or mark the query unanswerable. Add stable cases to the judged set, then test a proposed parser, index or ranking change against old and new slices. Counterfactual tests expose whether the change merely overfits familiar examples. Keep evaluation data versioned; otherwise an apparent gain may come from changed labels rather than a better retriever.

Worked contract

from collections import defaultdict

def slice_recall(records: list[tuple[str, bool, bool]],
                 minimum_cases: int = 3) -> dict[str, tuple[int, int]]:
    counts = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0])
    for query_slice, has_judged_answer, answer_found in records:
        if not has_judged_answer:
            continue
        counts[query_slice][1] += 1
        counts[query_slice][0] += int(answer_found)
    return {name: (hits, total) for name, (hits, total) in counts.items()
            if total >= minimum_cases}

judgments = [
    ("serial-id", True, True), ("serial-id", True, False),
    ("serial-id", True, True), ("recent-policy", True, True),
    ("recent-policy", True, True), ("recent-policy", True, True),
    ("recent-policy", False, False),
]
report = slice_recall(judgments)
assert report == {"serial-id": (2, 3), "recent-policy": (3, 3)}

Performance and operating cost

For Q judged queries, this single-pass slice calculation takes O(Q) time and O(S) space for S slices. Running two retrievers in shadow can nearly double retrieval compute for sampled traffic, plus trace storage and review work; sample deliberately and cap latency impact. The example reports counts instead of a bare percentage and excludes no-answer cases from answer-recall. Evaluate abstention separately, because excluding no-answer cases does not make false answers harmless.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling clicks a relevance label without accounting for position and presentation.
  • Comparing raw scores from different ranking models as if their scales matched.
  • Shadowing a candidate without the current permission filters.
  • Triggering a rollback from a tiny slice sample without examining its counts and source context.

Validation drill

Shadow 71 redacted queries across four named slices. Compare candidate overlap and judged recall, report counts with p95 latency and freshness, then adjudicate five disagreements before deciding on a rollout.

title: Faceted retrieval: trustworthy counts under permission filters
summary: Compute evidence-type and revision facets from the authorized result set without leaking restricted document counts.
body:
Compute evidence-type and revision facets from the authorized result set without leaking restricted document counts.

A facet describes the candidate set

A facet groups search matches by a field such as document type, plant, revision or language. It is a navigation control, not a relevance score. If a query returns maintenance notes and incident reports, a type facet tells the reader how many eligible documents of each kind remain. Define whether counts apply before or after a selected facet: both are useful, but silently mixing them makes the interface inconsistent. For a retrieval answer, the same metadata can steer query routing toward a source type without replacing the relevance judgment.

Authorize before counting

Count only documents the requester may see at this moment. A hidden document must not appear in a facet count even if its text never appears in results; a count of one can reveal that a confidential investigation exists. Apply tenant, document-status and access filters before aggregation, then compute buckets from the filtered candidate set. If permissions change, invalidate cached counts with the search result. Document lifecycle includes deletion and revocation, both of which change counts.

Keep a stable counting unit

One source manual may produce 70 chunks, while a short incident note produces one. Counting passages would suggest 70 manuals unless the interface clearly labels the unit as passages. For a document-type facet, deduplicate by source document ID and revision policy first; for an answer-span facet, passage counts may be appropriate. Decide whether two revisions are separate documents or one current logical document. The decision should match the result list and citations. Chunk identity provides the parent IDs required for correct grouping.

Choose fields and cardinality deliberately

Use exact metadata values for facets; analyzed body text is a poor source of category keys. A plant name may contain punctuation that a full-text analyzer splits, and a free-form document title can create nearly one bucket per record. Cap visible buckets and expose a separate search within a high-cardinality facet when needed. Distributed top buckets can have approximate counts if shards truncate their local candidates. When exact counts drive a legal or operational decision, use a compatible exact aggregation path and report its extra cost. Shard failures must make counts incomplete rather than silently authoritative.

Test facets alongside ranking

Create judged searches with multiple document types, one restricted record, duplicate chunks and an old revision. Verify that results, counts and selected filters all share the same authorized snapshot. A user selecting a facet should see a result set that equals the stated count under the same query, subject to pagination and any explicit approximate-count label. Do not compute counts from only the top-K ranked hits unless the UI says top-K: that measures the preview window, not all eligible matches. Stable pagination keeps the same filter and snapshot across pages.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceRecord:
    document_id: str
    passage_id: str
    tenant: str
    kind: str
    current: bool

def document_facets(records: list[EvidenceRecord], tenant: str,
                    matching_passages: set[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
    visible_documents = {}
    for record in records:
        if record.tenant != tenant or not record.current:
            continue
        if record.passage_id not in matching_passages:
            continue
        visible_documents[record.document_id] = record.kind
    return dict(Counter(visible_documents.values()))

records = [
    EvidenceRecord("manual-p47", "m47-a", "north", "manual", True),
    EvidenceRecord("manual-p47", "m47-b", "north", "manual", True),
    EvidenceRecord("incident-83", "i83-a", "north", "incident", True),
    EvidenceRecord("private-12", "p12-a", "south", "incident", True),
    EvidenceRecord("retired-4", "r4-a", "north", "manual", False),
]
counts = document_facets(records, "north", {r.passage_id for r in records})
assert counts == {"manual": 1, "incident": 1}

Performance and operating cost

For P matched passage records, this demonstration takes O(P) time and O(D) space for D distinct visible documents. A production index can aggregate metadata without loading every passage, but exact distinct-document counts and high-cardinality fields can consume memory and network work across shards. Count only after authorization. The example's tenant check is a teaching stand-in; a real service must also enforce per-document access and current revocation state before the bucket stage.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting chunks while labeling the number as documents.
  • Computing facet buckets before access filtering.
  • Treating counts from the top-K preview as all query matches.
  • Showing exact-looking counts after a shard timed out or returned truncated buckets.

Validation drill

Index 89 passages from 23 documents with two revisions and four restricted records. Compare facet counts with an independently authorized document list, then remove a shard and confirm the UI marks counts incomplete.

title: Multi-tenant retrieval: isolate indexes, routes and noisy neighbors
summary: Choose shared or separate indexes using permission boundaries, shard fanout, tenant size and deletion requirements.
body:
Choose shared or separate indexes using permission boundaries, shard fanout, tenant size and deletion requirements.

Tenant filtering is a security boundary

A multi-tenant retriever serves several organizations from one application. Every query, suggestion, cache entry and evidence citation must carry the authenticated tenant, regardless of any tenant value typed into the search box. A filter added after candidate generation may already be too late if the vector backend explores or logs unauthorized candidates. Where supported, constrain the index or shard search before ranking and recheck document permissions before returning evidence. Corpus permissions still apply within a tenant; tenancy alone is not document authorization.

Choose an index layout from workload facts

A separate index per tenant gives a clear deletion and capacity boundary, but thousands of tiny indexes can waste metadata, shards and warm memory. A shared index with an indexed tenant key reduces per-tenant overhead; it demands strict filtering and makes one large tenant a possible noisy neighbor. A hybrid layout puts large or regulated tenants in their own indexes and small tenants in a shared pool. Document the migration path for a tenant that grows. Do not choose the layout from row count alone: query volume, vector memory, update rate and retention policy matter.

Use routing to limit work, not to grant access

Routing records for one tenant to a subset of shards can reduce query fanout, but a routing key is not an authorization check. A malicious or mistaken client can provide another key unless the server derives it from the authenticated identity. Very large tenants may overload one shard, so size routing buckets and rebalance with measured limits. Queries across allowed shared collections may need several shard keys and an explicit merge policy. Shard fanout explains the latency and partial-result behavior once a request crosses partitions.

Keep generations and caches tenant-scoped

A lexical index migration, vector model upgrade or deletion replay may finish for one tenant before another. Record generation and watermark per tenant, not as a misleading global number. Cache keys need tenant, permission revision, query, filters and index generation; otherwise a cached answer can cross an access boundary after a cutover. Permission-aware caching provides the full revocation contract. Trace storage deserves the same isolation as the content index because raw queries may contain private identifiers.

Test failures that look like success

Seed two tenants with the same document title but different contents. Search by title, use autocomplete, paginate and revoke a document while holding a cursor. None of the surfaces should disclose the other tenant's title, count or snippet. Then send a burst from the large tenant and measure the smaller tenant's p95 latency to expose noisy-neighbor effects. Test deletion and rollback too; a tenant moved to a new index must not leave an older copy searchable. Index cutovers need this per-tenant deletion proof.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TenantPassage:
    tenant: str
    passage_id: str
    words: frozenset[str]

def authorized_candidates(passages: list[TenantPassage],
                          authenticated_tenant: str,
                          query_words: set[str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(passage.passage_id for passage in passages
                  if passage.tenant == authenticated_tenant
                  and passage.words & query_words)

index = [
    TenantPassage("north", "north-p47", frozenset({"seal", "limit"})),
    TenantPassage("south", "south-p47", frozenset({"seal", "contract"})),
]
assert authorized_candidates(index, "north", {"seal"}) == ["north-p47"]
assert authorized_candidates(index, "south", {"seal"}) == ["south-p47"]

Performance and operating cost

The list scan takes O(N) time for N passages and O(K) output space for K authorized matches. An indexed tenant partition or routed shard narrows the scanned candidates, but per-tenant indexes add fixed metadata and operational cost. The example shows the invariant that the tenant comes from authentication; it does not provide a secure search index. Enforce the same tenant scope at suggestion, aggregation, cache and citation boundaries, then measure tail latency under competing tenants.

Common Mistakes

  • Trusting a tenant ID supplied in a search parameter.
  • Using routing as the only permission check.
  • Moving a tenant between indexes without replaying deletions and clearing old caches.
  • Testing average latency only while one tenant saturates a shared shard.

Validation drill

Populate two tenants with 41 similarly named documents. Exercise search, facets, suggestions, pagination, rollback and deletion; assert zero cross-tenant IDs while one tenant generates five times the query load.

title: Retrieval autocomplete: useful suggestions without query leaks
summary: Build prefix suggestions from approved vocabulary, bind them to access scope and prevent private search histories from surfacing.
body:
Build prefix suggestions from approved vocabulary, bind them to access scope and prevent private search histories from surfacing.

Suggestion sources have different risks

An autocomplete menu may suggest known document titles, curated subject labels or popular past queries. Titles and labels can be approved at publication; raw query logs can contain names, account IDs and confidential incidents. Never turn query logs into public suggestions merely because the terms are frequent. Start with an approved catalog and a clear deletion path. If popularity is used, apply privacy review and minimum aggregation thresholds before a phrase enters the suggestion index. Safe query parsing still handles the submitted search after the user accepts or edits a suggestion.

Filter at candidate generation

A suggestion can leak a restricted document before the user submits a search. Build tenant-scoped suggestion collections or apply an authorization filter inside the suggestion query and recheck access before display. A site-specific prefix should never enumerate another site's vocabulary. Permission revisions and document deletion must invalidate suggestion caches. If a backend's completion feature cannot enforce the needed access boundary, do not index private titles in it. Tenant isolation covers the surrounding index and routing choices.

Match intent without damaging identifiers

For ordinary words, prefix and infix matching help when the user types the middle of a title. For serials and codes, preserve punctuation and case-normalization rules that fit the identifier scheme; a generic tokenizer may split P-47/AC into unrelated fragments. Rank suggestions by exact prefix, approved category and currentness before popularity. A suggestion is a proposed query, not an answer. Display its source type so a document title is not confused with a verified fact. Lexical identifier safety provides the corresponding search behavior.

Bound work at typing speed

Autocomplete runs for partial inputs, so it can issue many requests per user. Require a meaningful minimum prefix, debounce client requests, cancel stale responses and cap returned items. The server must still rate-limit and enforce length limits because clients can bypass the browser. A trie, edge n-gram index or specialized completion structure can avoid scanning the full vocabulary. Compare its memory and rebuild cost with observed traffic; a small approved catalog may work with a simple sorted prefix scan.

Evaluate visibility and usefulness separately

Test suggestions for common prefixes, typos, IDs, multilingual scripts and document removals. Verify that a restricted title never appears in another tenant's menu, network response or analytics log. Measure acceptance and downstream search success by query slice, but do not treat acceptance as relevance proof: prominent suggestions can influence what users choose. Position bias applies to menus too. A suggestion that raises clicks while suppressing rare but valid queries can make retrieval worse.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ApprovedSuggestion:
    text: str
    tenant: str
    current: bool

def suggest(prefix: str, authenticated_tenant: str,
            catalog: list[ApprovedSuggestion], limit: int = 5) -> list[str]:
    normalized = prefix.strip().casefold()
    if len(normalized) < 3 or not 1 <= limit <= 8:
        return []
    matches = (item.text for item in catalog
               if item.tenant == authenticated_tenant and item.current
               and item.text.casefold().startswith(normalized))
    return sorted(set(matches), key=lambda value: (len(value), value))[:limit]

catalog = [
    ApprovedSuggestion("Pump P-47 seal guide", "north", True),
    ApprovedSuggestion("Pump P-48 pressure limits", "north", True),
    ApprovedSuggestion("Pump P-47 incident", "south", True),
    ApprovedSuggestion("Pump P-42 retired", "north", False),
]
assert suggest("Pump P-4", "north", catalog) == [
    "Pump P-47 seal guide", "Pump P-48 pressure limits"]

Performance and operating cost

This demonstration scans A approved suggestions in O(A) time and uses O(M) memory for M matched strings before sorting them in O(M log M) time. A prefix index can reduce lookup work, but consumes storage and must track updates and revocations. The same current authorization check remains necessary after lookup. Client-side debouncing reduces normal request volume, not server-side abuse; rate limits and minimum prefix length must be enforced by the service.

Common Mistakes

  • Building public suggestions directly from raw search logs.
  • Filtering restricted suggestions only after returning them to the browser.
  • Assuming browser autocomplete settings protect server-side query history.
  • Letting a generic tokenizer strip significant punctuation from product IDs.

Validation drill

Create 74 approved titles, 12 removed titles and two tenant scopes. Test 20 prefixes, including punctuation-heavy IDs and a restricted unique prefix; inspect both response payloads and logs for leaks.

title: HNSW retrieval: candidate budgets, graph cost and recall curves
summary: Tune approximate vector search against an exact baseline while separating construction, traversal and filter effects.
body:
Tune approximate vector search against an exact baseline while separating construction, traversal and filter effects.

Approximate search trades work for missed neighbors

An HNSW index connects vectors in a layered graph so a search can follow promising neighbors instead of scoring every vector. The returned top-K is approximate: a closer vector may remain unexplored. Increasing the search candidate budget often improves recall but adds distance computations, memory traffic and tail latency. The exact baseline is a full similarity scan over the eligible corpus. A graph result should be measured against that baseline using the same embedding version and permission filters. Filtered ANN covers the additional difficulty of finding neighbors after an access or metadata filter.

Separate build knobs from query knobs

The graph connection limit controls how many edges a node retains, while a construction search width controls how broadly neighbors are considered as the index is built. Larger values can improve connectivity but raise memory and ingestion work. The query-time candidate budget controls exploration for one search; changing it does not rebuild a poor graph. Implementations use different parameter names and defaults, so record the actual backend version and settings with each benchmark. Embedding version must be held fixed while tuning the graph.

Measure recall by query slice

For each judged query, compare approximate top-K IDs with exact top-K IDs and compute overlap or labeled relevant-document recall. Include dense clusters, rare outliers, near duplicates and recently inserted vectors. Report p50 and p95 latency, distance computations, graph bytes and index build time for each budget. An average score can hide a recall collapse on filtered or rare-identifier queries. If vectors are quantized, isolate compression loss by comparing exact search on compressed vectors with exact search on original vectors. Quantization is a separate source of error.

Do not confuse global recall with authorized recall

An unrestricted graph can find nearby documents that a user cannot view. Removing them after top-K may leave too few eligible hits. Raise the exploration budget, use an engine with filter-aware traversal, or search a suitable tenant partition; benchmark each choice at a fixed latency cap. The final result must pass a fresh authorization check even when traversal used an authorized partition. Tenant layout changes both recall and security boundaries.

Use a controlled sweep, then freeze a gate

Sweep several search budgets while keeping corpus, queries, model, K and hardware fixed. Reject settings that fail a minimum recall slice or p95 latency budget. Re-run after large ingestion batches, graph rebuilds and backend upgrades, because segment layout and deleted-node patterns can change traversal. Use a smaller candidate budget only when measured savings matter and the lost evidence is acceptable. Release gates should capture that decision rather than one attractive benchmark chart.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def cosine(left: tuple[float, ...], right: tuple[float, ...]) -> float:
    numerator = sum(a * b for a, b in zip(left, right))
    left_norm = sqrt(sum(value * value for value in left))
    right_norm = sqrt(sum(value * value for value in right))
    if left_norm == 0 or right_norm == 0:
        raise ValueError("zero vector has no cosine similarity")
    return numerator / (left_norm * right_norm)

def exact_top_k(query: tuple[float, ...],
                vectors: dict[str, tuple[float, ...]],
                allowed_ids: set[str], k: int) -> list[str]:
    if k < 1 or not query or not all(len(v) == len(query) for v in vectors.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid vector dimensions or K")
    scored = [(item_id, cosine(query, vector))
              for item_id, vector in vectors.items() if item_id in allowed_ids]
    return [item_id for item_id, _ in sorted(
        scored, key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))[:k]]

vectors = {"pump-p47": (.9, .1), "pump-p48": (.5, .5),
           "pump-p49": (.1, .9), "private-plan": (1.0, 0.0)}
gold = exact_top_k((1.0, .1), vectors,
                   {"pump-p47", "pump-p48", "pump-p49"}, 2)
approximate = ["pump-p48", "pump-p47"]
recall_at_two = len(set(gold) & set(approximate)) / len(gold)
assert gold == ["pump-p47", "pump-p48"]
assert recall_at_two == 1.0

Performance and operating cost

For N eligible vectors of dimension D, the exact baseline takes O(ND + N log N) time with full sorting and O(N) space for scores; top-K selection can reduce the ranking term. HNSW typically visits far fewer vectors, but its practical work depends on graph connectivity, candidate budget, filtering and segment layout rather than a universal constant bound. The code computes an exact benchmark, not an HNSW implementation. The candidate list represents output from an ANN engine and must be obtained from that engine in a real sweep.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a larger query budget a fix for an incompatible embedding version.
  • Measuring overlap against an unrestricted exact baseline when users have access filters.
  • Reporting only average latency while p95 degrades.
  • Attributing quantization errors to graph traversal without a separate exact comparison.

Validation drill

For 97 labeled queries, sweep four candidate budgets with K fixed at 12. Report exact-overlap recall and judged recall by tenant and rare-query slice, plus p95 latency, build time and graph memory.

title: Vector similarity metrics: normalization changes the ranking
summary: Choose cosine, inner product or L2 from the embedding contract and test exact rankings before building an ANN index.
body:
Choose cosine, inner product or L2 from the embedding contract and test exact rankings before building an ANN index.

The metric is part of the embedding contract

A vector index needs a comparison rule. Cosine similarity compares direction after accounting for vector length; inner product combines direction and magnitude; Euclidean distance measures geometric separation. None is universally best for retrieval. An embedding model may assume normalized outputs or use vector length as a signal. If that contract changes, the same passage vectors can rank differently even when their dimensions match. Record the metric, normalization rule, model revision and dimension together. Embedding migrations should reject an index whose metric or normalization rule differs from the serving query encoder.

Normalize both sides when cosine is the goal

For nonzero unit vectors, the inner product equals cosine similarity. Squared L2 distance then equals two minus twice the inner product, so all three produce equivalent orderings when applied consistently to those unit vectors. That equivalence does not hold when only queries are normalized or when passage magnitudes vary. Normalize vectors before indexing and before querying if the backend implements cosine through inner product. A zero vector cannot be normalized; reject it and inspect the encoder pipeline rather than silently inserting it.

Compare exact scores before ANN tuning

An approximate index can miss a neighbor because of graph traversal, quantization or filters. First run exact search under the intended metric; then compare ANN results to that baseline at a fixed K and permission scope. Otherwise a rank change caused by accidental normalization may be blamed on a candidate budget. HNSW budgets affect exploration, while quantization affects stored precision. Keep these experiments separate.

Do not mix metric scores across branches

An L2 distance is smaller when better; cosine and inner product are larger when better. Their numeric scales differ and may vary by model or collection. A hybrid ranker cannot add raw values from these branches and expect a meaningful order. Convert each branch to a common calibrated signal using judged data, or combine ranks while keeping branch score interpretation intact. Fusion calibration handles this final step. A threshold learned for cosine cannot be copied to an inner-product index without reevaluation.

Test distributions and exceptions

Measure exact top-K recall on paraphrases, rare identifiers and out-of-domain text; compare score distributions before setting any answer threshold. Include zero vectors, NaNs, dimension mismatches and vectors whose magnitudes differ sharply. Check whether the embedding provider normalizes outputs at each version, but verify actual stored vectors rather than relying on a name. If magnitude is useful, cosine may discard a valuable signal. If magnitude is accidental, inner product may let unusually large vectors dominate. The decision belongs to measured retrieval quality, not a formula alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def scores(query: tuple[float, ...], passage: tuple[float, ...]
           ) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    if not query or len(query) != len(passage):
        raise ValueError("dimension mismatch")
    if not all(isfinite(value) for value in query + passage):
        raise ValueError("non-finite coordinate")
    query_norm = sqrt(sum(value * value for value in query))
    passage_norm = sqrt(sum(value * value for value in passage))
    if query_norm == 0 or passage_norm == 0:
        raise ValueError("zero vector")
    dot = sum(left * right for left, right in zip(query, passage))
    squared_l2 = sum((left - right) ** 2
                     for left, right in zip(query, passage))
    return dot, dot / (query_norm * passage_norm), squared_l2

query = (1.0, 0.0)
aligned = (4.0, 0.0)
nearby = (1.0, .3)
assert scores(query, aligned)[0] > scores(query, nearby)[0]
assert scores(query, aligned)[1] > scores(query, nearby)[1]
assert scores(query, aligned)[2] > scores(query, nearby)[2]

Performance and operating cost

Computing any one score for D-dimensional vectors takes O(D) time and O(1) extra space. Exact ranking across N passages takes O(ND) score work plus top-K selection or sorting; normalization can be precomputed at ingestion but still costs O(D) per new vector. ANN reduces comparisons at the cost of approximate recall and index memory. The example deliberately shows that inner product and cosine favor the long aligned vector while L2 favors the shorter nearby one; those are different ranking contracts, not a contradiction.

Common Mistakes

  • Normalizing queries but leaving indexed passages unnormalized when expecting cosine order.
  • Comparing a smaller-is-better L2 distance directly with larger-is-better cosine scores.
  • Changing metric settings without rebuilding or validating the indexed vectors.
  • Passing zero, non-finite or wrong-dimensional vectors into a search index.

Validation drill

On 67 judged queries, compare exact cosine, inner-product and L2 top-12 results under one embedding version. Report per-slice recall and vector norm distributions before selecting the production metric.

title: Spelling correction in retrieval: suggest a fix, preserve the original
summary: Recover ordinary misspellings without silently rewriting part numbers, names or exact-match evidence.
body:
Recover ordinary misspellings without silently rewriting part numbers, names or exact-match evidence.

Correction is a candidate branch

A misspelled word can create a zero-result query even when the right document is indexed. A correction service proposes alternatives from a controlled vocabulary; it does not establish what the user intended. Search the original text first or alongside a suggested form, then present the correction explicitly when it changes results. A silent rewrite can retrieve the wrong part or person. Safe query parsing defines the user's literal request; correction must preserve that record for tracing and evaluation.

Protect identifier-shaped tokens

Maintenance IDs, invoice numbers, code symbols and legal clauses often differ by one character. Edit distance would call them close, but their meaning may be unrelated. Route tokens with digits, punctuation or recognized identifier patterns through exact fields, with correction disabled unless a domain-specific alias registry says otherwise. Ordinary words can be considered for correction after a lexical miss. Identifier-safe lexical search protects the corresponding index fields. Keep case and punctuation rules consistent with each identifier family.

Generate and rank alternatives conservatively

Edit distance is a candidate generator, not a relevance score. Limit candidate vocabulary by language, source status and permission scope, then use term frequency and contextual fit only within that allowed set. One edit in a short word may be more dangerous than two edits in a long word. Correct at most a bounded number of tokens so a long noisy query does not explode into combinations. The query expansion guardrail applies: record which branch added a candidate and what evidence it returned.

Choose the display contract

If the original search has strong exact matches, do not replace it. If correction produces better results, label them as results for the corrected text and offer a one-click return to the original. Show one or a few alternatives, not a hidden substitution chain. For a retrieval-based answer, a candidate corrected query still needs claim-level source support; higher result count alone does not justify an answer. Evidence-bound answering can abstain when both branches fail.

Evaluate false corrections explicitly

Build separate test slices for typos, rare names, serial numbers, multilingual terms and already-valid but uncommon words. Count successful recovery and harmful rewrites, not just suggestion acceptance. A model can over-correct rare valid terms toward popular words, especially after popularity ranking. Test newly added vocabulary and deleted documents, because a correction index can lag the retrieval index. A suggestion pointing to removed or forbidden content is still a leak. Private autocomplete has the same vocabulary and permission boundary.

Worked contract

import re

IDENTIFIER = re.compile(r"(?=.*[0-9])[A-Za-z0-9/-]{3,}$")

def edit_distance(left: str, right: str) -> int:
    previous = list(range(len(right) + 1))
    for row_number, left_char in enumerate(left, 1):
        current = [row_number]
        for column_number, right_char in enumerate(right, 1):
            current.append(min(current[-1] + 1,
                               previous[column_number] + 1,
                               previous[column_number - 1]
                               + (left_char != right_char)))
        previous = current
    return previous[-1]

def suggest_spelling(token: str, approved_terms: set[str]) -> str | None:
    if IDENTIFIER.fullmatch(token) or len(token) < 4:
        return None
    candidates = [(edit_distance(token.casefold(), term.casefold()), term)
                  for term in approved_terms]
    close = sorted((distance, term) for distance, term in candidates
                   if distance == 1)
    return close[0][1] if close else None

assert suggest_spelling("presure", {"pressure", "seal"}) == "pressure"
assert suggest_spelling("P-47/AC", {"P-48/AC"}) is None
assert suggest_spelling("seal", {"seal"}) is None

Performance and operating cost

The two-row edit-distance routine uses O(LR) time and O(R) space for token lengths L and R. Scanning V approved terms multiplies that work by V; a production dictionary uses length buckets, prefix indexes or a specialized candidate structure before exact distance checks. Preserve the original query branch so the suggestion can be rejected. The example returns one candidate only and does not implement contextual ranking, authorization or a search engine.

Common Mistakes

  • Silently replacing a user's serial number with the nearest popular code.
  • Treating edit distance alone as proof of intended meaning.
  • Building the suggestion dictionary from restricted or deleted content.
  • Measuring only recovered queries while ignoring harmful corrections of valid rare words.

Validation drill

Label 81 queries: ordinary typos, rare valid terms, multilingual words and one-character-different IDs. Measure recovered top-12 recall and harmful-rewrite rate with the original branch retained.

title: Retrieval tombstones: compact indexes without reviving deleted evidence
summary: Distinguish logical deletion from physical reclamation and verify that a compacted generation preserves current access rules.
body:
Distinguish logical deletion from physical reclamation and verify that a compacted generation preserves current access rules.

Deletion has two clocks

A source can be removed from search results before its bytes are physically reclaimed. A logical tombstone marks it ineligible; segment merge or full index rebuild later removes obsolete postings and vector entries. A privacy or compliance request cannot wait for compaction before stopping disclosure. Enforce deletion in the authoritative eligibility layer immediately, then track physical reclamation under a separate deadline. Document lifecycle defines the access decision; compaction changes storage and performance, not the authority of that decision.

Rebuild from authoritative live records

A compactor must read a consistent source snapshot plus all later delete and update events up to a recorded watermark. Copying only old index entries can revive a document that was deleted while the build ran. Stable document IDs and revision numbers make replay idempotent. When the candidate generation catches up, compare its active-ID set against the authoritative source and tombstone ledger before traffic moves. Ingestion delete races explain why event order and repeated deliveries must be accounted for.

Graph and lexical cleanup are different operations

An inverted index may retain deleted postings until a segment merge. An ANN graph can retain unreachable or masked nodes and may need a backend-specific rebuild to recover memory and search quality. Do not assume an index force-merge command handles vector graph layout exactly as it handles text postings. Measure deleted-record ratio, storage bytes, candidate visits and recall on an exact baseline before scheduling maintenance. HNSW recall curves can show whether stale graph structure affects retrieval.

Cut over with a deletion proof

A new compacted generation is not ready because its build job succeeded. It must pass source-count checks, sampled document hashes, permission tests, delete proofs and a freshness watermark. Pin in-flight requests, then switch the serving pointer to the verified generation. Retain rollback only if the old generation still applies current tombstones and access filters. Alias cutovers describe the pointer operation; the deletion proof guards what that pointer exposes.

Schedule physical work without hiding failures

Merge or rebuild work consumes I/O, CPU and temporary disk. Running it on every delete can harm ingestion and p95 query latency; never running it can inflate storage and graph traversal. Set thresholds from measured delete ratio, disk headroom and latency, and keep a separate deadline for permanent erasure when required. If a build fails halfway, keep the current serving generation and its tombstone filter. Observability should report both eligibility latency and bytes remaining, because a zero-result query does not prove physical deletion.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class SourceRevision:
    document_id: str
    revision: int
    text: str

def compact(source_rows: list[SourceRevision],
            deleted_ids: set[str]) -> dict[str, SourceRevision]:
    active = {}
    for row in source_rows:
        if row.document_id in deleted_ids:
            continue
        current = active.get(row.document_id)
        if current is None or row.revision > current.revision:
            active[row.document_id] = row
    assert not active.keys() & deleted_ids
    return active

history = [SourceRevision("pump-p47", 1, "old seal rule"),
           SourceRevision("pump-p47", 2, "current seal rule"),
           SourceRevision("private-plan", 1, "restricted plan")]
generation = compact(history, {"private-plan"})
assert generation["pump-p47"].revision == 2
assert "private-plan" not in generation

Performance and operating cost

Scanning R source revisions takes O(R) time and O(D) memory for D retained documents; writing a real index adds tokenization, embedding, posting and graph-build costs. A tombstone lookup can be near constant time with a suitable set, but maintaining it across every serving path has operational cost. The example assumes one authoritative delete set at a fixed snapshot. A production build must replay later changes and verify a watermark before cutover; physical byte removal depends on the backend's storage lifecycle.

Common Mistakes

  • Waiting for physical compaction before suppressing a deleted document in search.
  • Building from stale source snapshots without replaying newer tombstones.
  • Assuming a clean query result proves the underlying bytes were erased.
  • Rolling back to a generation that lacks current deletion and permission filters.

Validation drill

Create 123 source revisions, delete eight during a rebuild and replay out-of-order updates. Compare active IDs with the authoritative ledger before and after cutover; inspect disk bytes and top-12 recall separately.

title: Retrieval deadlines: cancel optional work and label incomplete evidence
summary: Divide a request deadline across retrieval stages, prevent queued work from outliving the user and make partial results explicit.
body:
Divide a request deadline across retrieval stages, prevent queued work from outliving the user and make partial results explicit.

One request has one deadline

A retrieval-based answer may run query parsing, lexical search, vector search, reranking, evidence packing and generation. Giving each stage its own full timeout can multiply the user's wait. Start with one end-to-end deadline and pass the remaining time to every downstream operation. Reserve time for mandatory authorization and evidence checks; optional reranking can be skipped when the budget is nearly spent. Reranker budgeting handles the quality cost of a smaller or absent rerank stage.

Admission control comes before expensive work

If the system is saturated, admitting every request can increase queueing delay for all users. Cap concurrent expensive branches, reject or shed excess optional work and return a clear retryable status when the required search cannot finish. A cancellation signal should reach the search backend and any embedding call, not merely stop waiting in the frontend while the work continues. Record queue delay separately from execution time. Shard fanout shows how one slow branch can dominate the tail.

Required evidence is not optional

A timeout in one shard or source may leave an apparently plausible top-K list that omits the only relevant document. Decide in advance whether partial results may be displayed for navigation, and label coverage when they are. Do not feed an incomplete candidate set into a confident answer without an explicit support and abstention policy. An authorization timeout should fail closed; it cannot be treated like an optional reranker. Evidence-bound answering sets the final response rule.

Budget stages by their tail behavior

Allocate deadlines using measured p95 and p99 latency per stage and query slice, not a uniform split. A rare filtered vector query may need more candidate exploration than a common lexical query. If optional work is skipped, log the decision, residual candidate count and index generation so later evaluation can separate quality changes from model changes. A fixed budget should be revisited after corpus growth, shard movement or a new embedding model. Retrieval traces hold those facts.

Exercise slow and failed branches

Simulate a delayed shard, an overloaded embedding service, a cancelled client and a permission store that does not respond. Verify that backend jobs stop, partial evidence is labeled, and private data never crosses a failed authorization boundary. Test retries with idempotency: a user retry must not create duplicate ingestion or repeated paid work. An end-to-end timeout is an operating contract, not a substitute for measuring actual answer support and recall under degraded conditions.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetrievalStage:
    name: str
    estimated_ms: int
    required: bool

def plan_budget(stages: list[RetrievalStage], total_ms: int
                ) -> tuple[list[str], list[str]]:
    if total_ms <= 0:
        raise ValueError("deadline must be positive")
    remaining = total_ms
    run, skipped = [], []
    for stage in stages:
        if stage.estimated_ms < 0:
            raise ValueError("negative stage estimate")
        if stage.estimated_ms > remaining:
            if stage.required:
                raise TimeoutError(f"required stage lacks budget: {stage.name}")
            skipped.append(stage.name)
            continue
        run.append(stage.name)
        remaining -= stage.estimated_ms
    return run, skipped

pipeline = [RetrievalStage("authorization", 19, True),
            RetrievalStage("lexical", 31, True),
            RetrievalStage("vector", 39, True),
            RetrievalStage("rerank", 47, False)]
assert plan_budget(pipeline, 99) == (
    ["authorization", "lexical", "vector"], ["rerank"])

Performance and operating cost

Planning S stages takes O(S) time and O(S) output space. The example uses estimates, not actual timing or cancellation; a real service computes remaining time from a monotonic deadline and passes it to backend calls. Skipping an optional stage saves its work but may reduce ranking quality. Backend cancellation, concurrency limits and bounded queues are needed to stop abandoned work from consuming capacity. Treat missing required evidence or authorization as a failure, not as a fast answer.

Common Mistakes

  • Giving every downstream stage the full request timeout.
  • Stopping the HTTP wait while backend queries continue to run.
  • Treating a timed-out authorization check as permission to proceed.
  • Presenting incomplete shard results as if the full corpus was searched.

Validation drill

Replay 59 queries with injected delays at authorization, vector search and reranking. Record p95 latency, cancellation success, skipped stages and answer support; require explicit failure for missing mandatory work.

title: BM25 ranking: tune term saturation and document length by field
summary: Understand why repeated terms stop adding much score, why long fields are discounted and how to test lexical settings against judged queries.
body:
Understand why repeated terms stop adding much score, why long fields are discounted and how to test lexical settings against judged queries.

BM25 scores terms within a field

BM25 is a lexical ranking function built from term frequency, document frequency and field length. A query term receives more weight when it is uncommon in the indexed corpus; repeated occurrences in one document help, but their marginal gain shrinks. A length factor limits the advantage of a long document that mentions many terms by chance. The exact implementation depends on the search backend, its analyzer, field mapping and shard statistics. Do not treat a BM25 score as a probability or compare it directly with an embedding cosine score. Fusion calibration needs a separate contract for combining those branches.

Separate title and body behavior

A short title and a long manual chapter should not share an unquestioned relevance policy. A repeated word in the chapter is less surprising than the same word in the title, while a title may contain only three useful tokens. Tune fields separately and establish whether title boosts, body norms and exact identifier fields serve different intents. Field scoring and identifier safety covers the mapping boundary: a serial number belongs in an exact field even when nearby descriptive words use BM25. Otherwise a nearly matching serial can outscore the literal one.

What the two controls actually change

The parameter k1 controls term-frequency saturation. A larger k1 lets repeated appearances continue contributing for longer; a smaller one reaches a plateau sooner. The parameter b controls the strength of field-length normalization, from no length adjustment at zero to full adjustment at one. Both interact with average field length and the analyzer's token stream. If you change stemming, stopwords or synonym expansion, the underlying frequencies and lengths change too. Hold the analyzer fixed while testing k1 and b, then retest after an analyzer revision. Shadow evaluation can expose unintended ranking movement.

Use judged queries, not one convincing result

Build query slices for brief titles, long procedures, rare exact terms, repeated boilerplate and misspelled language. Compare recall at the candidate cutoff, nDCG after ranking and the downstream answer support rate. Repeated footer text can inflate term counts; remove it at extraction or use a separate low-weight field before adjusting k1 to compensate. Watch the rank of a passage that contains the entire answer once versus a long page that repeats one query word many times. Judged labels make the comparison inspectable rather than anecdotal.

Keep the scoring boundary visible

The example below computes a small-corpus BM25 term score so the parameter effect is observable. It is not a substitute for your engine's explain output: production engines may use field-specific norms, shard-local statistics, overlap-token rules or different treatment of query-term frequency. Record the index generation, analyzer revision, field, k1 and b with every experiment. Run the same permissions and filters in both variants. Otherwise a relevance regression may actually be a candidate-set change. If BM25 recall is weak for paraphrases, add a vector branch and judge its contribution; do not force lexical tuning to solve semantic mismatch.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import log

def bm25_rank(query: str, manuals: dict[str, str],
              k1: float = 1.3, b: float = 0.68) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    if not manuals or k1 <= 0 or not 0 <= b <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid corpus or BM25 settings")
    tokens = {manual_id: text.casefold().split()
              for manual_id, text in manuals.items()}
    average_length = sum(map(len, tokens.values())) / len(tokens)
    query_terms = set(query.casefold().split())
    scores = []
    for manual_id, words in tokens.items():
        counts = Counter(words)
        length_factor = 1 - b + b * len(words) / average_length
        score = 0.0
        for term in query_terms:
            document_frequency = sum(term in other for other in tokens.values())
            if not document_frequency or not counts[term]:
                continue
            idf = log(1 + (len(tokens) - document_frequency + .5)
                      / (document_frequency + .5))
            score += idf * counts[term] * (k1 + 1) / (
                counts[term] + k1 * length_factor)
        scores.append((manual_id, score))
    return sorted(scores, key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))

manuals = {"pump-47": "seal pressure service",
           "pump-81": "seal seal seal inventory inventory inventory"}
ranked = bm25_rank("seal pressure", manuals)
assert ranked[0][0] == "pump-47"
assert ranked[0][1] > ranked[1][1]

Performance and operating cost

This deliberately small implementation tokenizes T total words in O(T) time and stores O(T) tokens. It scans all N documents for document frequency inside every document/query-term pair, so scoring takes O(N squared times Q plus T) time for Q distinct query terms; sorting adds O(N log N). A real inverted index stores document frequency once and scores only candidate postings. Field norms and postings use storage, while larger candidate windows increase latency. Tune on measured queries before spending search capacity on a larger window.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a BM25 score as a calibrated probability or adding it directly to a vector score.
  • Tuning k1 to hide repeated footer text instead of cleaning the indexed field.
  • Changing the analyzer and BM25 parameters in the same evaluation run.
  • Applying body-field length settings to short titles and exact identifiers without separate tests.

Validation drill

For 83 judged maintenance queries, compare two k1/b pairs while holding tokenization and filters fixed. Report candidate recall at 24, nDCG at 8 and the number of exact identifiers displaced. Inspect at least ten individual ranking explanations before release.

title: Phrase and proximity retrieval need a token-position contract
summary: Store positions when word order matters, keep analyzer behavior consistent and test phrase boundaries before using matches as evidence.
body:
Store positions when word order matters, keep analyzer behavior consistent and test phrase boundaries before using matches as evidence.

A term match forgets order

A record-level inverted index can find documents containing both words but cannot tell whether they occur together. A phrase query needs token positions, or a slower scan of candidate text. A proximity query also asks how far apart matching terms may be. These are materially different retrieval contracts: a maintenance note about a pressure seal and a note about pressure testing a different seal may share terms without containing the requested phrase. Lexical field mappings should declare which fields retain positions and which remain exact identifiers.

Index-time positions must match query analysis

Lowercasing, punctuation splitting, stemming, synonyms and stopword removal affect the position stream. If stopwords are removed, preserving their position gaps avoids treating two formerly separated words as adjacent. Query analysis must apply the intended counterpart of the index analyzer; mismatched tokenization can make a visible phrase unsearchable. Synonyms with multiple tokens need explicit position handling, not a string replacement that loses order. For code, part numbers and quoted literals, an exact subfield may be safer than a linguistic analyzer. Literal query parsing keeps quotation marks from becoming accidental broad search.

Scope positions to an evidence unit

A phrase must not cross from one field into another or from one unrelated document chunk into the next. Store positions within a field and keep a stable document or passage identity alongside them. If a long manual is split into passages, a phrase at the split boundary can be missed; controlled overlap or parent-document verification can recover it. Chunk boundary tests quantify that tradeoff. Conversely, concatenating unrelated fragments can manufacture a phrase that no source actually says. Show the source span that matched before using it in an answer.

Proximity is not proof of a relationship

Allowing a few positions between terms can improve recall for expressions such as 'seal at high pressure', but a wide window may join terms from separate clauses or opposite statements. Decide whether order matters, define an explicit distance or slop policy, and test negation and section boundaries. Backends differ in how they count a transposition or removed stopword; copy neither a numeric setting nor an intuition between engines without fixtures. Claim support checks still have to read the actual sentence. A positional hit is only a retrieval signal.

Measure the storage and latency price

Positions increase posting size compared with document-only or frequency-only indexing. Phrase evaluation first intersects candidate postings, then checks compatible positions; common terms and wide proximity windows can still be expensive. Keep the phrase field narrow when possible and add budgets for broad queries. Compare exact phrase recall, near-phrase recall and false joins on judged queries. A high match count may mean the analyzer removed discriminating tokens. Inspect the position stream and original character offsets separately; token positions locate a term order, whereas offsets locate text for highlighting. Snippet offsets have their own redaction rules.

Worked contract

import re
from collections import defaultdict

def tokenize(value: str) -> list[str]:
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", value.casefold())

def positional_index(notes: dict[str, str]
                     ) -> dict[str, dict[str, list[int]]]:
    postings = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))
    for note_id, text in notes.items():
        for position, term in enumerate(tokenize(text)):
            postings[term][note_id].append(position)
    return postings

def exact_phrase(postings: dict, phrase: str) -> set[str]:
    terms = tokenize(phrase)
    if not terms:
        return set()
    candidates = set(postings.get(terms[0], {}))
    for term in terms[1:]:
        candidates &= set(postings.get(term, {}))
    return {note_id for note_id in candidates
            if any(all(start + offset in postings[term][note_id]
                       for offset, term in enumerate(terms))
                   for start in postings[terms[0]][note_id])}

notes = {"work-47": "Inspect the pressure seal before restart",
         "work-81": "Seal the valve after pressure testing"}
postings = positional_index(notes)
assert exact_phrase(postings, "pressure seal") == {"work-47"}
assert exact_phrase(postings, "seal pressure") == set()

Performance and operating cost

Building positions for T tokens takes O(T) time and O(T) posting entries. This simple phrase check intersects document sets and then scans first-term positions; list membership is linear, so a document with many repeated terms can require O(P times Q times P) work for P first-term positions and Q phrase terms. Production engines use ordered or compressed positional postings and merge walks to avoid those repeated linear membership checks. Indexing offsets as well as positions raises storage further. Phrase query cost should be measured on common-term and long-field slices.

Common Mistakes

  • Assuming a document-level term intersection proves that the words form a phrase.
  • Removing stopwords while collapsing the position gaps they occupied.
  • Allowing a phrase to span unrelated chunks or fields.
  • Treating a proximity hit as proof that the retrieved sentence supports an answer.

Validation drill

Create 71 phrase queries that include punctuation, stopwords, part numbers, negation and a passage boundary. Compare exact matches against the visible source text, then measure false joins when allowing one and three extra positions.

title: Collapse retrieval results by document without losing the best passage
summary: Group passage hits by a stable parent ID, budget enough candidates for distinct documents and keep permission filtering ahead of grouping.
body:
Group passage hits by a stable parent ID, budget enough candidates for distinct documents and keep permission filtering ahead of grouping.

Passage rank is not document rank

A long source can contribute many similar passages to the top results. If the interface promises a set of documents but displays every passage separately, one manual may occupy the entire first page. Result collapse selects one representative hit per stable parent document, commonly the highest-ranked eligible passage. That improves source variety for browsing, but it can hide a second passage from the same document that contains another required fact. Evidence packing should retain supporting spans when answer generation needs them even if navigation shows one card per document.

Filter before choosing representatives

Permission and deletion checks apply to every candidate passage before grouping. A private high-score passage must not be selected as the document representative, and its existence must not leak through group counts or 'more from this document' links. Use a tenant-scoped document key where IDs can collide across tenants. A representative should carry its passage ID, source revision and the exact score branch that produced it. Corpus permissions and delete tombstones remain authoritative even when a grouping API operates inside the search engine.

Candidate depth sets the diversity ceiling

Collapsing a top-12 passage pool cannot return twelve documents if ten passages came from one manual. Retrieve deeper, group, then take the requested number of distinct parents, or use a backend feature that performs collapse before final top-K selection. Oversampling has a latency cost and no fixed multiplier guarantees diversity for every query. Track unique-parent count at several candidate depths. If a rare document never entered the pool, post-processing cannot recover it. Reranker windows need the same distinction between passage count and unique-source count.

Choose a deterministic representative

Within a group, rank by the retrieval score or a reranked score under one stable policy, then break ties by passage ID or source order. Keep the original passage score visible to diagnostics. When multiple passages from the same source answer different aspects, offer an explicit expansion rather than quietly merging fragments into one invented excerpt. Near-duplicate documents from distinct parents require a separate duplicate policy. Independent support explains why two copies of the same text are not two independent sources. Collapse is for presentation and candidate allocation; it does not establish source independence.

Counts and pagination require a contract

A result count before collapse may describe passages, not distinct documents. Facet counts can also reflect the uncollapsed set, depending on the backend. Label the unit in the UI and avoid promising an exact number of groups unless you compute it. Paginating grouped hits needs a stable sort and a consistent index view; a changing candidate pool can repeat or skip documents. Point-in-time pagination sets that boundary. Evaluate grouped recall and answer support alongside visual variety, because hiding duplicate cards is useful only when important evidence remains reachable.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class PassageHit:
    tenant_id: str
    document_id: str
    passage_id: str
    score: float
    permitted: bool

def distinct_documents(hits: list[PassageHit], limit: int
                       ) -> list[PassageHit]:
    if limit < 0:
        raise ValueError("negative result limit")
    best = {}
    for hit in hits:
        if not hit.permitted:
            continue
        key = (hit.tenant_id, hit.document_id)
        current = best.get(key)
        if current is None or (-hit.score, hit.passage_id) < (
                -current.score, current.passage_id):
            best[key] = hit
    return sorted(best.values(), key=lambda hit: (
        -hit.score, hit.tenant_id, hit.document_id, hit.passage_id))[:limit]

hits = [PassageHit("plant-a", "manual-47", "p2", .81, True),
        PassageHit("plant-a", "manual-47", "p4", .88, True),
        PassageHit("plant-a", "manual-81", "p1", .95, False),
        PassageHit("plant-a", "manual-94", "p3", .76, True)]
chosen = distinct_documents(hits, 2)
assert [(hit.document_id, hit.passage_id) for hit in chosen] == [
    ("manual-47", "p4"), ("manual-94", "p3")]

Performance and operating cost

For C candidate passages, grouping takes O(C) expected time and O(G) space for G eligible parent groups; sorting those groups costs O(G log G). The code assumes the caller already fetched candidates and made permission decisions. A deeper candidate pool increases search, transport and rerank costs, while backend inner-hit expansion may issue additional searches. Measure distinct-parent yield at each depth and keep a latency budget. If authorization is unavailable, fail closed before this function rather than treating an absent permission as true.

Common Mistakes

  • Collapsing before permission checks and leaking the identity of a private document.
  • Fetching only K passages and assuming K distinct parent documents will remain.
  • Reporting raw passage hit counts as distinct-document counts.
  • Discarding other passages from a parent when the answer requires evidence from more than one span.

Validation drill

Construct 64 queries whose top 30 passages include repeated manuals and near duplicates. Compare document recall at 8, unique-parent yield and answer support before and after grouping; inject one forbidden highest-scoring passage per test group.
