title: Restore a retrieval index with schema, deletion and relevance proofs
summary: Treat a backup as a candidate generation: verify its metadata, replay later changes and test search quality before cutover.
body:
Treat a backup as a candidate generation: verify its metadata, replay later changes and test search quality before cutover.

A snapshot is not an answer-ready index

A backup can preserve index bytes while still being too old, mapped to the wrong embedding model or missing the latest permission and deletion events. Define recovery point and recovery time objectives for the retrieval service, then name every component needed to meet them: source documents, lexical and vector indexes, analyzers, embedding version, access-control state, aliases and change logs. An index archive alone cannot prove that restored results are safe. Embedding version contracts must match the query encoder before vector traffic returns.

Capture a consistent generation

Record an index generation ID, source watermark, schema revision, tokenizer or analyzer revision, embedding dimension, metric and document count with the backup. Use the backend's supported snapshot mechanism rather than copying live index files while writers are active. Protect the backup repository and test that its credentials and keys are available during recovery. A snapshot taken before an ingestion event is valid only if later events can be replayed from a durable log. Watermarks show what the restored service has and has not seen.

Restore beside production first

Restore into a separate generation or name so the current serving alias remains unchanged. Verify manifest checksums and active document IDs, then replay updates and tombstones through the target watermark. A stale backup must not revive a deleted document, even temporarily. Apply the current permission policy and compare source revisions, not just document totals; equal counts can conceal one missing and one duplicated record. Deletion proof is mandatory before the target accepts user queries. The old serving generation remains available until cutover checks pass.

Run retrieval and access canaries

A restored index may open successfully but rank badly because field norms, vector metric, analyzers or reranker inputs changed. Run exact identifier queries, phrase queries, filtered ANN probes and judged answer-support tests under the restored generation. Include forbidden-document canaries and intentionally deleted IDs. Compare top-K overlap and important slices against the last known good release, while allowing expected freshness changes after replay. Release gates define minimum quality; a green cluster status is not a relevance proof.

Switch, observe, and rehearse

Move the serving alias only after eligibility, freshness and quality checks pass. Pin or finish in-flight requests so a single answer does not combine evidence from different generations. Keep a rollback target only if it also applies the current tombstones and permissions; an unsafe rollback is not a recovery path. Alias cutover covers the pointer switch. Rehearse restore regularly, measuring time to first safe query, missing-event replay duration and storage headroom. A backup that has never been restored is an untested assumption.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class IndexedRecord:
    document_id: str
    revision: int
    content_digest: str

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RestoreManifest:
    source_watermark: int
    schema_revision: str
    embedding_revision: str
    active_digest: str

def active_digest(records: list[IndexedRecord],
                  deleted_ids: set[str]) -> str:
    active = [record for record in records
              if record.document_id not in deleted_ids]
    keys = [(record.document_id, record.revision, record.content_digest)
            for record in active]
    if len({key[0] for key in keys}) != len(keys):
        raise ValueError("duplicate active document")
    payload = "\n".join(f"{item[0]}:{item[1]}:{item[2]}"
                       for item in sorted(keys))
    return sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()

def verify_restore(records: list[IndexedRecord],
                   manifest: RestoreManifest, deleted_ids: set[str],
                   required_watermark: int) -> None:
    if manifest.source_watermark < required_watermark:
        raise ValueError("event replay is incomplete")
    if (manifest.schema_revision != "schema-7" or
            manifest.embedding_revision != "encoder-4"):
        raise ValueError("incompatible retrieval contract")
    if any(record.document_id in deleted_ids for record in records):
        raise ValueError("deleted document remains in index")
    if active_digest(records, deleted_ids) != manifest.active_digest:
        raise ValueError("restored content differs from manifest")

restored = [IndexedRecord("manual-47", 3, "sha-47")]
manifest = RestoreManifest(219, "schema-7", "encoder-4",
                           active_digest(restored, set()))
verify_restore(restored, manifest, {"withdrawn-81"}, 219)

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N active record descriptors for the digest takes O(N log N) time and O(N) memory; a backend can use ordered scans and streaming hashes to reduce extra memory. Snapshot creation, transfer, replay and vector reconstruction have separate I/O and CPU costs that depend on the engine. The code checks metadata and a manifest digest but does not perform storage-level restore, cryptographic signature verification, authorization or relevance tests. Those remain required gates before alias cutover. Track both recovery time and the age of the latest safe recovered watermark.

Common Mistakes

  • Copying a live index directory as if it were an atomic backup.
  • Restoring old data without replaying later deletions and permission changes.
  • Checking document counts but not IDs, revisions, schema and model compatibility.
  • Switching the serving alias before access canaries and judged retrieval tests pass.

Validation drill

Restore a backup from 47 ingestion events before the current watermark into a separate generation. Replay those events, delete seven records, run permission canaries and 39 judged queries, and record the time until the restored service can answer safely.

  • Index watermarks: measure what the retriever has actually seen
  • Retrieval tombstones: compact indexes without reviving deleted evidence
  • Retrieval release gates: evaluate slices before changing an index

title: IVF vector search: train centroids, budget probes, measure misses
summary: Use an inverted-file vector index when partition scans beat a full scan, and evaluate the recall cost of probing fewer cells.
body:
Use an inverted-file vector index when partition scans beat a full scan, and evaluate the recall cost of probing fewer cells.

IVF partitions vector space

An inverted-file vector index assigns each stored embedding to a coarse centroid and keeps a posting list for each centroid. At query time, it finds nearby centroids and scans only their lists. The number of lists is commonly called nlist; the number searched for one query is nprobe. Fewer probes reduce candidate distance calculations but can miss a nearest vector assigned to a neighboring cell. This is an approximate candidate-generation decision, not an answer-quality guarantee. Compare results with exact search under the same vector metric and normalization contract before drawing conclusions about recall.

Train on the distribution you intend to serve

Coarse centroids need representative training vectors from the corpus and embedding model that will actually populate the index. Training only on the first ingestion batch, one language or one high-volume tenant can leave later material in badly balanced cells. Record model revision, dimension, metric, normalization, sample selection and training seed with the index generation. If the embedding distribution changes enough, a fixed centroid set can produce long lists or poor recall even when index size stays constant. Embedding migrations should rebuild and evaluate the coarse assignment alongside the stored vectors.

Probe count trades work for recall

With a small nprobe, a query scans few lists and risks missing candidates near cell boundaries. A larger nprobe visits more lists, costs more CPU and memory bandwidth, and usually improves recall until gains flatten. If nprobe approaches every list, an uncompressed IVFFlat search approaches an exhaustive vector scan while adding coarse-routing overhead. An IVF index with compressed payloads can still differ from an exact flat index because compression changes distances. Quantization and exact reranking should be measured as a separate source of error rather than folded into the probe-count result.

Filters and skew alter the effective budget

A query restricted to one tenant or status may have few eligible vectors in the first probed cells. Some backends filter before vector search, others overfetch and filter afterward; the two plans have different recall and latency behavior. List imbalance also matters: probing four huge cells may scan more vectors than probing eight small ones. Measure eligible candidate count, list-size distribution, probes visited, p95 latency and exact top-K recall by filter slice. Filtered ANN tests expose an apparently fast configuration that returns too few authorized results. Never compensate for a failed permission filter by searching a broader scope.

Use a release gate, not a magic nprobe

Select several probe budgets and compare them against exact top-K results on representative queries: common intents, rare terms, new content, multilingual requests and difficult filter combinations. Record both passage recall and downstream supported-answer rate. The best value can differ by index size, hardware and query slice, but per-query adaptation needs a clear ceiling so tail latency remains bounded. HNSW candidate budgets have a related speed-versus-recall shape but use a different search structure. Review both index memory and build time before deciding that IVF is preferable to a graph or flat index.

Worked contract

from math import dist

def probe_cells(query: tuple[float, ...],
                centroids: dict[str, tuple[float, ...]],
                postings: dict[str, list[tuple[str, tuple[float, ...]]]],
                nprobe: int, limit: int) -> list[tuple[str, float]]:
    if not query or nprobe < 1 or limit < 1 or nprobe > len(centroids):
        raise ValueError("invalid query or search budget")
    if any(len(vector) != len(query) for vector in centroids.values()):
        raise ValueError("centroid dimension mismatch")
    cells = sorted(centroids, key=lambda cell: (dist(query, centroids[cell]), cell))
    candidates = []
    for cell in cells[:nprobe]:
        for document_id, vector in postings.get(cell, []):
            if len(vector) != len(query):
                raise ValueError("passage dimension mismatch")
            candidates.append((document_id, dist(query, vector)))
    return sorted(candidates, key=lambda item: (item[1], item[0]))[:limit]

centroids = {"west": (0.0, 0.0), "east": (8.0, 0.0)}
postings = {"west": [("manual-47", (2.5, 0.0))],
            "east": [("manual-81", (4.1, 0.0))]}
query = (3.95, 0.0)
assert probe_cells(query, centroids, postings, 1, 1)[0][0] == "manual-47"
assert probe_cells(query, centroids, postings, 2, 2)[0][0] == "manual-81"

Performance and operating cost

For C centroids, the toy code scores and sorts all centroids in O(CD + C log C) time for D dimensions, then scores M vectors in the selected lists in O(MD) and sorts them in O(M log M). It uses O(C + M) temporary space. Real implementations use trained coarse quantizers, compressed lists and efficient top-K selection, but the fundamental probe-versus-recall tradeoff remains. The demonstration does not train centroids or enforce filters; those are production responsibilities. Log actual scanned-vector count, because nprobe alone hides cell-size skew.

Common Mistakes

  • Training centroids on vectors from an old embedding model or an unrepresentative tenant.
  • Reporting ANN recall against another approximate index instead of an exact baseline.
  • Assuming the same nprobe scans the same amount of work for every filtered query.
  • Attributing compressed-distance errors entirely to the IVF probe setting.

Validation drill

Train one IVF generation on a stratified corpus sample, then test 93 judged queries at four probe budgets. Report exact top-12 recall, eligible-candidate counts, list-size skew and p95 latency by tenant and language. Repeat after the next substantial ingestion wave.

  • Vector compression: spend memory without losing the answer
  • Embedding migrations: keep query and document vectors in one space
  • HNSW retrieval: candidate budgets, graph cost and recall curves

title: Lexical term coverage: require enough words without losing valid hits
summary: Treat term-coverage thresholds as a candidate rule, keep authorization separate and define what happens when analysis removes every query token.
body:
Treat term-coverage thresholds as a candidate rule, keep authorization separate and define what happens when analysis removes every query token.

Term coverage is a retrieval gate

A lexical query with several terms can use an all-terms rule, an any-term rule or a threshold between them. All terms can miss a useful document when one word is absent or stemmed differently. Any term can return a large set of weak matches dominated by a common word. A minimum-term threshold requires a chosen number of optional clauses to match before a passage becomes a candidate. The threshold controls eligibility, not just score. BM25 ranks the surviving lexical candidates; it cannot rescue a relevant document removed by a too-strict coverage rule.

Separate required constraints from optional evidence

Tenant, access level, deletion state and document type are hard filters with independent authority. They must never be converted into optional text clauses to raise recall. Likewise, a quoted part number or a user-requested exact phrase may be mandatory even when descriptive words are optional. Parse the query into typed constraints and text clauses before applying a threshold. Literal query parsing prevents punctuation and quotation marks from being silently rewritten into broad term matches. A rule such as 'two of three text words' cannot replace an exact serial-number check.

Analyzer output determines the denominator

Minimum-should-match settings act on the clauses produced after analysis, not necessarily on the number of words typed by the user. Stopword removal, stemming and multi-term synonyms can change clause counts or group clauses differently. A query reduced to zero terms needs an explicit policy: return no lexical matches, route to another safe branch or ask for clarification. A match-all fallback can turn a blank or stopword-only query into a costly full-corpus request and may expose unrelated navigation results. Analyzer contracts must be versioned with the query policy.

Test short and long queries separately

A two-word query requiring both words can be much stricter than a six-word query requiring four. Fixed percentages also round differently at small clause counts, so write out the exact rule per length. Evaluate rare identifiers, negation, spelling mistakes and long natural-language questions as distinct slices. Start with a bounded lexical candidate pool and measure recall before reranking. Candidate recall is the upper bound on what a downstream reranker can recover. If recall falls, broaden optional term coverage or add a semantic branch without weakening mandatory filters.

Keep operators explicit in diagnostics

A broad OR query is often useful for candidate generation, while an AND query can be appropriate for a narrow technical phrase. Neither is a universal default. Log analyzed clauses, required filters, threshold, candidate count and the ranker's winning terms so an engineer can explain why a page appeared. A user-visible advanced query language should escape reserved syntax rather than treating arbitrary user text as executable query operators. Phrase matching applies when order matters; term coverage alone cannot establish adjacency or source support.

Worked contract

import re

STOPWORDS = {"a", "of", "the"}

def lexical_candidates(query: str, passages: dict[str, str],
                       required_terms: set[str], minimum_optional: int
                       ) -> list[tuple[str, int]]:
    optional_terms = set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", query.casefold()))
    required = {term.casefold() for term in required_terms}
    optional_terms -= required
    optional_terms -= STOPWORDS
    if not optional_terms and not required:
        return []
    if minimum_optional < 0 or minimum_optional > len(optional_terms):
        raise ValueError("invalid optional-term threshold")
    matches = []
    for passage_id, text in passages.items():
        words = set(re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.casefold()))
        if not required <= words:
            continue
        coverage = len(words & optional_terms)
        if coverage >= minimum_optional:
            matches.append((passage_id, coverage))
    return sorted(matches, key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))

passages = {"note-47": "Pressure seal replacement for pump P47",
            "note-81": "Pressure regulator inspection for pump P81",
            "note-94": "Seal inventory for pump P47"}
assert lexical_candidates("pressure seal", passages, {"p47"}, 1) == [
    ("note-47", 2), ("note-94", 1)]
assert lexical_candidates("the", passages, set(), 0) == []
assert lexical_candidates("", passages, set(), 0) == []

Performance and operating cost

For N passages with T total tokens and Q query terms, this direct scan takes O(T + NQ) expected time for tokenization and set intersections and O(Q + maximum passage vocabulary plus output) extra space per passage if processed sequentially. A real inverted index intersects required postings and counts optional postings without scanning every document. This example intentionally omits authorization and stemming; its tiny stopword set only illustrates the zero-term policy. Apply a separate mandatory permission filter before returning candidates. A zero-term query returns no hits rather than scanning everything.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating access-control conditions as optional clauses when trying to improve recall.
  • Applying a percentage threshold to raw input words instead of analyzed clauses.
  • Allowing a zero-term query to fall through to an unbounded match-all search.
  • Assuming a document containing enough terms also contains the requested phrase or supports the answer.

Validation drill

Build 79 queries across one-word identifiers, two-word technical phrases and longer questions. Compare all-term, any-term and length-aware thresholds on authorized candidate recall at 30, false-match rate and lexical execution cost. Include stopword-only and quoted-identifier cases.

  • Safe search query parsing: operators, filters and literal identifiers
  • Phrase and proximity retrieval need a token-position contract
  • Retrieval design: compare lexical, semantic and reranked candidates

title: Conflicting retrieved claims: compare scope before choosing an answer
summary: Represent claims with units, time, source revision and authority; resolve only explicit precedence and abstain when evidence still conflicts.
body:
Represent claims with units, time, source revision and authority; resolve only explicit precedence and abstain when evidence still conflicts.

High rank cannot settle a factual conflict

Two retrieved passages can disagree while both are topically relevant. One may state a retired pressure limit, another a current limit, or both may describe different machines with similar names. Embedding similarity and BM25 score measure retrieval fit, not truth. Before answering, extract the exact claim, subject, unit, scope, valid time and source revision from each candidate. Then distinguish a real contradiction from a comparison of different periods or entities. Temporal retrieval handles as-of questions; this lesson handles the remaining conflict after scope has been aligned.

Preserve the evidence chain

Keep every competing claim tied to a stable passage ID, document version and accessible source span. A summary that strips those identifiers can merge incompatible facts into a plausible but unsupported sentence. The answer layer should know whether a value came from a signed operating procedure, a field note or a user comment, and whether the source is current for the requested asset. Passage provenance supplies the chain; claim support checks confirm that the final wording matches a cited span. Never present the model's synthesis as a new source.

Precedence needs an explicit policy

A policy may prefer an approved revision of an operating manual over an older superseded revision for a specific plant. It should not prefer a source merely because the document is newer or its vector score is higher. A later discussion post may be less authoritative than an older still-valid standard. Encode precedence by source type, approval status, entity scope and validity interval, then test it with known cases. If two active approved sources disagree at the same scope, leave the conflict visible and escalate. Document lifecycle determines whether a source is even eligible for this decision.

Normalize values before declaring disagreement

Numerical claims require units, tolerances and measurement conditions. A value in kilopascals and one in bars can be equivalent after conversion; a temperature setpoint and a maximum safety limit are different predicates despite sharing a number. Preserve the original text and compute a normalized comparison only when the conversion rule is known. Do not erase ranges, qualifiers or uncertainty. The example compares exact normalized values under one subject and predicate; a production system also needs approved unit conversions and tolerance bands. Numeric cell context prevents a table header from being dropped while extracting a value.

Abstention is a valid result

If conflicting eligible sources cannot be resolved by an approved rule, return a concise conflict report with both source spans and the missing decision, or ask a domain owner. Do not average incompatible limits or pick the first result. A bounded follow-up search may find a superseding revision, but stop after a stated budget and avoid turning repeated retrieval into manufactured certainty. Corrective retrieval controls that retry; evidence-bound answering defines the final refusal to assert an unsupported value. Track unresolved-conflict rate alongside answer accuracy during release testing.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Claim:
    asset_id: str
    predicate: str
    value_kpa: int
    valid_from: int
    valid_until: int | None
    approved: bool
    passage_id: str

def resolve_limit(claims: list[Claim], asset_id: str, as_of: int
                  ) -> tuple[int | None, list[str]]:
    eligible = [claim for claim in claims
                if claim.asset_id == asset_id
                and claim.predicate == "maximum_pressure"
                and claim.approved and claim.valid_from <= as_of
                and (claim.valid_until is None or as_of < claim.valid_until)]
    if not eligible:
        return None, []
    readings = {claim.value_kpa for claim in eligible}
    sources = sorted(claim.passage_id for claim in eligible)
    if len(readings) != 1:
        return None, sources
    return readings.pop(), sources

claims = [Claim("pump-47", "maximum_pressure", 620, 100, None,
                True, "manual-v3-p6"),
          Claim("pump-47", "maximum_pressure", 590, 100, None,
                True, "bulletin-12-p2"),
          Claim("pump-47", "maximum_pressure", 570, 20, 100,
                True, "retired-v1-p4")]
assert resolve_limit(claims, "pump-47", 123) == (
    None, ["bulletin-12-p2", "manual-v3-p6"])
assert resolve_limit(claims, "pump-47", 55) == (570, ["retired-v1-p4"])

Performance and operating cost

Filtering C extracted claims takes O(C) time; sorting E eligible passage IDs costs O(E log E) and requires O(E) memory. Claim extraction, unit normalization, source validation and additional retrieval are separate costs. This example abstains when two active approved claims disagree and does not implement an authority hierarchy. A production resolver must log policy version, source revisions and scope, and must reject missing or uncertain units rather than silently treating them as comparable. More retrieval can increase the chance of finding a superseding source but also consumes latency and can surface new conflicts.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing the higher-ranked passage as truth when two eligible sources disagree.
  • Comparing numbers without units, predicate and operating conditions.
  • Discarding source revision or passage identity during answer synthesis.
  • Averaging two incompatible safety limits instead of reporting the unresolved conflict.

Assemble 53 asset-limit questions with superseded revisions, equivalent converted units, conflicting current approvals and wrong-asset distractors. Measure correct resolution, false certainty and source-span accuracy; require abstention for unresolved active conflicts.

title: Maximal marginal relevance: diversify retrieval without losing support
summary: Select a relevant but less repetitive evidence set, calibrate the novelty penalty and preserve essential corroborating passages.
body:
Select a relevant but less repetitive evidence set, calibrate the novelty penalty and preserve essential corroborating passages.

MMR is a second-stage selection rule

Maximal marginal relevance chooses one result at a time from an already retrieved candidate set. It balances query relevance against similarity to material already selected. With relevance weight lambda, a common form is lambda times query relevance minus one minus lambda times the maximum similarity to any selected result. A high lambda favors the original ranking; a lower one rewards novelty. This does not find passages absent from the candidate pool. If candidate recall is weak, tune the first-stage search before applying diversity. Run authorization and deletion filters before this selection rule.

The two scores need compatible meaning

A BM25 score can span a different scale from cosine similarity or token overlap. Plugging raw values into the formula makes lambda meaningless. Convert query relevance and passage-passage similarity to stable ranges using judged data, and record the score versions. The example uses bounded relevance values and Jaccard token overlap solely to make the behavior inspectable. A production selector may use embedding similarity, lexical overlap, lineage or a combination. Fusion calibration explains why numeric scale is a policy, not a label. One duplicate detector should not accidentally penalize unrelated facts that use the same technical vocabulary.

Diversity is not the same as independent evidence

Two passages from different documents can repeat one syndicated announcement. Conversely, two passages in one manual can provide distinct facts needed to answer a multi-part question. MMR's similarity penalty is a ranking signal, not proof of source independence. Preserve document revision, lineage and passage identity in the selected packet. Independent-support checks decide whether sources truly corroborate a claim. Document grouping is a presentation rule; it should not silently discard a second passage required for an answer.

Choose the evidence budget deliberately

The first selected item normally has no novelty penalty. Later selections can trade a small relevance drop for a new angle, but an aggressive penalty may push a weak or unrelated passage into a short context window. Reserve slots for mandatory exact matches and explicitly requested sources before running diversity over the remaining eligible pool. Keep conflicting evidence visible when the user asks for comparison or when active sources disagree. Claim-conflict handling must see the competing claims rather than receive a falsely tidy packet. Inspect the final ordered context, not merely the selection scores.

Evaluate both variety and answer support

Measure unique-parent count, near-duplicate rate and intent coverage at a fixed K, then check whether answer-bearing spans and contradictions survived. A higher diversity number can coexist with lower supported-answer rate. Compare several lambda values under the same first-stage pool and token budget. Log the relevance and novelty component for each chosen passage so a missing citation can be diagnosed. Context packing then assigns actual token slots and may reject a selected item that is too large. MMR improves candidate mix only when the final evidence remains sufficient.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Passage:
    passage_id: str
    relevance: float
    terms: frozenset[str]
    permitted: bool

def overlap(left: Passage, right: Passage) -> float:
    union = left.terms | right.terms
    return len(left.terms & right.terms) / len(union) if union else 0.0

def select_mmr(candidates: list[Passage], limit: int,
               relevance_weight: float) -> list[Passage]:
    if limit < 0 or not 0 <= relevance_weight <= 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid selection settings")
    remaining = [item for item in candidates if item.permitted]
    if any(not 0 <= item.relevance <= 1 for item in remaining):
        raise ValueError("relevance must be normalized")
    chosen = []
    while remaining and len(chosen) < limit:
        winner = max(remaining, key=lambda item: (
            relevance_weight * item.relevance
            - (1 - relevance_weight) * max(
                (overlap(item, prior) for prior in chosen), default=0.0),
            item.passage_id))
        chosen.append(winner)
        remaining.remove(winner)
    return chosen

hits = [Passage("seal-v3-a", .92, frozenset({"seal", "pressure"}), True),
        Passage("seal-v3-b", .89, frozenset({"seal", "pressure"}), True),
        Passage("pump-81", .78, frozenset({"pump", "inspection"}), True),
        Passage("private-note", .99, frozenset({"seal"}), False)]
assert [hit.passage_id for hit in select_mmr(hits, 2, .6)] == [
    "seal-v3-a", "pump-81"]

Performance and operating cost

For N candidates and K selected passages, this direct implementation compares each remaining candidate with every selected item on every round. If token-set comparison costs L, time is O(K squared times N times L) in the worst case and the remaining/chosen lists use O(N + K) space beyond stored terms. Incrementally storing each candidate's maximum similarity to chosen items can reduce repeated work to O(KNL) and O(N) extra state. Pairwise precomputation costs O(N squared times L) time and memory. Keep N bounded, because diversity selection is a reranking step, not a replacement for first-stage retrieval.

Common Mistakes

  • Applying MMR before permission filtering and allowing a private passage to influence public ranking.
  • Combining unscaled BM25 and bounded similarity values as if lambda had a stable interpretation.
  • Treating a novel result as independent corroboration without checking lineage.
  • Optimizing unique-source count while dropping the only passage that supports a required claim.

Validation drill

For 61 multi-aspect queries, compare three relevance weights at the same top-30 candidate pool and six-passage context budget. Record unique source lineages, supported-answer rate, omitted contradictions and p95 selection time.

title: Wildcard retrieval: bound prefix expansion and keep identifiers literal
summary: Control term-dictionary fanout, reject broad patterns and keep expansion behind the same access and query-parsing boundaries as ordinary search.
body:
Control term-dictionary fanout, reject broad patterns and keep expansion behind the same access and query-parsing boundaries as ordinary search.

A wildcard expands a query into terms

A trailing prefix pattern asks a search engine to find indexed terms that start with a given sequence, then search their postings. An infix or leading wildcard can require examining far more of the term dictionary. This differs from autocomplete, which suggests text to a user while typing; a wildcard query actually broadens the candidate set used for ranking or answering. A short pattern can match thousands of terms, creating a large Boolean expansion, latency spike or relevance drift. Treat the expansion as a bounded query-planning operation, not a harmless character in a string.

Do not run user syntax through an unrestricted parser

Accept an explicit, small pattern language rather than letting raw user text become a backend regular expression or query-string program. A conservative interface might allow one trailing star after at least three letters and reject leading stars, multiple wildcards, punctuation and overlong tokens. Escape or reject reserved syntax at the trust boundary. Safe query parsing keeps the user's literal request separate from search operators. For part numbers, route to an exact field unless the product has a documented prefix-search mode; a broad expansion of one digit can bring back a different device.

Expand only within the allowed vocabulary

An approved term dictionary must reflect tenant scope, published status and current deletion state. Generating a broad global list and filtering retrieved documents later can leak private vocabulary through expansion counts, logs or timing. Apply mandatory filters in the actual search backend as well; an authorized suggestion list alone does not authorize documents. Corpus lifecycle supplies the current eligibility rule. If the expansion limit is exceeded, return a clear request to narrow the prefix instead of silently taking the first few terms, which produces unstable and incomplete results.

Budget clauses and postings together

A limit on expanded term count is useful but not sufficient. Ten common expansions can touch more postings than a hundred rare ones. Set a query deadline, clause or automaton complexity cap, and maximum candidate work. Prefix indexes or specialized n-gram fields can reduce lookup cost, but they consume storage and may broaden matching semantics. Record expansion count, estimated postings, execution time and cancellation outcome. Deadline budgeting must include term expansion, not just document ranking. A timeout should not be disguised as an empty answer.

Judge recovery against accidental matches

Create tests for incomplete product names, valid rare codes, short prefixes and patterns containing punctuation. Compare recovered relevant documents with false positives and backend cost. A wildcard branch can complement spelling correction for exploratory search, but it does not prove that a user intended any particular expanded term. Show the interpreted query when it materially changes results. If the branch feeds an answer, keep the actual matched source span and do not imply that a wildcard match itself supports a factual claim.

Worked contract

import re

def expand_prefix(prefix: str, approved_terms: set[str],
                  max_terms: int) -> list[str]:
    if max_terms < 1:
        raise ValueError("positive expansion cap required")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]{3,24}", prefix):
        raise ValueError("only bounded lowercase prefixes are supported")
    expanded = sorted(term for term in approved_terms
                      if term.startswith(prefix))
    if len(expanded) > max_terms:
        raise OverflowError("narrow the prefix before searching")
    return expanded

visible_vocabulary = {"sealing", "seal", "sealed", "sensor", "private-seal"}
assert expand_prefix("sea", visible_vocabulary, 3) == [
    "seal", "sealed", "sealing"]
try:
    expand_prefix("s", visible_vocabulary, 3)
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("short prefixes must be rejected")
try:
    expand_prefix("sea", visible_vocabulary, 2)
except OverflowError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("over-budget expansion must fail")

Performance and operating cost

This standard-library demonstration scans V approved vocabulary terms in O(VP) worst-case prefix-comparison work for prefix length P, sorts M matches in O(M log M), and uses O(M) output space. A production ordered term dictionary can seek to a prefix and enumerate matching terms closer to O(log V + M) plus postings work. The toy approved set is already scoped; it does not implement access control or actual document search. A backend must enforce the same authorization at retrieval time and cap work beyond the term dictionary. Rejecting an over-budget expansion is safer than silently truncating its terms.

Common Mistakes

  • Allowing a leading wildcard or unrestricted regular expression over a large text index.
  • Truncating expansions to a few alphabetically first terms and presenting the results as complete.
  • Expanding from a global vocabulary before applying tenant and deletion rules.
  • Treating a serial-number prefix match as an exact device identity.

Validation drill

Replay 73 prefixes from real search tasks, including two-character strings, rare serials and terms with punctuation. Record expansion count, postings scanned, p95 latency and useful-result rate. Require explicit rejection for patterns above the agreed cost ceiling.

title: Retrieval metrics: read Recall, MRR and nDCG without hiding misses
summary: Choose metrics that match the product task, state the judgment set and treat unjudged results as unknown rather than wrong.
body:
Choose metrics that match the product task, state the judgment set and treat unjudged results as unknown rather than wrong.

Metrics answer different questions

Recall at K asks what fraction of all known relevant evidence appears in the first K results. It matters when a downstream reranker or answer generator needs enough candidates to work with. Reciprocal rank asks how early the first relevant item appears; mean reciprocal rank averages that value across queries. It is useful for a task where one good hit suffices, but it ignores a second missing support passage. Normalized discounted cumulative gain uses graded relevance and discounts lower ranks, so it can distinguish a direct answer from a merely related source. Answer evaluation remains separate: a good list does not prove a supported answer.

Define the judged universe and K

A recall denominator needs the known relevant set for each query. If judgments were pooled only from one old search system, a new system can retrieve an unjudged but valid document; scoring that as irrelevant creates bias. Record document or passage identity, corpus generation, permissions, as-of time and judgment policy. Label adjudication establishes those facts. Report the cutoff explicitly: Recall at 20 is not interchangeable with Recall at 5. A query with no relevant evidence needs a separate no-answer evaluation policy rather than a forced zero denominator.

MRR can reward the wrong release

Suppose the first result is somewhat relevant, while the only passage supporting a required number is missing. MRR can still be one because it cares only about the first relevant rank under a binary label. If a task requires multiple facts or independent sources, also report answer-span coverage, multi-hop completion or recall of required evidence units. Multi-hop retrieval makes that dependency explicit. Keep a miss ledger with query slices so an average improvement cannot hide a collapse on rare identifiers or filtered tenants.

nDCG depends on the grade definition

A graded label might use zero for unrelated, one for contextual, two for partially useful and three for a directly supporting passage. Discounted cumulative gain then rewards high grades near the top; dividing by the ideal possible gain makes scores comparable within the same judged query. But grade policies, gain formula and cutoff must stay fixed across releases. Unjudged results should be reviewed or reported as unknown, not silently mapped to grade zero. Copied evidence may require a separate diversity or lineage measure: nDCG does not automatically penalize repeating the same source.

Use release slices and uncertainty

Calculate query-level metrics first, then aggregate by intent, language, corpus age and permission slice. Keep the exact same queries and judgments for a paired comparison, and inspect differences rather than trusting a single global mean. Bootstrap intervals or paired randomization can help separate noise from a real improvement when enough independent queries exist. Do not repeatedly tune on a fixed held-out set until it becomes development data. Release gates should specify minimum recall and answer support for protected slices, while an online test monitors latency and user behavior separately.

Worked contract

from math import log2

def retrieval_scores(grades: dict[str, int],
                     ranked_ids: list[str], cutoff: int
                     ) -> tuple[float, float, float] | None:
    if cutoff < 1:
        raise ValueError("invalid cutoff")
    window = ranked_ids[:cutoff]
    if len(set(window)) != len(window):
        raise ValueError("repeated result in scored window")
    if any(document_id not in grades for document_id in window):
        raise ValueError("unjudged result in scored window")
    if any(grade < 0 for grade in grades.values()):
        raise ValueError("negative relevance grade")
    relevant = {document_id for document_id, grade in grades.items()
                if grade > 0}
    if not relevant:
        return None  # evaluate no-answer behavior separately
    recall = len(set(window) & relevant) / len(relevant)
    first_rank = next((rank for rank, document_id in
                       enumerate(window, 1) if document_id in relevant), None)
    reciprocal_rank = 1 / first_rank if first_rank else 0.0
    def gain(values: list[int]) -> float:
        return sum((2 ** grade - 1) / log2(rank + 1)
                   for rank, grade in enumerate(values, 1))
    observed = gain([grades[document_id] for document_id in window])
    ideal = gain(sorted(grades.values(), reverse=True)[:cutoff])
    return recall, reciprocal_rank, observed / ideal if ideal else 0.0

grades = {"manual-47": 3, "manual-81": 1, "manual-94": 0}
recall, mrr, ndcg = retrieval_scores(
    grades, ["manual-81", "manual-94", "manual-47"], 2)
assert recall == .5 and mrr == 1.0 and 0 < ndcg < 1

Performance and operating cost

For J judged documents and K displayed results, this direct calculation uses O(J log J + K) time because it sorts all judged grades for ideal nDCG and checks the ranked window; its extra space is O(J + K). For many queries, cache each query's ideal gain under an immutable judgment set. Judgment collection and adjudication cost much more than arithmetic. The code rejects unjudged top-K results instead of falsely assigning them zero, but a real evaluation pipeline can queue those results for judging and report the unknown rate. The returned tuple is query-level; macro averages must account for no-answer queries explicitly.

Common Mistakes

  • Reporting Recall at K without stating whether the known relevant set is complete.
  • Calling MRR an evidence-coverage metric when only the first relevant hit affects it.
  • Treating unjudged new results as irrelevant in an incomplete judgment pool.
  • Comparing nDCG values across changed grade scales, corpus generations or cutoffs.

Validation drill

Score 91 judged questions at K equal to 5 and 20. Report recall, reciprocal rank and graded nDCG per slice, plus the count of unjudged top-K results. Audit ten queries where the metrics disagree and record whether the generated answer has enough support.

title: Time-series charts: distinguish missing days, zeros and provisional periods
summary: Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.
body:
Build a complete display calendar, preserve gaps, and label the clocks behind each point.

A line implies continuity

A time-series chart maps measurements to ordered instants or calendar periods. Connecting two observed points across an unobserved day implies a path that was never measured. A recorded zero is different: it says the instrument or process observed the period and counted none. Store both the period key and an observation-status field before drawing the line. The observation calendar defines which periods were expected. Use a visible break, hollow mark, or separate missingness strip when a period has no measurement; do not silently replace it with zero.

Name the two clocks

Operational data often has an event timestamp and a processing timestamp. A refund received late may belong to Tuesday's customer cohort but be visible only on Thursday's dashboard. Choose the clock that answers the chart's question and label it in the axis or subtitle. When bucketing timestamps into local days, choose one time zone and convert before taking the date. Daylight-saving changes make a local day shorter or longer than 24 hours in some regions. An elapsed-duration chart should use instants; a calendar-day chart should use dates in the declared zone.

Mark provisional periods

A current day is incomplete even when its count is known so far. Drawing it with the same line and scale as closed days invites a false decline. Carry a finalized flag from the data source, and either exclude the open interval or render it with a different stroke and an explicit as-of time. Late corrections can reopen an earlier point, so the chart's data-version label matters. A reader must know whether yesterday is final, not only whether the plotting job ran.

Protect the comparison

Never join lines across a product outage, a changed population, or a denominator change without an annotation or split. Keep the y-axis unit and calculation stable across the displayed range. If one week contains 42, 47 and 51 eligible cases while the next has a different intake rule, raw counts compare different populations. The aggregation contract should produce both numerator and denominator where a rate is intended. A moving average may reduce noise, but its window, edge behavior and missing-day policy must be stated.

Check the drawn output

Test an interior missing day, an observed zero, an incomplete final day, a late revision, and a daylight-saving boundary for the region being displayed. Confirm that hover text, downloadable data and the axis all use the same period key. A chart-library setting that connects nulls can undo a carefully prepared missingness contract. Inspect the rendered image, not only the input array. The text alternative should report the gap and the as-of timestamp too.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(observed: dict[date, int],
                          start: date, end: date) -> list[tuple[date, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(count < 0 for count in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid date range or count")
    if any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("observation outside display range")
    return [(start + timedelta(days=offset),
             observed.get(start + timedelta(days=offset)))
            for offset in range((end - start).days + 1)]

points = complete_daily_series(
    {date(2026, 8, 11): 47, date(2026, 8, 13): 0},
    date(2026, 8, 11), date(2026, 8, 13))
assert [count for _, count in points] == [47, None, 0]

Performance and operating cost

For D expected periods and O observed keys, validation plus calendar completion takes O(D + O) time and O(D) output space. The code assumes an already chosen calendar zone and one authoritative count per day. Converting event timestamps and resolving duplicates belong upstream. For a long history, query only the visible interval, and keep finalization state beside each point; creating a million empty periods in a browser is a serving error, not a charting technique.

Common Mistakes

  • Converting an unobserved period into zero and drawing a continuous line.
  • Bucketing by server time zone while labeling the axis with the user's local dates.
  • Treating today's partial count as a completed daily value.
  • Using a rolling average without showing its window and missing-period rule.

Validation drill

Plot a 29-day refund series with one observed zero, two missing days and a provisional last day. Export the period keys and states, then verify that the line breaks only where observation is absent.

title: Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
summary: Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.
body:
Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.

Overplotting changes what a point means

A scatterplot maps paired values to two position channels. When thousands of records land on the same pixels, the visible mark count no longer approximates the record count. Transparency can expose a dense center, but repeated strokes saturate and rare points can disappear beneath it. Before changing the mark style, count records per screen-space cell and inspect whether the question is about density, outliers, groups or exact cases. The chart question determines whether a point cloud is still the right view.

Bin at a declared resolution

A two-dimensional density grid counts observations inside fixed x and y intervals. It can show population structure without rendering every dot. The cells need axis units, bounds and bin width; changing cell size changes the picture. A cell count is not a probability unless divided by the declared population or area. Use the same grid for comparisons across cohorts, otherwise apparent hot spots may be a change in binning. Preserve a drill-down path to the original records where access rules permit it. A heatmap of density has the same color-domain obligations as any other heatmap.

Sampling is a data product

Uniform sampling can make a common cluster readable yet omit a rare but important failure mode. If the operational question concerns unusual refunds, retain those cases deliberately and label the sample design. A stratified sample can hold a fixed number from each category, but its plotted mix no longer reflects population proportions unless weights or counts are shown. Never present sampled points as the full dataset. Record the random seed, inclusion rule and population size. The sampling frame matters even when the result is only exploratory.

Separate trend from uncertainty

A diagonal cloud does not by itself establish a causal effect. Outliers, groups and repeated measures can alter the apparent slope. Show marginal distributions or group facets when one cluster masks another. If a fitted trend is added, distinguish raw marks from the fitted line and state whether the fit is weighted, filtered or calculated on the visible sample. Influence checks are needed before treating that line as a stable summary. A truncated axis can also make a weak relation seem strong.

Validate at the pixel budget

Test identical coordinates, boundary points, non-finite values and a small rare cohort. Count how many records end in each visible density cell, then reconcile the total with the filtered input. Hovering a cell should report its count and ranges, not invent a single representative record. At high density, compare a grid and a sampled-point layer side by side: the grid describes mass, while the points retain individual exceptions. On a small screen, favor one readable layer over simultaneous translucent layers that obscure both.

Worked contract

from math import floor, isfinite

def density_cells(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                  x_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  y_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  columns: int, rows: int) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    x_low, x_high = x_bounds
    y_low, y_high = y_bounds
    if columns < 1 or rows < 1 or x_low >= x_high or y_low >= y_high:
        raise ValueError("invalid grid")
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for amount, handling_minutes in points:
        if not all(map(isfinite, (amount, handling_minutes))):
            raise ValueError("non-finite observation")
        if not (x_low <= amount <= x_high and
                y_low <= handling_minutes <= y_high):
            raise ValueError("point outside declared domain")
        column = min(columns - 1, floor((amount - x_low) * columns / (x_high - x_low)))
        row = min(rows - 1, floor((handling_minutes - y_low) * rows / (y_high - y_low)))
        counts[(column, row)] = counts.get((column, row), 0) + 1
    return counts

cells = density_cells([(47, 18), (47, 18), (81, 39)],
                      (0, 100), (0, 50), 5, 5)
assert sum(cells.values()) == 3 and max(cells.values()) == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N points and C occupied cells, fixed-grid counting takes O(N) time and O(C) memory, with C no larger than the number of grid positions. Rendering one rectangle per occupied cell can be much cheaper than rendering N circles. The example rejects out-of-domain points; a production view may instead maintain an explicit overflow bucket, but it must label that choice. Recompute bins when the axis domain or pixel resolution changes, and do not confuse screen-density counts with a probability density estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Lowering opacity and assuming the visible marks still represent all records.
  • Sampling rare cases away while evaluating an exception-handling workflow.
  • Comparing density grids built with different bounds or cell widths.
  • Calling a fitted slope causal based on a crowded scatterplot.

Validation drill

Generate 4,700 routine handling cases plus 31 rare high-delay cases. Compare raw points, a fixed grid and a seeded stratified sample; report whether each view keeps the rare cluster visible and whether displayed counts reconcile.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

Validation drill

Facet five depot delay series on one weekly calendar. Produce a shared-scale view for absolute comparison and a labeled independent-scale view for within-depot variation; write down which conclusions differ.

title: Heatmaps: make missing cells, rates and color domains explicit
summary: Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.
body:
Construct a complete matrix and keep unmeasured cells separate from zero-valued measurements.

A cell needs two keys and one measure

A heatmap is a matrix of marks whose position comes from two discrete dimensions and whose fill encodes a value. The first decision is the unit of a cell: one depot-day, one product-hour, or one model-class pair. Build the complete expected key grid before coloring it. Otherwise an absent record disappears, compresses the layout, or is mistaken for a low value. A white cell may mean zero, unobserved, unavailable or suppressed; these states require separate labels or patterns. Calendar completeness matters when columns are days.

Rates need their denominators

A defect-rate cell with 4 defects in 8 inspections and another with 40 in 800 inspections should not be interpreted as equally reliable even if their colors reflect 50% and 5%. Carry inspected count into a tooltip, visible annotation, or companion display. If no inspections occurred, the rate is undefined rather than zero. Measure grain determines whether the numerator and denominator belong to the same cell. If filters remove rows, recompute both counts instead of averaging precomputed cell percentages.

Fix the color domain for comparison

An automatically rescaled palette can make the same value change color when the viewer filters a subset. For cross-filter or before-after comparisons, set a stable domain and show its endpoints. A sequential palette fits a nonnegative rate; a diverging palette needs a meaningful center such as zero difference or target variance. Quantile coloring gives bins with similar record counts, not equal numeric widths. Label the bin rule. Accessible encodings add text or pattern cues so the chart still works without color.

Choose ordering deliberately

Alphabetical row order is reproducible, but ordering by a stable baseline can expose patterns. Clustering rows by similarity can reveal structure yet change the question: adjacent rows no longer imply geographic or operational proximity. If an algorithm orders rows, record its input period and freeze the order for comparisons. Keep hidden categories and totals visible. A truncated matrix that shows only the busiest depots is a selected population, not the entire network. Facet-order discipline applies here too.

Test the matrix contract

Include an observed zero, a missing key, a present key with zero exposure, an invalid negative count and a high-rate low-volume cell. Confirm each has a distinct state. Check the matrix against a long-form data table with the same row and column order. On mobile, provide axis labels that remain visible while scrolling; a distant legend is not enough. Exported CSV should retain status, numerator and denominator rather than only a color code.

Worked contract

def inspection_matrix(
    observations: dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[int, int]],
    depots: list[str], days: list[str]
) -> dict[tuple[str, str], tuple[str, float | None, int | None]]:
    expected = {(depot, day) for depot in depots for day in days}
    if len(expected) != len(depots) * len(days) or set(observations) - expected:
        raise ValueError("duplicate labels or unexpected cell")
    grid = {}
    for key in expected:
        if key not in observations:
            grid[key] = ("missing", None, None)
            continue
        defects, inspected = observations[key]
        if not 0 <= defects <= inspected:
            raise ValueError("invalid cell counts")
        grid[key] = ("no-exposure", None, 0) if inspected == 0 else (
            "observed", defects / inspected, inspected)
    return grid

matrix = inspection_matrix(
    {("north", "Mon"): (0, 47), ("north", "Tue"): (0, 0)},
    ["north"], ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"])
assert matrix[("north", "Mon")] == ("observed", 0.0, 47)
assert matrix[("north", "Tue")][0] == "no-exposure"
assert matrix[("north", "Wed")][0] == "missing"

Performance and operating cost

For R row labels, C column labels and M supplied observations, building the expected grid takes O(RC + M) time and O(RC) space. Large sparse matrices should keep sparse storage and generate only visible tiles, but must still represent missing cells and axis positions correctly. The demonstration returns status, rate and denominator; a production export should also retain the numerator and source snapshot. Color scaling and rendering add work proportional to visible cells, not merely to supplied observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Assigning the same white fill to an observed zero and an absent cell.
  • Changing the color domain after filtering without warning the reader.
  • Averaging cell percentages instead of recomputing counts for a new group.
  • Sorting rows by one selected day, then describing the layout as a stable geographic order.

Validation drill

Build a depot-by-day inspection matrix with 6 depots and 17 days. Insert one missing cell, one zero-exposure cell and one observed zero. Verify their states in both chart legend and exported data.

title: Choropleth maps: normalize counts and audit boundary coverage
summary: Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.
body:
Join measures to the right polygons, use a stated denominator, and distinguish unmapped places from zero-valued regions.

Area color is not an event count

A choropleth fills geographic regions according to a measure. Large polygons occupy more pixels and can dominate attention even when they contain few people or events. Raw incident counts often track exposure, such as population or active deliveries, more than risk. For a comparable rate, carry numerator and denominator for each polygon and specify the period. Exposure-based rates explain why 8 incidents across 47,000 trips differ from 8 across 470 trips. A map can still show counts when workload is the question; label it as a count map.

Join by stable region identity

Names drift, abbreviations collide, and administrative boundaries change. Join facts to geometry with stable region IDs and a boundary version. Report unmatched fact IDs, polygons with no measure, duplicate assignments and overlapping boundaries before rendering. Spatial joins are a separate operation from coloring polygons; they can duplicate a record if geometries overlap. If one region splits midyear, a before-after map needs a common boundary basis or an explicit break. Do not let a chart library silently drop unmatched regions.

Projection and extent shape perception

A projection transforms coordinates into map space. It can distort area, shape or distance; no flat map preserves everything. For regional comparison, keep the same projection, extent and viewport across panels, and avoid interpreting the visible area of a polygon as its population. Insets for distant regions need clear labels and scale context. If exact comparison of rates matters more than location, provide a sorted bar chart alongside the map. Choose the visual that serves the question, not merely the available geometry.

Class breaks are an editorial decision

Equal-width bins, quantile bins and fixed policy thresholds answer different questions. A quantile palette can assign different colors to tiny numeric differences when many regions cluster tightly; fixed thresholds can leave some colors unused. Print numeric breakpoints and keep them stable when comparing dates. Use a separate treatment for missing data and low-exposure suppression. Color-domain rules carry over to map legends. Keep the original rate in the accessible table and tooltip; color bins are a summary, not the data.

Protect sensitive locations

Very small denominators can make rates unstable and expose information about a few people or facilities. Define a minimum publishable group size, aggregate or suppress as appropriate, and show a visible suppressed state. Do not infer that a blank region has zero risk. Location privacy and small-sample display belong to the same release review. Test a region with no geometry, a polygon with no observation, a zero numerator and a zero denominator separately.

Worked contract

def regional_rates(
    boundary_ids: set[str],
    incident_counts: dict[str, tuple[int, int]]
) -> dict[str, tuple[str, float | None]]:
    unknown = set(incident_counts) - boundary_ids
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"facts without geometry: {sorted(unknown)}")
    result = {}
    for region_id in boundary_ids:
        if region_id not in incident_counts:
            result[region_id] = ("missing", None)
            continue
        incidents, trips = incident_counts[region_id]
        if not 0 <= incidents <= trips:
            raise ValueError("invalid regional counts")
        result[region_id] = ("no-exposure", None) if trips == 0 else (
            "observed", incidents / trips)
    return result

rates = regional_rates({"zone-47", "zone-81", "zone-94"},
                       {"zone-47": (8, 470), "zone-81": (0, 81)})
assert rates["zone-47"][1] == 8 / 470
assert rates["zone-81"] == ("observed", 0.0)
assert rates["zone-94"] == ("missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For B boundary IDs and M measured regions, this join-and-rate check takes O(B + M) expected time and O(B) output space using hash sets. Rendering cost depends on polygon vertex count, projection and viewport clipping, none of which this code performs. Simplify geometry only to a documented tolerance and keep an exact source for hit tests. A cached tile or geometry file must carry the same boundary version as the measures. The code distinguishes zero and missing; a real publication layer also enforces suppression and uncertainty policy.

Common Mistakes

  • Coloring raw counts as if the map showed per-person or per-trip risk.
  • Joining on human-readable region names without checking unmatched and duplicated keys.
  • Treating a missing polygon or missing measure as zero.
  • Changing map bounds or class breaks between comparison dates.

Validation drill

Map 23 service zones with one split boundary, one missing measure and one zone below the publishable exposure threshold. Reconcile region IDs and rates before drawing polygons; add a sorted rate table for exact comparison.

title: Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters
summary: Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.
body:
Make selections compose predictably, recalculate numerators and denominators, and expose the active state.

A selection changes the population

Linked filtering lets a selection in one view constrain another. Clicking a depot, brushing a date range or choosing a channel changes the cohort behind every plotted metric. The interaction contract must specify whether filters combine with AND or OR, whether a second click toggles, and whether an empty selection means all or none. Show active filters in text and offer a clear reset. Dashboard provenance needs the same filter state that the user sees; otherwise a shared screenshot cannot be reproduced.

Recompute base counts

A precomputed overall completion percentage cannot simply be filtered and averaged. Reapply the filter to eligible records, then sum timely and eligible counts for the selected cohort. If a record appears in both a status log and an order table, deduplicate to the declared unit before counting. Grain and denominator rules are the invariant under interaction. A filtered group with zero eligible records should display an undefined rate and zero denominator, not a zero-percent success rate.

Synchronize every view

When a brush narrows a chart, its companion count, data table, map and export must use the same selected IDs or query predicate. Some dashboards filter the marks but leave the headline KPI unfiltered; users then compare incompatible populations. Carry one normalized state object and one data-version token into each query. If a backend response arrives after the user changes filters again, discard the stale response instead of replacing a newer view. A request ID or abort signal can enforce this. Large-series rendering may be approximate, but filter semantics must remain exact.

Make selection discoverable and reversible

Hover-only behavior hides controls from touch and keyboard users. Provide visible filter chips, keyboard-operable controls, focus cues and a readable selection summary. Color should not be the sole indication of selected marks. A reset should restore the documented default and preserve the date or snapshot policy, not silently switch to today's data. Accessible chart controls include data values outside the plotted canvas. Keep the browser back button or a shareable query state when deep analysis paths matter.

Test the state machine

Exercise no filters, one filter, two intersecting filters, mutually exclusive filters, a zero-eligible result, and rapid filter changes. Compare chart, KPI and export row counts for each state. For a selected region and channel, check that removing one chip broadens the cohort only along that dimension. Record the expected query predicate alongside a screenshot in a release test. If the chart is based on sampled or aggregated data, do not use a pixel brush to imply record-level exactness unless the backend can resolve it.

Worked contract

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReviewRecord:
    receipt_id: str
    region: str
    channel: str
    eligible: bool
    timely: bool

def filtered_completion(records: list[ReviewRecord],
                        regions: set[str], channels: set[str]
                        ) -> tuple[int, int, float | None]:
    if len({record.receipt_id for record in records}) != len(records):
        raise ValueError("duplicate receipt identity")
    selected = [record for record in records
                if (not regions or record.region in regions)
                and (not channels or record.channel in channels)
                and record.eligible]
    if any(record.timely and not record.eligible for record in records):
        raise ValueError("timely receipt cannot be ineligible")
    timely = sum(record.timely for record in selected)
    eligible = len(selected)
    return timely, eligible, timely / eligible if eligible else None

receipts = [ReviewRecord("r-47", "north", "web", True, True),
            ReviewRecord("r-81", "north", "store", True, False),
            ReviewRecord("r-94", "south", "web", True, True)]
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"north"}, {"web"}) == (1, 1, 1.0)
assert filtered_completion(receipts, {"south"}, {"store"}) == (0, 0, None)

Performance and operating cost

For N records, duplicate validation and filtering take O(N) expected time and O(N) temporary space in this direct version; the selected list can be avoided with streaming counters to use O(N) identity state and O(1) additional cohort state. For a remote dashboard, query cost and transfer volume usually dominate. Cache only by normalized filters, authorization context and data version. Never reuse a cached result across tenants or revisions merely because the visible filter chips match.

Common Mistakes

  • Filtering colored marks while leaving headline metrics on the full population.
  • Averaging cached percentages after a filter instead of summing base counts.
  • Treating an empty cohort as a measured zero-percent rate.
  • Letting an older network response overwrite the result of a newer selection.

Validation drill

Connect a weekly trend, region bar chart and completion KPI. Test six filter states and verify the same eligible count in the chart tooltip, KPI, table and CSV export for each state.
