title: Dual-axis charts: test whether two series really need one plot
summary: Independent vertical scales can manufacture alignment; compare shared-time alternatives first.
body:
Independent vertical scales can manufacture alignment; compare shared-time alternatives first.

Two axes create a choice

A dual-axis chart places two measures against a shared horizontal dimension while giving each its own vertical scale. It can be compact, but independent scale ranges allow almost any pair of trends to look aligned or opposed. State both units, put each series next to its axis label, and inspect the same data as separate aligned panels before publishing. Small multiples preserve time alignment without implying that pixel height has a shared meaning.

Audit the apparent correlation

The eye can mistake coincident peaks for a relationship when one series has been shifted, smoothed or clipped. If the question is whether the measures co-vary, use paired observations in a scatter plot and name any lag rather than inferring it from two lines. Correlation coverage matters when dates are missing from one source. Do not quietly forward-fill one series to align timestamps. Carry measurement cadence and missingness into the displayed record.

When shared axes are possible

If the two series have the same unit and meaning, use a single axis. If they differ only by a constant conversion, convert one before plotting and disclose the conversion. If they have unrelated units but the question is relative change from a baseline, an indexed chart can be clearer, provided the base period and undefined zero-base cases are stated. Transformed scales also demand explicit zero handling. A second axis is not a shortcut around incompatible denominators.

Keep exports and text independent

When a second axis is justified by a particular reading task, export both raw series, scale domains, ticks and units. Use distinct line patterns, not just colors, and name the axes in a text summary. Test the chart with one series removed; readers should still know which axis belongs to the remaining series. The chart manifest should record every transformation and scale domain. Check mobile width: overlapping axis labels can erase the distinctions that made the chart defensible.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def paired_series_rows(
    first: dict[str, float], second: dict[str, float]
) -> tuple[list[tuple[str, float, float]], list[str]]:
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in [*first.values(), *second.values()]):
        raise ValueError("series values must be finite")
    shared = sorted(first.keys() & second.keys())
    missing = sorted(first.keys() ^ second.keys())
    return [(period, first[period], second[period]) for period in shared], missing

requests = {"week-47": 81, "week-48": 97, "week-49": 113}
latency = {"week-47": 59, "week-49": 68, "week-50": 83}
pairs, unpaired = paired_series_rows(requests, latency)
assert pairs == [("week-47", 81, 59), ("week-49", 113, 68)]
assert unpaired == ["week-48", "week-50"]

Performance and operating cost

For A and B keyed observations, set intersection and sorting use O(A+B+K log K) time and O(A+B) additional space for K paired periods. This preparation does not select axis domains or establish a correlation. It prevents silent alignment by index position. A production chart should also validate time-zone and aggregation-period equivalence before treating two keys as the same time.

Common Mistakes

  • Choosing independent axis domains solely to align peaks.
  • Forward-filling missing dates without a stated imputation rule.
  • Using two axes for measures that share a convertible unit.
  • Relying on color alone to tie each line to its axis.

Validation drill

Plot weekly requests and latency for 47 weeks as separate aligned panels and as a dual-axis view. Remove two latency weeks and verify the paired observation count changes visibly.

title: Beeswarm plots: show individual values without inventing spread
summary: Keep the measured axis exact, treat sideways displacement as layout, and disclose how many marks are present.
body:
Keep the measured axis exact, treat sideways displacement as layout, and disclose how many marks are present.

A dot is an observation

A beeswarm places individual observations along a measured axis and moves marks sideways only enough to reduce overlap. The lateral coordinate is not a second measured variable. State that in the axis caption, because a wide swarm can otherwise be mistaken for more variation. If the mark count exceeds the display's collision capacity, use a declared sample or a distribution summary instead of silently dropping points. Overplotting and sampling bias determine whether the displayed dots still represent the underlying population. Report the raw count and the displayed count for every group.

Preserve ties and identity

Repeated equal measurements should remain repeated observations. A deterministic layout lets an analyst compare revisions without random movement that looks like new data. Stable IDs matter when a reader selects or exports a point. If several rows share the same subject and timestamp, decide whether they are repeated measurements or duplicates before drawing. The plot cannot make that data decision. The export manifest should preserve observation ID, group, measured value, sampling rule and layout version. A text alternative can list the median, range, count and number of tied values.

Collision radius is a visual parameter

A beeswarm solver needs marker diameter in display pixels as well as the scale that maps values to pixels. Zooming, resizing or switching to mobile changes collision geometry. Thus an offset computed for one viewport cannot safely be reused for another. Cap the lateral spread only if the chart explicitly allows overlap after that cap; hiding dots is not acceptable. Accessible mark encodings need a visible outline or shape difference when groups share a panel. Test the chart at the narrowest intended width.

Compare with a distribution summary

The swarm is good for a few hundred visible records, particularly when outliers and ties are the story. At larger scale it becomes slow to lay out and hard to read. A box, violin or ECDF can summarize shape, while a small sample of dots reveals examples without pretending to be complete. Box and violin plots have their own bandwidth and whisker decisions; they are not interchangeable with raw observations. If groups have unequal sample sizes, annotate counts next to labels so width is not mistaken for prevalence.

Worked contract

from hashlib import sha256
from math import isfinite

def stable_strip_positions(records: list[tuple[str, str, float]],
                           spread: float = 0.38) -> list[tuple[str, str, float, float]]:
    if not 0 <= spread <= 0.5:
        raise ValueError("spread must fit inside one category")
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("observation IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not group or not isfinite(value) for _, group, value in records):
        raise ValueError("group and measured value must be valid")
    placed = []
    for record_id, group, value in records:
        digest = sha256(record_id.encode("utf-8")).digest()
        fraction = int.from_bytes(digest[:8], "big") / (2**64 - 1)
        placed.append((record_id, group, value, (2 * fraction - 1) * spread))
    return placed

service_times = [("ticket-47", "priority", 81.0),
                 ("ticket-59", "priority", 81.0),
                 ("ticket-83", "standard", 97.0)]
positions = stable_strip_positions(service_times)
assert len(positions) == 3 and positions[0][2] == positions[1][2]
assert positions == stable_strip_positions(service_times)

Performance and operating cost

Preparing N stable strip positions takes O(N) expected time and O(N) output space. This code produces reproducible jitter; it is not a collision-solving beeswarm. A true beeswarm needs screen-space marker geometry and may require O(N squared) comparisons in a simple placement algorithm. Do not label the jittered result collision-free. Preserve exact measured values and IDs in the export, and recalculate visual offsets when the display scale changes.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading sideways jitter as a measured quantity.
  • Suppressing overlapped observations without recording the omitted count.
  • Reseeding random positions on every redraw, making stable records appear to move.
  • Calling deterministic jitter a collision-free beeswarm without checking marker radius.

Draw 81 support-ticket response times across three queues. Keep equal values as separate dots, show each queue's count and compare a narrow mobile layout with a distribution summary.

title: Calendar heatmaps: distinguish an empty day from an absent day
summary: Generate the full date grid, fix the reporting time zone and encode missing observations separately from zero.
body:
Generate the full date grid, fix the reporting time zone and encode missing observations separately from zero.

A blank square has several meanings

A calendar heatmap arranges daily values in a weekly grid. A white day could mean zero events, no feed, a day outside the reporting range or a suppressed value. Those states cannot share one silent color. Generate every expected local date first, then join observations and label each cell's status. Missing-cell heatmaps need the same distinction. For a support operation, a zero confirmed ticket count is evidence; an uncollected Saturday is not. Show the number of complete days beside any annual total.

Choose the reporting day

An event at 00:20 UTC may belong to the prior local day. Convert timestamps to the declared reporting zone before aggregating, and record the zone in the export. Daylight-saving changes produce 23- or 25-hour local days in some regions; counts remain counts, but per-hour rates need an exposure adjustment. A calendar grid without its time-zone contract can move incidents across cells and distort weekday patterns. Time-series calendar rules cover incomplete current periods and delayed arrivals. Mark provisional days rather than painting them as final.

Keep color comparable

Fix the numeric color domain across years or related teams when the goal is comparison. Otherwise each year may assign the darkest shade to a different count. If the distribution has a long tail, state any transform or clipped maximum. A daily rate requires the matching daily denominator; weekend exposure often differs from weekday exposure. Grain and denominator come before color selection. A tooltip should expose date, value, status, denominator if used and refresh time, while a text table remains available for keyboard and screen-reader users.

Week structure is a locale decision

Some audiences expect Monday-first weeks; others expect Sunday-first. Label weekdays, show month boundaries and test leap years, year transitions and ISO week edges. Do not infer a causal weekday pattern from a few colored streaks. A release schedule, holiday closure or data-delivery gap may explain the pattern. Event annotations should state what happened without claiming effect. Export an explicit date-status table so another analyst can reconstruct the image rather than reverse-engineering its colors.

Worked contract

from datetime import date, timedelta

def complete_daily_series(start: date, end: date,
                          observed: dict[date, int | None]
                          ) -> list[tuple[date, str, int | None]]:
    if end < start or any(day < start or day > end for day in observed):
        raise ValueError("dates must fall inside the requested period")
    if any(value is not None and (not isinstance(value, int) or value < 0)
           for value in observed.values()):
        raise ValueError("daily counts must be nonnegative integers")
    result = []
    day = start
    while day <= end:
        value = observed.get(day)
        status = "missing" if value is None else "observed"
        result.append((day, status, value))
        day += timedelta(days=1)
    return result

calendar_rows = complete_daily_series(
    date(2026, 10, 1), date(2026, 10, 4),
    {date(2026, 10, 1): 47, date(2026, 10, 2): 0,
     date(2026, 10, 4): 59})
assert calendar_rows[1] == (date(2026, 10, 2), "observed", 0)
assert calendar_rows[2] == (date(2026, 10, 3), "missing", None)

Performance and operating cost

For D days and O observed keys, validation and completion take O(D+O) time and O(D) output space. This code assumes the input keys already represent the correct reporting-zone dates; timestamp conversion belongs upstream. If a source uses null to mean suppression rather than missing delivery, give it its own status before calling this function. Store daily exposure separately when coloring rates.

Common Mistakes

  • Turning missing days into zeros.
  • Aggregating UTC dates and labeling the result as a local calendar.
  • Allowing each year to auto-scale its colors during comparison.
  • Treating a partly reported current day as final.

Validation drill

Build a 47-day operations calendar with a confirmed zero, a late feed, a holiday closure and one provisional day. Export the four states and explain the color domain.

title: Parallel coordinates: make every axis conversion inspectable
summary: Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.
body:
Compare multivariate profiles only after documenting normalization, axis order and missing-value treatment.

A polyline is one record

Parallel coordinates display one entity as a line crossing several vertical axes. Its crossings are the entity's values; line slopes between axes are visual connectors, not measured rates of change. Before drawing, name every metric and unit. A route whose five service measures have incompatible units cannot be read honestly on one raw height scale. Scale integrity applies independently to every axis. Put the raw value in a tooltip or adjacent table so a normalized line does not erase the original measurement.

Normalization changes the question

Min-max normalization maps each axis to a shared display interval, but a single extreme entity can compress all others. Fixed policy bounds may be more stable than bounds computed from the current filter. If lower is preferable for one metric, invert its display direction and label that inversion. Never silently reverse an axis just to make good records form a tidy line. Target-oriented KPI charts may be clearer if the decision is only whether a threshold was met. Keep the bounds, direction and unit beside each dimension in exported metadata.

Axis order and brushing are analytic choices

Swapping two adjacent axes changes which relationships are visually easiest to see, even though the data stay unchanged. Pick an order tied to the question, such as intake, response, resolution and cost, then preserve it across comparable views. Brushing one range selects entities; a linked table should show which IDs remain and how many were excluded. Linked filters require explicit cohort state. Avoid drawing every record at full opacity: a thousand crossing lines become an opaque band. Sampling must retain a visible selected count and a full-population summary.

Missing values must not become fabricated paths

A line should break or be omitted with an explicit reason when one dimension is absent; zero is not a replacement for missing. Check whether the missingness is related to the outcome being inspected. If only high-cost projects fail to report quality, excluding incomplete records changes the apparent relationship. An export manifest should name complete-case rules, filter state, axis order, bounds and transformed values. For accessibility, offer a sortable table of the underlying records and a concise summary of which dimensions separate selected groups.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def normalize_profile(profile: dict[str, float | None],
                      axes: dict[str, tuple[float, float, bool]]
                      ) -> dict[str, float | None]:
    if set(profile) != set(axes):
        raise ValueError("profile dimensions must match axis declarations")
    normalized = {}
    for metric, (low, high, lower_is_better) in axes.items():
        value = profile[metric]
        if not all(isfinite(bound) for bound in (low, high)) or high <= low:
            raise ValueError("axis bounds must be finite and ordered")
        if value is None:
            normalized[metric] = None
            continue
        if not isfinite(value) or not low <= value <= high:
            raise ValueError("measurement outside declared axis")
        position = (value - low) / (high - low)
        normalized[metric] = 1 - position if lower_is_better else position
    return normalized

axes = {"response_minutes": (0, 120, True),
        "resolved_percent": (0, 100, False)}
depot_profile = normalize_profile(
    {"response_minutes": 47, "resolved_percent": 81}, axes)
assert round(depot_profile["response_minutes"], 4) == 0.6083
assert depot_profile["resolved_percent"] == 0.81

Performance and operating cost

For D dimensions in one record, normalization takes O(D) time and O(D) output space; N records take O(ND). Rendering N polylines can dominate interaction cost, especially when brushing triggers full redraws. The code rejects values outside policy bounds rather than clipping them invisibly. If clipping is intended, export both raw and displayed values and count clipped records by axis.

Common Mistakes

  • Interpreting connector slope as a real-world rate of change.
  • Recomputing axis bounds after a filter and comparing line heights as if scale stayed fixed.
  • Silently reversing one axis or replacing missing with zero.
  • Drawing all records at full opacity and calling the dense band a cluster.

Validation drill

Compare 59 depots on response time, resolution rate and cost. Publish fixed axis bounds, invert only metrics where lower is better, then brush a subgroup and reconcile its ID count to the table.

title: Bump charts: show rank movement without losing ties or entrants
summary: Declare the ranking metric, tie policy and eligible entities for each period before connecting positions.
body:
Declare the ranking metric, tie policy and eligible entities for each period before connecting positions.

Rank is an ordering, not a magnitude

A bump chart connects an entity's ranks across periods. A move from third to first may reflect a tiny absolute difference or a major change; the line does not tell you which. Name the ranked measure and link to values behind each position. Paired-change charts work better when the actual size of change matters. If a new entity enters the cohort, existing ranks can fall without their own measurements changing. Display entrants and exits as membership events rather than implying deterioration.

Ties need a written rule

Equal measurements can share a rank, be assigned adjacent ranks by a secondary key, or be shown in a tied band. These choices produce different line paths. Competition ranking gives equal values the same rank and skips the next position; dense ranking does not skip. Neither should be selected by accident inside a plotting library. Preserve raw values and the chosen tie rule in the export. Reproducible chart exports also need source period and eligibility criteria. Test ties at both top and bottom before publishing.

Hold the cohort question steady

A panel can rank the same fixed set of entities every period or rank whoever was eligible at the time. The first view tracks a stable cohort; the second reflects changing membership. State which one readers see. If a missing measurement removes an entity from one period, show a line break or missing marker rather than assigning last place. Provisional periods and data gaps are especially easy to hide in a rank-only display. Mark a period as provisional when its numerator or denominator can still change.

Limit crossings and preserve access

Many crossing lines defeat tracing. Highlight a small set chosen by a documented rule, fade the remainder and let the reader search by entity ID. A table with period, rank, value and membership status is essential, because color-only line identity and hover-only labels fail on touch and assistive technology. Text alternatives should call out the biggest rank rise, biggest fall, ties and entrants. Do not claim a trend from two ranks alone; a third period or actual values may tell a different story.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def competition_ranks(scores: dict[str, float]) -> dict[str, int]:
    if any(not entity for entity in scores):
        raise ValueError("entity IDs must be nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in scores.values()):
        raise ValueError("scores must be finite")
    ordered = sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    ranks = {}
    prior_score = None
    current_rank = 0
    for position, (entity, score) in enumerate(ordered, start=1):
        if prior_score is None or score != prior_score:
            current_rank = position
        ranks[entity] = current_rank
        prior_score = score
    return ranks

week_47 = competition_ranks({"north": 81, "south": 81,
                             "west": 59, "east": 47})
assert week_47 == {"north": 1, "south": 1, "west": 3, "east": 4}

Performance and operating cost

Ranking N entities costs O(N log N) time and O(N) output space per period; connecting P periods takes O(PN) output storage for a fixed cohort. The code uses higher-score-first competition ranks and stable ID ordering only for reproducible output. It does not fill absent entities. Before rendering, validate that every period uses the same score definition and disclose whether the eligible set is fixed or variable.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading a one-place rise as a fixed-size improvement.
  • Allowing a chart library to break ties arbitrarily.
  • Assigning missing entities last place.
  • Comparing periods with changing eligibility without labeling entrants and exits.

Validation drill

Rank 47 service depots over six weeks with two ties and one new entrant. Reconcile every rank to its score and show how the entrant changes the apparent position of unchanged depots.

title: P charts: account for varying denominators before flagging a rate
summary: Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.
body:
Use a declared baseline and period-specific limits for binomial proportions, then investigate signals without inventing causes.

A rate needs its opportunity count

A p chart follows a proportion such as defective shipments divided by inspected shipments. Forty-seven defects in 470 inspections and 47 in 4,700 do not carry the same sampling uncertainty. Plot the period denominator or put it in a table, and calculate limits from the baseline proportion using each period's sample size. Denominator discipline is the first check. Do not mix units such as orders and line items, or change the defect definition midway through the series.

Freeze the baseline before judging a new point

Choose a stable historical interval and document excluded outages, policy changes and incomplete periods. Pool baseline defects over baseline opportunities for a center line. Calculating a fresh center from every newly flagged point can move the goalposts. A period beyond an approximate three-standard-error limit is a signal to investigate; it does not prove a specific cause. Event annotations should distinguish observed timing from causal evidence. A confirmed process change may justify a new baseline, but record where the old phase ends.

Know the approximation's limits

The simple p-chart formula assumes independent, comparable Bernoulli opportunities and a fairly stable underlying probability. Correlated batches, rare events or extra variation can make the limits misleading. Tiny sample sizes produce wide limits; values must still stay between zero and one. If repeated points reveal more variation than the model allows, investigate the collection process or choose a method suited to overdispersion. Small-sample displays help communicate why a large-looking percentage swing may be weak evidence. A control limit is not a target or a confidence interval for a business decision.

Explain the chart without color

Show the center line, period-specific bounds, actual rate, numerator and denominator in the export. Mark flagged points with shape and text, not red alone. If a late-arriving batch changes a historical numerator, recompute the affected point and disclose the revision. Provisional periods should be clearly separate from finalized ones. An accessible summary can state which periods crossed limits and which lacked enough data, while leaving the causal diagnosis to the investigation.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt

def p_chart_rows(baseline: list[tuple[int, int]],
                 periods: list[tuple[str, int, int]]
                 ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float, bool]]:
    def valid(defects: int, inspected: int) -> bool:
        return (isinstance(defects, int) and isinstance(inspected, int)
                and inspected > 0 and 0 <= defects <= inspected)
    if not baseline or any(not valid(d, n) for d, n in baseline):
        raise ValueError("baseline requires valid defect counts")
    if any(not label or not valid(d, n) for label, d, n in periods):
        raise ValueError("period counts or labels are invalid")
    center = sum(d for d, _ in baseline) / sum(n for _, n in baseline)
    output = []
    for label, defects, inspected in periods:
        radius = 3 * sqrt(center * (1 - center) / inspected)
        lower, upper = max(0.0, center - radius), min(1.0, center + radius)
        rate = defects / inspected
        output.append((label, rate, lower, upper, rate < lower or rate > upper))
    return output

baseline = [(47, 470), (59, 590), (81, 810)]
signals = p_chart_rows(baseline, [("week-47", 47, 470),
                                  ("week-48", 3, 470)])
assert round(signals[0][1], 4) == 0.1
assert signals[1][-1] is True

Performance and operating cost

For B baseline periods and P plotted periods, this calculation takes O(B+P) time and O(P) output space. The three-standard-error limits are an approximation under an independent binomial model; the code does not test independence, estimate overdispersion or infer a cause. A production pipeline should version the baseline and defect definition, enforce finalized counts, and show denominator size with every point.

Common Mistakes

  • Comparing percentages while concealing sharply different sample sizes.
  • Recomputing the baseline after every flagged period.
  • Calling a control limit a business target.
  • Treating a signal as proof of the annotated event's effect.

Validation drill

Track 59 weekly inspection proportions with variable sample sizes. Freeze a baseline, flag points beyond their own limits and investigate a week whose rate is high but denominator is small.

title: Pareto charts: reconcile the cumulative line to the categories
summary: Sort one additive measure, retain the whole denominator and make the category boundary explicit.
body:
Sort one additive measure, retain the whole denominator and make the category boundary explicit.

Start with an additive question

A Pareto chart ranks categories by a nonnegative contribution and traces their cumulative share of the total. The measure could be incident count, repair hours or cost; those are different prioritization questions. State the unit and aggregation grain before sorting. If one ticket appears under several causes, the category totals may exceed the number of tickets. Either allocate each ticket once or label the chart as multi-tag occurrences. Aggregation and denominator rules determine whether the cumulative line has a meaningful one-hundred-percent endpoint.

Keep the total visible

Calculate the percentage from all eligible categories, including the long tail. Grouping minor categories into Other can make a useful display, but the grouped value must equal the sum of the hidden categories and the full total must remain unchanged. A threshold line at eighty percent is only a reading aid; it does not prove an eighty-twenty distribution. Report the smallest number of categories needed to cross the chosen threshold, and name the threshold as a policy choice. Composition charts face the same problem when categories enter or leave the frame.

Separate bar scale from share scale

Bars encode the additive quantity, while the cumulative line encodes a percentage. These are different units, so label both axes and give the percentage line an explicit zero-to-one-hundred range. A dual-axis overlay can be compact, but lines and bars should remain legible independently. Dual-axis integrity matters here because changing the right axis can make the cumulative curve look steeper. A companion table with category, contribution, cumulative contribution and share makes the chart auditable without decoding line height.

Handle ties, zeros and time changes

When two categories have equal contributions, use a stable secondary key so repeated renders keep the same order. Zero categories may remain in the export even if the display omits them. If the chart is refreshed weekly, changing rank order is expected; do not compare bar positions as though category identity stayed fixed. Rank-movement charts are better for that question. If the total is zero, a cumulative percentage is undefined. Show the count table and an explicit no-contributions state rather than drawing a flat zero-percent line.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def pareto_rows(contributions: dict[str, float]
                ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float]]:
    if not contributions or any(not name for name in contributions):
        raise ValueError("categories must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0
           for value in contributions.values()):
        raise ValueError("contributions must be finite and nonnegative")
    total = sum(contributions.values())
    if total <= 0:
        raise ValueError("a zero total has no cumulative share")
    ordered = sorted(contributions.items(), key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
    running = 0.0
    result = []
    for category, value in ordered:
        running += value
        result.append((category, value, running / total))
    return result

repair_hours = {"pump seals": 47, "sensor faults": 81,
                "cable damage": 29, "other": 43}
priority = pareto_rows(repair_hours)
assert priority[0] == ("sensor faults", 81, 0.405)
assert priority[-1][2] == 1.0

Performance and operating cost

For C categories, sorting costs O(C log C) time and output takes O(C) space. Floating-point sums can round slightly for large fractional inputs; use exact decimal or integer minor units for financial totals. The example requires nonnegative additive contributions and rejects an all-zero chart. Production exports should retain category membership, source period and any Other grouping rule so cumulative shares can be reproduced.

Common Mistakes

  • Using overlapping cause tags while claiming the bars count unique incidents.
  • Removing the long tail before calculating percentages.
  • Treating an eighty-percent crossing as a universal law.
  • Leaving the two axes unlabeled or suppressing the all-zero state.

Validation drill

Rank 47 maintenance causes by total repair hours, then by incident count. Reconcile both denominators and explain why the first three categories differ between the two charts.

title: Asymmetric error bars: tell readers what each endpoint means
summary: Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.
body:
Carry lower and upper endpoints with every estimate, and never relabel arbitrary spread as uncertainty.

The interval needs a type

An error bar may encode a standard deviation, a confidence interval, a prediction interval, an instrument tolerance or a minimum-to-maximum range. These answer different questions. Put the interval type, level where applicable, method and sample size in the chart caption. Uncertainty displays explain why a narrow-looking interval does not automatically mean a precise individual prediction. A bar without that contract invites the reader to supply the wrong interpretation. If the calculation is model-based, identify the population and conditions under which it applies.

Keep the endpoints, not just a radius

Some intervals are asymmetric around the estimate, especially near natural boundaries or after a nonlinear transform. Export estimate, lower and upper as three separate numbers. A renderer may ask for downward and upward distances, which can be derived from those endpoints without losing meaning. An estimate outside its own stated interval is a data error for many common interval definitions and should be stopped or explained. Forecast fan charts make this distinction even more important because uncertainty often widens with horizon.

Draw limits honestly

If an endpoint falls beyond the plotted axis, do not clip it silently. Extend the axis, use a visible arrow with the endpoint value, or choose another layout. A log axis cannot display zero or negative endpoints; transforming the point and interval requires the same transformation applied to both, with the method stated. Log and symmetric-log scales are not cosmetic switches. The chart should show whether a bound is physical, statistical or merely the display edge.

Compare groups without overclaiming

Overlap of two intervals is not a general significance test, and non-overlap is not the only way to establish a difference. If the decision concerns the difference between groups, estimate and plot that difference with its own interval. Signed differences put zero at the relevant comparison point. Check whether the same subjects appear in both groups; paired data require a paired calculation. For accessible reading, list each estimate and its endpoints in text, with units and the interval definition repeated where the chart may be shared alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def errorbar_distances(rows: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]
                       ) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("estimate labels must be unique and nonempty")
    output = []
    for name, estimate, lower, upper in rows:
        if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (estimate, lower, upper)):
            raise ValueError("estimate and bounds must be finite")
        if not lower <= estimate <= upper:
            raise ValueError("estimate must lie within its interval")
        output.append((name, estimate, estimate - lower, upper - estimate))
    return output

service_intervals = errorbar_distances([
    ("priority queue", 81, 59, 113),
    ("standard queue", 97, 83, 149),
])
assert service_intervals == [
    ("priority queue", 81, 22, 32),
    ("standard queue", 97, 14, 52),
]

Performance and operating cost

Preparing N intervals takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code validates geometry but cannot establish that endpoints were calculated with the right statistical method. Keep the original endpoints and method metadata even if the chart library wants only positive distances. Avoid computing an interval from a small sample with an unverified shortcut just because the renderer accepts two numbers.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling a range or standard deviation a confidence interval.
  • Forcing asymmetric endpoints into equal visual arms.
  • Clipping a bound at the axis edge without a marker or label.
  • Inferring a group-difference test only from overlap of separate intervals.

Validation drill

Show 59 response-time estimates with asymmetric intervals. Identify five bounds outside the current axis and revise the view without hiding those endpoints.

title: Q–Q plots: compare distribution shape beyond one summary number
summary: Pair probabilities rather than row positions, state the reference distribution and inspect tail behavior separately.
body:
Pair probabilities rather than row positions, state the reference distribution and inspect tail behavior separately.

A quantile is an ordered position

A Q–Q plot compares quantiles from two distributions at the same cumulative probabilities. It does not pair individual records, even if both samples have the same size. State whether the horizontal axis is an observed reference group or a theoretical distribution, and label units on both axes. ECDF and percentile reading provide the underlying probability view. A line of points near a diagonal suggests broadly similar locations and spreads only if both axes use the same unit and scale; otherwise the reference may have a non-unit slope.

Choose a quantile convention

Software packages differ in how they interpolate between observations. Write down the convention when results will be compared across tools. Repeated values produce repeated or flat stretches; adding random jitter to hide ties changes the apparent pattern. For samples of different sizes, evaluate a common probability grid rather than aligning the first observation of each sorted list. Do not include probability zero or one in a theoretical distribution whose inverse CDF is infinite there. Box and violin views are useful companions when the Q–Q plot is too technical for a general audience.

Read center and tails separately

A nearly straight center with an upward bend in the high tail may indicate more large values in the vertical sample. A shift can move all points above the reference; a scale difference can change the slope. Avoid treating visual departures as an automatic hypothesis test. With a small sample, endpoints are unstable; with a huge sample, slight departures may be practically irrelevant. Sample-size uncertainty belongs in the caption. If the question is about service-level failures, count observations beyond a meaningful threshold as well as inspecting tail curvature.

Keep the comparison reproducible

Filter both samples by the same eligibility and time-window rules, then report their sizes and missing-value counts. If one group contains outages and the other excludes them, the plot is comparing policies as well as distributions. A chart export manifest should include filters, quantile grid, interpolation rule and transformed values. Provide a compact table of selected quantile pairs so a reader can inspect exact numbers without relying on hover or color. Never reverse the axes silently between reports.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def interpolate_quantile(sorted_values: list[float], probability: float) -> float:
    if not sorted_values or not 0 <= probability <= 1:
        raise ValueError("sample and probability are required")
    index = (len(sorted_values) - 1) * probability
    low = int(index)
    high = min(low + 1, len(sorted_values) - 1)
    return sorted_values[low] + (index - low) * (sorted_values[high] - sorted_values[low])

def paired_quantiles(reference: list[float], current: list[float],
                     probabilities: list[float]) -> list[tuple[float, float, float]]:
    if not reference or not current or any(not isfinite(value)
                                            for value in reference + current):
        raise ValueError("samples must contain finite values")
    if any(not 0 <= probability <= 1 for probability in probabilities):
        raise ValueError("probabilities must be inside zero and one")
    first, second = sorted(reference), sorted(current)
    return [(p, interpolate_quantile(first, p), interpolate_quantile(second, p))
            for p in probabilities]

quantile_pairs = paired_quantiles([47, 59, 81, 97, 113],
                                 [52, 61, 83, 101, 129], [0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
assert quantile_pairs == [(0.25, 59, 61), (0.5, 81, 83), (0.75, 97, 101)]

Performance and operating cost

Sorting reference and current samples of sizes A and B takes O(A log A + B log B) time; Q paired probabilities take O(Q) additional time and output space. The code uses linear interpolation at index (N minus one) times probability. It compares two empirical distributions, not a theoretical normal curve or a significance test. Preserve the method and sample sizes with the plot.

Common Mistakes

  • Pairing rows by index instead of pairing equal probabilities.
  • Switching interpolation methods between reports without disclosure.
  • Jittering ties until they look like genuine tail structure.
  • Calling every visible bend a statistically important deviation.

Validation drill

Compare 81 delivery-time records before and after a routing change. Plot common percentiles, report sample counts, and inspect whether the upper tail moved more than the median.

title: Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
summary: Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.
body:
Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.

A symbol has a location contract

A circle over a map may represent a precise facility, a regional centroid or an approximate address. Those are not equivalent. State what the coordinate means and how much location precision the data support. Choropleth maps color whole regions; proportional symbols encode a value at a point or chosen anchor. Do not place a regional total at a centroid without telling the reader that the circle summarizes an area. If location is sensitive, aggregate or coarsen before publication rather than relying on small marker size to conceal it.

Area should represent quantity

If a symbol encodes a nonnegative count, its visual area should be proportional to that count. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four, exaggerating the larger value. Compute radius from the square root of value relative to a declared maximum. Use a visible reference legend with at least two example magnitudes. A zero count should remain a recorded zero, even if its circle has no area; a tiny outline or table entry may be needed to keep the location discoverable. Scale integrity also means fixing the size domain across maps intended for comparison.

Overlapping circles need an explicit policy

Dense areas can hide smaller symbols under larger ones. Drawing order, opacity and zoom can all change what a reader sees. Try smaller maximum radius, outlines, clustering with disclosed counts, or an alternate ranked table. Do not let overlap remove records from the export. Hexbin density may be better when the question is where point events concentrate, while a proportional-symbol map is better when each point already has a meaningful aggregate. Test overlapping facilities at the closest supported zoom and on a narrow phone viewport.

Count and rate are different maps

A large population center may dominate a count map while having a modest per-person rate. A rate can be mapped with symbol size only if the legend names its denominator and the sampling uncertainty is not buried. Often a count-sized symbol plus a separately encoded rate is too much for one map; use paired maps or a table. The denominator contract must follow the geography and period. Export ID, coordinate meaning, count, denominator, computed rate, symbol radius and suppression state, so the map can be checked without its pixels.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def area_scaled_radii(values: dict[str, float],
                      maximum_radius: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    if not isfinite(maximum_radius) or maximum_radius <= 0:
        raise ValueError("maximum radius must be positive")
    if not values or any(not place for place in values):
        raise ValueError("locations must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in values.values()):
        raise ValueError("mapped values must be finite and nonnegative")
    maximum_value = max(values.values())
    if maximum_value == 0:
        return {place: 0.0 for place in values}
    return {place: maximum_radius * sqrt(value / maximum_value)
            for place, value in values.items()}

service_calls = {"north depot": 47, "south depot": 188, "west depot": 0}
radii = area_scaled_radii(service_calls, 20)
assert radii["south depot"] == 20
assert radii["north depot"] == 10
assert radii["west depot"] == 0

Performance and operating cost

For N locations, finding the maximum and calculating radii takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code sizes nonnegative values by area and leaves geographic projection, collision handling and legend generation to the map renderer. A production map must keep one fixed reference maximum across views that readers are expected to compare; recalculating it after every filter changes apparent size.

Common Mistakes

  • Making radius proportional to count and thereby exaggerating area.
  • Treating a regional centroid as an exact event location.
  • Letting large symbols cover small ones without a table or overlap strategy.
  • Comparing maps whose size domains were auto-scaled independently.

Validation drill

Map 59 service depots with zero, small and large call counts. Use area-scaled circles, disclose the location meaning and produce a fixed-size legend for two reporting periods.

title: Gantt timelines: make task dates and dependencies auditable
summary: Define interval boundaries, separate planned from actual work and verify dependency logic before drawing bars.
body:
Define interval boundaries, separate planned from actual work and verify dependency logic before drawing bars.

Bars are intervals

A Gantt-style timeline uses a horizontal interval for each task. Decide whether the end timestamp is exclusive or inclusive; an end-exclusive interval allows one task to end exactly when another begins without overlap. State the time zone and whether a displayed day means a calendar day or working day. Calendar semantics matter when a task crosses holidays or daylight-saving changes. Never reduce an actual timestamp to a date label before checking that its start and end still make sense.

Plan and actual are different records

A baseline plan should remain visible after work slips. Store planned start and finish separately from actual start and finish, and mark unfinished work as open rather than inventing an actual end at today. A progress fill is a third measurement, not a substitute for dates. Annotations can identify approvals, outages and scope changes, but placing them near a delay does not establish causation. Report the date at which the displayed project state was captured so a screenshot can be interpreted later.

Dependencies are a graph

A predecessor relationship means the successor has a scheduling constraint, not merely that its bar appears later on the page. Validate referenced task IDs, detect cycles and apply the chosen lag rule before rendering arrows. When a dependency is violated, show the violation rather than nudging a bar into a visually tidy position. Network identity rules apply: stable task IDs are safer than matching labels, which may change. For a crowded plan, show a selected path and a searchable dependency table instead of drawing every connector.

Resource overlap is not always an error

Two tasks can run concurrently on different teams; two tasks assigned to one exclusive machine cannot. Declare resource capacity before flagging overlap. A timeline sorted by start date may be useful for operations, while sorting by workstream may be better for planning; document the order so movement is not mistaken for a schedule change. Linked selection state should preserve which tasks and resources are visible. Provide an accessible task table with interval, status, predecessor and resource fields, and test the mobile view where narrow bars become untappable.

Worked contract

from datetime import datetime

def exclusive_resource_conflicts(
    tasks: list[tuple[str, str, datetime, datetime]]
) -> list[tuple[str, str, str]]:
    identifiers = [task_id for task_id, _, _, _ in tasks]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)):
        raise ValueError("task IDs must be unique")
    by_resource = {}
    for task_id, resource, start, end in tasks:
        if not task_id or not resource or start.tzinfo is None or end.tzinfo is None:
            raise ValueError("tasks need IDs, resources and zoned dates")
        if end <= start:
            raise ValueError("end-exclusive interval must have positive duration")
        by_resource.setdefault(resource, []).append((start, end, task_id))
    conflicts = []
    for resource, intervals in by_resource.items():
        ordered = sorted(intervals)
        for index, previous in enumerate(ordered):
            for current in ordered[index + 1:]:
                if current[0] >= previous[1]:
                    break
                conflicts.append((resource, previous[2], current[2]))
    return conflicts

from datetime import timezone
utc = timezone.utc
inspection = ("inspect-47", "crane-A", datetime(2026, 10, 8, 8, tzinfo=utc),
              datetime(2026, 10, 8, 11, tzinfo=utc))
repair = ("repair-59", "crane-A", datetime(2026, 10, 8, 10, tzinfo=utc),
          datetime(2026, 10, 8, 13, tzinfo=utc))
assert exclusive_resource_conflicts([inspection, repair]) == [
    ("crane-A", "inspect-47", "repair-59")
]
short_job = ("check-83", "crane-A", datetime(2026, 10, 8, 10, 30, tzinfo=utc),
             datetime(2026, 10, 8, 10, 45, tzinfo=utc))
assert len(exclusive_resource_conflicts([inspection, repair, short_job])) == 3

Performance and operating cost

For N tasks, sorting costs O(N log N); enumerating every conflicting pair takes O(N squared) time in the worst case and O(N plus K) space for K reported pairs. When many tasks overlap, K itself can be quadratic. This check is not a dependency scheduler or a capacity planner. Validate dependency references and cycles separately before publishing arrows, and preserve planned and actual intervals in the export.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing inclusive and exclusive task end dates.
  • Overwriting the original plan with actual dates.
  • Drawing dependency arrows without validating task IDs or cycles.
  • Calling every overlap an error without a resource-capacity rule.

Validation drill

Plot 47 maintenance tasks with planned and actual dates, two exclusive machines and three predecessor chains. Flag interval conflicts and an unfinished task without assigning it a fake actual end.

title: Ridgeline plots: compare distributions without hiding their size
summary: Use shared units and smoothing, disclose whether each ridge has unit area, and make overlaps readable.
body:
Use shared units and smoothing, disclose whether each ridge has unit area, and make overlaps readable.

First decide what height means

A ridgeline plot stacks several distribution curves along one shared horizontal measure. Each ridge can be a normalized density or a count-scaled curve. Those choices answer different questions. Unit-area curves compare shape but erase group size; count-scaled curves retain volume but can bury small groups. Put the choice beside the chart and list group counts. A ridge with 47 observations should not appear as equally well supported as one with 4,700 just because both curves reach the same height. Box and violin displays offer a less overlapping alternative when the group count grows.

One bandwidth across comparable groups

A density ridge depends on the smoothing bandwidth. A narrow bandwidth can turn individual observations into false-looking peaks; a wide one can erase real mixtures. If the goal is comparison, use one documented bandwidth in the same units for every group, then inspect the underlying counts and a histogram or ECDF. Near a hard lower bound such as zero minutes, a symmetric kernel can place visual density below zero. Clip display only with an explicit boundary rule, or use a boundary-aware estimator. ECDFs avoid bandwidth choice entirely and are useful for checking tail claims.

Overlap is a design parameter

The vertical offset between ridges changes what is concealed. With heavy overlap, the front ridge can cover a smaller peak in the ridge behind it. Keep a thin outline, enough transparency and a stable layer order. Do not use color alone for identity; label each ridge on its own baseline. For a screen reader or a small phone, publish a companion table of group size, median and selected percentiles. Accessible chart alternatives help preserve the comparison when curves cannot be seen or hovered.

Keep populations and windows aligned

A weekly ridge may show an apparent shift because the eligible population changed, not because individual values moved. Define the event, unit, missing-value rule and period before comparing curves. If a week has too few valid observations, mark it as insufficient rather than creating a smooth curve from a handful of points. Keep the horizontal domain fixed across a report; otherwise a later ridge can look compressed only because its axis changed. Aggregation grain and period completeness should accompany the exported chart data.

Worked contract

from math import exp, isfinite, pi, sqrt

def gaussian_ridge(samples: list[float], grid: list[float],
                   bandwidth: float) -> list[float]:
    if not samples or not grid or not isfinite(bandwidth) or bandwidth <= 0:
        raise ValueError("samples, grid and positive bandwidth required")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in samples + grid):
        raise ValueError("values must be finite")
    scale = len(samples) * bandwidth * sqrt(2 * pi)
    return [sum(exp(-0.5 * ((position - value) / bandwidth) ** 2)
                for value in samples) / scale for position in grid]

weekly_minutes = {"week 47": [27, 31, 35, 41],
                  "week 48": [31, 37, 43, 49]}
grid_minutes = [30, 40, 50]
ridge_rows = {week: gaussian_ridge(values, grid_minutes, 8)
              for week, values in weekly_minutes.items()}
assert len(ridge_rows["week 47"]) == 3
assert all(height > 0 for heights in ridge_rows.values() for height in heights)
assert ridge_rows["week 47"][0] > ridge_rows["week 48"][0]

Performance and operating cost

For G groups, M grid positions and N total observations, direct Gaussian evaluation takes O(MN) time and O(GM) output space. The sample lists also occupy O(N) memory. A histogram convolution or a vetted density library is preferable for a very large grid. The code estimates unbounded Gaussian densities; it does not correct a physical zero boundary or choose a statistically justified bandwidth. Save the bandwidth, group counts, grid and raw eligibility rule with every export.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-height, unit-area ridges as equal numbers of events.
  • Using a different automatic bandwidth for each group while comparing peaks.
  • Allowing overlap to hide a smaller group without outlines or a table.
  • Treating a four-record smooth curve as stable evidence of several modes.

Validation drill

Compare 59 weekly response-time groups. Mark weeks with fewer than 47 valid records, hold the unit and horizontal range fixed, and verify one apparent tail shift with an ECDF.

title: Regression overlays: separate fitted trend from individual spread
summary: Fit on a declared population, show the data behind the line, and keep confidence and prediction bands distinct.
body:
Fit on a declared population, show the data behind the line, and keep confidence and prediction bands distinct.

Define the fit population

A line on a scatterplot is a model output, not a property of the pixels. State which rows entered the fit, the x and y units, the time window and exclusions. If the visible chart filters to one region while the line is still fitted across all regions, label that difference or refit intentionally. A pooled line can hide opposing group trends. Plot groups separately before deciding whether a shared slope is defensible. Overplotting and sampling can make a line look better supported than the visible points imply.

Do not mix two kinds of band

A confidence band for the conditional mean describes uncertainty in the estimated average curve under the model. A prediction band for a new observation includes individual variation and is normally wider. Label the band type, level and fitting method; never call an arbitrary shaded region a confidence interval. Interval endpoints should be retained in the exported data. A narrow mean band does not promise that the next delivery will land near the line.

Check influential points and model shape

One distant x value may pull a straight line through a cloud that otherwise has little trend. Inspect residuals and report the fit's valid x range. If the relationship bends, a straight line can be a poor summary even when it is easy to draw. Do not extend the overlay far beyond observed x values unless extrapolation is the explicit task and its uncertainty is shown. Q–Q diagnostics can reveal distribution departures in residuals but do not repair confounding or nonlinearity.

Keep explanation separate from causation

A rising line means the plotted variables co-vary in the selected records. It does not establish that changing x will change y. Annotate outages, policy changes or cohorts where they matter, but do not turn temporal coincidence into a mechanism. Event annotations have the same limit. Publish the coefficients and row count alongside the plot, and offer a table of fitted values if the chart is interactive. A model revision should change its version in the export so the old and new lines can be reproduced.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def fit_straight_line(points: list[tuple[float, float]]) -> tuple[float, float]:
    if len(points) < 3 or any(not (isfinite(x) and isfinite(y))
                              for x, y in points):
        raise ValueError("at least three finite pairs required")
    mean_x = sum(x for x, _ in points) / len(points)
    mean_y = sum(y for _, y in points) / len(points)
    xx = sum((x - mean_x) ** 2 for x, _ in points)
    if xx == 0:
        raise ValueError("x values need variation")
    slope = sum((x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) for x, y in points) / xx
    return mean_y - slope * mean_x, slope

dispatch_records = [(2, 47), (3, 59), (4, 71), (5, 83)]
intercept, slope = fit_straight_line(dispatch_records)
assert (intercept, slope) == (23.0, 12.0)
assert intercept + slope * 6 == 95.0

Performance and operating cost

Computing a simple least-squares line takes O(N) time and O(1) extra space for N pairs. The code deliberately does not calculate uncertainty bands: those require a named model, assumptions, residual variance and an interval method. It is only a descriptive fit; the four exact points are a code check, not evidence of predictive accuracy. Keep the raw rows or an auditable snapshot when shipping a chart with a fitted overlay.

Common Mistakes

  • Fitting on all rows while displaying only a filtered subset without saying so.
  • Calling a mean-confidence band a prediction interval for the next record.
  • Extrapolating a straight line beyond observed x values as though support were unchanged.
  • Interpreting an association line as proof of a causal effect.

Validation drill

Fit dispatch delay against queue depth for 188 records. Compare pooled and depot-specific slopes, identify the most influential record, and label any uncertainty band with its exact meaning.

title: Map boundaries: handle antimeridian crossings before drawing routes
summary: Normalize longitude, split crossings and treat projection distance as a display property.
body:
Normalize longitude, split crossings and treat projection distance as a display property.

Longitude has a seam

A route from 177 degrees east to 178 degrees west crosses a narrow part of the Pacific. A renderer that simply connects numeric longitudes may draw a line across nearly the entire map. Choose a longitude convention, validate it at ingestion, and split a crossing before sending geometry to the visual layer. Keep the original coordinates as well as display segments. Symbol maps also need a clear coordinate meaning; a route line needs the additional seam rule.

A bounding box can wrap

For an antimeridian-spanning area, a western longitude numerically greater than the eastern longitude can describe a small region. Do not automatically swap the two values or calculate width by direct subtraction. Compute wrapped angular span and tell a mapping library whether its viewport crosses the seam. A naive min-to-max bounding box may zoom to almost the whole world. Region boundaries need the same care when a polygon is split into multiple pieces for display.

Projection changes visual geometry

A flat map projects a curved surface. Pixel distance, area and direction can vary with projection and latitude. Use a projection appropriate to the question, and avoid estimating physical travel distance with screen coordinates. A straight segment drawn in longitude and latitude is not automatically the shortest path on Earth. When a route represents measured travel, retain the actual track; when it represents an abstract connection, label it as such. Scale integrity applies to maps as well as charts.

Preserve identity across pieces

After a crossing is cut into two display segments, both pieces must retain one route ID so a tooltip, filter and export refer to the same underlying trip. A segment count is not a trip count. Include source coordinate order, time zone for event timestamps, geometry version and wrapping method in the export. Test endpoints exactly at positive and negative 180 degrees. The export manifest should record enough to reproduce the same viewport and splitting rule after a map library upgrade.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def split_dateline_segment(west: tuple[float, float],
                           east: tuple[float, float]
                          ) -> list[list[tuple[float, float]]]:
    lon_a, lat_a = west
    lon_b, lat_b = east
    if not all(isfinite(value) for value in (*west, *east)):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    if not (-180 <= lon_a <= 180 and -180 <= lon_b <= 180
            and -90 <= lat_a <= 90 and -90 <= lat_b <= 90):
        raise ValueError("longitude or latitude outside range")
    difference = lon_b - lon_a
    if abs(difference) <= 180:
        return [[west, east]]
    adjusted_b = lon_b - 360 if difference > 180 else lon_b + 360
    seam = -180 if adjusted_b < lon_a else 180
    fraction = (seam - lon_a) / (adjusted_b - lon_a)
    seam_lat = lat_a + fraction * (lat_b - lat_a)
    opposite = 180 if seam == -180 else -180
    return [[west, (seam, seam_lat)], [(opposite, seam_lat), east]]

shipping_route = split_dateline_segment((177, -17), (-178, -18))
assert shipping_route == [
    [(177, -17), (180, -17.6)],
    [(-180, -17.6), (-178, -18)],
]

Performance and operating cost

Splitting one two-point segment is O(1) time and space; a route with N points needs O(N) processing and output. The interpolation is linear in longitude and latitude for display geometry, not a geodesic calculation. For long-distance navigation or polar tracks, densify with a suitable geographic method before projecting. A production pipeline must define how exact-seam endpoints, multi-segment tracks and duplicate 180-degree coordinates are serialized.

Common Mistakes

  • Drawing a nearly global line between two points that are close across the seam.
  • Swapping wrapped bounding-box longitudes and accidentally selecting most of the world.
  • Measuring real distance from flat-map pixels.
  • Counting two rendered pieces as two journeys.

Validation drill

Draw 47 shipping tracks with three seam crossings. Keep one ID per journey, verify wrapped viewport width, and compare the exported track length with the number of display segments.

title: Event-aligned charts: choose a baseline before comparing trajectories
summary: Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.
body:
Align observations to a real event, retain calendar context and make missing periods explicit.

Event time is not calendar time

An event-aligned chart puts each subject's event at relative time zero. This lets a reader compare trajectories before and after events that occurred on different calendar dates. Store the actual event timestamp as well as the relative offset; otherwise seasonality, outages and policy changes disappear. Specify whether an offset means elapsed hours, calendar days or complete reporting periods. Time-series period rules are essential when the event occurs late in a day or across a daylight-saving change.

Fix the baseline rule

A common display subtracts each subject's pre-event value or divides by it. These produce different shapes and units. Select the baseline window before inspecting outcomes, report how many valid observations contributed to it, and reject a percentage change when the baseline is zero. If one subject has only one pre-event measurement and another has 47, their aligned curves carry different reliability. Denominator and grain rules should stay visible with the chart. Plot absolute values alongside normalized values when the magnitude of the original series matters.

Missing is not flat

Do not fill missing pre-event days with the baseline or connect a line across an unobserved outage without a marker. A cohort average at relative day five may use fewer subjects than at day one because follow-up ends; show the contributing count by offset. Attrition can make a trend look like improvement. Small-sample uncertainty belongs near sparse tails, and forecast intervals must not be substituted for missing actual observations.

The line does not prove an effect

A change at time zero can reflect selection into the event, a concurrent intervention, regression to the mean or ordinary seasonality. An annotation identifies timing, not causality. Compare a relevant untreated group or a pre-specified benchmark if the decision requires an effect estimate, and state the assumptions of that comparison. Annotation and causal-claim boundaries apply here. Export subject ID, event date, relative offset, original value, baseline window, normalized value and eligibility state so every plotted line can be reconstructed.

Worked contract

from datetime import date
from math import isfinite

def event_aligned_change(event_day: date, observations: dict[date, float],
                         baseline_days: tuple[date, ...]
                        ) -> list[tuple[int, float, float]]:
    if not baseline_days or len(set(baseline_days)) != len(baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline days must be distinct")
    if any(day >= event_day or day not in observations for day in baseline_days):
        raise ValueError("baseline must be observed before the event")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for value in observations.values()):
        raise ValueError("observations must be finite")
    baseline = sum(observations[day] for day in baseline_days) / len(baseline_days)
    return sorted(((day - event_day).days, value, value - baseline)
                  for day, value in observations.items())

incident_counts = {
    date(2026, 10, 5): 47, date(2026, 10, 6): 59,
    date(2026, 10, 8): 38, date(2026, 10, 9): 35,
}
aligned = event_aligned_change(
    date(2026, 10, 7), incident_counts,
    (date(2026, 10, 5), date(2026, 10, 6)),
)
assert aligned == [(-2, 47, -6), (-1, 59, 6), (1, 38, -15), (2, 35, -18)]
assert all(offset != 0 for offset, _, _ in aligned)

Performance and operating cost

For N observations and B baseline days, validation and averaging take O(N+B) time; sorting relative periods takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. The function leaves missing event day zero absent instead of inventing a value. Calendar dates are appropriate only when day-level reporting is the contract; intraday events need zoned timestamps and a declared binning method. Subtracting a baseline describes change, not a causal estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Discarding calendar dates after alignment and losing concurrent-event context.
  • Choosing a favorable baseline window after seeing the result.
  • Drawing a continuous line over days with no observations.
  • Calling a post-event change proof that the event caused it.

Validation drill

Align 81 facilities around a maintenance intervention. Show each facility's baseline window and post-event coverage, then recompute the cohort curve using only facilities observed through day 14.

title: Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer
summary: Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.
body:
Treat focus, selection and the data table as part of the chart's public interface.

Hover is not access

A tooltip visible only on pointer hover excludes keyboard and many touch users. Give each interactive mark a reachable focus target, a meaningful accessible name and the same detail on focus as on hover. Arrow keys can move within a series, while Home and End can jump to its bounds; publish the key rules next to the chart. Keep a visible focus indicator. Color and text alternatives cover the static layer, but a chart with filters and selections also needs an interaction contract.

Separate focus from selection

Focus says where keyboard input will act. Selection says which records are included in the current analysis. Do not silently change the filter merely because focus moved to another point. If Enter selects a point, announce the new selection and update the related table or summary. A selected range should survive a resize and a redraw by stable record IDs rather than pixel coordinates. Linked filters and cohort state should make the selected population and denominator visible across all charts.

Avoid a thousand tab stops

Putting every mark in the page's normal Tab sequence can make a dense chart unusable. A single chart entry point followed by arrow-key movement may be better, provided the active point's name and value are exposed, the user can exit with Tab, and the navigation order is predictable. Do not trap focus inside the plot. For large series, offer direct search, a bounded table, or a downloadable data file so a user does not have to press an arrow 4,700 times. Large-series reduction must preserve access to underlying records when visual points are aggregated.

The table is a first-class view

An accessible data table should use the same filters, units, missing-value markers and ordering as the chart. If the chart displays a sampled or binned series, identify that fact and provide a route to full records when appropriate. Do not generate a table from SVG positions; derive both views from one data model. Export provenance should include the selection, filter and sort state so a shared screenshot and a CSV tell the same story. Test with only a keyboard, at narrow width, and with zoom before publication.

Worked contract

function nextChartPoint(currentIndex, pointCount, key) {
  if (!Number.isInteger(pointCount) || pointCount < 1 ||
      !Number.isInteger(currentIndex) || currentIndex < 0 ||
      currentIndex >= pointCount) {
    throw new RangeError("chart point state is invalid");
  }
  if (key === "ArrowRight" || key === "ArrowDown") {
    return Math.min(currentIndex + 1, pointCount - 1);
  }
  if (key === "ArrowLeft" || key === "ArrowUp") {
    return Math.max(currentIndex - 1, 0);
  }
  if (key === "Home") return 0;
  if (key === "End") return pointCount - 1;
  return currentIndex;
}

const visibleRecordIds = ["depot-47", "depot-59", "depot-83"];
let focusedIndex = 0;
focusedIndex = nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "End");
if (visibleRecordIds[focusedIndex] !== "depot-83") {
  throw new Error("keyboard focus must follow chart order");
}
if (nextChartPoint(focusedIndex, visibleRecordIds.length, "ArrowRight") !== 2) {
  throw new Error("focus must stop at the last record");
}

Performance and operating cost

A key transition takes O(1) time and space; the displayed order and accessible table require O(N) record storage for N visible points. The pure function handles movement only. The browser component must connect it to focus, accessible names, announcement text and selection state, and must retain Tab exit. If a virtualized chart reorders records, map stable IDs to the new order before restoring focus. Treat the table as the source-aligned view, not as a decorative duplicate.

Common Mistakes

  • Making hover-only tooltip content unavailable on focus and touch.
  • Changing the selected cohort whenever a user merely moves focus.
  • Adding every dense-series mark to the Tab order with no shortcut or data table.
  • Restoring focus by pixel position after filter changes instead of stable record identity.

Validation drill

Audit a 188-point chart using only keyboard navigation. Verify focus visibility, Enter selection, Tab exit, a synchronized table and stable record identity after a filter change.

title: Forest plots: align estimates, intervals and the no-effect value
summary: Compare like-for-like effects on one scale and explain what each interval and marker means.
body:
Compare like-for-like effects on one scale and explain what each interval and marker means.

Choose one effect measure

A forest plot places estimates on a shared horizontal scale with an interval beside each estimate. Mean differences, risk ratios and odds ratios cannot be mixed as though their numbers shared a unit. State the effect measure, population, comparison direction and interval method before plotting. The no-effect value is zero for an additive difference and one for a multiplicative ratio. A log-scaled ratio axis often makes equal proportional changes on either side of one visually comparable; it cannot accept zero or negative endpoints. Signed differences have a different zero reference and should not inherit ratio-axis labels.

Keep the interval type attached

A horizontal line may be a confidence interval, a credible interval, a sensitivity range or something else. Say which. Do not infer that a row with an interval touching the no-effect line is equivalent to a row with a wide interval far beyond it. Both estimate magnitude and precision matter. Asymmetric error bars explain why endpoints must be kept as numbers, not reconstructed from a visual radius. When an interval exceeds the plot boundary, use a clipped-end marker and print its true endpoint. Never replace the endpoint with the axis maximum in the underlying data.

Marker area needs a contract

A larger square can indicate greater analytic weight, sample size or merely visual emphasis. Those are not interchangeable. If marker area represents a weight, name the weighting method and provide the numeric weights. A pooled estimate at the bottom is a separate calculation, not the average of x positions on the screen; omit it when the included rows are not meaningfully combinable. Area-scaled symbols follow the same rule: doubling a marker radius quadruples its area. A plain point estimate with equal marker size is safer when weights are not part of the analysis.

Sort without changing meaning

Sorting rows by effect size can make a striking ladder but may hide prespecified groups or study chronology. Declare the row order, retain stable IDs, and distinguish subgroups without implying that adjacency is evidence of similarity. A plot of model variants should note which intervals are correlated because they share data; counting each variant as an independent result overstates evidence. Uncertainty and sample-size displays help explain sparse rows. Supply an accessible table with row ID, estimate, lower and upper bounds, unit, interval type and weight, then compare the chart against that table before publishing.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, log

def ratio_forest_positions(
    rows: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]
) -> list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]:
    names = [name for name, _, _, _ in rows]
    if len(names) != len(set(names)) or any(not name for name in names):
        raise ValueError("row names must be unique and nonempty")
    output = []
    for name, estimate, lower, upper in rows:
        if not all(isfinite(value) and value > 0
                   for value in (estimate, lower, upper)):
            raise ValueError("ratio estimates and endpoints must be positive")
        if not lower <= estimate <= upper:
            raise ValueError("estimate must lie within its interval")
        output.append((name, log(estimate), log(lower), log(upper)))
    return output

depot_comparisons = ratio_forest_positions([
    ("north depot", 1.25, 1.06, 1.47),
    ("south depot", 0.80, 0.65, 1.03),
])
assert depot_comparisons[0][1] > 0
assert depot_comparisons[1][1] < 0
assert log(1) == 0

Performance and operating cost

Validating and transforming N rows takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code prepares positive ratio estimates for a log axis; it does not calculate intervals, pool rows or assign weights. Keep original ratio values in the export because logarithmic positions are drawing coordinates. If a row has a zero, negative or undefined ratio, investigate the estimator rather than forcing it onto the log plot.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing additive differences and ratios on one unlabeled axis.
  • Drawing the no-effect line at zero for a raw ratio plot.
  • Using square size as weight without stating the weighting rule.
  • Silently truncating interval endpoints or treating related model variants as independent studies.

Validation drill

Compare 47 depot-level rate ratios with intervals. Identify rows that need clipped-end markers, then explain why a pooled diamond should not be drawn until the estimands and weights are reviewed.
