title: Scatterplot matrices: disclose which rows support each pair
summary: Treat pairwise missingness, scales and the number of comparisons as part of the matrix.
body:
Treat pairwise missingness, scales and the number of comparisons as part of the matrix.

Each cell has its own population

A scatterplot matrix shows pairwise relationships among several variables. If missing values differ by column, the cell for queue depth versus delay may use different records from the cell for delay versus cost. A common complete-case filter makes populations consistent but may discard many rows. Pairwise deletion retains more data but changes the population from cell to cell. State which policy was used and print the valid count in every cell. Correlation heatmaps face the same coverage problem but hide the underlying point clouds.

Use one variable scale across its row and column

A variable appearing on several axes should keep a common unit and domain where possible. Otherwise the apparent slope and spread change as a reader moves across the grid. Label only the outer axes if the layout is tight, but keep units available in a companion table. Transformations such as logarithms must be consistent for every appearance of the variable, and invalid nonpositive values need an explicit exclusion count. Log-scale boundaries should be chosen for the data, not merely to make a diagonal cluster look tidy.

A matrix multiplies visual tests

With seven variables there are 21 distinct off-diagonal pairs. One remarkable-looking cell may occur by chance, especially after inspecting many matrices, filters and periods. Use the display to generate questions rather than to announce discovered laws. Annotate pre-specified comparisons, and follow up with a model or analysis suited to the decision. Regression overlays need their own fit population and assumptions; a line in every cell can overwhelm the matrix and invite unsupported causal readings.

Control density and reading order

Plotting the same large cohort in 42 mirrored cells can be expensive and visually opaque. Use the lower triangle for points and reserve the diagonal for univariate distributions or compact count summaries. Sample only with a declared rule, preserving rare groups if that is part of the question. Overplotting techniques can reveal concentration without creating false individual positions. Sort variables in a stable, meaningful sequence and offer a per-cell data table or drill-down so the matrix remains usable at phone width and high zoom.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def pairwise_points(records: list[dict[str, float | None]],
                    horizontal: str, vertical: str
                   ) -> list[tuple[float, float]]:
    if not horizontal or not vertical or horizontal == vertical:
        raise ValueError("two distinct variable names required")
    points = []
    for record in records:
        x_value, y_value = record.get(horizontal), record.get(vertical)
        if x_value is None or y_value is None:
            continue
        if not isfinite(x_value) or not isfinite(y_value):
            raise ValueError("non-finite values require an explicit policy")
        points.append((x_value, y_value))
    return points

depot_rows = [
    {"queue": 47.0, "delay": 31.0, "cost": 81.0},
    {"queue": 59.0, "delay": None, "cost": 97.0},
    {"queue": 83.0, "delay": 43.0, "cost": None},
]
assert pairwise_points(depot_rows, "queue", "delay") == [(47, 31), (83, 43)]
assert pairwise_points(depot_rows, "queue", "cost") == [(47, 81), (59, 97)]

Performance and operating cost

For P variables and N records, preparing every unique pair costs O(P squared times N) time. Retaining all displayed points for the lower triangle can take O(P squared times N) space; stream or aggregate when that footprint is too large. The example uses pairwise deletion and makes no correlation or significance claim. Report the per-cell count and dropped-row policy so two adjacent clouds are not mistaken for identical cohorts.

Common Mistakes

  • Reporting one global sample size when cells use different valid rows.
  • Auto-scaling the same variable differently across matrix cells.
  • Treating the most striking of many inspected pairs as confirmed evidence.
  • Rendering mirrored dense cells without a detail view or sampling record.

Validation drill

Build a lower-triangle matrix for seven operational measures. Put valid-row counts in all 21 cells, fix each variable's scale across appearances and identify three relationships chosen before viewing the grid.

title: Streamgraphs: preserve totals behind a moving baseline
summary: Use a centered stack for shape exploration, but give readers a separate way to inspect the total.
body:
Use a centered stack for shape exploration, but give readers a separate way to inspect the total.

The baseline is a layout choice

A streamgraph stacks nonnegative category values over time around a moving or centered baseline. Its flowing shape can help reveal broad category shifts, but the vertical position of a layer is partly an artifact of the baseline calculation. Layer thickness represents value; the upper edge alone does not. Do not label the vertical axis like an ordinary zero-based stacked area chart unless it actually has a fixed zero. Stacked composition explains why categories and their denominator must be stable enough to compare.

Totals still need a view

Centering a total of 47 and a total of 188 both around the same midpoint can make the chart attractive while hiding the operational difference. Include a separate total line, a compact table or a conventional zero-based stacked view when volume matters. A streamgraph is a poor sole view for audit questions such as whether all categories reconcile to the source total. Waterfall reconciliation handles additive changes with a more explicit baseline. For each time bin, validate that layer values sum to the reported total before calculating any layout offset.

Order controls readability

A layer buried in the middle may be easier to follow than one whose boundaries both move erratically, but changing the order between frames makes categories impossible to track. Select a stable order and color identity for the whole time range. If categories enter or leave, distinguish true zero from missing data; an absent category record should not silently become a zero-thickness layer. Missing periods and provisional bins require an explicit display state, even in a decorative-looking flow chart.

Keep the raw table accessible

Layer thickness is hard to read precisely, particularly on a narrow viewport. Provide a table with period, category, value, total and any excluded share. Label categories directly where possible and offer keyboard-accessible inspection for the rest. Interactive chart access should preserve each period and category ID when focus moves. Export the stacking order and baseline algorithm so an updated chart library cannot silently change the shape while the underlying observations stay fixed.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def centered_stack(categories: list[str],
                   periods: list[dict[str, float]]
                  ) -> list[dict[str, tuple[float, float]]]:
    if not categories or len(categories) != len(set(categories)):
        raise ValueError("ordered categories must be unique")
    output = []
    for period in periods:
        if set(period) != set(categories):
            raise ValueError("each period needs every category, including real zeros")
        if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in period.values()):
            raise ValueError("values must be finite and nonnegative")
        baseline = -sum(period.values()) / 2
        layers = {}
        for category in categories:
            upper = baseline + period[category]
            layers[category] = (baseline, upper)
            baseline = upper
        output.append(layers)
    return output

service_mix = centered_stack(
    ["routine", "urgent"],
    [{"routine": 47, "urgent": 59}, {"routine": 81, "urgent": 97}],
)
assert service_mix[0] == {
    "routine": (-53.0, -6.0), "urgent": (-6.0, 53.0)
}
assert service_mix[1]["urgent"][1] == 89.0

Performance and operating cost

For T periods and C categories, validation and centered stacking take O(TC) time and O(TC) output space. This code uses a simple centered baseline, not an optimized wiggle offset; those two layouts differ. It requires a complete category set per period and rejects negative measures. Keep the original values and totals for accessibility and reconciliation. For large C, crowded labels and thin layers may make small multiples or a ranked table clearer.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading the moving layer boundary as a zero-based value.
  • Using a centered streamgraph alone when the decision depends on total volume.
  • Changing category order across periods and making colors switch identity.
  • Replacing missing category records with zero without a recorded rule.

Validation drill

Show 47 reporting periods and eight service classes. Reconcile each total, hold category order fixed and place a separate total-volume line beside the centered streamgraph.

title: Horizon charts: trade vertical space for a harder value lookup
summary: Explain the baseline, band width and color order so compact time series remain decodable.
body:
Explain the baseline, band width and color order so compact time series remain decodable.

Folded bands need a key

A horizon chart divides a value's distance from a baseline into bands and overlays those bands in a short row. It can fit many series in little vertical space, but a reader must decode band color as well as vertical shape. State the baseline and numeric size of one band. If the chart shows deviations from 47 incidents per day, a value of 87 occupies two 20-unit bands above that reference, not 87 units of vertical height. Baseline integrity matters more when the display has been folded.

Positive and negative need separate meaning

For signed deviations, use distinguishable sequences for above and below the baseline, not just a lighter and darker tint of one hue. Include text labels for the sign and a small decoding key with concrete values. A monochrome or color-vision test should still allow readers to distinguish the two directions through texture, labels or a paired table. Accessible color alternatives are a requirement of the underlying comparison, not a finishing layer. Missing observations need a gap; they are not zero deviation.

Fix a common band domain

If each row chooses its own band width, the darkest color represents a different numeric amount in each series. That defeats cross-row comparison. Choose a shared band width and number of bands for all rows being compared, and decide how out-of-range values are signaled. Clipping an extreme silently is worse than showing an overflow marker and its numeric value. Extrema-preserving reduction helps keep short-lived spikes when a long series must be downsampled before folding.

Use compactness only when it helps

A horizon chart is suited to scanning many similarly scaled time series for timing and magnitude patterns. It is weak for exact readout, unfamiliar audiences and small numbers of series, where an ordinary line chart is easier. Keep a linked detail view or accessible table with timestamp, original value, baseline, signed deviation and band encoding. Small multiples are the natural comparison when there is enough vertical space. Document the folding rule in the export so future renders preserve the same visual thresholds.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def horizon_bands(value: float, baseline: float,
                  band_width: float, band_count: int
                 ) -> tuple[str, list[float], bool]:
    if not all(isfinite(number) for number in (value, baseline, band_width)):
        raise ValueError("values must be finite")
    if band_width <= 0 or not isinstance(band_count, int) or band_count < 1:
        raise ValueError("positive band width and count required")
    delta = value - baseline
    remaining = abs(delta)
    heights = []
    for _ in range(band_count):
        height = min(remaining, band_width)
        heights.append(height)
        remaining -= height
    sign = "above" if delta > 0 else "below" if delta < 0 else "at"
    return sign, heights, remaining > 0

assert horizon_bands(87, 47, 20, 3) == ("above", [20, 20, 0], False)
assert horizon_bands(18, 47, 20, 2) == ("below", [20, 9], False)
assert horizon_bands(130, 47, 20, 3)[2] is True

Performance and operating cost

Encoding N observations with B bands takes O(NB) time and O(NB) output space when every band height is retained. The overflow flag prevents silent saturation but the rendering layer must draw a visible marker and numeric value. This function returns a sign and positive band heights; the renderer chooses color and clipping. Do not compare rows using different baselines or band widths unless the chart explicitly separates those views.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading folded height as the full original value.
  • Changing band width from row to row while reusing one color key.
  • Letting values above the maximum band range saturate without an overflow label.
  • Encoding missing as a zero deviation from baseline.

Validation drill

Display 59 equipment series around a shared service threshold. Check the band key against five exact values, mark overflows and offer a full-height line chart for one selected machine.

title: Animated charts: do not let motion invent data
summary: Keep record IDs, scales and frame provenance stable; offer pause and a static path through the same observations.
body:
Keep record IDs, scales and frame provenance stable; offer pause and a static path through the same observations.

Frames are data snapshots

An animated chart displays a sequence of observations, not a continuous measurement just because movement looks continuous. Store the date, source revision, eligibility rule and unit for every frame. When data exist only at two dates, intermediate positions are visual interpolation and must not be described as observed measurements. A bar that grows from 47 to 81 may imply smooth change even if the underlying quantity jumped at one import. Time-series completeness should determine which frames can be compared and which remain provisional.

Identity must survive reordering

Use stable entity IDs across frames. A ranked bar animation may reorder entities; if color or label is assigned by array position, it can appear that one entity changes into another. Match records by ID, separate newly entering and exiting entities, and never fill a missing measurement with zero unless zero is a real observation. Rank movement charts are often better as a static alternative when the main question is who changed position. Keep the selection anchored to ID if a user pauses halfway through a transition.

Lock the scale or disclose change

An axis that rescales independently at every frame can make a flat series appear to surge or a large decline look minor. Fix a domain across the full sequence when the comparison is meant to be quantitative. If an extreme new value requires a domain change, pause, label the change and provide the numeric context. Axis integrity applies to every frame, and extrema checks must run before the domain is chosen. Keep category colors, units and legend order stable too.

Motion is optional

Provide play, pause, next-frame and previous-frame controls that work with a keyboard. Do not trap focus on the chart. Respect reduced-motion preference and offer a static small-multiple view or data table that carries the same observations. A paused live feed should indicate whether resuming continues from the pause point or jumps to the latest state. Keyboard and table contracts keep the analysis available without timed interaction. Export frame ID, timestamp, scale domain and source record IDs so a particular visual state can be cited and reproduced.

Worked contract

function pairedFrameValues(previousFrame, nextFrame) {
  const previous = new Map(previousFrame.map(record => [record.id, record.value]));
  const next = new Map(nextFrame.map(record => [record.id, record.value]));
  if (previous.size !== previousFrame.length || next.size !== nextFrame.length) {
    throw new Error("each frame needs unique record IDs");
  }
  const paired = [];
  for (const [id, earlierValue] of previous) {
    if (next.has(id)) {
      const laterValue = next.get(id);
      if (!Number.isFinite(earlierValue) || !Number.isFinite(laterValue)) {
        throw new Error("frame values must be finite");
      }
      paired.push({id, earlierValue, laterValue});
    }
  }
  return paired;
}

const pairedDepots = pairedFrameValues(
  [{id: "north-47", value: 47}, {id: "south-59", value: 59}],
  [{id: "south-59", value: 81}, {id: "north-47", value: 52}],
);
if (pairedDepots[0].id !== "north-47" || pairedDepots[0].laterValue !== 52) {
  throw new Error("records must match by identity, not array position");
}

Performance and operating cost

Building two ID maps and pairing N previous records with M next records takes O(N+M) time and space. This code deliberately omits entering and exiting entities from interpolation; the view should represent them with explicit entry or exit states, not fabricate an earlier zero. A full animation also needs frame controls, reduced-motion handling, stable scales and a static equivalent. The pairing function is the data boundary that prevents position-based identity errors.

Common Mistakes

  • Presenting interpolated in-between positions as measured observations.
  • Matching reordered rows by array index so entities switch labels or colors.
  • Auto-scaling every frame while inviting quantitative comparison.
  • Autoplaying without a working pause and static way to inspect the data.

Validation drill

Animate 47 weekly depot snapshots. Lock the quantity scale, audit entry and exit states, pause on a chosen week and confirm the static table reports the same IDs and values.

title: Survival curves: show who remains at risk after each event
summary: Build a step curve from observed events, keep censoring visible and stop trusting a thin tail.
body:
Build a step curve from observed events, keep censoring visible and stop trusting a thin tail.

Define the event and the clock

A survival curve estimates the share of a starting cohort that has not yet experienced a specified event by elapsed time. A device-failure chart, for instance, needs a clear start such as commissioning and an event such as first unrecoverable shutdown. Mixing calendar dates with elapsed operating days changes the risk set. Units matter too: a device observed for 47 calendar days but active for 31 operating days is not interchangeable with one observed continuously. Event-aligned time series can show measurements around a milestone, while a survival curve asks when the first event occurs. Decide how replacement devices, repeat failures and delayed entry will be treated before fitting the curve; the simple right-censored calculation below assumes every device enters at elapsed time zero.

A censor mark is not a failure

Right censoring means observation ended without the event being seen. A study cutoff, withdrawal or lost sensor feed can create one, but those reasons need separate counts because their relationship to failure risk may differ. The Kaplan–Meier step drops only when events occur. A censor at time 59 leaves the height unchanged while reducing the group available for later event times. When events and censors share a recorded time, declare whether events are processed before same-time censors; the code uses that convention. Put the censor marks on the curve and provide an at-risk table at chosen time ticks. Missing periods are a different data problem: do not silently turn an unobserved failure time into a clean censor without checking what was actually known.

Read the tail against its denominator

A flat tail can look reassuring even when only two devices remain under observation. Show the number at risk at regular, meaningful intervals and consider ending the displayed curve where support becomes too sparse for the decision. Do not stretch the last estimated step into a guarantee beyond follow-up. If two cohorts enter in different years or face different servicing policies, their curves are descriptive until the cohort definitions and confounding are reviewed. Small-sample uncertainty belongs beside the estimate, and a confidence band needs a stated method. An ordinary percent-without-failure line is not equivalent when follow-up lengths differ because it treats early withdrawals as though they had complete observation.

Keep the underlying event ledger

The plot is a compression of the event ledger, not a substitute for it. Preserve device ID, entry time, exit time, event flag, censor reason, cohort, and data-cutoff date. Reconcile the at-risk count before each event: prior risk minus prior events and censors must equal the next risk count. If failures can be precluded by a different event, a conventional one-event survival curve may answer the wrong question; define a competing-event analysis instead. Empirical CDFs are useful when event times are fully observed, but they do not automatically handle censoring. Export a table of each step time, event count, censor count, risk count and estimated survival so a reader can audit every drop without estimating coordinates from pixels.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import isfinite

def device_survival_steps(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]]):
    identifiers = [device_id for device_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("device IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(duration) or duration < 0 or type(failed) is not bool
           for _, duration, failed in records):
        raise ValueError("duration and event flags must be valid")
    events = Counter(duration for _, duration, failed in records if failed)
    censors = Counter(duration for _, duration, failed in records if not failed)
    risk_count, survival, steps = len(records), 1.0, []
    for duration in sorted(events.keys() | censors.keys()):
        failed_count = events[duration]
        censored_count = censors[duration]
        survival *= 1 - failed_count / risk_count
        steps.append((duration, risk_count, failed_count,
                      censored_count, survival))
        risk_count -= failed_count + censored_count
    return steps

depot_devices = [
    ("station-47", 3, True), ("station-59", 4, False),
    ("station-83", 4, True), ("station-97", 7, False),
]
depot_steps = device_survival_steps(depot_devices)
assert depot_steps[0] == (3, 4, 1, 0, 0.75)
assert depot_steps[1] == (4, 3, 1, 1, 0.5)
assert depot_steps[-1][-1] == 0.5

Performance and operating cost

Counting and sorting N event or censor records takes O(N log N) time and O(N) space. The function returns every observed exit time so censors can be marked even when the step height stays level. It assumes entry at time zero, one terminal event, and a declared event-before-censor tie rule; it does not calculate confidence limits or correct informative censoring. Validate the event ledger and at-risk table before drawing smooth-looking output.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating a censored record as an observed failure or as complete follow-up.
  • Omitting at-risk counts while interpreting the last flat segment.
  • Combining elapsed operating time with calendar time on one axis.
  • Comparing cohorts without checking different entry policies, follow-up windows or censor reasons.

Validation drill

Audit 47 devices across two installation cohorts. Print the risk set at months 0, 6, 12 and 18, mark withdrawals, then explain where the tail no longer supports a useful comparison.

title: Mosaic plots: make cell area match the underlying count
summary: Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.
body:
Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.

Choose a denominator before drawing tiles

A two-way mosaic plot partitions one rectangle by a contingency table. Each first-category column gets width proportional to its count in the full data set. Within that column, second-category tile heights represent conditional shares. Multiplying width by height yields the cell's share of the grand total. That area contract is the point of the chart. If the column widths are all equal instead, the display answers a different question: it emphasizes within-group composition and conceals unequal group sizes. Stacked bars are often easier to read when exact conditional rates are the primary comparison, while treemaps use area for hierarchical totals rather than a two-way cross-classification.

Declare the table grain

Count one unit only once in the table unless the chart explicitly represents events rather than entities. If a shipment can appear in several outcome categories, a standard contingency table is not valid until a mutually exclusive rule is chosen. A missing outcome is its own category or an explicit exclusion; quietly dropping it changes every tile's area. Aggregation grain and denominator should be fixed upstream. Record the category order even if one group has a zero count, and distinguish a true zero cell from a category never collected. Reconcile each column subtotal with source records before calculating widths, then reconcile all columns to the grand total. A plot that looks rectangular can still be numerically wrong.

Read association without mistaking size for rate

A wider group contributes more observations, while a taller tile within that group represents a larger conditional share. Readers often compare tile heights across groups and forget the width, or compare areas when the question is only about rates. Label both count and within-group percentage in a companion table. If a tiny tile cannot hold text, put the label outside or leave it to an accessible table rather than enlarging the tile. Heatmaps can encode a rate in color, but their equal-size cells do not show count automatically. Do not imply statistical significance from a striking mosaic pattern; sampling design, uncertainty and multiple subgroup inspections remain separate questions.

Keep order and coverage stable

A mosaic is more legible with a limited number of well-defined categories. Many thin columns or slivers make the visual fragile on phones and at high zoom. Sort categories by a declared business order, not by whichever tile creates the strongest pattern in each filter state. If a dashboard filter removes units, recompute column totals and display the new grand total; a stale denominator can make area and labels disagree. Linked filters should expose which cohort is selected. Export the exact cross-tabulation with count, row total, grand total, conditional percentage and excluded count so the visible geometry can be independently reconstructed.

Worked contract

def mosaic_tiles(table: dict[str, dict[str, int]],
                 outcomes: list[str]):
    if not table or not outcomes or len(outcomes) != len(set(outcomes)):
        raise ValueError("groups and ordered outcomes are required")
    if any(set(cells) != set(outcomes) for cells in table.values()):
        raise ValueError("every group needs every outcome, including zeros")
    if any(type(count) is not int or count < 0
           for cells in table.values() for count in cells.values()):
        raise ValueError("counts must be nonnegative integers")
    group_totals = {group: sum(cells.values()) for group, cells in table.items()}
    if any(total == 0 for total in group_totals.values()):
        raise ValueError("empty groups need a separate missing-data state")
    grand_total = sum(group_totals.values())
    tiles, left = [], 0.0
    for group, cells in table.items():
        right = left + group_totals[group] / grand_total
        bottom = 0.0
        for outcome in outcomes:
            top = bottom + cells[outcome] / group_totals[group]
            tiles.append((group, outcome, left, right, bottom, top,
                          cells[outcome]))
            bottom = top
        left = right
    return tiles

review_counts = {
    "early shift": {"accepted": 47, "returned": 13},
    "late shift": {"accepted": 20, "returned": 20},
}
review_tiles = mosaic_tiles(review_counts, ["accepted", "returned"])
early_accepted = review_tiles[0]
assert abs((early_accepted[3] - early_accepted[2]) *
           (early_accepted[5] - early_accepted[4]) - 0.47) < 1e-12
assert review_tiles[-1][-1] == 20

Performance and operating cost

For G groups and K outcome categories, validation and tile construction take O(GK) time and O(GK) output space. The positions are normalized to a unit square; the first tile covers 47 percent of the area because 47 of 100 reviewed shipments fall in that cell. Floating-point boundaries are drawing coordinates, not replacement counts. Keep the integer table available for labels and audit exports.

Common Mistakes

  • Making every group equally wide while claiming tile area represents total count.
  • Dropping unknown outcomes without updating the denominator and exclusion note.
  • Enlarging tiny tiles to fit labels, which breaks the area contract.
  • Reading an attractive pattern as evidence of association without examining uncertainty or sampling.

Validation drill

Cross-tabulate 83 inspected shipments by shift and disposition, including an unknown disposition. Reconcile the grand total and verify that each tile area equals its cell count divided by 83.

title: Ternary plots: preserve the total behind a three-part composition
summary: Map three nonnegative parts into a triangle only after defining what the whole contains.
body:
Map three nonnegative parts into a triangle only after defining what the whole contains.

The triangle represents a closed whole

A ternary plot places three nonnegative components of one whole at a point inside a triangle. A point near a corner has a large share of the component named at that corner. The chart requires a real closure rule: if raw materials, labor and transport make only 83 percent of a project budget, normalizing those three to 100 percent silently discards the remainder. Add a declared other category, change the question or use a different display. Stacked composition is easier when the reader needs several exact shares. A ternary plot earns its space when the trade-off among exactly three parts is itself the question and the total is comparable or available elsewhere.

Keep the raw total next to normalized shares

Closure removes scale. A project costing 47 units and another costing 470 can occupy the same triangle point when their ratios match. Preserve total cost as a table column, size encoding with a disclosed area scale, or a linked separate chart. Do not let marker color quietly reintroduce a fourth variable without a readable legend and accessible alternative. Area-scaled markers explain why marker radius is not proportional to magnitude. Zeros are legitimate triangle-edge cases, whereas negative components or a zero total cannot be mapped as shares. Before plotting, decide whether a recorded zero is a real absence, a rounded small positive amount or missing data; these cases should not share one symbol.

A trend can be a denominator effect

If one component's share rises, at least one other share must fall even when its raw amount is unchanged. That closure constraint can manufacture apparent negative relationships between parts. Compare raw components and totals before attributing a movement to a process change. Correlation heatmaps on closed shares need special care for exactly this reason. If several periods are shown, connect points only when each project ID and period order are stable. Label direction and elapsed time; a long geometric move is a large change in composition, not necessarily a large change in dollars or units. The triangle should not be used as a causal diagram.

Fix corners, orientation and precision

Choose a component order and corner labeling once for every panel and export. Reordering corners rotates the apparent story even when the numbers are unchanged. Use meaningful tick spacing and consistent normalization, preferably with a table reporting the original values and resulting shares to a stated precision. When values are rounded, their displayed shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1; keep full precision for coordinates and explain display rounding. Parallel coordinates offer another way to inspect several components without enforcing a three-part closure. For accessible interaction, keyboard focus should reveal all three components, the raw total and the record ID, not just an unlabeled point location.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def triangle_positions(records: list[tuple[str, float, float, float]]):
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("composition IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    points = []
    for record_id, materials, labor, transport in records:
        parts = (materials, labor, transport)
        if any(not isfinite(part) or part < 0 for part in parts):
            raise ValueError("components must be finite and nonnegative")
        total = sum(parts)
        if total <= 0:
            raise ValueError("a zero total has no composition")
        x_position = (labor + transport / 2) / total
        y_position = (sqrt(3) / 2) * transport / total
        points.append((record_id, x_position, y_position, total,
                       tuple(part / total for part in parts)))
    return points

budget_points = triangle_positions([
    ("depot-47", 47, 31, 22),
    ("depot-59", 94, 62, 44),
])
assert abs(budget_points[0][1] - 0.42) < 1e-12
assert budget_points[0][1:3] == budget_points[1][1:3]
assert budget_points[0][3] == 100
assert budget_points[1][3] == 200

Performance and operating cost

Validating and normalizing N compositions costs O(N) time and O(N) output space. The two budgets share coordinates because their proportions match, yet their totals differ by a factor of two. The function supplies plotting coordinates for corners materials-left, labor-right and transport-top; it does not determine whether the three categories truly exhaust the business total. That semantic check belongs at the data boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Normalizing an incomplete three-part subset without naming the omitted share.
  • Comparing triangle distance as though it represented absolute amount.
  • Treating closure-induced negative relationships as independent evidence.
  • Changing corner order between panels or hiding raw totals after normalization.

Validation drill

Plot 59 project budgets using three exhaustive cost components. Identify any zero-total or negative record, retain the raw totals and explain why two projects with identical shares can require different spending decisions.

title: CUSUM charts: accumulate small departures from a stable target
summary: Define the reference process, update rule and alert threshold before reading a rising trace.
body:
Define the reference process, update rule and alert threshold before reading a rising trace.

A cumulative trace needs a frozen baseline

A cumulative-sum chart can detect a sustained small departure that a point-by-point threshold misses. Start with a process metric measured at consistent intervals and a target estimated from an independent, stable baseline period. A cumulative sum of raw values will drift simply because the metric is positive; subtract the target and a reference allowance before accumulating evidence of an upward shift. Use a separate lower trace for downward shifts. P charts handle varying binomial denominators; their rate and limits should not be replaced by a CUSUM of unadjusted percentages. If observation precision or exposure changes across periods, standardize or model that change before applying a fixed CUSUM rule.

The allowance and threshold are design choices

In a tabular upper CUSUM, each new value adds its deviation from the target minus an allowance, and negative running totals reset to zero. A lower CUSUM mirrors the logic for downward movement. The allowance controls the size of shift the chart is tuned to notice; the decision threshold controls when an alert is raised. Neither number is a universal constant. Calibrate them against the operational false-alarm rate and detection delay the team can tolerate, using an appropriate baseline model. Uncertainty displays help explain how noisy short runs can be. The worked numbers below demonstrate mechanics only and must not be copied as an alert policy for another process.

A signal is a review trigger

Mark the exact first threshold crossing on the chart. Keep every earlier point and the zero resets visible; truncating the history can make the signal look instantaneous. An alert says the observed sequence is unusual under the chosen reference model, not that a particular maintenance event caused it. Event annotations need timestamps and a caution about causal interpretation. If a baseline is re-estimated after every signal, the chart can absorb the very drift it was intended to detect. Version the target, allowance, threshold and any planned reset date. When a legitimate process change establishes a new operating state, start a documented new chart rather than silently splicing scales.

Audit the measurement pipeline

A sustained run of delayed, duplicated or missing readings can resemble a process shift. Validate sampling cadence, units, sensor identity and data revision status before interpreting the trace. Time-series gaps must remain gaps or be handled by an explicit rule; inserting zero will push a lower trace down for the wrong reason. Serial correlation also changes the false-alarm behavior of a rule calibrated for independent observations. Keep an export with period ID, raw reading, target version, upper and lower cumulative values, and alert state. Chart manifests make the calculation reproducible after a dashboard or threshold update.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def process_shift_trace(readings: list[float], target: float,
                        allowance: float, threshold: float):
    if (not all(isfinite(value) for value in [*readings, target,
                                               allowance, threshold])
            or allowance < 0 or threshold <= 0):
        raise ValueError("finite readings, nonnegative allowance and positive threshold required")
    upper = lower = 0.0
    trace = []
    for period_index, reading in enumerate(readings, start=1):
        upper = max(0.0, upper + reading - target - allowance)
        lower = max(0.0, lower + target - reading - allowance)
        trace.append((period_index, upper, lower,
                      upper >= threshold, lower >= threshold))
    return trace

depot_trace = process_shift_trace([48, 49, 52, 54],
                                  target=47, allowance=2, threshold=8)
assert depot_trace[:2] == [(1, 0.0, 0.0, False, False),
                           (2, 0.0, 0.0, False, False)]
assert depot_trace[-1] == (4, 8.0, 0.0, True, False)

Performance and operating cost

Updating N readings takes O(N) time and O(N) space when the full trace is retained; an online alarm needs O(1) state. The sequence reaches the illustrative upper threshold only after two larger readings accumulate. No false-alarm guarantee follows from those values. Choose target, allowance and threshold from the real measurement process and validate assumptions such as independence or expected exposure before production alerts.

Common Mistakes

  • Using a target recomputed from the same drifting window being monitored.
  • Copying example allowance and threshold values into a live alert without calibration.
  • Filling missing readings with zero or treating duplicate periods as independent evidence.
  • Calling the first alert proof of a specific cause rather than a trigger for investigation.

Validation drill

Monitor 47 daily throughput readings. Freeze a baseline version, compare an upper and lower trace, record every reset, and test how one missing day changes the alert when it is omitted versus incorrectly filled with zero.

title: Chord diagrams: audit directed flows before drawing ribbons
summary: Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.
body:
Turn a directed source-to-destination matrix into an auditable chord layout without hiding self-flows or double-counting totals.

Fix the unit and direction first

A chord diagram curls a square flow matrix around a circle. One row identifies the source; one column identifies the destination. A matrix entry can represent parcels moved between depots, but it cannot mix parcel count with shipment value. Decide whether the story is directed before any ribbons are drawn: a transfer from North to East is not the same record as East to North. If the values describe mutual relationships rather than movements, use an undirected contract and explain how two mirrored cells are consolidated. Network graphs emphasize topology; chords emphasize the volume between a manageable set of named groups. Their apparent symmetry can mislead readers when source and destination have different meanings, so label the ends or use a visible directional cue.

Reconcile sectors and ribbons

For a directed matrix, the outbound total of a group is its row sum and inbound total is its column sum. Decide whether each sector encodes outbound alone or inbound plus outbound; otherwise a sector width may appear to contradict its label. The worked contract below reports both. A transfer from a group to itself belongs on the diagonal and must be kept or explicitly excluded. Draw a self-loop distinctly because it can consume a large share of an arc without crossing the center. A ribbon should have an auditable value in an accompanying table. Sankey diagrams are often clearer when a process has ordered stages and conservation across them must be inspected.

Keep categories and filters stable

Arc order changes which ribbons overlap and can make the same data look dense or sparse. Set one documented category order across periods and filtered views. If an unseen group is grouped into Other, publish which group IDs it contains and keep its membership fixed when comparing periods. An interaction should reveal source, destination, amount, unit, time window and whether the value is a self-loop. It should also disclose the current filter cohort. Linked filter state is part of the reading contract: a selected destination must not silently redefine the total behind each sector. Export the full matrix rather than only the visible top ribbons.

Use density as a stopping rule

With 47 groups, there can be 2,209 directed cells before any filtering. Even a complete and accurate chord can become an unreadable knot. Start with a ranked table, a small set of stable groups or a matrix heatmap when precise cell comparisons matter. Heatmaps preserve a fixed row-column grid and make absent flows easier to spot. If the chord is retained, annotate whether zeros mean no observed movement or unavailable data, and provide text alternatives for keyboard and screen-reader access. Test the display at narrow widths; hiding labels does not remove the underlying ambiguity.

Worked contract

def directed_flow_ledger(groups: list[str],
                         flows: dict[tuple[str, str], int]):
    if not groups or len(groups) != len(set(groups)) or any(not name for name in groups):
        raise ValueError("group names must be unique and nonempty")
    known = set(groups)
    if any(source not in known or target not in known or
           type(amount) is not int or amount < 0
           for (source, target), amount in flows.items()):
        raise ValueError("flow endpoints and amounts must be valid")
    matrix = [[flows.get((source, target), 0) for target in groups]
              for source in groups]
    outbound = {source: sum(matrix[index])
                for index, source in enumerate(groups)}
    inbound = {target: sum(matrix[index][column]
                           for index in range(len(groups)))
               for column, target in enumerate(groups)}
    assert sum(outbound.values()) == sum(inbound.values())
    return matrix, outbound, inbound

depots = ["North", "East", "West"]
transfers = {("North", "East"): 47, ("East", "North"): 13,
             ("North", "North"): 5, ("West", "East"): 29}
matrix, outbound, inbound = directed_flow_ledger(depots, transfers)
assert matrix[0] == [5, 47, 0]
assert outbound["North"] == 52
assert inbound["East"] == 76
assert sum(outbound.values()) == 94

Performance and operating cost

For G groups, matrix construction takes O(G²) time and O(G²) space even when most flows are zero. The sparse input map is better for storage and for very large networks; the dense matrix is useful only when the chosen renderer requires it. The ledger counts each directed transfer once, including a self-loop, and proves that aggregate outbound equals aggregate inbound. It does not turn the chart into a conservation model across time: inventory changes and external entries still require their own rows.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding both directions into one ribbon while calling the result directed.
  • Dropping self-loops because they do not cross the circle.
  • Changing arc order or the membership of Other between comparison panels.
  • Treating an unavailable matrix cell as an observed zero.

Validation drill

Audit 59 transfer routes between five depots. Reconcile each outbound and inbound subtotal, then compare a chord with a matrix table at phone width.

title: Bivariate choropleths: map two rates with a readable joint legend
summary: Classify two regional rates independently, then document all nine combinations, denominators and missing regions.
body:
Classify two regional rates independently, then document all nine combinations, denominators and missing regions.

Make each variable a comparable regional rate

A bivariate choropleth gives each area one color based on two measurements. First establish a meaningful rate for each variable, with its own numerator, denominator, period and units. Coloring counties by raw counts mainly maps population size, while comparing a rate from 2024 with another from 2026 can imply a joint pattern that never existed at one time. Check whether the geography is identical for both data sets and whether boundary changes have been resolved. Single-variable choropleths explain why boundary version and denominator belong in the legend. If two measures cannot be made comparable, separate maps with explicit units are the honest choice.

Classify each axis before mixing color

A typical joint legend has three classes for the horizontal measure and three for the vertical measure. That yields nine named combinations, such as low–high, not nine unlabeled shades. Declare two cut points per variable and how exact boundary values are handled. The code uses lower-inclusive classes: a value equal to the first cut moves into the middle class. Choose cut points against the analytic question, then freeze them across panels. Recomputing quantiles on every filter action can cause a region's color to change even when its rate does not. Shared scales apply to map panels too. A 3×3 legend should label both axes, their directions and the numeric boundaries.

Separate missingness from low values

A region missing either measure has no joint class. Give it a separate visible symbol and a table row explaining which measure is missing. A zero is a valid numeric value only when the upstream measurement process really observed zero. Suppression of small counts is not zero, and imputing it can distort a rate. Heatmap missing cells face the same distinction. Reconcile the number of mapped, missing, suppressed and excluded regions before styling. If an area has a tiny denominator, attach count and uncertainty in a companion table so its saturated color is not mistaken for strong evidence.

Use the map for patterns, the table for values

Nine colors are hard to decode from memory, especially when several patches are similar or the map is viewed on a small display. Test the palette under common color-vision differences and in grayscale; provide class text and both exact rates on focus or in a linked table. A bivariate map can suggest a spatial association, but it does not establish that one measure causes the other. Large regions occupy more screen area regardless of population, and neighboring regions are not independent evidence by default. Accessible color and text alternatives should be part of the export, not an afterthought. Include the breakpoints, data period, geographic key and unmapped-count summary with every image.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def joint_rate_classes(regions: list[tuple[str, float | None, float | None]],
                       first_cuts: tuple[float, float],
                       second_cuts: tuple[float, float]):
    if not (first_cuts[0] < first_cuts[1] and second_cuts[0] < second_cuts[1]):
        raise ValueError("each pair of cuts must increase")
    if len({region for region, _, _ in regions}) != len(regions):
        raise ValueError("region keys must be unique")
    cells = []
    for region, first_rate, second_rate in regions:
        if not region:
            raise ValueError("region key is required")
        if first_rate is None or second_rate is None:
            cells.append((region, None, first_rate, second_rate))
            continue
        if not isfinite(first_rate) or not isfinite(second_rate):
            raise ValueError("rates must be finite")
        first_class = sum(first_rate >= cut for cut in first_cuts)
        second_class = sum(second_rate >= cut for cut in second_cuts)
        cells.append((region, (first_class, second_class),
                      first_rate, second_rate))
    return cells

service_regions = [("ward-47", 12.0, 31.0),
                   ("ward-59", 19.0, 45.0),
                   ("ward-83", None, 24.0)]
classified = joint_rate_classes(service_regions, (12.0, 18.0), (25.0, 40.0))
assert classified[0][1] == (1, 1)
assert classified[1][1] == (2, 2)
assert classified[2][1] is None

Performance and operating cost

Classifying R regions takes O(R) time and O(R) output space; the nine-color lookup is constant size. The function preserves exact rates and missingness alongside class coordinates, and its assertions pin the breakpoint tie rule. It assumes both inputs are already compatible rates. Validate numerators, denominators, units, boundary version and time window upstream before interpreting any mapped class.

Common Mistakes

  • Mixing raw counts with rates in one joint legend.
  • Recomputing class breaks separately for each period while comparing colors.
  • Coloring a suppressed or absent rate as low.
  • Shipping nine colors without numeric boundaries or an accessible table.

Validation drill

Classify 47 wards for two service rates. Report all nine cell counts plus missing regions, and test whether the map stays interpretable in grayscale.

title: Dendrograms: read merge height without overreading leaf order
summary: Audit distance, linkage and cut height before labeling clusters from a hierarchical tree.
body:
Audit distance, linkage and cut height before labeling clusters from a hierarchical tree.

A tree is built from a distance rule

A dendrogram shows a sequence of cluster merges. Its shape depends first on what distance means: Euclidean distance on raw fields lets large-unit features dominate, while a domain-specific distance may weight errors or missingness differently. Standardize only when that operation fits the question and record the fitted scaling parameters. Then choose a linkage rule. Single linkage merges by the nearest pair of members and can chain points; complete linkage uses the farthest pair; average linkage uses the mean of pair distances. These are different cluster definitions, not styling options. Correlation heatmaps often sit next to a dendrogram, but the correlation-to-distance transformation must be stated if it creates the tree.

Read height, not horizontal spacing

The vertical coordinate of a merge records the linkage distance at which its child clusters join. Horizontal leaf placement is usually a layout choice: sibling branches can be rotated without changing any membership or merge distance. Do not infer that two neighboring leaf labels are the closest original pair merely because they appear adjacent. Put the distance metric and linkage rule in the caption, and label the merge-height axis with units or a dimensionless scale. A flat cut at a chosen height partitions the leaves, but that height is a decision threshold, not a statistical test. The chart question should say whether the reader needs a hierarchy, a fixed number of groups or actual pairwise distances.

Inspect unstable merges

Small changes in records or scaling can reorder merges near the same height. A visually dramatic split is not automatic evidence of a natural population boundary. Refit after reasonable perturbations, compare membership and report how often groups persist; keep the data snapshot fixed while changing one assumption at a time. If a leaf represents a collapsed branch, show how many original members it contains. Truncating a large dendrogram can hide lower merges, so label contracted nodes explicitly. Uncertainty displays are useful when the tree is used to support a decision, especially with few observations or noisy distances. Keep an accessible membership table for every cut shown.

Choose the right comparison view

A tree can hold many leaves but becomes difficult to read at phone width. For a few entities, a labeled distance matrix may answer the exact-pair question faster. For many groups, a cut-level summary and downloadable membership table are more useful than microscopic text. In linked views, selecting a branch should highlight its exact IDs in the associated chart without recomputing the clustering under the cursor. Linked filters should disclose whether they merely highlight a fixed tree or rebuild it from a filtered population. Rebuilding changes the merge history and needs a new analysis version in the export.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def average_linkage_merges(values: dict[str, float]):
    if len(values) < 2 or any(not label or not isfinite(value)
                              for label, value in values.items()):
        raise ValueError("at least two finite labeled observations are required")
    clusters = {label: (label,) for label in values}
    merges = []
    while len(clusters) > 1:
        candidates = []
        labels = sorted(clusters)
        for left_index, left in enumerate(labels):
            for right in labels[left_index + 1:]:
                distances = [abs(values[first] - values[second])
                             for first in clusters[left] for second in clusters[right]]
                candidates.append((sum(distances) / len(distances), left, right))
        height, left, right = min(candidates)
        members = tuple(sorted(clusters.pop(left) + clusters.pop(right)))
        cluster_id = "|".join(members)
        clusters[cluster_id] = members
        merges.append((members, height))
    return merges

sensor_offsets = {"sensor-47": 4.0, "sensor-59": 5.0,
                  "sensor-83": 19.0, "sensor-97": 21.0}
merges = average_linkage_merges(sensor_offsets)
assert merges[0] == (("sensor-47", "sensor-59"), 1.0)
assert merges[1] == (("sensor-83", "sensor-97"), 2.0)
assert merges[2][1] == 15.5

Performance and operating cost

This transparent teaching implementation recomputes all candidate average distances at every merge. For N observations it uses O(N³) time in the worst case and O(N²) temporary space: each merge compares pair distances across the current partition; use a tested clustering library for real data. Its scalar absolute-distance rule is deliberately narrow. The output provides memberships and heights, not leaf x-coordinates. Those can be rearranged without changing the hierarchy.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading adjacent leaves as the closest original observations.
  • Changing the distance metric or scaling without documenting a new tree.
  • Treating a chosen cut height as a significance threshold.
  • Truncating branches without their member counts or a membership table.

Validation drill

Cluster 47 sensor offsets using two distance definitions. Save both trees, compare cut memberships and explain which merges changed because of the metric.

title: Probability calibration plots: compare predicted risk with observed frequency
summary: Build a reliability table with honest bin counts, event rates and a fixed evaluation cohort.
body:
Build a reliability table with honest bin counts, event rates and a fixed evaluation cohort.

Separate ranking from calibrated probability

A score can rank likely events well yet overstate their chance. A calibration plot asks whether cases assigned a given probability experience the event at approximately that frequency. For an equipment-alert model, a group with average predicted failure probability 0.31 should have an observed failure share near 0.31 over a sufficiently large, representative evaluation set. This is not a claim about any single device. Regression overlays often invite a best-fit line; a calibration plot instead compares observed and predicted rates against the identity diagonal. Ranking metrics, decision thresholds and the cost of false alarms answer different questions and should be displayed separately.

Construct bins without concealing support

Partition predictions with a stated rule. Equal-width bins have stable numeric boundaries but may leave some bins thin; equal-count bins balance support yet their boundaries move between cohorts. For each nonempty bin, plot mean predicted probability on x and observed event fraction on y. Include count and event count in a table or label, because a point based on 7 cases is not as stable as one based on 700. Do not join empty bins with a line. The code uses fixed equal-width bins and makes p=1 belong to the final bin. Small-sample displays explain why approximate agreement needs interval context, especially near the extremes.

Protect the evaluation split

Calibration estimated on the same records used to fit or tune a model is optimistic. Hold out an evaluation period or cohort and keep its definition stable. If scores are recalibrated, fit that transformation on a separate calibration set, then evaluate it on untouched data. Log model version, score timestamp, outcome window and censoring or delayed-label policy. A device marked as no failure before its observation window closes is not a verified negative. Provisional periods must be separated from complete labels. Also show prevalence: when base failure rate shifts between cohorts, the curve may move even if the model's ranking stays useful.

Inspect slices and drift carefully

A global curve can hide one badly miscalibrated plant or device family. Compare slices only when each has enough cases, and keep the same bin boundaries and evaluation window. Report omitted records and missing scores. Point movement between months may be sampling noise, model drift or a change in who gets scored; the plot alone cannot distinguish them. Small multiples with shared scales make comparisons less deceptive, while an export manifest keeps model and data versions attached to the image. Provide the underlying bin table so readers can check the plotted rates rather than measuring the diagonal by eye.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def calibration_bins(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]], width: int = 5):
    if type(width) is not int or width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("bin count must be positive")
    identifiers = [device_id for device_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not item for item in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("device IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    bins = [[0, 0.0, 0] for _ in range(width)]
    for _, probability, failed in records:
        if (not isfinite(probability) or not 0 <= probability <= 1
                or type(failed) is not bool):
            raise ValueError("probabilities and event flags must be valid")
        bucket = min(int(probability * width), width - 1)
        bins[bucket][0] += 1
        bins[bucket][1] += probability
        bins[bucket][2] += failed
    return [(bucket, count, score_sum / count, events / count, events)
            for bucket, (count, score_sum, events) in enumerate(bins)
            if count]

inspection_results = [("unit-47", 0.22, False),
                      ("unit-59", 0.31, True),
                      ("unit-83", 0.37, False),
                      ("unit-97", 1.0, True)]
reliability = calibration_bins(inspection_results)
assert reliability[0] == (1, 3, 0.3, 1 / 3, 1)
assert reliability[1] == (4, 1, 1.0, 1.0, 1)

Performance and operating cost

For N predictions and B fixed bins, accumulation takes O(N + B) time and O(B + N) space because unique IDs are validated. Empty bins are omitted rather than invented. The four-record check demonstrates bin assignment and arithmetic, not credible calibration evidence; real evaluation needs sufficient support, a held-out cohort and uncertainty intervals. The function does not estimate those intervals or repair delayed labels.

Common Mistakes

  • Using training records as the final reliability evaluation.
  • Plotting one bin point without its case count or event count.
  • Calling a high-ranking score calibrated without comparing observed frequency.
  • Treating unfinished outcome windows as verified negatives.

Validation drill

Hold out 470 device predictions. Build fixed bins for two months, print counts and event rates, then identify whether a shifted curve also coincides with changed prevalence or incomplete labels.

title: Precision–recall curves: preserve threshold ties and class prevalence
summary: Build an auditable precision–recall staircase from held-out scores, then read average precision against the actual event rate.
body:
Build an auditable precision–recall staircase from held-out scores, then read average precision against the actual event rate.

Start with the decision population

A precision–recall curve describes a ranked binary score across possible alert thresholds. Precision is true alerts divided by all alerts; recall is true alerts divided by all actual events. They answer different questions. If a maintenance team can inspect 47 machines per shift, the useful region may be the high-precision, low-recall end, while a safety review may tolerate many inspections to find nearly every fault. Define the event, prediction timestamp, outcome window, eligible population and positive class before plotting. Probability calibration answers whether a score of 0.30 corresponds to about 30% observed risk; a precision–recall curve asks how selected alerts trade false alarms for captured events. A ranking can be useful and still be poorly calibrated.

Sweep tied scores as one threshold

Sort records by decreasing score. At each distinct score, include all records with that score before measuring precision and recall. Splitting tied cases in arbitrary input order invents operating points that no threshold can achieve. Add a no-alert endpoint at recall zero and precision one only as a plotting convention: it does not mean the model has already found an event. At the opposite end, all eligible records are selected and precision equals the cohort event rate. The stepwise curve must retain its actual points; smoothing or interpolating precision can imply a threshold that never existed. An empirical CDF uses a similar idea of preserving observed steps rather than drawing a continuous story through discrete decisions.

Interpret area and baseline carefully

Average precision weights precision at each achieved recall increment. It is not always the same number as trapezoidal area under a line interpolated between curve points, and neither is classification accuracy. The event prevalence is a useful no-skill reference when scores are independent of labels; if prevalence changes from one plant to another, the apparent precision of the same ranking can change too. Put both event count and total eligible count beside every panel. Compare models on the same untouched evaluation cohort, outcome definition and time window. Shared small-multiple scales stop separate panels from hiding the difficult low-recall region. When costs matter, also show the selected operating threshold and its alert volume rather than publishing only a scalar summary.

Expose uncertainty and selection limits

Few positives produce large stair steps: one additional true event can move recall markedly. Bootstrap or another justified interval method may describe sampling uncertainty, but resample at the correct independent unit, such as machine or customer, when multiple records belong to one unit. Delayed outcomes, unreviewed alerts and selectively labeled negatives can bias the curve; an apparent negative is not a confirmed one merely because a record is old. Small-sample uncertainty and provisional periods need explicit treatment. A companion table should give threshold, true positives, false positives, precision, recall and selected count at a few operationally relevant cuts.

Worked contract

def precision_recall_steps(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]]):
    from math import isfinite
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("record identifiers must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(score) or type(event) is not bool
           for _, score, event in records):
        raise ValueError("finite scores and boolean labels are required")
    positives = sum(event for _, _, event in records)
    if positives == 0:
        raise ValueError("recall requires at least one positive")
    ranked = sorted(records, key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    points = []
    true_positives = false_positives = cursor = 0
    while cursor < len(ranked):
        threshold = ranked[cursor][1]
        while cursor < len(ranked) and ranked[cursor][1] == threshold:
            true_positives += ranked[cursor][2]
            false_positives += not ranked[cursor][2]
            cursor += 1
        selected = true_positives + false_positives
        points.append((threshold, true_positives / selected,
                       true_positives / positives, selected))
    average_precision = sum(
        precision * (recall - (points[index - 1][2] if index else 0))
        for index, (_, precision, recall, _) in enumerate(points))
    return points, average_precision, positives / len(records)

inspection_scores = [("press-47", 0.91, True),
                     ("press-59", 0.73, False),
                     ("press-83", 0.73, True),
                     ("press-97", 0.22, False)]
steps, average_precision, prevalence = precision_recall_steps(inspection_scores)
assert len(steps) == 3
assert steps[1] == (0.73, 2 / 3, 1.0, 3)
assert abs(average_precision - 5 / 6) < 1e-12
assert prevalence == 0.5

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N records takes O(N log N) time. The threshold sweep is O(N), while the sorted copy and output need O(N) space; unique-ID validation also needs O(N) space. The sample's average precision is 5/6 because recall rises first by one half at precision one and then by one half at precision two thirds. Four records demonstrate arithmetic and tie handling, not a credible model comparison. The function assumes labels are complete and the evaluation cohort has already been held out.

Common Mistakes

  • Breaking equal scores in row order and presenting unreachable thresholds.
  • Calling trapezoidal interpolation average precision without defining the calculation.
  • Comparing curves built from cohorts with different prevalence or outcome windows.
  • Reading the no-alert plotting endpoint as measured model performance.

Validation drill

Evaluate 470 held-out inspection scores with 59 confirmed events. Print every attainable tied-score threshold, mark the 47-alert operating point, and compare its event capture with the full curve.

title: Bland–Altman plots: assess paired measurement agreement
summary: Compare paired device readings with signed bias, agreement limits and a check for magnitude-dependent error.
body:
Compare paired device readings with signed bias, agreement limits and a check for magnitude-dependent error.

Pair the same specimen under both methods

A method-agreement plot starts with two readings of the same item under conditions that make comparison meaningful. Put their mean on the horizontal axis and the signed difference, new instrument minus reference instrument, on the vertical axis. A scatterplot or high correlation between devices can coexist with a large systematic offset, so correlation is not an agreement test. Define the acceptable difference in the original unit before seeing the result. For a temperature probe, an average offset of 0.8 degrees may matter or not depending on the process tolerance; a statistically precise estimate does not make an operationally unsafe offset acceptable. Paired-change charts show each item's two readings, while this plot concentrates on the distribution of pairwise error across the measurement range.

Compute bias and descriptive limits

The horizontal reference line is the mean signed difference, or bias. Under assumptions including approximately stable difference variance and a suitable difference distribution, conventional agreement limits are bias plus or minus 1.96 sample standard deviations of differences. Those lines describe the spread expected for individual differences under the model. They are not confidence intervals for the mean bias and are not a pass/fail tolerance supplied by the process owner. Report the number of pairs, direction of subtraction and raw units with the limits. Interval labeling matters here: a reader must be able to tell agreement limits from uncertainty about where those limits lie. A small sample makes estimated limits unstable.

Look for error that changes with magnitude

A fan-shaped cloud suggests that larger measurements have greater absolute disagreement; a sloped pattern suggests proportional bias. One global pair of horizontal limits can then misrepresent both ends of the range. Inspect residual patterns and consider a justified transformation or a model in which spread depends on magnitude. Do not automatically use percent difference: dividing by a near-zero mean can explode, and a ratio may be inappropriate for values that cross zero. Regression overlays can reveal a trend, but a line drawn through differences is only descriptive until its assumptions and uncertainty are examined. Mark outliers for investigation without quietly deleting them.

Respect independent units and coverage

Repeated measurements from the same machine are correlated. Treating 47 repeated readings from one unit as 47 independent machines understates uncertainty. Choose a design that separates repeatability within each method from agreement between methods, or analyze at the proper unit. Check whether pairs cover the full operating range; limits estimated from a narrow band cannot be claimed for extreme values never sampled. An accessible table should list specimen ID, both values, pair mean, signed difference and any excluded or missing reading. An export manifest should preserve calibration date, units, method versions and the subtraction direction, because reversing that direction changes the sign of bias and both limit labels.

Worked contract

from math import sqrt, isfinite

def agreement_summary(pairs: list[tuple[str, float, float]]):
    identifiers = [specimen_id for specimen_id, _, _ in pairs]
    if len(pairs) < 2 or len(set(identifiers)) != len(pairs) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("at least two uniquely identified pairs are required")
    if any(not isfinite(reference) or not isfinite(candidate)
           for _, reference, candidate in pairs):
        raise ValueError("all paired readings must be finite")
    points = [(specimen_id, (reference + candidate) / 2,
               candidate - reference)
              for specimen_id, reference, candidate in pairs]
    bias = sum(difference for _, _, difference in points) / len(points)
    variance = sum((difference - bias) ** 2
                   for _, _, difference in points) / (len(points) - 1)
    spread = sqrt(variance)
    return points, bias, (bias - 1.96 * spread, bias + 1.96 * spread)

probe_pairs = [("batch-47", 41.0, 42.0),
               ("batch-59", 54.0, 55.0),
               ("batch-83", 63.0, 66.0)]
points, bias, limits = agreement_summary(probe_pairs)
assert points == [("batch-47", 41.5, 1.0),
                  ("batch-59", 54.5, 1.0),
                  ("batch-83", 64.5, 3.0)]
assert abs(bias - 5 / 3) < 1e-12
assert limits[0] < 0 < limits[1]

Performance and operating cost

For N pairs, constructing points and calculating sample variance each take O(N) time. The returned plot table takes O(N) space; streaming just the bias and variance is possible with O(1) extra space when individual points are not needed. The three-pair check fixes the sign convention and sample-variance denominator. It is too small to justify operational agreement limits and does not account for repeated measures or magnitude-dependent spread.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling high correlation proof that two methods agree.
  • Confusing agreement limits for individual differences with confidence limits around mean bias.
  • Reversing the subtraction direction between chart and report.
  • Counting repeated readings from one item as independent specimens.

Validation drill

Pair 59 items across two measurement devices. State a tolerable difference first, then plot signed differences, check for magnitude-dependent spread and report which items fall outside that tolerance.
