title: UpSet plots: count exact intersections without double counting
summary: Turn overlapping memberships into exclusive intersection bars with a stated universe and reproducible set order.
body:
Turn overlapping memberships into exclusive intersection bars with a stated universe and reproducible set order.

Define one universe of unique entities

An intersection plot is useful when a Venn drawing becomes too crowded. Consider support tickets tagged Billing, Delivery or Returns. Each ticket needs a stable unique ID and a documented observation period; multiple log rows for the same ticket should not become multiple members. Decide whether the universe is all tickets, all tagged tickets or only tickets passing an eligibility filter. That choice changes the meaning of the empty-membership group. Aggregation grain and denominator apply before any bars are drawn. A set-size bar counts every ticket in a set, including tickets in other sets; summing set-size bars therefore double-counts overlap by design.

Distinguish exact from inclusive intersections

An exact intersection for Billing and Returns contains tickets with those two tags and no other displayed tag. An inclusive intersection contains those tickets even when they also carry Delivery. UpSet-style bars often use exact membership masks, but analysts sometimes compute inclusive intersections in SQL and label them as exact. State which contract each bar uses. The worked function returns an exact mask for every record and excludes the all-false mask from plotted bars while retaining its count in the audit. The sum of all exact masks must equal the size of the universe, including items outside all displayed sets. Mosaic plots offer a different view of joint categories, but they also require a clear rule for empty cells and denominators.

Keep column and set order stable

Sort intersections by count for exploration, then freeze a documented column order when comparing periods. Otherwise a bar that moves horizontally can be mistaken for a membership change. Order the set rows consistently, and show the connected dots or a textual equivalent beneath each bar. A bar for no sets can be meaningful if every ticket belongs to the universe regardless of tagging; do not silently discard it from reconciliation. Stable facet order helps the same reader compare versions. A companion table should give exact mask, count, period, filters, and the underlying entity IDs or an authorized export path.

Stop before combinations swamp the chart

With K sets there are up to 2^K exact masks, including the empty mask, even though many may have zero observations. An unreadable wall of tiny bars is not comprehensive communication. Select a justified subset of sets, group lower-value combinations with a visible membership rule or offer a searchable intersection table. Do not hide suppressed small groups inside a falsely labeled zero. Keyboard and table access matters because a dot matrix alone cannot expose exact membership to every reader. If the set definitions drift across months, a stable-looking bar chart can still compare different concepts; publish the rule version beside the counts.

Worked contract

def exact_intersections(records: dict[str, set[str]],
                        sets_in_order: list[str]):
    if not sets_in_order or len(sets_in_order) != len(set(sets_in_order)):
        raise ValueError("set names must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not name for name in sets_in_order):
        raise ValueError("set names must be nonempty")
    known = set(sets_in_order)
    if any(not ticket_id or not membership <= known
           for ticket_id, membership in records.items()):
        raise ValueError("ticket IDs and memberships must be valid")
    counts = {}
    for membership in records.values():
        mask = tuple(name in membership for name in sets_in_order)
        counts[mask] = counts.get(mask, 0) + 1
    assert sum(counts.values()) == len(records)
    return counts

ticket_tags = {"ticket-47": {"Billing", "Returns"},
               "ticket-59": {"Billing", "Returns", "Delivery"},
               "ticket-83": {"Delivery"}, "ticket-97": set()}
set_order = ["Billing", "Delivery", "Returns"]
intersections = exact_intersections(ticket_tags, set_order)
assert intersections[(True, False, True)] == 1
assert intersections[(True, True, True)] == 1
assert intersections[(False, False, False)] == 1
assert sum(intersections.values()) == 4

Performance and operating cost

For N records and K named sets, computing membership masks takes O(NK) time and O(MK) space for M observed masks, with M at most min(N, 2^K). The worst-case chart itself becomes difficult well before that bound. The function assumes each record key is already a unique entity and its tag collection is a set. It counts exact intersections, not inclusive overlaps, and deliberately retains the empty mask for reconciliation.

Common Mistakes

  • Summing set-size bars as if their members were disjoint.
  • Labeling an inclusive SQL overlap as an exact intersection.
  • Dropping the no-set group without explaining the changed universe.
  • Reordering sets or redefining tags across comparison panels without a version note.

Validation drill

Build an exact-mask ledger for 470 tickets and four tags. Reconcile every mask to the eligible universe, then compute one inclusive overlap separately and explain why the two counts differ.

title: Contour plots: respect measured grids and interpolation boundaries
summary: Read isolines and filled bands against a regular grid, declared contour levels and explicit missing-cell masks.
body:
Read isolines and filled bands against a regular grid, declared contour levels and explicit missing-cell masks.

Know what a contour line represents

A contour line joins locations estimated to share one value of a continuous field. A filled contour uses bands between stated levels. Both require a coordinate system and an underlying surface. In a warehouse temperature survey, readings at sensor positions are observations; color between sensors is an interpolation model, not another measurement. If observations sit on an irregular mesh, state how they were gridded before rendering. A heatmap shows cell values directly and may be more honest when only measured cells matter. Contours are appropriate when spatial continuity is scientifically defensible and the uncertainty between samples is acceptable for the question.

Choose levels and preserve the numeric domain

Use one ascending level list across panels that readers will compare. Automatic levels chosen independently for each frame can make unchanged values move to new colors. The legend should give units, exact boundaries and what happens below the first or above the last level. Do not choose dozens of bands merely to create a smooth-looking gradient; more colors do not add measurements. Shared scales and panels apply to contours as well. Preserve the aspect ratio if x and y use comparable spatial units, and label a transformed coordinate axis if a map projection or other conversion changes distance. Separate contour lines from the base grid in an accessible data export.

Mask gaps rather than inventing a bridge

Missing readings can create holes in the surface. Mark unavailable grid cells and state whether the renderer masks a cell, a vertex or any quadrilateral touching it; these policies have different visible footprints. Never replace an absent observation with zero just to satisfy a plotting library. A sensor fault along a wall can create an apparent cold band if imputed as zero. Missing mapped regions present the same honest-versus-smooth choice. Show the sampled domain boundary and avoid extrapolating contours far outside the convex hull of observations unless an explicit physical model supports it.

Treat interpolation as a model to validate

Linear interpolation within each grid cell can create straight segments even when the real field bends; smoothing can conceal localized peaks. Keep point markers or a linked table to show where measurements actually exist. Cross-validate by withholding sensors in several areas, compare predicted values against withheld readings and investigate systematic error near edges. Uncertainty grows where sensors are sparse, while render provenance should record grid version, interpolation method, level list and mask policy. For a decision about safety limits, publish the original measurements and margin near the threshold instead of relying on the contour image alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def contour_cells(x_coordinates: list[float], y_coordinates: list[float],
                  values: list[list[float | None]], levels: list[float]):
    if len(x_coordinates) < 2 or len(y_coordinates) < 2:
        raise ValueError("a contour grid needs at least two points per axis")
    if any(not isfinite(position) for position in x_coordinates + y_coordinates):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    if any(right <= left for left, right in zip(x_coordinates, x_coordinates[1:])):
        raise ValueError("x coordinates must increase")
    if any(top <= bottom for bottom, top in zip(y_coordinates, y_coordinates[1:])):
        raise ValueError("y coordinates must increase")
    if len(values) != len(y_coordinates) or any(len(row) != len(x_coordinates) for row in values):
        raise ValueError("grid dimensions do not match axes")
    if len(levels) < 2 or any(not isfinite(level) for level in levels) or any(
            upper <= lower for lower, upper in zip(levels, levels[1:])):
        raise ValueError("at least two increasing finite levels are required")
    if any(reading is not None and not isfinite(reading)
           for row in values for reading in row):
        raise ValueError("observed values must be finite")
    usable = []
    masked = []
    for row in range(len(y_coordinates) - 1):
        for column in range(len(x_coordinates) - 1):
            corners = (values[row][column], values[row][column + 1],
                       values[row + 1][column], values[row + 1][column + 1])
            cell = (column, row)
            (usable if all(value is not None for value in corners) else masked).append(cell)
    return usable, masked

sensor_grid = [[18.0, 20.0, 22.0], [19.0, None, 24.0], [20.0, 23.0, 25.0]]
usable, masked = contour_cells([0.0, 47.0, 94.0], [0.0, 59.0, 118.0],
                               sensor_grid, [18.0, 21.0, 24.0, 27.0])
assert usable == []
assert masked == [(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)]

Performance and operating cost

Validating a grid with X columns, Y rows and L contour levels takes O(XY + X + Y + L) time and O(XY) output space for the cell audit. An actual contour renderer adds work that depends on its interpolation and line-tracing algorithm. This standard-library check does not draw isolines; it makes the mask rule explicit: any cell touching a missing corner is unavailable. A single missing center reading masks all four neighboring cells in the sample, rather than fabricating a continuous field.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating interpolated values as if they were sensor readings.
  • Changing levels between comparison panels without announcing the change.
  • Filling missing cells with zero and displaying a false low region.
  • Drawing contours beyond the sampled domain without a model and uncertainty statement.

Validation drill

Map 47 warehouse sensors on a fixed coordinate system. Hide three sensors, audit the masked cells, compare two fixed level sets, and record held-out interpolation error near the perimeter.

title: ROC curves: read attainable thresholds and false-positive rates
summary: Build a binary ROC curve without splitting tied scores, then place AUC beside the operating point and cohort counts.
body:
Build a binary ROC curve without splitting tied scores, then place AUC beside the operating point and cohort counts.

Define both error denominators

A receiver operating characteristic curve plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate as a score threshold moves. True-positive rate divides captured events by all actual events. False-positive rate divides false alerts by all actual non-events. The latter is not the fraction of alerts that are false. State which label is positive, when the score was produced and when outcomes became final. A hospital or factory may need a low false-positive rate because follow-up capacity is limited, but the curve alone cannot decide the cost of an alert. Precision–recall curves put false alerts in the denominator of precision and often make alert workload easier to see. A confusion matrix makes the counts behind one selected threshold explicit.

Sweep score ties as a single decision

Sort evaluation records by descending score. Start at the no-alert point, false-positive rate zero and true-positive rate zero. Add every record at a distinct score together; equal scores cannot be separated by a threshold that uses the score alone. After each group, divide cumulative true positives by the total positives and cumulative false positives by total negatives. The last point is one, one when every eligible record has a finite score. Retain the actual staircase vertices. A plotting package may remove intermediate collinear points for display, but the operational threshold table must keep enough detail to identify each attainable selection. A score need not be a calibrated probability to produce an ROC curve. Calibration plots test that separate question.

Keep AUC in its place

Trapezoidal ROC AUC summarizes ranking over the full false-positive-rate range. It can be interpreted as the probability that a randomly selected positive outranks a randomly selected negative, with half credit for a tie, under the evaluation population. A high overall AUC may still conceal weak performance in the low-false-positive region where the system can operate. If only that range matters, specify its bounds and normalization before reporting a partial AUC, and show the actual portion of the curve. Compare models on the same held-out records and labels. The ROC axes use rates that do not algebraically contain prevalence, yet precision and the number of false alarms at deployment do depend on the population mix. Print counts and the intended threshold beside AUC.

Test slices and uncertain tails

A curve built from 47 positives can jump by more than two percentage points with each newly captured positive. Likewise, one false alert has a large horizontal effect when few negatives were evaluated. Publish total positives, negatives and score coverage; use uncertainty intervals or unit-level resampling when records are clustered by customer, machine or site. Avoid comparing curves whose outcome windows or eligibility filters differ. Uncertainty displays need to reveal thin support, while shared axes matter when models or sites appear in separate panels. If labels are delayed, do not quietly count pending cases as negatives. A companion table should include threshold, selected count and all four confusion-matrix cells at the chosen operating points.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def roc_thresholds(records: list[tuple[str, float, bool]]):
    identifiers = [record_id for record_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("record IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    if any(not isfinite(score) or type(event) is not bool
           for _, score, event in records):
        raise ValueError("scores and labels must be valid")
    positives = sum(event for _, _, event in records)
    negatives = len(records) - positives
    if not positives or not negatives:
        raise ValueError("ROC needs both positive and negative records")
    ranked = sorted(records, key=lambda row: row[1], reverse=True)
    points = [(None, 0.0, 0.0, 0)]
    true_positives = false_positives = cursor = 0
    while cursor < len(ranked):
        threshold = ranked[cursor][1]
        while cursor < len(ranked) and ranked[cursor][1] == threshold:
            true_positives += ranked[cursor][2]
            false_positives += not ranked[cursor][2]
            cursor += 1
        points.append((threshold, false_positives / negatives,
                       true_positives / positives, cursor))
    area = sum((points[index][1] - points[index - 1][1]) *
               (points[index][2] + points[index - 1][2]) / 2
               for index in range(1, len(points)))
    return points, area

quality_scores = [("lot-47", 0.91, True), ("lot-59", 0.64, False),
                  ("lot-83", 0.64, True), ("lot-97", 0.18, False)]
points, area = roc_thresholds(quality_scores)
assert points[0] == (None, 0.0, 0.0, 0)
assert points[2] == (0.64, 0.5, 1.0, 3)
assert points[-1][1:3] == (1.0, 1.0)
assert area == 0.875

Performance and operating cost

For N labeled records, sorting takes O(N log N) time, and the grouped threshold sweep plus trapezoid sum take O(N). The sorted records, uniqueness set and output points need O(N) space. This four-record audit proves a tied score creates one shared threshold point and yields area 0.875. It does not estimate uncertainty, calibrate scores or determine a safe operating threshold. Those need an evaluation design and a stated decision cost.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling false positives divided by all alerts the false-positive rate.
  • Breaking score ties in input order and drawing unattainable thresholds.
  • Choosing a model by full AUC when only a narrow false-positive range is usable.
  • Comparing AUCs from different label windows or evaluation cohorts.

Validation drill

Score 470 held-out production lots with confirmed outcomes. Mark every tied threshold, report the four confusion-matrix counts at the 47-alert operating point, and inspect the first 0.05 of false-positive rate separately.

title: Confusion matrices: fix class order, denominators and abstentions
summary: Build a classification error ledger with actual rows, predicted columns, fixed labels and visible support for every class.
body:
Build a classification error ledger with actual rows, predicted columns, fixed labels and visible support for every class.

Make axes a written contract

A confusion matrix is a count ledger, not merely a colored square. Fix the class vocabulary and its order before comparing model versions. This lesson puts actual class on each row and predicted class on each column. A cell at row Delivery, column Returns therefore means a real Delivery ticket routed to Returns. Swapping axes changes the question while leaving a superficially similar image. Use the same class keys in tables, hover text, screen-reader descriptions and any export. Heatmap color scales should make count ranges readable, but numerical labels must remain available. On a sparse matrix, zero means no observed cases; it does not prove an error is impossible.

Keep counts and row rates together

Raw counts show workload. Row-normalized values divide each cell by the number of actual cases in its row, making recall-like class comparisons possible. Column normalization divides by the number predicted as that class, answering a precision-like question. Whole-matrix normalization divides by all cases and answers a third question. Never label all three simply 'accuracy.' Print row totals and column totals so readers can audit the denominators. A model that gets 9,400 common cases right and misses 47 rare cases can have impressive overall accuracy but fail the rare-class task. Denominator design and precision–recall analysis provide the neighboring view for rare binary outcomes. If a class has zero actual cases, its row rate is undefined, not zero.

Treat abstention and missing truth separately

Some classifiers can decline to assign a class. Represent abstain as a predicted column and report coverage, the share of eligible records receiving a concrete prediction. Do not drop abstentions before calculating performance unless a separate coverage-conditioned table is clearly labeled. Missing ground truth is different: those records cannot enter a verified confusion matrix at all, and their count should be disclosed alongside the eligible population. In a human-review workflow, only the reviewed cases may have labels, creating selection bias. A matrix built from those cases is not automatically representative of all incoming work. Linked filters should make this labeled-cohort restriction visible at all times.

Compare the errors that matter

The diagonal marks correct classifications; off-diagonal cells identify which mistakes occur. A stable class order and shared color domain let readers compare model versions without relearning the image. Sort classes by a documented domain order, not by each version's frequency. When there are dozens of labels, show a targeted subset or a table rather than shrinking every cell until it is unreadable. Report cost-relevant pairs explicitly: sending a fraud report to routine support may be more expensive than confusing two routine categories. Small multiples help comparisons, while text alternatives carry exact counts where color alone cannot. The matrix describes a fixed decision rule; a threshold sweep needs a separate ROC or precision–recall view.

Worked contract

def classification_ledger(records: list[tuple[str, str, str]],
                          classes: list[str]):
    if (not classes or "Abstain" in classes or
            len(classes) != len(set(classes)) or any(not item for item in classes)):
        raise ValueError("class labels must be unique and nonempty")
    identifiers = [ticket_id for ticket_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(not key for key in identifiers):
        raise ValueError("ticket IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    actual_positions = {name: index for index, name in enumerate(classes)}
    predicted_positions = {name: index for index, name in
                           enumerate(classes + ["Abstain"])}
    counts = [[0 for _ in predicted_positions] for _ in classes]
    for _, actual, predicted in records:
        if actual not in actual_positions or predicted not in predicted_positions:
            raise ValueError("unknown actual or predicted class")
        counts[actual_positions[actual]][predicted_positions[predicted]] += 1
    row_rates = []
    for row in counts:
        support = sum(row)
        row_rates.append([value / support for value in row] if support else None)
    assert sum(map(sum, counts)) == len(records)
    return counts, row_rates

ticket_routes = [("ticket-47", "Billing", "Billing"),
                 ("ticket-59", "Billing", "Delivery"),
                 ("ticket-83", "Delivery", "Delivery"),
                 ("ticket-97", "Delivery", "Returns"),
                 ("ticket-101", "Returns", "Returns"),
                 ("ticket-131", "Returns", "Billing")]
labels = ["Billing", "Delivery", "Returns", "Technical"]
counts, row_rates = classification_ledger(ticket_routes, labels)
assert counts[0][:3] == [1, 1, 0]
assert row_rates[0][:3] == [0.5, 0.5, 0.0]
assert row_rates[3] is None
assert sum(counts[index][index] for index in range(4)) == 3

Performance and operating cost

For N records and K actual classes, ledger construction takes O(N + K²) time and O(N + K²) space: the unique-ID set stores N keys and each dense matrix has K rows and K+1 predicted columns, including Abstain. A sparse map can avoid empty cells when K is large. The code rejects an unknown actual or predicted label; missing actual labels require a separate exclusion ledger. The six-ticket assertion checks axis direction, row normalization and an undefined zero-support row, not model quality.

Common Mistakes

  • Flipping actual and predicted axes between dashboards.
  • Displaying row-normalized color without support counts.
  • Reporting an empty actual-class row as zero recall.
  • Discarding abstentions or unreviewed cases without changing the cohort label.

Validation drill

Audit 470 routed tickets across four service classes. Reconcile row and column totals, add an Abstain predicted column, and explain how coverage and per-class recall change between two model versions.

  • Interactive dashboards: recompute cohorts after linked filters

title: EWMA control charts: detect slow shifts against a frozen baseline
summary: Compute a time-ordered exponentially weighted trace with startup limits, then separate process signals from specification failures.
body:
Compute a time-ordered exponentially weighted trace with startup limits, then separate process signals from specification failures.

Freeze a trustworthy reference process

An exponentially weighted moving average, or EWMA, updates a running statistic from each new observation. Before monitoring, estimate or choose a target mean and process spread from an in-control reference period. Record the unit, subgroup definition, sampling interval, instrument version and baseline dates. A baseline contaminated by a slow fault will normalize that fault away. Control limits describe variation expected under the reference process; they are not engineering specification limits for an individual product. P charts handle binomial proportions with varying denominators, whereas this worked EWMA assumes comparable numeric observations with one historical spread estimate. A process can remain in statistical control while producing values outside a customer tolerance.

Weight recent values without erasing history

At time t, the statistic is lambda times the new reading plus one minus lambda times the previous EWMA. Lambda must be above zero and no greater than one. A smaller value smooths more and can highlight a sustained small shift, but it also delays a sudden jump and creates dependence between plotted points. Show raw readings or a linked table beside the smooth trace; smoothing alone can hide an isolated dangerous measurement. Preserving extrema matters even when the monitoring statistic does not alert. Compare each EWMA point with limits designed for that same time index. Startup limits widen toward steady-state limits when the statistic begins at the fixed target; using the asymptotic limit immediately changes early false-alarm behavior.

Keep time steps honest

A recurrence is defined over ordered observations, not an arbitrary display order. If two shifts are missing, do not quietly join the previous EWMA to the next reading as though no time passed. Decide whether the index counts samples or calendar periods, document any reset after maintenance, and mark instrument downtime. Time-series gaps need a visible policy. The code below treats every input reading as the next consecutive sample and rejects nonfinite values; it does not infer time gaps. If the monitoring interval or subgroup size changes, a single baseline spread may no longer apply. Freeze lambda, target, spread and limit multiplier before evaluating a future run, then version them whenever they change.

Investigate signals without chasing noise

An EWMA point beyond its control limit is a signal to investigate the process and measurement system, not proof of a particular cause. Repeated searching and changing limits after seeing a signal inflates false discoveries. Estimate false-alarm behavior and detection delay under a realistic process model before choosing lambda and limit width; independence and stable variance assumptions matter. CUSUM charts offer a related running-evidence design with a reference shift and reset rule. A published chart should include target, lambda, multiplier, baseline window, each raw reading, the EWMA value, both time-specific limits and the investigation outcome. The export manifest protects that state when charts are shared outside the monitoring system.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def ewma_trace(readings: list[tuple[str, float]], target: float,
               sigma: float, weight: float = 0.25, multiplier: float = 3.0):
    if not isfinite(target) or not isfinite(sigma) or sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("target and positive baseline spread are required")
    if not isfinite(weight) or not 0 < weight <= 1:
        raise ValueError("weight must be in (0, 1]")
    if not isfinite(multiplier) or multiplier <= 0:
        raise ValueError("limit multiplier must be positive")
    if len({sample_id for sample_id, _ in readings}) != len(readings) or any(
            not sample_id or not isfinite(value) for sample_id, value in readings):
        raise ValueError("sample IDs and readings must be valid")
    current = target
    ledger = []
    for index, (sample_id, value) in enumerate(readings, start=1):
        current = weight * value + (1 - weight) * current
        startup_spread = sigma * sqrt(weight / (2 - weight) *
                                      (1 - (1 - weight) ** (2 * index)))
        lower = target - multiplier * startup_spread
        upper = target + multiplier * startup_spread
        ledger.append((sample_id, value, current, lower, upper,
                       current < lower or current > upper))
    return ledger

probe_readings = [("shift-47", 52.0), ("shift-59", 53.0),
                  ("shift-83", 54.0), ("shift-97", 56.0)]
trace = ewma_trace(probe_readings, target=50.0, sigma=2.0)
assert trace[0][2:5] == (50.5, 48.5, 51.5)
assert abs(trace[2][2] - 51.84375) < 1e-12
assert [row[-1] for row in trace] == [False, False, False, True]

Performance and operating cost

For N ordered readings, the recurrence and time-specific limits take O(N) time and O(N) output space; streaming only the latest statistic and signal uses O(1) extra space. The four-reading check proves the startup-width calculation and a later alert under its chosen reference values. Those values are illustrative, not calibrated for a target false-alarm rate. The function assumes equally spaced independent baseline observations and does not solve missing periods, serial correlation or a drifting reference process.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating control limits as customer specification limits.
  • Estimating the baseline from the same visibly drifting period being monitored.
  • Changing lambda or limits after viewing alerts without versioning the rule.
  • Hiding raw spikes or missing periods beneath a smooth EWMA line.

Validation drill

Monitor 47 consecutive production shifts. Freeze a clean baseline first, compare startup with steady-state limits, flag gaps and resets, and explain each alert with the raw reading and investigation record.

title: Cumulative gains and lift: rank contacts without hiding score ties
summary: Turn a ranked response model into an auditable contact-capacity curve with attainable thresholds, cohort counts and a random-selection baseline.
body:
Turn a ranked response model into an auditable contact-capacity curve with attainable thresholds, cohort counts and a random-selection baseline.

Define the decision population

A cumulative gains chart asks how many confirmed responders appear among the highest-ranked share of eligible contacts. The horizontal axis is contacts selected divided by all eligible contacts. The vertical axis is responders captured divided by all confirmed responders. Lift at that point is gain divided by selected share. These are different denominators; mixing them produces an impressive-looking but meaningless line. Freeze the eligibility rule, scoring date, response window and label-maturity rule before ranking. An unobserved response is not automatically a negative response. Grain and denominator checks belong beside the chart, especially when one customer has several campaign records.

Use a reachable threshold

Sort by descending score and advance one whole score group at a time. Equal scores cannot be separated using the model score alone. A budget of 47 contacts might land inside a tie containing 11 people. Either contact the whole tied group, stop before it, or apply a declared secondary rule that the team can reproduce; do not show a fractional customer as an attainable decision. Plot points after complete groups, print the actual selected count, and draw the random-selection gain baseline as selected share. The random baseline has lift one at every positive selected share. ROC thresholds face the same tie issue, but their horizontal axis divides false alerts by actual non-events rather than contacts by all eligible records.

Read lift with capacity, not as a trophy

If the top quarter contains half of all responders, cumulative lift at that contact depth is two. It does not mean the model doubles every person's response probability. Cumulative lift generally approaches one when all eligible contacts are selected, so a large value at a tiny first group should not dominate the decision. Show selected count, captured responders, gain and lift at each usable capacity. If outreach cost varies by channel or customer, a count-based gain curve is insufficient; calculate expected net value under the actual contact rule. Precision–recall curves show positive yield among selected contacts and are a useful companion, while calibration asks whether the scores themselves can be read as probabilities.

Protect evaluation against selection bias

A campaign label is often observed only for people previously contacted. Ranking that historical contacted subset can make a new model appear stronger than it is for the full eligible population. Record who had a chance to respond, the old contact policy, and whether the evaluation uses randomized outreach or an appropriate correction. Compare candidate models on the same held-out cohort and response window. If outcome prevalence changes, gains and lift at a fixed share may shift because the target population changed. Slice by campaign, region or customer tenure only when each slice has enough confirmed responders to support the curve. Small-sample displays should expose the event counts behind sharp early jumps.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def gains_ledger(contacts: list[tuple[str, float, bool]]):
    contact_ids = [contact_id for contact_id, _, _ in contacts]
    if not contacts or len(contact_ids) != len(set(contact_ids)) or any(
            not contact_id for contact_id in contact_ids):
        raise ValueError("contacts need unique, nonempty IDs")
    if any(not isfinite(score) or type(responded) is not bool
           for _, score, responded in contacts):
        raise ValueError("scores must be finite and responses must be known")
    total_responses = sum(responded for _, _, responded in contacts)
    if total_responses == 0:
        raise ValueError("gain is undefined without responders")
    ranked = sorted(contacts, key=lambda record: record[1], reverse=True)
    selected = captured = cursor = 0
    points = [(None, 0, 0.0, 0.0, None)]
    while cursor < len(ranked):
        threshold = ranked[cursor][1]
        while cursor < len(ranked) and ranked[cursor][1] == threshold:
            captured += ranked[cursor][2]
            selected += 1
            cursor += 1
        share = selected / len(ranked)
        gain = captured / total_responses
        points.append((threshold, selected, share, gain, gain / share))
    return points

campaign_contacts = [("contact-47", 0.94, True),
                     ("contact-59", 0.87, False),
                     ("contact-83", 0.87, True),
                     ("contact-97", 0.61, False),
                     ("contact-101", 0.55, True),
                     ("contact-131", 0.31, False),
                     ("contact-149", 0.21, False),
                     ("contact-173", 0.08, False)]
trace = gains_ledger(campaign_contacts)
assert trace[2][:4] == (0.87, 3, 3 / 8, 2 / 3)
assert abs(trace[2][4] - 16 / 9) < 1e-12
assert trace[-1][1:] == (8, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)

Performance and operating cost

Sorting N contacts takes O(N log N) time; the grouped sweep takes O(N) time. The ranked records, ID set and returned points use O(N) space. The eight-contact check proves that a tied score contributes a single attainable point and gives lift 16/9 after selecting three contacts. That tiny ledger illustrates arithmetic only. It does not estimate campaign return or correct selective labels from past outreach.

Common Mistakes

  • Using responders among selected contacts as cumulative gain; that ratio is precision.
  • Splitting tied scores to make an exact budget look reachable without a secondary rule.
  • Comparing lift measured on different eligible populations or outcome windows.
  • Calling never-contacted people nonresponders when their outcome cannot be observed.

Validation drill

Take 470 eligible contacts with mature response labels and a fixed campaign window. Mark every tied threshold, then publish selected count, captured responders, gain, lift and outreach cost at capacities 47, 94 and 141; explain any capacity that falls inside a tie.

title: Regression residual plots: locate bias, spread and missing segments
summary: Build residual-versus-predicted coordinates and fixed-bin summaries from held-out records before interpreting a regression error plot.
body:
Build residual-versus-predicted coordinates and fixed-bin summaries from held-out records before interpreting a regression error plot.

Name the residual and the split

For this lesson, residual means observed value minus predicted value. A positive residual is an underprediction; a negative residual is an overprediction. Put predicted value on the horizontal axis and residual on the vertical axis with a visible zero line. State the outcome unit and whether the records are training, validation or a final held-out set. Training residuals can look artificially calm after model selection. If repeated measurements belong to the same account or machine, preserve that identity when splitting and when estimating uncertainty. Overplotting controls matter when thousands of residuals pile onto rounded predictions.

Inspect structure before a score

A curved center suggests the model misses a systematic relationship; a fan-shaped spread suggests error size changes with the predicted level. Bands or clusters may reveal a missing segment or a target recorded at only a few allowed values. None of these shapes by itself identifies a cause. Color or facet by a prespecified segment, but hold axes fixed across panels so one group's errors do not look small only because its scale expanded. Small multiples make that comparison testable. Plot residuals against time as a second view; time order can reveal drift that disappears when points are sorted by predicted value.

Pair points with fixed-bin summaries

Choose predicted-value bin boundaries before reading the result. For each bin, print support, mean signed residual, mean absolute error and perhaps an upper error quantile. The signed mean detects directional bias; the absolute mean cannot cancel positive and negative misses. A bin with three records should not receive the same visual authority as one with three thousand. Keep bins fixed when comparing model versions or periods and disclose records outside the chart domain. Population and denominator rules still apply: removing failed predictions changes the displayed population. Uncertainty views can show how unstable a sparse bin's mean is.

Do not turn every pattern into a linear-model violation

The familiar constant-variance diagnostic is useful for some regression assumptions, but count-like or positive skewed outcomes may naturally have error spread that grows with the expected value. The plot still documents operational error; interpreting it requires the loss function and data-generating process. Large residuals can be genuine costly cases, label errors or records outside the model's intended domain. Investigate with stable IDs, not anonymous dots. If the outcome was transformed during training, bring predictions and actuals back to a common declared scale before computing residuals. A Q–Q plot checks tail shape; it answers a different question from residual versus fitted value.

Worked contract

from bisect import bisect_right
from math import isfinite, sqrt

def residual_profile(records: list[tuple[str, float, float]],
                     edges: list[float]):
    if (len(edges) < 2 or any(not isfinite(edge) for edge in edges)
            or any(left >= right for left, right in zip(edges, edges[1:]))):
        raise ValueError("bin edges must be finite and strictly increasing")
    record_ids = [record_id for record_id, _, _ in records]
    if len(record_ids) != len(set(record_ids)) or any(not key for key in record_ids):
        raise ValueError("record IDs must be unique and nonempty")
    bins = [[] for _ in range(len(edges) - 1)]
    points = []
    for record_id, observed, predicted in records:
        if (not isfinite(observed) or not isfinite(predicted)
                or predicted < edges[0] or predicted > edges[-1]):
            raise ValueError("record is invalid or outside the plot domain")
        residual = observed - predicted
        index = min(bisect_right(edges, predicted) - 1, len(bins) - 1)
        bins[index].append(residual)
        points.append((record_id, predicted, residual))
    summaries = []
    for index, errors in enumerate(bins):
        count = len(errors)
        summaries.append((edges[index], edges[index + 1], count,
                          sum(errors) / count if count else None,
                          sum(abs(error) for error in errors) / count
                          if count else None,
                          sqrt(sum(error * error for error in errors) / count)
                          if count else None))
    return points, summaries

shipment_estimates = [("shipment-47", 23, 20), ("shipment-59", 31, 32),
                      ("shipment-83", 44, 48), ("shipment-97", 68, 60),
                      ("shipment-101", 69, 72), ("shipment-131", 78, 88)]
points, bands = residual_profile(shipment_estimates, [0, 50, 100])
assert points[3] == ("shipment-97", 60, 8)
assert bands[0][2:5] == (3, -2 / 3, 8 / 3)
assert bands[1][2:5] == (3, -5 / 3, 7.0)

Performance and operating cost

For N records and B fixed bins, assigning each prediction with binary search takes O(N log B) time and summarizing residuals takes O(N + B); storing the points, ID set and bin contents uses O(N + B) space. The six-shipment assertion checks sign convention and separates signed bias from absolute error. It does not diagnose serial correlation, supply uncertainty intervals or validate the model split. Those require a held-out design and more observations.

Common Mistakes

  • Switching residual sign between charts without changing the label.
  • Re-estimating bins for each model so apparent segment changes cannot be compared.
  • Dropping observations whose predictions lie beyond the drawn axis without an exclusion count.
  • Using only average signed residual when large positive and negative errors cancel.

Validation drill

Export 470 held-out shipment predictions with stable IDs and outcome times. Build residual-versus-predicted and residual-versus-time views, keep fixed bin edges and shared axes, and audit the three bins with the largest mean absolute error alongside their support counts.

title: Population pyramids: compare age bands without losing the denominator
summary: Build a mirrored age distribution with shared age bins, one total-population denominator and an explicit unrecorded-category ledger.
body:
Build a mirrored age distribution with shared age bins, one total-population denominator and an explicit unrecorded-category ledger.

A mirror is a layout, not a negative population

A population pyramid places age bands vertically and two recorded categories on opposite sides of a central zero line. One side is plotted with negative coordinates solely to mirror the bars; its underlying counts remain nonnegative. Name the categories as they were collected rather than guessing what a binary field means. The familiar pyramid shape is not a requirement: a region with older residents or migration concentrated in working ages may have a wide middle. Keep youngest ages at the bottom or label any reversed order prominently. Axis integrity matters because the left and right extents must have equal magnitude when their bar lengths are compared.

Choose count or share deliberately

Counts show service volume. Shares show age structure for differently sized places or years. If each bar uses a percent, choose a denominator and print it: this lesson divides every age-and-category count by the total recorded population, including people whose category is unrecorded. Dividing the left side by its own category total and the right side by another total answers a different conditional question and makes widths deceptively comparable. For two places, use identical bin widths, axis limits and denominator definitions; show the underlying total of each place nearby. Shared-scale panels prevent a small district from visually matching a large city by accident.

Reconcile coverage before drawing

Age bands must cover the intended population once each without overlaps or gaps, and the reporting date must be the same across both sides. A top band such as 85 and older is open-ended; preserve that label rather than pretending it spans the same number of years as a five-year band. Unknown ages need an exclusion count and explanation outside the plotted bands. An unrecorded category is also not a third side; print its total and age-band breakdown in a companion table so the two mirrored sides do not silently claim to represent everyone. Composition charts offer another view when more than two categories are central to the question.

Treat small counts as data, not shape

A one-person change can visibly reshape a small-area band. Consider disclosure rules and uncertainty when publishing small geographies; combining bins may protect privacy and reduce noise, but the regrouping must apply to every compared area and year. Suppressed cells are not zero. Printed counts and an accessible table let readers distinguish a narrow bar from a missing value. Accessible alternatives should give the age band, each count, total and percentage without relying on color or left-right position alone. A smooth outline drawn through sparse age groups adds no information and can imply detail the input never had.

Worked contract

def pyramid_ledger(age_bands: list[tuple[int, int, int, int, int]]):
    if not age_bands:
        raise ValueError("at least one age band is required")
    ordered = sorted(age_bands)
    for index, (start_age, end_age, male, female, unrecorded) in enumerate(ordered):
        if (type(start_age) is not int or type(end_age) is not int
                or start_age < 0 or end_age <= start_age or
                any(type(count) is not int or count < 0
                    for count in (male, female, unrecorded))):
            raise ValueError("invalid age boundary or count")
        if index and start_age != ordered[index - 1][1]:
            raise ValueError("age bands must be contiguous and nonoverlapping")
    population = sum(male + female + unrecorded
                     for _, _, male, female, unrecorded in ordered)
    if population == 0:
        raise ValueError("percentage denominator cannot be zero")
    bars = [(start_age, end_age, -male / population,
             female / population, unrecorded / population)
            for start_age, end_age, male, female, unrecorded in ordered]
    assert abs(sum(right - left + missing
                   for _, _, left, right, missing in bars) - 1) < 1e-12
    return population, bars

catchment_counts = [(0, 18, 47, 45, 3), (18, 65, 141, 138, 5),
                    (65, 85, 29, 35, 2)]
population, bars = pyramid_ledger(catchment_counts)
assert population == 445
assert bars[0] == (0, 18, -47 / 445, 45 / 445, 3 / 445)
assert sum(band[4] for band in bars) == 10 / 445

Performance and operating cost

For B age bands, sorting and validating the intervals takes O(B log B) time; the ledger needs O(B) output space. If input is already sorted and validated upstream, the count sweep is O(B). The 445-person check proves that both mirrored sides and the ten unrecorded-category records share one denominator. The code accepts only closed, finite upper age boundaries; an open-ended oldest band needs a separately labeled representation rather than a fabricated endpoint.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading negative drawing coordinates as negative people.
  • Using each side's own total while labeling bars as shares of the whole population.
  • Changing age-band widths between places or treating suppressed cells as zero.
  • Dropping unrecorded categories while claiming the visible bars sum to the entire population.

Validation drill

Compare two synthetic clinic catchments with 445 and 1,410 registered residents. Reconcile every age-band count to its population total, draw count and percentage versions on shared axes, and print unrecorded-category counts beside both charts.

title: Lorenz curves: audit ranked shares before quoting a Gini value
summary: Construct cumulative population and amount shares with an equality reference, a declared observation unit and an explicit zero-value policy.
body:
Construct cumulative population and amount shares with an equality reference, a declared observation unit and an explicit zero-value policy.

Fix the population and the quantity

A Lorenz curve ranks units from the smallest nonnegative amount to the largest, then plots cumulative population share against cumulative amount share. The unit might be a household, customer, shipment or location; the amount might be income, support hours or energy consumption. State both. A curve over customers cannot be compared directly with one over invoices when some customers generate many invoices. Start at zero, zero and finish at one, one. The diagonal is an equal-share reference, not a fitted trend. Grain and denominator decisions determine the curve before a single point is drawn. Print the total amount, number of units, observation window and eligibility exclusions beside the chart.

Keep zero values and define negative values

A unit with zero amount still occupies population share. It produces a horizontal segment at the bottom of the curve, often an important feature rather than noise to filter out. Negative amounts break the ordinary nonnegative Lorenz interpretation: debt, net profit and refunds need a separately defined policy, not an unannounced absolute value or shift. Missing amounts are different again. Disclose their count and decide whether the published population excludes them, estimates them, or uses a sensitivity range. If the source is a survey with weights, each unit's horizontal step is its normalized sampling weight; an unweighted curve like the code below must not be labeled as a population-weighted estimate. An empirical CDF ranks values too, but its vertical axis counts units rather than their cumulative share of an amount.

Calculate area on the points actually shown

For nonnegative individual amounts with equal unit weight, the Gini value is one minus twice the area under the piecewise-linear Lorenz curve. Calculate that area from every sorted unit boundary, not from a handful of plotted labels or a smoothed curve. A summary rounded to two decimals can hide a change that matters to policy, so show the underlying curve and selected checkpoints such as the bottom half's amount share. A Gini value near zero means the measured amount is distributed more evenly across the included units. It says nothing by itself about whether total resources are adequate. Uncertainty and support deserve attention when comparing small places or sampled populations.

Compare periods without swapping the denominator

Two curves can cross; then one scalar Gini cannot describe which segment has a larger share at every population depth. Put both periods on identical zero-to-one axes, retain the same unit definition and describe major population or data-collection changes. A rising total can coexist with a more bowed curve, and a falling total with a straighter one. Show totals as a separate companion view rather than asking normalized curves to reveal volume. If a few units dominate the tail, provide a table of their share without exposing private identities. Shared-scale panels and text alternatives keep the comparison readable without relying on line color alone.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def lorenz_ledger(amounts: list[tuple[str, float]]):
    unit_ids = [unit_id for unit_id, _ in amounts]
    if not amounts or len(unit_ids) != len(set(unit_ids)) or any(
            not unit_id for unit_id in unit_ids):
        raise ValueError("units need unique, nonempty IDs")
    if any(not isfinite(amount) or amount < 0 for _, amount in amounts):
        raise ValueError("ordinary Lorenz amounts must be finite and nonnegative")
    total = sum(amount for _, amount in amounts)
    if total <= 0:
        raise ValueError("positive total amount is required")
    ranked = sorted(amounts, key=lambda record: record[1])
    points = [(0.0, 0.0)]
    cumulative = 0.0
    for position, (_, amount) in enumerate(ranked, start=1):
        cumulative += amount
        points.append((position / len(ranked), cumulative / total))
    doubled_area = sum((points[index][0] - points[index - 1][0]) *
                       (points[index][1] + points[index - 1][1])
                       for index in range(1, len(points)))
    return points, 1 - doubled_area

district_amounts = [("district-47", 47.0), ("district-59", 59.0),
                    ("district-83", 83.0), ("district-211", 211.0)]
curve, gini = lorenz_ledger(district_amounts)
assert curve[2] == (0.5, 106 / 400)
assert curve[-1] == (1.0, 1.0)
assert abs(gini - 0.3225) < 1e-12
assert lorenz_ledger([("empty-47", 0.0), ("full-59", 47.0)])[0][1] == (0.5, 0.0)

Performance and operating cost

For N units, sorting takes O(N log N) time and the cumulative sweep plus trapezoidal area take O(N). The ranked records, uniqueness set and point list need O(N) space. The four-district check yields bottom-half share 0.265 and Gini 0.3225; a separate zero-amount check proves that zero units remain in the population. This code is deliberately unweighted and rejects negative amounts. Survey weights or negative wealth require a different declared calculation and interpretation.

Common Mistakes

  • Ranking invoices while describing the horizontal axis as households.
  • Removing zero-amount units because they make a flat segment.
  • Calculating Gini from smoothed drawing coordinates instead of the ranked data.
  • Comparing two normalized curves without reporting totals and population coverage.

Validation drill

Build two yearly curves for 470 synthetic service districts. Reconcile every amount to the published total, include zero-use districts, show bottom-half and top-decile shares, and explain any missing or negative records before comparing Gini values.

title: Individuals and moving-range charts: monitor level and local variation
summary: Pair single-observation measurements with successive absolute differences while freezing baseline center and limits before monitoring begins.
body:
Pair single-observation measurements with successive absolute differences while freezing baseline center and limits before monitoring begins.

Use the pair when each period has one reading

An individuals chart plots one measurement per ordered sampling point. A companion moving-range chart plots the absolute difference between consecutive readings, so it can reveal a jump that deserves attention even when the level remains inside its own limits. The pair is useful when rational subgroups of repeated measurements are unavailable. Do not substitute it for a subgroup chart when several readings are deliberately sampled within each period; averaging or selecting one would discard within-period variation. A p chart instead monitors proportions with varying denominators. Time-series gap rules apply before any adjacent difference is calculated.

Freeze a credible baseline

Estimate a center from an earlier stable phase. For moving ranges of two successive baseline observations, divide their mean by the appropriate two-point constant to estimate short-term standard deviation; three such estimated standard deviations on either side of the center give illustrative individuals limits. The moving-range chart has its own upper limit and a zero lower bound under this standard pairing. Record the baseline IDs, sampling interval, calibration version and exclusions. Do not recompute limits after every surprising new point, because an actual shift would then move the reference line along with it. CUSUM and EWMA can complement this pair when small persistent shifts matter more than isolated jumps.

Do not bridge missing or changed periods

A moving range is meaningful only between adjacent observations of the process under the chosen sampling plan. If one shift is missing, comparing the readings on either side spans a longer interval and should not silently become an ordinary two-point range. Start a new run after a known process reset or measurement-system change, and mark the gap on the chart. Serial correlation can make the textbook limits misleading: slowly drifting readings have small successive differences even when the process is no longer stable. Inspect raw points and time spacing, and validate false-alert behavior on a clean baseline before operational use. Control limits describe process behavior under assumptions; they are not product acceptance specifications.

Make alerts inspectable

Show the measurement, moving range, reference center, both limit sets and which rule triggered. A point outside a limit is a signal to investigate, not proof of a faulty product or a named root cause. Record investigation outcome and subsequent measurement rather than redrawing away a signal. For small baselines, estimates can be unstable; the six-point demonstration below is an arithmetic check, not a recommended operational baseline size. A chart export manifest should carry the baseline version and missing-period policy so another reader can reproduce the same alarms. Use text flags as well as colored markers.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def individual_range_ledger(baseline: list[tuple[str, float]],
                            monitoring: list[tuple[str, float]]):
    all_readings = baseline + monitoring
    identifiers = [sample_id for sample_id, _ in all_readings]
    if len(baseline) < 5 or len(identifiers) != len(set(identifiers)) or any(
            not sample_id or not isfinite(value)
            for sample_id, value in all_readings):
        raise ValueError("use valid unique samples and at least five baseline readings")
    baseline_values = [value for _, value in baseline]
    ranges = [abs(current - previous)
              for previous, current in zip(baseline_values, baseline_values[1:])]
    center = sum(baseline_values) / len(baseline_values)
    mean_range = sum(ranges) / len(ranges)
    if mean_range == 0:
        raise ValueError("zero baseline variation needs an investigation")
    sigma_estimate = mean_range / 1.128
    individual_limits = (center - 3 * sigma_estimate,
                         center + 3 * sigma_estimate)
    range_limits = (0.0, 3.267 * mean_range)
    last_value = baseline_values[-1]
    plotted = []
    for sample_id, value in monitoring:
        moving_range = abs(value - last_value)
        plotted.append((sample_id, value, moving_range,
                        value < individual_limits[0] or value > individual_limits[1],
                        moving_range > range_limits[1]))
        last_value = value
    return center, mean_range, individual_limits, range_limits, plotted

reference_shifts = [("shift-47", 47.0), ("shift-59", 49.0),
                    ("shift-83", 48.0), ("shift-97", 50.0),
                    ("shift-101", 49.0), ("shift-131", 51.0)]
new_shifts = [("shift-149", 52.0), ("shift-173", 54.0)]
center, average_range, bounds, range_bounds, marks = individual_range_ledger(
    reference_shifts, new_shifts)
assert center == 49.0 and average_range == 1.6
assert bounds[0] < 47 < bounds[1] < 54
assert marks == [("shift-149", 52.0, 1.0, False, False),
                 ("shift-173", 54.0, 2.0, True, False)]

Performance and operating cost

With B baseline readings and M monitored readings, calculating center, successive baseline ranges and alerts takes O(B + M) time. The returned monitor ledger uses O(M) space, while ID validation uses O(B + M); streaming from a prevalidated unique-ID source needs only constant additional state. The eight-reading check detects a level signal at 54 while both observed moving ranges remain below their own limit. Its baseline is intentionally too small for a reliable operating rule. Validate a longer stable phase and the sampling schedule before treating limits as alarms.

Common Mistakes

  • Including new alarm points in the baseline average and moving limits.
  • Treating a missing shift as though its two neighbors were adjacent samples.
  • Calling a control limit a product specification or a guaranteed false-alarm probability.
  • Ignoring serial correlation because the moving ranges happen to be small.

Validation drill

Use 47 verified stable production shifts as a frozen baseline, then monitor 83 later shifts. Mark gaps and equipment resets, display both charts with versioned limits, and explain every alert with its raw reading, adjacent reading and investigation state.

title: Tornado charts: keep scenario ranges attached to their assumptions
summary: Rank one-factor-at-a-time output changes around a reproducible baseline without mistaking a wide input range for causal importance.
body:
Rank one-factor-at-a-time output changes around a reproducible baseline without mistaking a wide input range for causal importance.

Start at a reproducible base case

A tornado chart compares how a model output changes when each input is moved to a declared low and high scenario while every other input stays at its baseline. Write down the model version, baseline inputs, output unit and evaluation date first. The central line is the base-case output, not automatically zero. A bar may extend mainly to one side if the output response is asymmetric. Keep the low-input and high-input labels with their actual output values; for a cost input, increasing the input may move profit left instead of right. Diverging bars explain signed changes, but a tornado's reference is an output produced by a specific model state.

Make ranges comparable before sorting

The width of a sensitivity bar depends on both the model and the tested range. Comparing an input moved by 47 percent with another moved by 2 percent and calling the wider result 'more important' confuses scenario design with model sensitivity. Use justified low and high bounds such as operational limits or prespecified uncertainty ranges, and print them in a table. Sort bars by a declared measure, such as maximum absolute movement from the base case; retain a stable secondary order for ties. If different input units matter, a percentage change can help explain the scenario but must be defined even when the baseline is zero. Axis integrity requires one output scale across all rows.

Do not present one-factor variation as a forecast

One-factor-at-a-time bars hold other inputs fixed. They miss interactions: a lower order count and a lower margin together may hurt more than either separate bar suggests. They also ignore correlations and the probability of a scenario. A bar should not be read as a confidence interval or as the expected range of outcomes. Show combined scenarios separately when constraints tie inputs together, and use an uncertainty method suited to the actual model if probability statements are needed. Forecast bands encode a different claim. Interval labels help prevent scenario ranges from masquerading as statistical error bars.

Audit the model calls behind the picture

Evaluate the base case once and each low and high scenario with all other inputs unchanged. Store every exact input vector and output before sorting for display; otherwise a later reader cannot reproduce why a bar moved. Validate that the baseline lies within each scenario's declared range, and reject nonfinite model results. Include the actual input units and whether a low scenario means 'better' or simply a smaller number. For crowded dashboards, show the largest few bars with a link or table containing the rest instead of silently dropping variables. An export manifest can retain input range, model revision and ordering rule. A clear table is also a text alternative to colored bars.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def margin_model(inputs: dict[str, float]) -> float:
    return inputs["weekly_orders"] * inputs["unit_margin"] - inputs["fixed_cost"]

def tornado_ledger(baseline: dict[str, float],
                   bounds: dict[str, tuple[float, float]]):
    if set(baseline) != set(bounds) or not baseline or any(
            not isfinite(value) for value in baseline.values()):
        raise ValueError("every finite baseline input needs one scenario range")
    base_output = margin_model(baseline)
    rows = []
    for name, (low, high) in bounds.items():
        if (not isfinite(low) or not isfinite(high) or
                low > baseline[name] or high < baseline[name]):
            raise ValueError("scenario must bracket its baseline input")
        low_case = dict(baseline)
        high_case = dict(baseline)
        low_case[name] = low
        high_case[name] = high
        low_output = margin_model(low_case)
        high_output = margin_model(high_case)
        if not isfinite(low_output) or not isfinite(high_output):
            raise ValueError("model result is not finite")
        impact = max(abs(low_output - base_output),
                     abs(high_output - base_output))
        rows.append((name, low, high, low_output, high_output, impact))
    rows.sort(key=lambda row: (-row[-1], row[0]))
    return base_output, rows

base_inputs = {"weekly_orders": 47.0, "unit_margin": 83.0,
               "fixed_cost": 1700.0}
scenario_bounds = {"weekly_orders": (42.0, 52.0),
                   "unit_margin": (74.0, 92.0),
                   "fixed_cost": (1500.0, 1900.0)}
baseline_output, rows = tornado_ledger(base_inputs, scenario_bounds)
assert baseline_output == 2201.0
assert [row[0] for row in rows] == ["unit_margin", "weekly_orders", "fixed_cost"]
assert rows[0][3:6] == (1778.0, 2624.0, 423.0)
assert rows[-1][3:5] == (2401.0, 2001.0)

Performance and operating cost

For P inputs and model-evaluation cost C, the base plus two scenarios per input take O(P·C) model time; copying P-element input maps for each scenario also costs O(P²) in this small standard-library implementation. The row list is O(P) space, with O(P) temporary space per call. The worked weekly margin model returns base output 2,201, correctly orders the three tested ranges and shows that lower fixed cost raises profit. For expensive models, keep the same scenario contract while avoiding unnecessary full-map copies in the evaluation adapter.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling the longest bar the most important variable without comparing the ranges tested.
  • Assuming low input always produces the left endpoint of the output bar.
  • Reading one-factor-at-a-time scenarios as joint uncertainty or prediction intervals.
  • Sorting a published tornado by a new rule without preserving scenario values and model version.

Validation drill

For a synthetic service operation, freeze 47 weekly orders and a 2,201-unit base margin. Evaluate every low and high scenario independently, add one combined worst-case scenario to expose interactions, and give readers an exact input-output table beside the sorted bars.

title: Unequal-bin histograms: make rectangle area carry frequency
summary: Compute density heights for unequal intervals, document edge inclusion and reconcile plotted area to the measured population.
body:
Compute density heights for unequal intervals, document edge inclusion and reconcile plotted area to the measured population.

Define the measured population before the bins

A histogram partitions a numerical measure into adjacent intervals. Each observation belongs to one interval, and the shape depends on the chosen boundaries. Specify the observation unit, measurement unit, eligibility window and treatment of missing values before drawing. A delivery-latency chart over requests differs from one over customers even if both use milliseconds on the horizontal axis. Fixed bin edges let readers compare weeks without interpreting a shifted boundary as a changed distribution. Do not silently trim values outside the visible domain; either expand the domain or label the excluded count and range. Grain and denominator choices come first, and outlier displays can preserve extreme values that a compact histogram hides.

For unequal widths, height is a density

When widths vary, raw counts cannot be the rectangle heights if the picture is supposed to preserve frequency. Divide each bin's count by its width for count density, or divide again by the total number of included observations for probability density. The rectangle area then equals its count or share. A 40-unit-wide bin containing two requests and an 80-unit-wide bin containing four requests have equal probability-density height, although the second contains twice as many requests. Print counts or shares on demand; height alone is easy to misread. State whether intervals are left-closed and right-open, and make the final upper boundary inclusive if that is the published rule. Axis integrity requires a labeled density unit, such as share per millisecond, rather than a mislabeled 'number of requests' vertical axis.

Choose edges without chasing the answer

A histogram with very wide bins buries local peaks. Very narrow bins turn sampling noise into apparent structure. Pick boundaries using measurement resolution and a declared analytical purpose, then inspect sensitivity using another reasonable fixed bin plan. Do not search many boundaries and publish only the one that makes a preferred group look unusual. For side-by-side cohorts, use shared edges and a shared vertical density scale; sample-size differences belong in annotations and raw-count tables. If an interval is open-ended, it has no finite width and cannot receive an ordinary density rectangle. Split it at a finite bound, or display its count separately. Shared-scale small multiples make the bin plan visible across groups.

Reconcile the chart before interpretation

The bin ledger should sum to the included record count. For a probability-density histogram, the sum of height times width should equal one apart from floating-point rounding. Those checks catch dropped boundary observations, double assignment and a denominator that includes records outside the plotted range. The code below rejects out-of-range measurements rather than making an attractive but incomplete chart. A separate report can show excluded or invalid records under a declared policy. Give readers an accessible interval table with bounds, counts, shares and density; a smooth overlay is a different estimate with its own bandwidth and should not erase the measured bins. Density bandwidth and text alternatives cover those follow-on decisions.

Worked contract

from bisect import bisect_right
from math import isfinite

def histogram_ledger(latencies_ms: list[float], edges_ms: list[float]):
    if (not latencies_ms or len(edges_ms) < 2 or
            any(not isfinite(edge) for edge in edges_ms) or
            any(left >= right for left, right in zip(edges_ms, edges_ms[1:]))):
        raise ValueError("supply observations and strictly increasing finite edges")
    counts = [0] * (len(edges_ms) - 1)
    for latency in latencies_ms:
        if not isfinite(latency) or latency < edges_ms[0] or latency > edges_ms[-1]:
            raise ValueError("every observation must be finite and inside the domain")
        index = min(bisect_right(edges_ms, latency) - 1, len(counts) - 1)
        counts[index] += 1
    total = len(latencies_ms)
    ledger = [(left, right, count, count / total,
               count / (total * (right - left)))
              for left, right, count in zip(edges_ms, edges_ms[1:], counts)]
    assert sum(row[2] for row in ledger) == total
    assert abs(sum((row[1] - row[0]) * row[4] for row in ledger) - 1) < 1e-12
    return ledger

request_latencies = [47, 59, 83, 97, 131, 149, 173, 211, 227, 251]
bins = histogram_ledger(request_latencies, [40, 80, 160, 320])
assert [row[2] for row in bins] == [2, 4, 4]
assert bins[0][4] == bins[1][4] == 0.005
assert histogram_ledger([40, 80, 160, 320], [40, 80, 160, 320])[-1][2] == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N measurements and B bins, binary search assigns each observation in O(log B) time, so the sweep costs O(N log B); constructing the ledger costs O(B). The returned counts and rows need O(B) extra space. The ten-request check gives bin shares 0.2, 0.4 and 0.4, while the first two densities both equal 0.005 share per millisecond. The boundary assertion places 80 in the second interval and includes 320 in the final interval. Preserve this boundary policy when computing comparison charts.

Common Mistakes

  • Using raw counts as rectangle heights when widths differ.
  • Labeling a probability-density vertical axis as a count axis.
  • Dropping the last-edge observation or assigning an internal edge twice.
  • Changing bin boundaries between cohorts and reading the changed geometry as changed behavior.

Validation drill

Measure 470 request latencies, declare three unequal finite intervals and audit every boundary value. Publish an interval ledger, an excluded-record count, a fixed-edge comparison for a second week and a density-area check that equals one.

  • Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
